The prosecution argued that Bamber – a skilled huntsman – had to be the killer, because Caffell was insufficiently experienced with a rifle to have a 100% hit rate. The defence argued that Caffell did have limited knowledge of handling .22 rifles because she had grown up on the farm and attended rural shoots.

The bullets identified by Carney-Gannon imply that the shooter was less skilled than has been suggested. After all, not only does Carney-Gannon suspect that some bullets missed June Bamber, she believes June probably moved around for some time after being shot.

Carney-Gannon’s findings support a forensic investigation the Guardian commissioned from the prestigious forensic physician Professor Jason Payne-James, earlier this year, into whether or not a silencer was used in the shooting of Caffell.

The silencer in question was found three days after the massacre, in a downstairs storage cupboard at White House Farm, by relatives who went on to inherit from the Bamber estate. This silencer was crucial in the case against Bamber. The prosecution argued that Caffell’s arms were not long enough to kill herself had the silencer been attached to the rifle, and, if she had shot herself, she would obviously have been unable to replace the silencer in the downstairs cupboard. At trial, it was stated that blood belonging to Caffell was found inside this silencer.

Mr Justice Drake told the jury that if they were convinced beyond reasonable doubt that a silencer was used, then Bamber was guilty of the murders. Minutes before they convicted Bamber, the jury returned to ask whether the blood in the silencer definitely belonged to Caffell. The judge told them it did. In fact, it was merely her blood grouping, which she shared with Robert Boutflour, who regularly used the guns. Later testing suggested the blood found in the silencer might not even be human.

Payne-James concluded that a silencer had not been used, and that the two shots to Caffell’s neck and chin were either contact or close-contact wounds. This dismantled much of the prosecution’s case against Bamber, and is consistent with Carney-Gannon’s view.

The new findings will be handed to the Criminal Cases Review Commission, the body responsible for investigating alleged miscarriages of justice and referring them to the Court of Appeal if it concludes there is a “real possibility” that a conviction may be unsafe. The commission spent four years examining four out of 10 points in the latest submission by Bamber, before rejecting them.

After being criticised for its low referral record in recent years (1.5% of total applications in 2023/24 were referred to the Court of Appeal), the CCRC’s chair and CEO were forced to resign last year. Under the leadership of interim chair Dame Vera Baird KC, there has been a sharp increase in referrals – 45 cases were referred in the 2025/26 financial year, compared with 31 in 2024/25. Baird accused the previous regime of “almost looking for reasons not to refer”.

It is hard to see how the commission will not be swayed by Carney-Gannon’s findings, especially under its new leadership. After all, the new evidence regarding stray bullets that were shot at the bed; June Bamber sitting down and walking around after being hit by an unskilled shooter; and, most importantly, the blood stains suggesting that Sheila Caffell shot herself, turns the case on its head.

A spokesperson for the Jeremy Bamber Innocence Campaign says: “This report supports what Jeremy has said all along, that he did not murder his family. The report is clear that the blood patterns present at the scene are consistent with the initial conclusion drawn by the police at the scene, that his seriously mentally ill sister Sheila killed her family and then herself. These two terrible tragedies have been compounded by how long it is taking the appeal system to recognise this in the light of the scientific evidence now available.”

https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/o.title: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 review – a thrilling airport novel of a game
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/o.author: Keith Stuart
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/o.text:
Activision; PC, PS5, Switch 2, XboxFrom parkour over Manhattan rooftops and car chases in Paris to the climactic battle at a North Korean air base, the developers have thrown absolutely everything at the game

And so we return perhaps one final time to Call of Duty’s Modern Warfare strand, with stories, “ripped from the newspaper headlines”, featuring shady terror organisations, nefarious rogue states and the brutally capable, monosyllabic war fighters who stand between us and Armageddon. Last year’s Black Ops 7 instalment was a sales disappointment for Activision, and that has no doubt put extra pressure on Infinity Ward, the studio leading Modern Warfare 4 development. Fortunately, this developer – like series heroes Price, Gaz and Ghost – seems to thrive on pressure.

As you may have read, this year’s campaign is based around a fictitious North Korean ruling family that has seized an opportunity to invade its southern neighbour. Amid the chaos, a small group of Korean and American marines must help lead the fightback, while in the shadows, SAS hard man John Price makes an unlikely new comrade in his own morally ambiguous quest to put the world to rights. Mads Mikkelsen pops up as evil mastermind The Archer, but like Kiernan Shipka in Black Ops 7 he’s rather wasted, with very little screen time.

Nevertheless, it’s a bombastic, thrilling airport novel of a game, crammed with classic CoD set pieces, including but not limited to parkour over Manhattan rooftops, a car chase in Paris and a shootout in a train yard that somehow feels like a cross between Frogger and Time Crisis. A climactic battle at a North Korean airbase throws absolutely everything at you from sniper firefights to helicopter gunship attacks.

There are also moments where you’re forced into stark unethical actions, faintly recalling the notorious “No Russian” mission from 2009’s Modern Warfare 2. Elsewhere, a whole open-world section lets you explore a snowy landscape, carrying out story missions and side quests to improve your armoury. It’s a nice break from corridor shooting, and somehow it doesn’t stall the game’s momentum. Throughout the six-hour campaign, bullets fly and buildings collapse, friends become enemies, enemies become friends, and a breathless story of geopolitical skullduggery emerges. It’s a shame, though, that the Capt Price arc gets a little overlooked toward the end and his denouement lacks the intended emotional clout, but it’s fun and at least a little bit emotional while it lasts.

The multiplayer mode is a refinement of the turbo-paced, ultra-lethal experience of Black Ops 7. Players are still extremely agile, able to vault over obstacles and skid around corners, blasting their guns like John Wick on a recently polished vinyl floor. But movement is a touch more naturalistic here, and weapons have a heft to them that makes you feel deadly, even if you’re getting shot in the face every five seconds.

Alongside all the classic modes there are decent newcomers, such as the epic, up-to-64-player, Combat Outpost, and Collateral, a round-based shootout where you buy new weapons and items at the start of each bout (the better you do, the more cash you get to spend on goodies). The highlight though is Kill Block, which takes place in a modular training centre where three landscape types are randomly selected from dozens of possibilities, then slotted in to a play space at the start of the round so you’re never sure how everything will fit together. You might have to move from a train yard to a storage depot to a trench network, and weapons are randomised too, so you could all be fighting with pistols or sniper rifles, adding to the unpredictable challenge.

The last part of the package is a reconstructed take on Call of Duty’s extraction shooter mode, DMZ. Taking place in and around Hajin City, abandoned during the events of the campaign, you parachute in with up to two teammates, then carry out various PvE missions to earn cash and gear, before calling in for air rescue – all while avoiding or attacking other players on the same map. New to this version is the Forward Operating Base, a safe house you return to after each expedition where you can upgrade your weapons, 3D print new gear and get info on the current roster of boss characters. There’s also a three-branch skill tree for your character, which you populate by earning in-game XP. This gives you a range of new abilities and improvements including taking more loot from downed enemies, faster revives and reducing damage from explosives.

DMZ, then, is a huge mode with lots to do, set in a dynamic world with a real-time weather system. So far, we’ve only been able to play an early access version, but exploring the world and gambling on just one final side quest before extraction promises to offer the sort of tension and excitement this genre thrives on. However, its success will depend on how many players Activision can attract and retain, and to survive it’ll surely have to tempt people over from established rivals such as Arc Raiders and Escape from Tarkov. That could be the toughest mission of all.

Infinity Ward and its co-developers have thrown everything they have at this game, and it shows. The campaign is short but polished, the multiplayer still grabs you by the neck and DMZ is richly detailed and exhaustive. It’s all rendered in incredible audiovisual detail, delivering the spectacle we expect from the series. I’m not sure it’ll bring in a vast new audience, especially with GTA 6 on the way – Call of Duty remains a gung-ho Hollywood fantasy of armed conflict that glorifies the military-industrial complex. But if it’s a glossy, bombastic thrill ride you’re after, there is plenty here to keep you locked and loaded for months to come.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Experience: I’ve climbed Mount Everest 20 times
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Kenton Cool
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
In 1996 doctors told me I wouldn’t walk again unaided, but in 2022 I took the record for the most Everest summits by a non-Sherpa

I grew up in Slough, Berkshire, in a bungalow beside a farm. My father was a scout leader, and I was always outside, building dams and dens, sleeping out and hiding in trees. In my teens, family holidays were two weeks in Wales. At home, nature was my playground.

When I was 17, a school friend took me to a climbing wall where he was a regular. I loved the physicality of it and trying to work out where to put my hands and feet next. We would go there twice a week. In sixth form, we headed to the south coast in Dorset for my first real climbing outing. The waves were crashing and it felt scary and exhilarating. I thought it was magical.

We would go climbing there or in the Peak District whenever we could. After A-levels, we caught a bus to Chamonix, in the Alps, for five weeks of camping; we climbed Mont Blanc and made stupid mistakes like starting too late in the day. It was a huge learning curve, but it was fabulous.

I did a geology degree at the University of Leeds and joined the climbing club. I wanted to see the Himalayas, so organised a trip to Pakistan. That was a turning point. The climbing was wonderful, but it was the people I fell in love with.

Over the next decade, I spent half my year working in ski and climbing shops, and the other half climbing across Europe, New Zealand and Asia. It was treacherous at times. In 1996 I fell from a rock face, shattering both heel bones, and was told I wouldn’t walk again unaided. After several surgeries and three months in a wheelchair, I defied doctors to climb – and even ski – some of the world’s highest peaks. A group of us took on harder and higher routes and were nominated for a Piolet d’Or – the Oscars of the climbing world – after establishing a trail on Annapurna III, a 7,555-metre peak in Nepal, in 2003.

That caught the attention of a Sheffield adventure company, which asked if I would guide an expedition of two to Everest. I was an accomplished climber, but I had never been to 8,000 metres or led at high altitude; it was a huge leap of faith.

The ascent took eight weeks and I relied heavily on Sherpa expertise. We climbed through the night, with thunderstorms and stars lighting the sky, and I soaked in the feeling of being on the summit at the highest point on the planet, looking down at the Himalayas spread below.

I loved facilitating someone else’s journey. I did three more Everest ascents for the company before setting up my own in 2006. Now I take on one client a year, preparing together for up to three years.

I’ve climbed Everest most years since that first time. This May, I clocked up my 20th summit. There have been testing times – once, we encountered a catastrophic oxygen delivery failure and had to share tanks.

But there have been beautiful moments, too. The best was in 2017: we had summit day to ourselves – warm, no wind and just the right amount of snow. I could see Kangchenjunga and Makalu, the third and fifth highest peaks, respectively, and into Tibet. In 2013, I climbed Everest’s neighbouring peak, Nuptse, looking back from 7,900 metres and recalling years of memories.

That same year, I encountered my hardest night when I came across a dying climber who passed away in my arms. Another time, I pulled a dead Sherpa off the fixed line ropes, the barriers designed to stop people falling. The mountain doesn’t respect whether you have climbed it 20 times or once – anybody can die there.

In 2022, I took the record for the most Everest summits by a non‑Sherpa after my 16th ascent. Meanwhile Kami Rita Sherpa holds the general record. I still hold mine, although it has never been about numbers; it’s about experiences.

There will be a time when I stop climbing Everest, but it won’t be soon. It has given me everything and I feel humbled by that. But it’s the place and its people that mean the most to me – Sherpas I have climbed with; locals who fed me in their homes or nursed me when I was ill; people who have become my friends. The mountain is simply the vehicle that got me there.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Heat killed ‘staggering’ 50,000 people in Europe’s cities this summer, scientists warn
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Ajit Niranjan
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
People succumbed to heat at highest rates in Malta, Italy and Hungary, with health issues, loneliness and poverty exacerbating toll

Heat killed a record 50,000 people in European cities this summer, new research suggests, with scientists blaming climate breakdown for two in every three of the deaths.

Morgues and funeral homes filled with bodies from June to August as the heat added by planet-baking pollution cut short an extra 32,000 lives in urban areas, the researchers found. Hot days pushed vulnerable bodies into overdrive and warm nights prevented them from recovering.

The “staggering” death toll, modelled using historical relationships between heat and health in 854 cities, was the worst on record, the study found. Hot weather marked by relentless heatwaves killed nearly twice as many people as it did in each of the two next most dangerous years.

“In some sense, the absolute numbers of the heat-related deaths estimated across the 854 urban areas are indeed staggering,” said Malcolm Mistry, a climate and health scientist at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, who co-authored the study. “But perhaps what is even more alarming is the proportion of these deaths that we attribute to anthropogenic climate change.”

The share of deaths due to climate breakdown has risen from about 40% at the start of the century to 65% this summer, the study found.

People succumbed to heat at the highest rates in Malta, Italy and Hungary, while absolute death tolls were greatest in Italy, France, Spain, Germany and the UK. Because death certificates rarely record contributing factors – such as dangerous temperatures that push a stroke victim or lung cancer patient past their limits – families rarely know that heat and human activity hastened their relatives’ death.

“These shocking figures represent thousands of families who have lost a loved one this summer due to the climate crisis,” said Katie White, the climate transition minister for the UK, where scientists estimated 4,354 heat deaths this summer.”

In Naples, the hardest-hit city on the continent, 815 people per million died from the heat, according to the study’s age-standardised estimates. Mario Guarino, an emergency doctor at Ospedale CTO in the north of the city, said he witnessed a 15% increase in emergency room visits during the hottest weeks.

The “defining characteristic” of the period was the complexity of health problems exacerbated by heat, he added, with loneliness and poverty worsening the situation further.

“We took in a terminal cancer patient who lived in a hot attic simply because his family couldn’t find a company to install air conditioning during the summer,” said Guarino. “An elderly man with dementia was abruptly abandoned by his Ukrainian caregiver who returned home to say goodbye to her son, who had been called to war. Emergency services found [the man] lying on the floor one night with a fractured pelvis, desperately trying to call the tenant next door.”

The study found people over the age of 85 made up almost half of the death toll, though younger people were not immune, with 833 people between the age of 20 and 44 also thought to have died due to the heat. The scientists said the death toll from the cities studied, which account for about 40% of the European population, could not be easily extrapolated to estimate the full death toll including those in towns and villages.

The scorching heat that persistently baked western Europe this summer was the worst on record, the EU’s climate monitoring service announced this month, with more than half the continent seared by “very strong” heat stress that felt hotter than 38C. Slightly less punishing temperatures in eastern Europe brought the continental average to its third-hottest level on record.

Greenhouse gases have warmed Europe about twice as fast as the global average, exposing more people to intolerably hot summers and fewer people to dangerously cold winters. While cold is a bigger killer than heat, scientists expect rising temperatures to claim more lives than they save, as heat deaths are projected to rise faster than cold deaths fall.

The study combined established relationships between heat and mortality with temperature data for 2026 to rapidly estimate the fallout from this summer’s heat. The death tolls for individual countries differ from what national public health agencies have calculated using their own methods.

David García-García, a researcher at the mortality monitoring system at the Carlos III health institute in Madrid, who was not involved in the study, said it was a “valuable contribution” that allowed for comparisons across the continent. “However, it is important to bear in mind that these are estimates based on observed temperatures and epidemiological models, which do not incorporate actual data on deaths occurring in the summer of 2026,” he said.

Doctors have urged governments to burn fewer fossil fuels – the core driver of rising temperatures – while bolstering health systems, greening cities, rolling out air conditioning and encouraging people to drink water and seek shade. They have also stressed the benefits of people checking in on vulnerable neighbours and family members so they can get help before tragedy strikes.

“The real epidemic these days is loneliness,” said Guarino. “Many elderly people are left alone during the summer, abandoned by their families, and due to their low income, they can’t afford air conditioning or, if they do have it, avoid turning it on because of the cost of electricity.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Liechtenstein prince’s ‘surreal’ abortion veto dismays campaigners
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Ashifa Kassam European community affairs correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Alois uses the first veto of his reign to quash parliament-approved bill backed by a national petition

The hereditary prince of Liechtenstein has used his veto for the first time in his reign to quash a bill aimed at bringing abortion laws in line with much of Europe.

The legislation was approved by Liechtenstein’s parliament last month after the presentation of a citizens’ initiative signed by roughly a quarter of the nation’s voters.

The news left campaigners in the principality, home to some of the strictest abortion laws in Europe, reeling. “We’re not really surprised, but still disappointed,” said Tatjana As’Ad, who led the initiative to overhaul the law and who works for the small leftwing party, Free List. “It’s surreal what’s happening right now in 2026 in a state in the middle of Europe.”

The veto would do little to actually prevent abortions from taking place, she said. “Liechtenstein will continue to have a situation where abortions are banned, but we know they’re happening. The veto just means they will continue to take place abroad.”

Abortions in the principality are allowed only in limited circumstances such as when a woman’s life is at risk or a pregnancy is the result of rape. Since 2015, women have been legally permitted to travel abroad to terminate a pregnancy to skirt around the restrictions.

After campaigners launched the citizen’s initiative in February, more than 4,970 people – far more than the 1,000 signatures needed to send it to parliament – backed the call to decriminalise abortion up to 12 weeks. The initiative also called for the procedure to be covered by health insurance and for a repeal of a nationwide ban on sharing information about abortion access.

The hope was to do away with the many barriers that women face by being forced to travel abroad, often to neighbouring Austria or Switzerland, which include the cost, the need to arrange childcare and the lack of a vehicle.

As the initiative gained steam, Liechtenstein’s hereditary prince, Alois, said he would use his veto to counter any overhaul of the laws. The promise loomed over the initiative, even as parliamentarians voted narrowly to back it and an August poll suggested that 62% of voters were in favour of reforming the law.

This week the royal house confirmed Alois’s decision to “withhold his sanction from the bill” in a statement. It said: “Following careful consideration, he remains convinced that the proposed reform is not compatible with ensuring adequate protection of unborn life as a fundamental legal value.”

The royal house did not respond to a further request for comment from the Guardian.

Campaigners, who said they had met Alois hours before he announced his decision, described it as a blow to Liechtenstein’s identity as a monarchy underpinned by democratic principles.

“A single individual is overriding a decision initiated by almost a quarter of eligible voters and passed by the parliament,” the committee behind the citizens’ initiative said in a statement.

“Hereditary Prince Alois has only threatened to veto legislation twice in his reign, and both times it concerned the legalisation of abortion,” the statement added, referring to a 2011 pronouncement by the regent.

“This is the first time he has actually exercised this veto. The conclusion is clear: when it comes to abortion, there is only one decision-maker.”

It was a nod to the tremendous power the monarchy holds over the Alpine nation, with the ruling prince able to appoint judges and fire the government or individual ministers, said Gabriella Alvarez-Hummel, a journalist and one of the campaigners behind the citizens’ initiative. “He has a veto over everything, really,” she said.

In 2012, voters cast their ballots overwhelmingly to uphold his veto powers, in a referendum that was described at the time as a proxy debate over whether or not Liechtenstein should have a monarchy.

Alvarez-Hummel described this week’s decision as “very troubling”, given that Liechtenstein was the last in Europe to grant women the right to vote in national elections in 1984.

“Liechtenstein has a history of being the last when it comes to women’s rights,” she said. “I had hoped that we wouldn’t be the last in abortion rights as well, but it doesn’t look good at the moment.”

The campaign had managed to chalk up a few successes, she said, pointing to how it had chipped away at the decades-long taboo in talking about the topic in the nation.

In his statement this week, Alois also said he was open to lifting the nationwide ban on information about abortion, suggesting that women might one day be able to consult their healthcare provider on where to access the procedure abroad and receive support afterwards.

Even so, Alvarez-Hummel worried that the estimated 40 women a year who are forced to carry out the procedure abroad would now face greater stigma and more deeply entrenched taboos.

“You live in a country where it is forbidden, where the prince who lives in a castle made sure it stayed forbidden,” she said. “The one time he used his veto was against this – I can only imagine how difficult it must be for them to know this.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Giorgia Meloni is Italy’s great political survivor. Could one man be about to bring her down? | Riccardo Alcaro
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Riccardo Alcaro
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
With elections looming in 2027, Roberto Vannacci’s new far-right movement could fatally outflank the prime minister

Giorgia Meloni’s government became the longest serving in Italy’s republican history last month. This unusual political longevity, a moderate foreign policy, a certain personal charisma and even a recent spat with Donald Trump have combined to sharpen Meloni’s profile as the go-to leader on the European right.

Meloni’s personal approval rating – at about 41% – is one of the highest among west European leaders. Her far-right Brothers of Italy party has retained most of its support – a striking feat in our anti-incumbent era and by Italian standards, an achievement.

Yet all this may not suffice for her ruling coalition to be returned to power at Italy’s next election, in 2027.

Even before this week’s riots in Milan, Meloni’s greatest challenge was emerging from her far right, in the form of a new movement led by the former army general, Roberto Vannacci. The firebrand demagogue will, like Marine Le Pen in France, certainly seek to exploit the unrest to promote his party’s law-and-order credentials. If he succeeds, it could come at the expense of Meloni’s ruling coalition.

Vannacci was a high-ranking officer of almost 40 years’ service when in 2023 he self-published Il mondo al contrario (The World Turned Upside Down). Filled with hyper-conservative misgivings about such supposed western ills as cosmopolitanism, multiculturalism and feminism, Vannacci’s book became a sensation and the general was suspended from the armed forces.

But Vannacci’s extreme positions and abrasive style quickly made him a regular media presence, and with public attention came political interest. Matteo Salvini, leader of the far-right League and a junior partner in Meloni’s coalition, calculated that pulling the general into his ranks could boost his dwindling ratings. Salvini’s instincts were not wrong: in 2024 Vannacci was elected to the European parliament. However, he soon quit the League and this year founded a new far-right party, National Future, to which, polls suggest, the League has been losing support, imperilling Meloni’s coalition’s chances of re-election.

Electoral logic and a common ideological background would point to a Meloni-Vannacci alliance, but Vannacci’s ideological extremism makes that difficult.

Vannacci has made the “remigration” of foreign nationals – an idea promoted by such radical forces as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) – a central plank of his programme. While opposition to migration is one of the defining features of Meloni’s government, it has never gone that far.

Vannacci’s emphasis on the traditional family is so uncompromising that he proposes giving parents additional votes in elections and an advantage in public recruitment. His programme insists that abortion “is not a right” while it promotes the so-called “Mediterranean patriarchy”, and advocates abolishing the specific crime of femicide. These positions sit uneasily with Meloni’s politics, which combine conservative values with her own self-image of female empowerment.

The sharpest divide relates to foreign policy. Vannacci aims at easing the burden of eurozone fiscal discipline and opposes plans for greater defence integration. Tellingly, he has joined the AfD-led Europe of Sovereign Nations grouping in the European parliament, a group shunned even by Salvini’s League, the most nativist member of the Meloni government. On Russia and Ukraine, the gap is wider still. Echoing the AfD, Vannacci has argued that Russia is not an imminent threat to Europe and has called for the reopening of trade and diplomatic channels with Moscow, including by buying Russian gas. Vannacci also opposes support for Ukraine. For Meloni, by contrast, backing Ukraine is a pillar of her international positioning, most recently attested by her open criticism of Trump’s decision to waive sanctions on Russian diesel exports, ahead of a hard winter for Ukraine.

Meloni’s reluctance to enter an alliance with Vannacci is understandable. Forza Italia, her centre-right coalition partner, fears it would drive away the moderate conservative vote. The League is so shaken that some of its members want to disavow Salvini’s nativist ideology and go back to the party’s roots, representing the interests of business and local communities in Italy’s northern regions.

For the time being, Meloni has responded to the far-right challenge by doubling down on migration. Vannacci’s presence in the electoral wings explains some of the background to her suspension of the Schengen free-movement rules for air and sea passengers from Spain after the Ceuta tragedy. The same applies to the recent decision to put a 30% ceiling on students of foreign origin in schools. But it is far from certain this strategy can work, and pressure to strike a deal with Vannacci may build, not least to prevent the former military man from claiming to be the only politician promising a hardline law and order response to vandalism and looting in Milan. Meloni’s dispatch of 500 troops to the city ahead of further planned cost-of-living demonstrations was aimed partly at taking the wind out of Vannacci’s sails.

While an alliance could increase Meloni’s chances of re-election Vannacci would be a restive and unreliable coalition partner.

The alternative is to delegitimise Vannacci as a nationalist force, pointing to his extremism and proximity to Russia. Meloni would hardly regain the most extreme nativist voters lost to Vannacci but could convince a section of the moderate electorate to choose her coalition over centrist parties.

This strategy entails a real risk that Meloni will lose the next election. Still, the onus is on her now to articulate why Vannacci’s mix of anti-EU nativism, homophobia and misogyny is incompatible with both her own brand of national conservatism and Italy’s place in Europe. Doing so would send a powerful message that the commitment to the EU’s democratic principles – and European cohesion – is a moral red line. It is also one that can be imposed by conservative nationalists like Meloni on fringe forces to their right. As the now-seasoned leader figures out how to juggle her political ambition against the challenge posed by Vannacci, she should consider how high the stakes are, not just for Italy, but for all of Europe.

Riccardo Alcaro is head of research at IAI, Istituto Affari Internazionali, in Rome

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: ‘Slow news day at the office’: LeBron James shrugs off Trump’s national anthem attack
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Guardian sport and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Donald Trump lashed out at NBA superstar LeBron James on Thursday for what he called disrespectful behavior during the playing of the national anthem.

Trump posted a video of the basketball legend making apparent warm-up movements while lined up with his Philadelphia 76ers teammates before their season opener against the New York Knicks on Tuesday.

“While listening to our National Anthem, LeBron James disrespects our Country! I said right from the beginning that he’s no good, a TOTAL DISGRACE,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social network.

“LeBron James should apologize to all of those Great American Warriors and Heroes who died for the American Flag, and all that our Country stands for!” he wrote.

The video used by Trump had an on-screen caption that read: “LeBron working on his golf swing pregame.” It showed him making lateral swinging motions and basketball shooting movements.

Trump, speaking at a campaign rally in Iowa on Thursday night, renewed the attack, calling James’s actions “a big scandal kind of a story”.

Trump and James have traded barbs before, and the NBA’s all-time leading scorer shrugged off the president’s latest criticism.

“It must be a slow news day at the office,” he said after the Sixers completed an epic comeback to beat the Cleveland Cavaliers 114-106 in Philadelphia. “Slow news day at the office.”

James, 41, is entering a record-extending 24th NBA season with his fourth team.

Sixers coach Nick Nurse said Trump’s comments were the kind of distractions he was schooling his team to tune out.

“I think that goes right in with other outside noise we’ve already had,” Nurse said. “I keep saying the same thing. All I really care about is getting to the practice floor, getting them in the film room, getting them to the game floor.

“The focus that they’ve had and the intent and all the stuff like that has been outstanding.”

Philadelphia’s win on Thursday marked both the largest comeback by the Sixers in the play-by-play era (since 1996-97) and the largest comeback win of James’s career.

James finished with 17 points, 10 rebounds, five assists and three steals, while Tyrese Maxey powered the rally with 32 points and a crucial defensive effort on James Harden. Jaylen Brown, also making his home debut in a 76ers uniform, scored 17 of his 21 points in the second half and 10 in the fourth quarter.

Trump has been critical of athletes before – particularly Black athletes – for their behavior during the playing of the Star-Spangled Banner before games.

During his first term, Trump singled out NFL star Colin Kaepernick for his decision to kneel during the Star-Spangled Banner to protest against racial injustice and police brutality.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: ‘Bespoke’ mRNA vaccine significantly reduces risk of melanoma recurrence or death, clinical trial shows
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Donna Lu Assistant editor, climate, environment and science
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Trial results represent ‘foundational shift’ in approach to cancer, allowing scientists to harness immune system in more personalised way

A personalised mRNA-based melanoma vaccine significantly reduces the risk of cancer recurrence or death within two years, new clinical trial results show.

The vaccine, intismeran, is custom-made to target genetic mutations unique to an individual’s melanoma. It is the first individualised cancer vaccine to show positive results in a phase III clinical trial.

The Australian-led trial included 1,137 patients whose melanoma had been surgically removed but were at high risk of it returning.

All were treated with an immunotherapy drug called pembrolizumab for twelve months, and some were also given the personalised intismeran vaccine.

The trial found that at two years post treatment, the combination of intismeran and pembrolizumab reduced the risk of melanoma recurrence or death by 42% compared with treatment with pembrolizumab alone.

Prof Georgina Long, medical director at the Melanoma Institute Australia and 2024 Australian of the Year, described the findings as “a foundational shift in our approach to cancer”, allowing scientists to “harness … the immune system in a more personalised way to reduce the risk of melanoma recurrence or death. This has not been achieved before in the history of cancer drug development.”

Long will present the results at the European Society for Medical Oncology’s annual congress in Madrid on the weekend.

The results have been accepted for publication in the New England Journal of Medicine and will need to go through a process of peer review.

Patients in the trial – conducted across 157 sites worldwide – had not previously received any cancer drug treatment. Of those receiving the combination of intismeran and pembrolizumab, 82% were alive and recurrence-free after two years, compared with 70% of participants treated with pembrolizumab alone.

In a phase III trial, a treatment is tested in a large group of people and compared with standard treatments; it is necessary before drug regulators can approve a medicine for use in the general population.

In recent years, developments in immunotherapy drugs have significantly increased survival rates for people with advanced melanoma.

Dr Jessamy Tiffen, acting deputy director of the Centre for Cancer Innovations at the Centenary Institute, who was not involved in the research, said what was “truly remarkable” about the vaccine was the “deeply personalised nature of the treatment, something cancer researchers have been striving to achieve for decades”.

“Where previously oncologists could pick a targeted therapy based on a single gene mutation present in the melanoma, this bespoke mRNA vaccine targets up to 34 gene mutations, unique to each patient. This vaccine, in combination with another type of immunotherapy, then trains the immune system to recognise and eliminate the melanoma, and most importantly, stop it from coming back.”

She noted that the treatment, if progressed, would not benefit all people with melanoma. “A significant portion do not respond to the vaccine in the first instance,” she said.

“Cancer cells also have an insidious ability to adapt and evade whatever treatment we throw at them. Only time will tell how effective the treatment is beyond two years, but the results are clear that the combination works better than immunotherapy alone, and that’s a very exciting development.”

The drug manufacturers said it was too early to tell from the data whether the combination treatment improved long-term survival.

Prof Christopher Sweeney, director of the South Australian immunoGENomics Cancer Institute at Adelaide University, described the vaccine as “a step-change approach for how to improve the body’s immune system to see cancer cells as foreign and then augment the ability to prevent the cancer cells growing and recurring”.

He said more research was needed to see if the approach was effective in patients “who have cancer we can see”, or who were not responsive to the immune enhancer pembrolizumab.

The personalised vaccine will not be available as a standard melanoma treatment until it has gone through further study and regulatory review, a process that may take several years.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Milan braces for more unrest as debate intensifies over Italy’s ‘lost generation’
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Angela Giuffrida in Milan
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Protests and fringe violence expose sharp divide between marginalised and immigrant youth and those with greater prospects

Martina Miccichè was filming riot police kicking and beating a teenager with batons as they dragged him along Piazza del Duomo, the central Milan square hosting its cathedral, when she was struck by a flying object, causing a deep gash and bruising near her right eye.

The journalist had joined hundreds of mostly young people marching through the northern Italian city on Saturday afternoon to protest over soaring living costs and unaffordable housing, echoing the wider wave of economic discontent fuelling protests across Europe.

It wasn’t the first time Italy’s youth have loudly aired their grievances during Giorgia Meloni’s four years as prime minister, despite the risk of falling foul of her ruling coalition’s ever-expanding crackdown on security and public dissent. On Saturday afternoon they plan to protest again in Milan and other major Italian cities.

Miccichè said the atmosphere last Saturday was peaceful until about 5pm, when police blocked access to Via Broletto, a street about a 10-minute walk away from Piazza del Duomo.

“People were angry because they were being repressed,” she said, claiming the police turned “suddenly violent” as they pushed the crowd back with their shields. “The violence escalated. They started to grab people at random, hitting and kicking them. It was shocking.”

As the clashes continued and police filled the square with teargas while astonished tourists looked on, a group of masked youths on the fringes headed to the surrounding fashion district, tearing down road signs, setting bins alight and smashing shop windows – among them Footlocker and Levi’s – then looting them.

The vandalism resumed on Sunday as the gangs – many baited by the promise of luxury goods through a network of social media chats – descended on the city centre again, mostly from marginalised areas on the outskirts.

During the two days of unrest, police detained more than 271 young people. Of those, 32 were arrested, including 23 minors and 13 foreign nationals.

As the Italian media published images of injured police officers, Meloni’s government rapidly enacted more measures targeting minors and further empowering the police – including holding parents financially accountable for their children’s vandalism and looting – while dispatching 500 troops to Milan.

The latest legislation also criminalises violent participation in ⁠a demonstration and toughens penalties for ⁠rioters.

Some of the government’s security measures are now being applied in the south of Italy, where lorry drivers have been protesting against high petrol prices for more than a week, blocking roads and disrupting supermarket supplies. In response, 71 people have been reported to judicial authorities and 242 fined over the blockades – a protest act made illegal in a previous security bill. A government official also warned the lorry drivers that obstructing public highways could carry jail terms.

“This government just tries to repress protesters instead of listening to them and addressing the issues,” said Miccichè, who needed stitches for her injury. “It is all connected. There is anger in the south over fuel prices and young people everywhere are angry – they don’t even have a chance to think about the future because they are so terrified of the present.”

Furthermore, “we are not feeling safe”, the 34-year-old added, “because we can see how much space the police have now and how shielded they are”. Racial profiling had become the norm in Milan, especially in the centre and close to its train stations, she claimed.

The weekend’s urban unrest, including protests in Turin and Bologna, has intensified debate over Italy’s “lost generation”.

Furthermore, the youth protests and subsequent fringe violence have exposed the sharp divide between Italy’s marginalised and immigrant youth and those with greater prospects.

Working-class Italians or third- and second-generation immigrants are regularly labelled by rightwing politicians and the press as maranza, a derogatory term used to describe groups of young people who usually congregate in city centres.

They come from areas like Barona, a sprawling council estate in the south-west of Milan. Young people there have been reflecting on the events of last weekend. “There is a lot of discontent – we are all children of this widespread malaise,” said Domenico Ricci, who along with Luca Orlando manages a bar that is part of Barrio’s, a cultural hub where the district’s youth come together.

Orlando believes the vandalism and looting were a symptom of anger and years of feeling unheard and invisible. “So when an opportunity arises, these kids take revenge. They don’t do it simply because they want to steal something. All this government does is introduce new crimes – they never listen or engage in dialogue.”

Orlando, whose parents came from Calabria, is feeling the nationwide discontent. “But the protests there [in the south-west] have hardly had any coverage,” he said. “And we are only talking about Milan because of the violence and not the real issues.”

Thomas, 18, who has grown up in Barona, is training to be a chef and wants to leave Italy “as soon as possible”. He said: “I see no future here.” His friend Mohamed, an Italian citizen of Moroccan origin, is still at high school and wants to become a lawyer. “If you make a mistake, then you must pay,” he said. “But this is also a characteristic of protests – the more a government doesn’t listen, the more people get angry.”

Mauro Magatti, a sociologist at Milan’s Catholic University of the Sacred Heart, said socioeconomic discomfort and a sense of abandonment affected “an entire generation” and responding to the anger with excessive repression risked enlarging the protest. “Violence always needs to be condemned but now we need to lower the tone to overcome this burst of anger and violence and focus on addressing the real problems,” he said.

Police and military presence in central Milan has been building in recent days before Saturday’s protest, organised by a new online movement which has pledged to gather each weekend “until this government of thieves falls”. Security guards stood outside shops that had been damaged or looted last weekend.

Italy’s politicians from across the spectrum must take heed, warned Miccichè, as the protests were only set to amplify ahead of general elections next year. “There is no perception at all of how young people feel,” she said. “Even if they took just a minute to listen, they will understand that it is a generation full of ideas – they just want to be heard.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: ‘The biggest motivation is fear’: High turnout among Israel’s Palestinians could unseat Netanyahu
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Emma Graham-Harrison and Quique Kierszenbaum in Kfar Qasim
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
The Knesset is up for grabs next week and the Arab community is desperate to topple the far-right ruling coalition

As the sun set over the town of Kfar Qasim, Palestinian citizens of Israel gathered over hot knafeh pastries and shots of strong cardamom-laced coffee to hear an urgent pitch for their votes.

Palestinians make up about 20% of Israel’s population and their votes are likely to be critical to efforts to unseat Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right coalition in elections next week.

“We are determined to do everything in order to bring this government down. And high turnout among the Arab community is one important tool in achieving this goal,” said Ahmad Tibi, a member of the Knesset for more than two decades as head of the Ta’al party.

Most polling shows Netanyahu’s coalition will lose its majority in the 120-seat Knesset but the Jewish Israeli opposition bloc will also fall short of the 61 seats needed to form a government.

Palestinian citizens of Israel are forecast to secure between 12 and 15 seats, divided between the Islamist Ra’am and the Joint List alliance of three smaller parties, one of which is Ta’al.

The mathematics of power are clear, even though most of the Jewish Israeli opposition has ruled out a coalition with Arab politicians, and Netanyahu and his allies have been doing everything they can to make such an alliance politically toxic.

Racist, fear-mongering campaigning includes posters reading “It’s [either] the right or Palestine”, while others on the right have coined the phrase “Bibi [Netanyahu’s nickname] or Tibi”, even though there is little chance Tibi will hold even a junior ministerial post.

In the history of the state of Israel, there have been just two Palestinian ministers: Raleb Majadele held the portfolio for sport for two years and Issawi Frej was in charge of regional coordination for just over one year.

There is recent precedent for breaking promises not to work with Palestinians, however. The Ra’am leader, Mansour Abbas, in 2021 took his party into a historic coalition government with Naftali Bennett, now part of the opposition bloc, and Netanyahu himself had previously started coalition negotiations with Abbas.

One prospective voter, Mohammed, works at a hi-tech company, managing both Jewish and Arab employees, which he sees as a template for a different future for Israel.

Although disappointed that most Jewish Israeli opposition parties have ruled out a coalition with Palestinian parties, he understands the political logic, and he expects their position to shift once results are in.

“At the end of the day, everything is mathematics, right? One plus one is two. They cannot do anything without [those seats]. So they must do [some kind of deal] and they will do it.”

He is voting and urging all his friends, Jewish and Palestinian, to do the same. “You can say, ‘OK, they don’t like me and I want to relocate’. But if you want to stay here, you must vote. You must do that. Because if this government stays in power, it will be a disaster,” he said.

For Palestinian politicians, any alliance with a Jewish-Israeli opposition is also challenging. None of the parties are calling for a two-state solution, most vigorously oppose a Palestinian state and most support the settlement movement in the occupied West Bank.

“It’s between bad and worse. Any new government will not be my cup of tea, but I am choosing between Netanyahu, [Bezalel] Smotrich, Itamar Ben-Gvir and the opposition,” Tibi said.

The scale of death and destruction in Gaza, militant violence and ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, and spiralling racism and discrimination inside Israel have created deep-rooted fears about what another four years of far-right ministers could bring.

“The biggest motivation is fear. It is more effective and important than our political parties or our campaigns or anything else,” said the Balad party leader, Sami Abu Shehadeh. “People are very politicised, and aware of the danger of what will happen if these criminals come back to rule again.”

Turnout has been suppressed in the past because some voters lost faith in a system that is stacked against Palestinians and their representatives.

Israel’s supreme court effectively forced Abu Shehadeh to drop out of the race last month over an article about the 7 October Hamas-led attacks, in a decision widely criticised for enshrining different standards of free speech for Jewish and Palestinian citizens of the state.

A motion to disqualify the national security minister, Itamar Ben Gvir, for racist language, including calls for ethnic cleansing, was not upheld.

Other Palestinians do not take part in elections on principle. Nagham Zbeedat, a journalist with Haaretz newspaper, laid out her opposition in an article earlier this year.

“I do not vote because I refuse to legitimize a system that treats my rights as favors, my safety as optional and my humanity as negotiable,” she wrote. “I refuse to be grateful for crumbs while Palestinians are erased – slowly here, violently elsewhere.”

There is a new urgency to voting this year, however, because a far-right coalition returned to power would have a renewed mandate to accelerate its policies of ethnic cleansing and annexation, said Amjed Iraqi, a senior analyst for Israel/Palestine at International Crisis Group.

In Kafr Qassim, the date of the election is a reminder of Palestinian vulnerability. Two days after voting, the town will remember one of the most notorious massacres in Israel’s history, when in 1956 border police killed 49 men, women and children, shot because they broke a curfew they didn’t know had been imposed on them.

“From a Palestinian perspective this election is arguably primarily about mitigation. Everyone understands fully what the opposition represents and yet, for all that, Palestinians in Israel can see the difference between a rightwing government and a far-right government,” Iraqi said.

“There’s the sense you need to make your presence known and heard and shown, in the face of the far right, just by going to the ballot. There’s no clarity about what comes afterwards but that’s how powerless I think a lot of people feel.”

https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.title: Murder on the dancefloor: are phones, drugs and chatter killing off dancing?
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.author: Oliver Keens
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.text:
Viral pleas for punters to stop yapping have divided clubland. With ketamine and social media also altering behaviour, DJs and dancers weigh in on how sacred a space the club should be

Towards the end of summer, a debate began raging in clubland, kick-started by an Instagram post from the esteemed DJ Jane Fitz. Ahead of the Houghton festival, where she is a regular fixture, she posted a request asking people to stop chatting so much during DJ sets.

“What I wrote was super respectful,” she tells me. “A bit of talking is obviously OK. But why would you stand completely still, where the sound is super loud, just to ask your mate about a new boyfriend or what they had for lunch? It’s called a dancefloor for a reason.”

Fitz’s plea exploded. It chimed with many, while others were up in arms, claiming that paying an entry fee allowed them to do whatever they wanted. “People were accusing me of being the fun police,” she says. “I’m not trying to stop your fun, mate. I’m trying to give you a better night out.”

“I think the dancefloor is dead,” Charli xcx sang on her tongue-in-cheek comeback single Rock Music this spring. Was she right? Many DJs and clubbers are worried it goes further than the yappers Fitz complained about, citing the rise of certain drugs – insular ketamine, chew-your-ear-off cocaine – and TikTok-boosted star DJs bringing in passive fans used to consuming dance music through a screen, who end up standing still filming the DJ and their visuals. Then there is the rising cost of clubbing, prohibiting younger, potentially bouncier dancers from attending raves.

As fewer purpose-made clubs have been built in recent years, clubbers have got used to squeezing into one-room raves often in converted arches, warehouses and garages. Josh Aitman, an organiser of the sober-friendly London queer party Good As You, complains that “some parties can be so packed in that I get looks just for dancing”. Separate bar areas are scarce and the 90s concept of a dedicated chill-out room is long gone, so the smoking area is often the only safe – if smelly – bet for a chat away from the music.

While the audiophilia boom has improved sound quality in many clubs, stricter council licensing demands often result in quieter dancefloors, making chat more liable to cut through and annoy other punters. One diehard group of clubbers detailed the science on cards they handed out this summer on dancefloors including at Houghton. One side read: “The Dance Floor Is For Dancing” with “Please take your conversation to the back” written underneath. The flipside featured a diagram of EQ curves. “Dance music is very bassy, meaning there’s loads of room on the top end of the EQ spectrum for vocals to punctuate,” says Paul M, one of the instigators of the cards.

“The sadistic side of me wishes I could just turn the music off for 10 minutes and give these people a lecture on all this so they understand,” says Paul. “The cards were a jokey way of doing that – but it’s no joke. I was watching a DJ I’d wanted to see for ages and two men next to me were having a 20-minute discussion about mortgage rates.” Astonishingly, this group of dancefloor activists wasn’t alone – someone else at Houghton gave out cards that just said: “Stop Talking.”

Not everyone in clubland wants the dancefloor to be treated as a sacred space. James Ronald, who plays as Hot Cross Fun and is a resident DJ for the nomadic party Disco Disco, posted a heartfelt rebuttal to Fitz’s post titled: “Please Talk on the Dancefloor.” It garnered a similarly huge reaction. “I get that you should be respectful,” says Ronald. “But she talked about treating it like a church, cinema or a theatre – places where you just observe and nobody communicates.”

Ronald tapped into an important reason why club culture is such a powerful force: the dancefloor is a place for people to connect. “Community is a really big part of clubbing,” he says. He defends the right for clubbers to get deep. “There’s been instances with a particular friend, for example, who only really opens up when he’s a bit wasted. We’ve had important chats about family and personal issues, chats we wouldn’t have had anywhere else.”

It’s a fairly new discussion and, apparently, an intractable one. Dan Beaumont, a DJ who is writing a history of London’s queer club culture, sees it like this: “Gossip is the glue that holds clubbing together. You need an equilibrium of yappers and dancers. Clubbing doesn’t work when it’s one and not the other.”

One possible way forward is for venues to set more direction for what they expect from punters. At Gaffe, an intimate DIY 150-capacity club in south London that opened in early 2025, a sign shows two arrows pointing in different directions. One says “Dancing”, the other “Yapping”.

“The sign is a bit tongue in cheek,” says founder Luca Marchal. “But the arrows point in different directions for a reason. We’re asking people to take the longer chats off the dancefloor. Having a proper catch up is a massive part of going out, so we want that to happen somewhere good.”

Until more venues spell it out quite so clearly with signs, interpersonal skills have become more important than ever in this delicate standoff, a challenge for conflict-averse Britons. Compare that with Berlin, where there is far less social stigma around asking someone to take their chat outside. “There’s a certain etiquette that leads to more satisfying and transformative experiences on the dancefloor,” says the British DJ Pandora, who is based in Berlin. “You’re more able to get into a flow state without the distraction of nearby conversations.”

British clubs have started to follow Berlin’s lead in banning phones on the dancefloor, a change that many have credited with restoring a bit of life. Michael Peacock, an almost ambassadorial figure for British clubbing, is one of those leading the charge. The 68-year-old likes to arrive at clubs barefoot, often wearing little, and proceeds to have the most fun in the room; he says his peak this summer was dancing for 30 straight hours.

In 2022, a video of Peacock going for it at Fabric in London was shared online by a punter with mocking intent. There was a huge outcry: not only are people not dancing because they are filming the DJ (or each other) but they may be worried about someone else filming them. “A lot of the debate on social media is about how phones destroy the vibe for the DJ,” says Peacock. “But there’s still scant regard for ravers who are filmed without their consent.”

Peacock now campaigns for less phone use in clubs. He praises Amber’s in Manchester which goes further than most “no-phones” clubs with a strictly enforced zero tolerance policy. “There are still times when I have to remonstrate with people,” he says with a sigh.

Sheffield DIY venue Plot 22 staff place a sticker over your phone camera on the way in, and will have a word if they catch you breaking the rules. “Our space is small and intimate,” says the venue’s manager, Mike Thompson. “Even just one person filming with a flash would really disrupt the vibe”. Co-owner Adam Seymour agrees: “People say they feel free to enjoy the dancefloor when you take away the ability to use their phone.”

If clubbing’s heyday was defined by ecstasy, today’s most popular drugs can pull the dancefloor in disparate and equally destructive directions. Many feel that the rise in ketamine use – a drug that creates a profound sense of dissociation – has made dancefloors markedly less buoyant in recent years.

Manchester DJ Luke Una stresses that he doesn’t want to be judgmental about drug use, but calls ketamine a “very solo” drug. “It breaks any sense of communal togetherness. For me, music has to be about connection. A nightclub should be about bringing people together and transcending and escaping together. The one time I had it, I’ll be honest with you, I thought I was listening to Underground Resistance for 12 hours until I came round and realised that I was listening to the air conditioning unit.”

Then there’s cocaine, the cost of which has plummeted in recent years and is now as omnipresent as ecstasy used to be. Clubbers have “gone from a drug that makes the music sound amazing, to a drug that makes you think you’re amazing and people need to listen to you instead,” says the DJ Wes Baggaley, a resident on NTS Radio, a London music station.

But Luke Una is keen to point out how a revival of a different drug is having the opposite effect. “In the last 12 months, there’s been a lot more unity, love, warmth and smiling – down to people taking mushrooms again. I played a party in Belfast and said to the person running it, ‘Why is everyone so fucking happy?” And he said, ‘Luke, they’re all on mushrooms.’ I’m not advocating using them – but you can see the difference.”

Now Jane Fitz feels optimistic: “We started a debate, which was a great first step. I have seen differences, I think people have realised there should be some kind of etiquette. During the breakdowns in songs, the dancefloor has been feeling quiet with people listening again.”

When a party pops off, Luke Una also sees optimism: “I believe something is going on which feels like a reaction to what has become a brutal, toxic world out there. It feels like people are coming back to life in 3D again, showing a need to be together and – without being cringe about it – to kind of transcend together too.”

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Apple Watch Ultra 4 review: longer battery life but still awaiting new features
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Samuel Gibbs Consumer technology editor
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Biggest Apple smartwatch gets better health tracking and new readiness tools with a battery and chip boost in preparation for controversial audio AI

As the Ultra enters its fourth year as Apple’s biggest and beefiest smartwatch it gets the best kind of spec upgrade – longer battery life – while waiting for something potentially more transformative.

That’s because several of the key features announced as part of Apple’s new smartwatch lineup for 2026 have yet to be enabled, awaiting updates towards the end of this year. That leaves the £749 (€899/$799/A$1,349) Apple Watch Ultra 4 the top dog, but basically the same as last year’s model.

The Ultra 4’s body, screen, colours and design are identical to the previous versions. It weighs about 1g more, but the bigger changes are on the back and inside.

Upgraded sensors on the back of the watch take heart rate (HR) readings every five seconds during the day, up from every five minutes on previous generation Apple Watches. They also enable the measurement of your heart rate variability (HRV) during the day, not only at night, which feeds into some new recovery metrics.

The Ultra 4 is the first Apple Watch in several generations to get a meaningfully faster chip with the new S11. The battery life for general use in my testing now stretches to 79 hours, too, meaning the watch lasted well into its third day between charges. Most will be able to charge it every third morning, or less if you use the low power modes, although that is far behind the week-plus stamina of top adventure watch rivals.

The new watch charges at 10W with its little magnetic puck, up from 5W of previous generations, and reached 82% in under an hour and 100% in less than 90 minutes.

The Apple Watch features some of the most comprehensive health tracking available on your wrist, which on the Ultra includes extremely accurate dual-band GPS tracking for exercise. The more frequent HR and HRV measurements enable a few new features for the Ultra 4. The Vitals app, which monitors your stats overnight, now works during the day giving you an assessment of your general health. It can let you know when your HR and HRV are outside your usual baseline, indicating strain or sickness that might be on the way.

The new readiness app adds a popular feature from sports watches, which looks at your activity, vitals and sleep and works out whether you have properly recovered from strenuous exercise or stressful days. It gives you a score out of 10 and some advice on how ready you are for exercise, which can be a useful tool for training for a race or goal.

The Ultra 4 runs watchOS 27, just like Apple Watches back to the Series 9 and Ultra 2, which includes Apple’s new Siri and improved AI tools, some of which are available now, while other exclusive features are awaiting updates planned for later this year.

The upgraded Siri is available to talk to and behaves very similarly to that on a modern iPhone, including the Siri app for reviewing previous interactions. The new Siri Modular watch face features the top timely widget, which has been surprisingly useful. It shows simple things such as the timer when you have one running, or the weather when it starts raining. It also puts your vitals front and centre in the morning, or your calendar if you have an upcoming event, replacing the need for multiple complications.

Shazam music recognition is now significantly faster, while the sound recognition accessibility feature, which listens out for certain sounds, such as a fire alarm, doorbell, car horn or baby crying, and sends an alert to your wrist could be very useful.

But the marquee “audio intelligence” features that could be transformative and controversial are not yet enabled, being expected in “late 2026”. Siri Recap promises to transcribe conversations all day before delivering them as an AI summary. It doesn’t record audio or keep full transcripts, just the text summaries, but the Live Rewind feature can show you a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation so you can see what you missed.

Apple says the battery should last more than 1,000 full charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity and can be replaced for £95. Damage repairs cost £539.

The watch contains more than 45% recycled material, which is broken down in its environmental impact report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling for devices.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 comes in a choice of two colours and multiple bands costing from £749 (€899/$799/A$1,349).

For comparison, the Apple Watch Series 12 costs from £369, the Watch SE 3 costs £219 and the Garmin Fenix 9 costs from £860.

The Ultra 4 is the best smartwatch Apple makes. It has a great screen, rugged looks and all the trappings of other Apple Watches, including Apple Pay, comprehensive health tracking and full integration with an iPhone.

The faster charging and longer battery life are welcome, lasting about six hours more for general use than previous versions in testing. The more frequent heart rate readings and daytime heart rate variability monitoring are additive rather than revolutionary. The readiness and recovery monitoring add to the existing suite of training tools to close the gap to top-tier sports watches from Garmin and others.

Upgraded Siri is more useful on your wrist, and the new Siri Modular watch face was a surprisingly good addition. But the new audio intelligence features are not here yet.

That makes the Ultra 4 a great Apple Watch, just not a significant upgrade on those that came before.

Pros: great screen, rugged yet sophisticated design, hands-free gestures, three-plus-day battery life, 4G/5G and satellite SOS/messaging, comprehensive health tracking, great activity tracking with dual-band GPS, recovery/readiness tracking, better Siri, extra action button, 100-metre water resistance and 40-metre dive-ready, long software support.

Cons: no big upgrade on previous model, very expensive, only works with an iPhone, no third-party watch faces, shorter battery life than adventure watch rivals, marquee AI features not yet available.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Can AI really predict cancer survival better than a doctor? I have my doubts | Devi Sridhar
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Devi Sridhar
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Take a selfie to see how healthy you are: the idea is enticing and this new research is promising. But so many factors have been ignored

The idea that a single selfie could predict how long someone with cancer may live sounds like an incredible breakthrough. AI is getting better at spotting patterns in medical data, but can it be used to reliably predict what will happen to an individual patient? I asked a clinical colleague what she thought about the recent headlines. She found it an interesting development given that doctors have long used facial appearance to assess patient health. For example, she noted that they may write “appears stated age” or “appears older than stated age” as a proxy for general health.

Now, researchers from Mass General Brigham, a healthcare institution in Massachusetts, have taken this idea a step further. They have developed an AI model trained on more than 40 million facial images – called FAHR-Face – to assess biological age and predict survival in cancer patients. For biological age, they developed FAHR-FaceAge, which estimates age from certain facial features such as the forehead, the wrinkles between the nose and mouth and the temples. For cancer survival, they developed FAHR-FaceSurvival, trained using almost 35,000 photos of cancer patients. This model focused more closely on the area below the eyes and the bridge of the nose – regions of the face “linked with dying”. Dr Raymond Mak, one of the study’s authors, noted that these parts of the face are the same as those referenced by Hippocrates in 400BC as signs of muscle wasting and mortality risk: “the nose sharp, the eyes sunken, the temples fallen in”.

The results, published in The Lancet Digital Health this month, are intriguing – but far from conclusive. Researchers found that AI-estimated facial age was significantly associated with survival in 18 of 28 cancer categories. So, basically, it works for some cancers, but not for others. In addition, Prof Miroslaw Bober noted, “The tool still needs testing against doctors’ own judgments and across different hospitals and patient groups. For example, the facial-age measure was not significantly associated with survival for Black patients after adjustment for other factors.” That finding adds to the growing concern that AI models can exhibit racial bias based on the data used to train them and underlying assumptions. For example, racial bias has been shown when AI models analyse cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) scans – used to diagnose and monitor heart disease.

Let’s go back to what the published study does and doesn’t tell us. These models are built on retrospective data looking at statistical associations across thousands of patients, and it’s a jump to then accurately predict future survival from this. A selfie may contain clues about a patient’s health, but that is a long way from being able to predict their future – and a longer way still from proving that the prediction is useful in clinical practice.

I also worry about how unreliable selfies are. Just think of the times you’ve met people in real life and compared them with their profile photos. Anyone who has tried one of the online AI “guess your age” tools will know how much the result varies with lighting, camera angle, facial expression or even time of day. And then there’s botox, fillers, facelifts and even GLP-1 drugs, which alter facial fat and shape. How much can a single photograph really tell us about someone’s underlying health?

As anti-ageing treatments become the norm, visible age and underlying health will become an increasingly complex relationship. A face in a selfie that looks younger may not be necessarily healthier. The researchers do note that they tested their age model against lighting, expression and cosmetic surgery – but if predictions are based on specific signs of ageing in parts of the face that those all affect, I can’t see how it would be possible to avoid a certain degree of error in AI estimates.

None of this means the research isn’t promising. This new tool and the research team behind it are impressive. Alongside other tests that a doctor may perform to assess a patient’s health and future prognosis, it could take some of the guesswork out of “looks stated age”. But the question is whether it’s actually useful in daily practice beyond what clinicians are already doing when using experience and years of training.

If you’re tempted to go to the project’s public website to find out your biological age, even just to brag to friends about how young it says you look, be aware that by uploading your selfie, you will become part of the study too, as their consent forms indicate. Your face is not only being assessed, it’s contributing to the data used to develop the technology. Currently, the tool will only tell you your biological age, but I would be sceptical of what that may tell you about your overall health.

Finally, a pop quiz (I’m in the middle of the teaching semester): what top three things did the researchers find made people’s face age? Alcohol, drugs and smoking. No surprise there, but possibly an explanation as to why doctors can broadly read someone’s health status from their face. Something that perhaps we didn’t need AI scanning 40m faces to tell us.

Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh

https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.title: Starlink access for Ukraine limited after Trump’s claims satellite service restored, officials say – Europe live
https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.author: Guardian Staff
https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.text:
The satellite service was still operating at a cap of 161km/hr, crippling key air defences

A quick update from what the Ukrainian and Russian officials are saying this morning on overnight attacks:

Ukraine says Russia targeted energy sites in six different regions. Currently more than 500,000 people are without power.

Russia’s defence ministry confirmed strikes on Vilkovo port in Odesa, a railcar depot in Poltava and a cargo vessel in the Black Sea.

A war of words has erupted between the Trump administration, officials in Kyiv and Elon Musk over who is to blame for limiting Ukraine’s access to Space X’s military-grade version of Starlink. The restrictions to Starshield have rendered many of the drones used by Kyiv to strike behind the frontlines inoperable and hampered air defence systems that stop Russian attacks, according to Ukrainian officials. The US president said on Thursday that the service was running again at full speed, but a European official speaking to the Associated Press denied the service was fully functioning. What has Trump said?

Trump initially denied any responsibility for the changes to Starshield, telling reporters last Friday: “I don’t know if it was anybody, but it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” referring to Musk, SpaceX’s CEO.

Trump’s cabinet backed him up, with secretary of state Marco Rubio saying on Wednesday: “What I can tell you with certainty is the president of the United States nor anyone in our system ever requested that any changes to that system be made.”

Rubio, however, also made a comment that threw suspicion on to Musk, the world’s richest man.

The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr Musk. That’s a private company. The president doesn’t run that company and can’t direct that company to do anything.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that the US president had asked Musk to restore the service, with Trump later telling reporters the system was “back”.

He refused to comment on whether he had spoken to Musk, but appeared to suggest the ultimate power to limit the service rested with the SpaceX CEO. “I guess the bottom line, he put it back,” Trump said, referring to Musk.

However, John Cornyn, a Republican who is in his final weeks as the US senator for Texas, told US media that he didn’t believe Musk would have acted “without at least the acquiescence of the White House”. What about Musk? Musk has supported Trump’s calls for Volodymyr Zelenskyy to be replaced and has been highly critical of the Ukrainian president. However, he was quick to blame the limits on Starshield on the Trump administration, writing on X last week that the systems were “owned and controlled by the US government”.

Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.

Musk – one of the Republican party’s biggest donors and a Trump ally – continued to deny responsibility for the changes. However, on Tuesday the Wall Street Journal reported that Musk made the order to slow down Starshield, with the paper’s sources in disagreement over whether this was made in concert with Trump.

Vice-president JD Vance backed Musk on Thursday, saying the billionaire “doesn’t want to get in the middle of what is a war between two state actors without the United States government effectively directing him on what to do”.

So I don’t think this is about Elon. I think it’s fundamentally what is America’s policy in Ukraine and Russia going to be.

Amid the war of words, civilian casualties in Ukraine have surged, and the question over who is ultimately responsible for limiting Kyiv’s access has remained unanswered.

Good morning and welcome to our Europe live blog, where we’ll begin in Ukraine.

Local authorities reported explosions overnight in Lutsk, a city not far from the Polish border, and in the central Poltava and southern Sumy regions. Russia this morning has also claimed strikes on ships in the Black Sea.

Both sides engaged in heavy strikes yesterday with Russia bombarding Kyiv with ballistic missiles and Ukraine sending swarms of drones to Moscow. Trump has declared that Starlink is once again running at full speed across Ukraine after the service was throttled last week -but Ukrainian and European officials say they haven’t seen that speed and functionality resume.

The satellite service was still only operating at a cap of 161km/hr, crippling key air defences and limiting mid-range strikes, a Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent after Trump’s comments. “Overall, nothing has changed anywhere,” the paper quoted the unnamed official saying.
