She told her newsletter subscribers the next day, “together with many celebrities and Trump supporters”, and “met Steve Bannon and Donald Trump Jr there, among others”.

On 14 February the vice-president, JD Vance, met Weidel on the sidelines of the Munich security conference. On 23 February the AfD doubled its vote and became the largest opposition party in the Bundestag.

In September 2025, the New York Times reported that in April, Von Storch and the AfD politician Joachim Paul had met the state department official Samuel Samson in Washington. “They took a lot of notes,” Paul said.

On 1 October Darren Beattie, then the acting under-secretary of state for public diplomacy, posted that he had met Frohnmaier and a second AfD MP, Jan Wenzel Schmidt, “to discuss U.S.-Germany relations, as well as shared priorities on cultural exchange and migration”. Beattie was fired as a White House speechwriter in 2018 after it emerged he had spoken on a panel with the white nationalist Peter Brimelow. On 13 December his successor, Sarah B Rogers, met Frohnmaier too; Frohnmaier posted on X that the exchange had “made clear that Washington is looking for a strong German partner that is ready to take on responsibility”.

The Guardian reported in February that Rogers, asked about the 2019 Russian documents, which argued for supporting his candidacy in the 2017 German election, said she had “sought guidance within the state department and determined” that the allegation was “unsubstantiated – and in any event, not a bar to a meeting”.

In an emailed response to a request for comment on the meeting, Rogers wrote “Mr Frohnmaier is the foreign policy spokesman for the most popular political party in Germany. He delivers AfD’s foreign policy positions in the Bundestag, and is the person German media call when they want a policy statement from AfD. For this reason, we talk to him in his official capacity to understand AfD’s positions.”

Rogers added: “During the ‘cancel culture’ era, there was a manic focus on reputational contagion that probably hurt American civic life, and is a poor fit for American diplomacy.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: The mega-Maga contender in deep-red Florida who doesn’t want to talk about Trump
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Richard Luscombe in Miami
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Byron Donalds removed mentions of the president from his website and has barely uttered his name – will his ploy prove successful in a tight governor’s race?

It took Byron Donalds, addressing a wildly supportive crowd at a rally in Florida’s bluest county, some time to list those he blamed for any “affordability” issues they might be experiencing.

Joe Biden, and the radical policies of the Democrats, were at fault, the Republican nominee for Florida governor insisted in his stump speech at Broward county’s Green Glades West ranch, even though neither has wielded power in Washington for almost two years.

Donalds also pointed a finger at other traditional betes noires of the modern Republican movement, New York’s democratic socialist mayor, Zohran Mamdani, and the despised Dr Anthony Fauci.

Another to receive a lengthy verbal lashing was David Jolly, his opponent in a closely watched race that will help gauge the strength of a Democratic resurgence in a state that has veered reliably red in recent years.

Yet one name – Donald Trump – remained conspicuously unspoken, as did any mention of the war in Iran, soaring gas prices, unaffordable healthcare premiums, or any number of issues that have caused the president’s approval rating to drop to new lows.

How to handle Trump has become something of a conundrum for Donalds, an ultra-Maga, three-term Republican congressman, as he navigates a race that remains much closer than he would like it to be.

Such is the president’s unpopularity that the Donalds campaign made the decision last month to purge almost every mention of Trump from his campaign website, including the removal of “enact the Trump agenda” as his top priority as governor.

That, and his notable reluctance to invoke his name, or policies, on the campaign trail, appeared to be working, until Trump announced that he would be coming to Fort Myers on Friday, a little more than a week from election day, on the latest stop of the president’s late red-state tour in support of vulnerable candidates.

Some prominent Republicans seeking election have chosen to be elsewhere when Trump comes to town. Perhaps in an effort not to be seen too closely aligned, the Texas governor, Greg Abbott, discovered an unavoidable commitment as Trump visited San Antonio this month.

“Of course I’m going to be there. What kind of question is that?” he snapped at a reporter after last Friday’s joint rally with the Republican senator Ashley Moody, who is also on the 3 November ballot.

Another journalist asked Donalds if his silence on Trump was a deliberate uncoupling from some of the president’s more unpopular policies, such as his immigration crackdown that is polling poorly with Florida’s large Latino and Hispanic voting blocs.

“This is what I’m talking about. You guys are so caught up in, ‘Do you agree with this, do you agree with that?’” he said, not answering the question. “I was giving a speech about my campaign for governor because I’m running for governor.”

The distancing is a calculated gamble that may prove inconsequential anyway, given that registered Republican Florida voters outnumber Democrats by more than 1.5 million.

But his snippy responses suggest he is aware that Trump is probably uppermost in voters’ minds as they decide whether to allow him to succeed Ron DeSantis, whose endorsement has replaced Trump’s on Florida TV ads, and extend the Republican grip on the governor’s mansion that dates to January 1999.

Donalds’s speech last Friday, which was warmly received by the mostly white, middle-aged and above audience at the private ranch lodge resembling an upmarket Cracker Barrel restaurant on the edge of the Everglades, contained plenty of what they wanted to hear, and nothing that they didn’t.

He did not touch the wars in Iran or Ukraine, or gas prices. Any extra financial burden on Florida’s families, he said, could be laid at the door of “the craziness from the previous administration”.

Political analyst Larry Sabato said the distancing was a ploy that will be quickly forgotten if Donalds wins.

“Donalds is super-Maga. This is just a campaign tactic being used by quite a few Republicans all across the country,” said Sabato, founder and director of the University of Virginia’s Center for Politics and author of the election analysis website Sabato’s Crystal Ball.

“Look, Donalds has no choice but to make the most out of Trump, but not be devoured by him. And you know it’s not easy to do. You’re walking a very fine line there.”

Democratic leaders point to Donalds’s ultra-conservative, pro-Maga positions during almost six years in Congress. They include refusing to certify Biden’s 2020 election win, arguing that undocumented immigrants are not entitled to due process, denying climate change is human-made, championing abortion restrictions, and opposing transgender women and girls in sport.

Nikki Fried, the chair of the Florida Democratic party, told a press conference Thursday, one day before Trump’s Fort Myers, visit that Donalds is not fooling voters.

“Even when Byron Donalds tried to distance himself from Trump by scrubbing the president from his website, he went running back into Daddy’s arms within hours, but there is no hiding from this presidency,” she said.

“Tomorrow, Donalds and the rest of the Florida Republicans will once again reveal their true loyalties. The people of our state are tired of spineless politicians who kiss the ring and fall in line instead of standing up.”

But several attenders at the rally at the ranch, hosted by the environmentalist and businessman “Alligator” Ron Bergeron, a close ally of DeSantis, said they were unbothered by Donalds’s avoidance of any Trump talk.

“We’re all on the same page with our president supporting what is right,” said Luis Breton, a Republican voter and US citizen originally from the Soviet Union.

Stella Patrick said she saw Donalds and Moody as fighting for Florida’s interests, while Trump was busy “defending the nation”. The Fort Lauderdale retiree said: “Byron Donalds doesn’t need Trump’s blessing to win, and I’m happy he spoke about what he’s going to do for us in Florida. That’s what matters to me.”

To win and become Florida’s first Black governor, Donalds cannot afford to lose huge chunks of the alliance that helped Trump win the state at three successive presidential elections, including Black voters and Hispanics.

According to polls, Hispanic voters appear to be wavering about sticking with the Republican cause, favoring Donalds 48%-43% in an NBC6/Telemundo 51 survey published last week. Support from Black voters looks to have slipped away, the same poll giving Jolly a 76-10 advantage.

Meanwhile, Democrats nationally see a tightening race, and on Tuesday pledged an extra million dollars to bolster Jolly in late campaigning.

Sabato’s Crystal Ball, and Fox News, list the Donalds-Jolly contest as “leans Republican”.

Sabato said the days when Florida could be considered a purple state are long gone. “It’s not even close,” he said. “Trump won it easily, and so you can’t underestimate the Republican vote there, or overestimate the Democratic vote.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Magnitude-7 earthquake hits Tibet, killing at least 16 and destroying hundreds of homes
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Search and rescue efforts under way after quake strikes region’s north, with at least seven aftershocks recorded

A magnitude-7 earthquake has hit Tibet, killing at least 16 people, injuring 54 and destroying hundreds of homes in the northern regional city of Nagqu, official media have said.

Search and rescue efforts continued after at least 339 homes and 20 livestock sheds collapsed, the Nagqu media office said, citing city government officials. It was the biggest quake in the region in the past five years, according to China’s national broadcaster CCTV.

More than 1,600 people from the local county were deployed to help rescue efforts. Supplies were also sent into the region, including 1,000 prefabricated housing units, about 3,000 tents, folding beds, torches and winter clothing.

The US Geological Survey said the quake occurred at 10.33pm local time on Thursday, with its epicentre 119 miles (191km) east-north-east of Nagqu, in a sparsely populated, high-altitude area of northern Tibet. It put the earthquake’s depth at 11 miles.

The agency recorded at least seven aftershocks of magnitudes between 4.3 and 5.2, all of them with a depth of 6 miles. Videos posted by CCTV showed workers running out of restaurants and objects falling off shelves at supermarkets when the quake struck.

China’s official Xinhua news agency said on Friday that communication in some areas hit by the quake was down. Local railway authorities had taken emergency actions to stop trains passing through the region.

More than 300 police officers were dispatched for relief work while the regional fire and rescue services had sent almost 350 personnel to the affected areas, Xinhua reported. Rescue workers clambered through damaged buildings, some with collapsed roofs, footage on CCTV showed.

The earthquake caused rockfalls, forcing local authorities to close a section of national highway 317, allowing only emergency, rescue and official support vehicles through as crews worked to clear debris, according to Xinhua. Intermittent snow was expected in the region over the next three days, Xinhua said.

China’s president, Xi Jinping, called for an all-out effort in the rescue operation and medical relief work.

Nagqu is more than 185 miles north of Tibet’s capital, Lhasa. Earthquakes are relatively common in China. In January 2025, at least 126 people were killed in one in Tibet’s rural Tingri county.

In August, a disastrous flood hit the border of Tibet and Nepal. China’s tight grip on information prevented international media from visiting the affected regions on the Tibetan side, obscuring the scale of the damage.

In December 2023, a quake in remote Gansu province in north-west China killed at least 134 people, state media said. That quake was China’s deadliest since 2014, when more than 600 people died in the south-western province of Yunnan.

Tibet is a particularly seismically active area. The high-altitude region was taken under Chinese control in the 1950s and its people, who are predominantly ethnic Tibetans, have had a tense relationship with the authorities in Beijing since. As well as being one of the poorest regions in China, many Tibetans reject Beijing-imposed controls on their culture and religion.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘They wanted to make a scene’: the 72-year-old paraded in dramatic arrest for ‘voter fraud’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Sam Levin in Los Angeles and Sam Levine in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Omar Muñoz, one of 28 people charged in California, speaks out about being dragged from his home in front of cameras as DoJ accused of ‘disgusting’ PR campaign

Omar Muñoz was getting ready to have his morning coffee just after 5am on Monday when he heard a loud bang at the front door of his Los Angeles home.

“Open up or else we’ll break down the door, and it’ll be bad for you,” the man on the other side yelled, Muñoz, 72, recalled.

Outside, Muñoz saw officers in police vests and opened the door. When they told him to put his hands up, he explained he was frail after six recent surgeries. He said something to the effect of, “I can’t walk fast, I can’t take long steps, to enter a car is painful,” he recalled. The officers nonetheless handcuffed him, he said, and when he stepped out into the street, he saw about six law enforcement cars. And cameras filming.

Photos taken by an Associated Press photographer show officers in the dark of morning, some with helmets, masks and shields, walking a shackled Muñoz out in the red pyjama pants he had slept in the night before.

A helicopter flew above and his street had already been taped off, he said: “It was staged and I’m the patsy … They wanted to make a scene.”

At that moment, Muñoz said he had no idea why he was being detained. He later learned he was one of 28 green card holders in California charged by the Trump administration with allegedly registering to vote unlawfully. Muñoz’s arrest was publicized a day later in a slickly edited Department of Justice (DoJ) promotional video, turning him into the face of the crack down.

The publicity around Monday’s events shocked experts who closely follow these kinds of cases.

“It’s disgusting,” said Justin Levitt, a professor at Loyola law school in Los Angeles and a former deputy assistant attorney general. “There’s no point other than partisan politics behind that sizzle reel. And DoJ is supposed to be forbidden from engaging in partisan politics in their enforcement actions.”

The arrests come as the Trump administration has ramped up efforts to criminally charge noncitizen voters ahead of the midterm elections, as part of an effort to create the impression that voter fraud is rampant while several studies have shown it is exceedingly rare.

In recent weeks, the administration has charged 40 people across the US for voter fraud, according to Seamus Hughes, who runs the news website Court Watch, which focuses on legal news. Around 170 people have been charged for illegal voting since the start of Trump’s second term, according to Hughes. There were more than 230m people registered to vote in the 2024 presidential election, according to the US election assistance commission.

In California, the DoJ has also sued the state, alleging there are 20,000 non-citizens on the state’s voter rolls and demanding the state be blocked from tabulating certain ballots the justice department claimed might belong to noncitizens. The 20,000 alleged non-citizens represent a tiny fraction of the more than 23m registered voters in the state.

State officials have forcefully rejected the federal government’s claims, saying the justice department had wrongly flagged US citizens and people whose voter registrations have already been cancelled as potential ineligible voters.

Muñoz, a lawful permanent resident and longtime Californian, is accused in a federal criminal complaint of fraudulently registering to vote and making false statements in a citizenship application where he claimed to have never voted. A Department of Homeland Security agent alleges he cast ballots several times since 2020. Green card holders have legal status, but are ineligible to vote. At his lawyer’s advice, Muñoz declined to comment on the specific fraud claims while the charges were pending.

The charges that the 28 California defendants face vary even though the accusations are similar. Muñoz and others charged in the central district of California, which covers Los Angeles, are facing felonies that carry maximum five-year prison sentences. Those who have been charged in the eastern district, which covers the Central valley region, have been charged with misdemeanors which carry maximum one-year sentences.

In the rare instances where noncitizens get registered to vote, it is often because they are confused, experts say. They may not know they are ineligible, or believe they can vote if someone offers them a chance to. California is one of 24 states that has automatic voter registration – a system in which people are automatically registered when they interact with certain state agencies unless they opt out.

Several people who were arrested in the California case this week have expressed confusion about the charges – one saying he mistakenly thought he could vote; another saying she had no recollection of registering to vote as the authorities had alleged; and another flatly denying voting as authorities had alleged.

Democracy and constitutional law experts said it was extraordinary for the federal government to launch a heavy-handed operation to detain someone accused of a nonviolent voting offense and stunning to see the justice department directly release a propaganda-style video of the arrest, particularly before the defendant has even been indicted. One former justice department attorney also said it was a significant departure from the department’s norms to pursue highly politicized cases during campaign season, particularly two weeks before a midterm election, with prosecutors traditionally avoiding actions that could be perceived as trying to influence the contests.

Voting rights’ advocates have raised concerns the Trump administration was trying to sow doubt about the integrity of the elections in the lead-up to the high-stakes midterms.

Levitt said the justice department’s video was designed to confuse the public about the prevalence of voter fraud. “The government wants the circus, because they like the circus. And that is wildly improper, because we pay for that.”

“This is all part of this PR campaign,” said Wendy Weiser, the vice-president for democracy at the Brennan Center for Justice. She was skeptical, however, that the campaign would succeed because there is broader awareness of the administration’s effort to create a false impression of voter fraud. “It will still yield some damage, and it debases the presidency and the Department of Justice too,” she added.

The justice department did not respond to inquiries about Muñoz’s case and about criticisms of its media strategy. A DHS spokesperson declined to answer questions about Muñoz, saying the department doesn’t comment on active investigations. The spokesperson said DHS is “actively rooting out and investigating election fraud wherever it can be found” and “aliens who vote ... will face the consequences – including criminal charges and deportation”.

Muñoz’s lawyer declined to comment. Los Angeles election officials did not respond to questions about his alleged voting record.

Muñoz, originally from Belize, said he has lived in the US for more than 50 years and has 10 grandchildren and 12 great-grandchildren. He retired in 2019 after a range of careers, including installing alarms and caretaking for people with disabilities, he said.

He recounted his ordeal to the Guardian while seated on a bench outside the front door of his home on a sleepy dead-end street in Commerce, an industrial city just outside of downtown LA. His birds chirped in a cage nearby and his pug, Daisy, napped on the pavement where a flurry of agents had gathered two days before.

“I’m a strong person, but I’m not doing well,” Muñoz said on Wednesday. “They had me dragged all throughout the media. They wanted to make a spectacle out of me.”

The video the justice department posted to its X account was edited with an upbeat rock song and captioned, “OPERATION PROTECT THE VOTE.” It showed neighbors looking on during Muñoz’s arrest, and included a series of clips of officers holding the elderly man as they escorted him to be processed before his first court appearance. The edit blurred his face.

Defense lawyers said typically in cases such as Muñoz’s, prosecutors would coordinate with federal defenders to have the defendants appear for a hearing.

“These folks are clearly not flight risks and weren’t accused of violent acts,” said Sergio Perez, a civil rights lawyer and former justice department attorney. “To enter into residential neighborhoods with this degree of militarized approach is unheard of.”

Perez, who worked as a justice department observer during the 2012 election, said the department would historically investigate claims of improper voting, but would not approach these cases in a theatrical manner, nor would prosecutors bring charges in the heat of campaign season, in an effort to avoid any appearance of meddling in elections.

Muñoz said he fell twice as he struggled to stand while being transported to a holding facility in downtown LA, and that more cameras awaited him there. While he waited to be brought into court, he was placed in additional chains around his waist and feet: “It was so tight, I could barely walk and I was hurting.” He said he suffers from bone disease and nerve pain and the shackles exacerbated his problems: “The pain just progressed more and more.” He was eventually given an apple and candy bar, his only food for the day, he said.

His family showed up to court to support him and he was released later on Monday, at which point he saw the news coverage and better understood why the government had put him in the spotlight: “This is about a fight between Trump and the Democrats,” he said.

Muñoz said the government could have sent him a letter asking him to come to court or dispatched one or two officers to his door without much fanfare. “I understand they have an allegation against me, that’s their job, but it’s the manner that they did this to me,” he said. “There were so many officers. How much taxpayer money went into that?”

Lliani Orantes, Muñoz’s daughter, who is a nurse, said that when her father was seen by doctors on Wednesday, discs in his spine appeared to be out of line in the area where he had a recent surgery, he was experiencing full-body trembles and his blood pressure was very high: “It’s hurtful he has to go through this.”

“Living with your wife for more than 50 years and being in there and not knowing anything, I don’t know,” he said. “I don’t know what I’d do. Would I die in there?”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: What’s up with Trump’s unhinged rants on male candidates’ bodies at rallies?
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Adam Gabbatt
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Trump’s latest tactic to champion Republicans at midterm rallies? Assessing men’s bodies in meticulous detail

Speaking at a rally in Youngstown, Ohio, earlier this month, to support the Republican senator Jon Husted, Donald Trump broke from his prepared remarks.

Trump said he had recently learned that Husted played football at university. The president, 80, said this had prompted him to conduct a physical assessment of Husted.

“I don’t do this with men very often. I started examining his body, because I didn’t know he was a great athlete. And I looked and I watched up and down. I looked at his ass and I looked at the whole – and then I looked at his hands. Look at his hands. He’s got these, like, claws,” Trump said.

It was just one example of Trump offering unsolicited, and increasingly unhinged, assessments of men’s bodies in the last two weeks, as he freewheels across the US attempting to drum up votes before November’s midterm elections.

With Republicans expected to struggle, it’s unclear whether Trump’s inspections are part of a carefully thought-out strategy or just a man indulging a pattern, but either way Husted, who has represented Ohio in the Senate since 2025, could be forgiven for wanting the president to stop paying him such close attention. Unfortunately, that seems unlikely to happen, because Trump has begun to speak of Husted’s charms even when he’s campaigning for other candidates in other states.

So it was that an audience in Kentucky this week heard Trump talking about Husted, with his appraisal taking on a more forensic nature.

“I examined his ass,” the president said of Husted, who was not at the event. “And then I looked at his shoulders. I looked at his feet. I looked at his hand. I looked at his jawline. Studied him. He’s got a jawline.”

Trump continued: “I then patted him on the shoulder, and it was like a piece of steel. I’m still recovering.”

Democrats are expected to comfortably win the House next month and could even clinch the Senate, with the party even having a chance of winning deep red states like Mississippi, Kansas and Kentucky. That’s prompted a flurry of activity from Trump, who has repeatedly told voters to pretend he is on the ballot – the president seemingly ignoring his own historically low popularity.

Whether this tactic of trumpeting men’s looks can turn Republicans fortunes around remains to be seen – but in any case, Trump shows no sign of slowing. And while it’s Husted’s physique that has most captivated him, the president has shown himself to be an aesthetic pluralist, with other candidates catching his eye. Those include Ed Gallrein, a 68-year-old Navy Seal turned dairy farmer who definitely does not color his hair.

“He’s going to be, he’s going to be a perfect man,” Trump said of Gallrein. Trump recalled when he was looking for a candidate to run against the incumbent Republican congressman Thomas Massie – whom Trump does not like – in Kentucky.

“I needed somebody good, and this guy walks through the door,” Trump said of Gallrein. “I said, look at this beautiful guy.”

Trump’s unusual behavior hasn’t gone unnoticed. Anderson Cooper, the CNN host, dubbed Trump the “assman-in-chief” as he played clips of his comments on air.

“There’s nothing at all unusual – and certainly nothing gay – about a president who dances daily to YMCA and who publicly pined for a reprise of Betty Buckley in Cats,” Cooper, who is gay, said.

On Fox News, meanwhile, host Jesse Watters attempted to normalize Trump’s comments.

“Trump says a lot of stuff we all think but we don’t say. Sometimes it sounds a little gay. But he can get away with it because he’s straight,” Watters said.

“This is what guys say,” Watters continued. “He was saying this guy John Husted is a phenomenal athlete, he was an all-American corner back, national champion, division three football player and he’s got what it takes.”

Still, we’re approaching a point where Trump breaking off to tout the looks of his Republican candidates is as much a feature of his speeches as are his dark warnings that Democrats are aiming to turn the US into a cross between Pol Pot’s Cambodia and the Australia of Mad Max.

On Friday, at a rally in Dalton, Georgia, he discussed the contrasting charms of Jon Ossoff, the state’s 39-year-old Democratic senator, and Mike Collins, the stilted Republican challenger who wears his white hair in a style approaching a mullet.

Early in his speech, Trump broke off from a plea for people to “really get out there” and vote to compare Ossoff’s appearance to Pee-wee Herman, the comedy character whose popularity peaked in the mid-1980s.

“Somebody said he’s a good-looking man,” Trump said of Ossoff. “I don’t think he’s a good-looking man. I actually think Mike Collins is a good-looking man – and he’s all man. He’s all man. I’m not sure about Ossoff.”

Trump then turned his attention to Rick Jackson, the 72-year-old billionaire Republican who is running for Georgia governor.

“I actually think that Rick Jackson’s a very handsome, distinguished, beautiful-looking guy,” Trump said.

The examples keep coming. Tim Sheehy, a US senator from Montana was ruled “a very handsome guy”. An unidentified group of generals were dubbed “beautiful guys”. There was praise for Ted Nugent’s “beautiful-looking son”.

It’s a pattern which might have reached its zenith at a rally in Oklahoma this month. During his speech Trump broke off from his planned remarks to praise three “big, strong, good-lucking guys” he had seen waiting in the line outside the event.

“Where are they?” Trump asked the crowd. “You can’t miss ’em: big, strong, handsome Oklahoma studs.”

The crowd laughed nervously, unsure how to react to this intimate scene. But perhaps they shouldn’t have been surprised. Perhaps this was just the natural culmination of one man’s growing fascination with asses, jawlines and steel-like shoulders, a preoccupation that Trump seems to enjoy, but which seems unlikely to help Republicans on 3 November.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Ukraine troops report ongoing problems with Starlink satellite network
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Pjotr Sauer
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Communications system still faces speed restrictions despite Trump claim that Musk had resumed full service

Ukrainian forces continue to report widespread disruptions to the Starlink satellite network, despite Donald Trump’s claim that Elon Musk had lifted restrictions on the service.

The slowdown, which has affected the key communications system used by Ukrainian troops, began last week after Trump and Starlink founder Musk publicly criticised Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, over continued strikes on Russian oil refineries.

The restrictions have raised questions and confusion about who ordered the slowdown and why, with both Trump and Musk denying responsibility.

“I don’t comment one way or the other,” Trump said on Thursday when asked about reports that he had personally called Musk to demand the restrictions be lifted.

But Ukrainian officials said on Friday morning that speeds remained capped at about 100mph, with no indication that the restrictions had been lifted.

“At present, we have not observed any lifting of the restrictions on Starlink,” said Serhii Beskrestnov, a military expert who advises Zelenskyy.

“There have been isolated cases in which Starlink has operated at speeds slightly above the imposed limits, but this is likely due to SpaceX’s algorithms or specific conditions of use, rather than any lifting of the restrictions,” Beskrestnov added.

The speed restrictions have prevented Ukrainian military equipment, including drones, from maintaining a connection to the satellite network when travelling at high speeds, hampering both offensive drone operations and efforts to intercept incoming Russian attacks.

The slowing down of Starlink, coupled with Zelenskyy’s complaints that Washington had temporarily suspended intelligence-sharing with Kyiv, have plunged relations between Ukraine and the US to a new low in recent days.

Tensions first flared after Washington’s surprise decision to lift sanctions on Russia and begin importing Russian diesel, as Trump sought to bring down US energy prices before the midterm elections. Maritime tracking data showed that the first tanker carrying Russian diesel was en route to New York on Thursday.

Meanwhile, Russia launched another overnight barrage against Ukraine, even as Moscow said a fresh round of US-brokered talks aimed at ending the war could take place next month.

The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said on Friday that trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US were expected to resume in Abu Dhabi in November. Previous rounds of negotiations have failed to produce a breakthrough, with Moscow and Kyiv far away over the terms of any peace settlement.

Among Russia’s maximalist demands are that Ukraine withdraw its forces from territory it still controls in the east of the country, drastically reduce the size of its military and adopt a neutral status that would rule out Nato membership.

Speaking to a Russian state television reporter late on Thursday, Putin once again questioned Ukraine’s sovereignty, echoing claims he has repeatedly made throughout the war.

“The lands lost by Kyiv are not their territory, they are Russia’s historical lands,” Putin said.

The Russian president also cited unspecified genetic research to revive his longstanding claim that Russians and Ukrainians were “one people”, before insisting that Moscow would achieve all the objectives of its full-scale invasion.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: Oil hits five-month high amid fears US will renew strikes on Iran
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Lauren Almeida
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
Brent crude rises to $114.72 a barrel after Tehran threatens retaliatory attacks on Gulf oil and tech facilities

Oil has hit its highest level in more than five months as fears of fresh escalation in the Middle East conflict grip the energy markets.

Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, rose by 1% on Friday morning to $114.72 a barrel – its highest level since May.

The increase came after Tehran said it would strike oil facilities, undersea cables, datacentres and AI facilities in the Gulf region if a new US-Israeli attack was launched against Iran.

“Widespread reports that the US is considering renewed military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections rather than pursuing a diplomatic route was enough for the price to pop, after what many had considered would be a brief conflict is now in its eighth month,” said Richard Hunter at the broker Interactive Investor.

Oil had traded at about $72 a barrel back in February, before the Iran war began, but soared to $126 a barrel by the end of April.

Tensions in the region have been rising this week; Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps claimed to have struck four commercial ships in the strait of Hormuz on Wednesday. The US state department ordered some diplomats and the families of US government employees to leave Saudi Arabia, which has faced continued attacks from Houthi rebels in Yemen.

Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategists at the broker Wealth Club, said fears were rising that American and Israeli forces would be ordered to launch strikes on Iran’s energy infrastructure after the US elections on 3 November.

“At the same time, the attacks on Saudi Arabia’s facilities by Houthi rebels have intensified this week, and for ships attempting to cross the strait of Hormuz, it’s still a dangerous journey, with projectiles still being fired,” she said.

Streeter said Ukraine’s bombardment of Russian diesel refineries was also adding to supply concerns.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Suit filed to force Trump administration to address cancer-linked pesticide pollution
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Tom Perkins
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Suit alleges EPA has for decades failed under the Clean Water Act to address surface-water atrazine pollution

A new lawsuit asks a federal judge to order the Trump administration to address widespread pollution from the hormone-disrupting pesticide atrazine – which has regularly been found at levels that threaten wildlife and human health.

The cancer-linked chemical is now contaminating nearly 25%, or about 860,000 miles, of all continental US rivers, according to a recent review of federal records. The waterways cover more than 20% of surface drinking water intakes across the country, and more than 675,000 private and commercial wells.

The suit alleges that the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has for decades failed under the Clean Water Act to address the surface-water pollution. It asks a federal court to order the EPA to develop quality standards for the chemicals.

The EPA was supposed to put a plan in place in 1999, but has not yet done so. Another plan it developed under the nation’s pesticide laws, instead of the water laws, would only address about 1% of atrazine pollution, according to a peer-reviewed study.

“It is absolutely insane that atrazine is one of the most widespread water contaminants and it isn’t even be properly regulated under the Clean Water Act,” said Nathan Donley, environmental health science director with the Center For Biological Diversity, a non-profit that is among the lead plaintiffs. “The fact that it doesn’t have any [limits] is bonkers and goes to show how little they’ve done.”

Atrazine is the second most widely used pesticide in the US, with about 70m pounds sprayed on the nation’s cropland annually. It can have severe impacts on human and animal hormones, especially for developing children. The pesticide was found to “chemically castrate” frogs and cause some to change sexes. It is so dangerous that it has been effectively banned in 60 countries, including the European Union, since 2003, and California this month proposed adding it to its carcinogen list.

The EPA’s plan to rein in pollution under the pesticide laws appears good on paper, but is “worthless” upon closer scrutiny, Donley said. It would require farmers who spray the maximum amount allowed under the law to reduce their use. But very few farmers spray the maximum amount, so the effect would be negligible, Donley said.

The EPA plan also offers a “menu” of about 30 actions from which farmers can choose to reduce the amount of atrazine runoff from farmland. But many of the options include actions like keeping a log of the amount of pesticide the farmer uses, which does not actually do anything to reduce runoff, Donley said.

“Where the rubber hits the road, the EPA plan does not do a damn thing,” Donley said. The chemical is such a problem because it is highly mobile and easily washes into waterways, and it is persistent, meaning it does not break down. The only real solution is ban, Donley said.

“The rest of the world is banning this incredibly dangerous pesticide. Why is Trump’s EPA continuing to push this poison on people?” he added.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/liv.title: Oil hits five-month high as global stocks wobble on AI fears; retail sales in Great Britain fall as shoppers cut back - business live
https://www.theguardian.com/business/liv.author: Lauren Almeida
https://www.theguardian.com/business/liv.text:
Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets, and the world economy.

A fresh wave of selling hit AI stocks around the world overnight, as investor grow increasingly anxious around the sustainability of AI-fuelled returns.

The Japanese and South Korean stock markets, which have been buoyed up by their exposure to the AI investment boom, fell before recovering some ground to trade broadly flat on the day.

And over in the US, the blue chip S&P 500 fell by 1.2%, its worst performance since July, and the tech heavy Nasdaq dropped by 2.6%, its biggest drop since June. The Philadelphia semiconductor index fell by a painful 6.7%, also its worst day since June.

Jim Reid, of Deutsche Bank, says our gloomy weather is reflected in the stock market:

double quotation markAs storm Austen hits these shores this morning, clouds kept darkening for markets yesterday, as the wobbles of recent weeks all collided at once. First, there was mounting stress around France, with the Franco-German 10yr spread (+14.8bps) seeing its biggest daily widening since the initial pandemic turmoil in March 2020.

Second, AI fears continued to gather pace, with the Philly semiconductor index (-6.72%) falling to its lowest level since July, which dragged down equities more broadly. And third, the latest geopolitical fears meant oil prices kept rising as well, with Brent crude (+4.00%) hitting a 5-month high of $113.17/bbl.

So collectively, those concerns drove a huge risk-off move, with the 10yr Treasury yield (-16.6bps to 4.95%) seeing its biggest daily decline since August 2024.

And in a further sign that investors are taking a decidedly more conservative approach – there has been a strong move towards US Treasuries, widely considered the best quality government debt in the market and a safe haven asset. Reid says:

double quotation mark…In the midst of all these market pressures, an interesting theme was the flight to US Treasuries, which returned to its traditional risk-off role in periods of turmoil. In fact, the 10yr yield fell -16.6bps to 4.95%.

Moreover, that came despite some strong US data, demonstrating how the financial stress was weighing on sentiment rather than the fundamentals. For instance, the weekly initial jobless claims fell to a 3-month low of 194k in the week ending October 17 (vs. 200k expected). And in turn, that pushed the smoother 4-week moving average to its lowest since September 2022, back when the unemployment rate was just 3.5%.

Ipek Ozkardeskaya, an analyst at Swissquote, says that the falling value of some of the biggest tech and AI stocks in the world suggests that the bubble in the sector is bursting.

double quotation markGiven the more than 50% retreat in memory chipmakers’ share prices from their peaks, we could now argue that their exponential rise was a bubble, and that the bubble has burst.

These memory chip companies continue to benefit from strong AI-related demand, and they’re trading at very low forward earnings multiples: Samsung and SK Hynix at around 3–4× — yes, 3–4 times! Alas, buyers are nowhere to be found.

Investors will be watching closely next week as Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Sandisk are all due to report their latest results.

Elsewhere this morning, British retail sales fell by ⁠0.4% in September, compared with expectations of a drop of 0.1%.

An unseasonably warm start to the autumn weighed on ⁠online clothing vendors ⁠and ​supermarkets also saw a drop in volumes, official figures showed on Friday.

double quotation markThe drop in retail sales in September and sharp fall in consumer confidence in October raises the risk that the economy’s recent run of resilience might be coming to an end.

At least part of the drop in retail sales in September can be attributed to warm weather dampening demand for winter clothing, which might reverse in October.

But retailers also reported lower footfall and customers cutting back, suggesting cost of living pressures might be starting to bite. Indeed, the slump in consumer confidence in October suggests that higher inflation and borrowing costs are now having a bigger impact on confidence and spending. Nervousness ahead of what seems likely to be another tax raising budget, may also be playing a role.

9.30am BST: Flash PMI for UK, construction statistics for Great Britain 2025

3pm BST: Flash PMI for US, University of Michigan’s US consumer confidence index

US stocks are poised to fall when the market opens later this afternoon, with futures for the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq down.

Susannah Streeter, of the broker Wealth Club, adds that the prospect of higher borrowing costs will unsettle investors betting on companies that are spending huge amounts on AI.

double quotation markInvestors have turned highly nervous again about the cost of the build out, and there’s likely to be little comeback today for tech stocks which have been severely tested this week. The Nasdaq Composite tumbled 2.6% to 26,009 and the S&P 500 fell 1.2% [on Thursday]. Futures markets point to a muted start for Wall Street with few sparks of hope around to ignite a meaningful recovery.

Heineken has warned British bars and pubs that the boom in popularity of weight-loss drugs could lead to a fall in sales of beer and cider.

The world’s second largest brewer sent a presentation to British hospitality customers earlier this month warning that GLP-1 use – led by Ozempic and Wegovy – can reduce the desire to drink alcohol, which could lead to “fullness and fewer serves” of pints in pubs and bars.

The document, revealed by Reuters, warned that the GLP-1 era could lead to the tradition of the multi-pint drinking session becoming a less frequent occurrence.

The Netherlands-headquartered company offered advice including promoting half pints, low- and zero-alcohol options and pairing drinks with small plates of food, or risk declines in customer visits and spending.

GLP-1 use has soared as consumers seek a quick, easy solution to rapid weight loss, with 10 million people turning to medication in the US last year, according to research by JP Morgan.

Heineken, the world’s second largest brewer after AB InBev, said the presentation was shared with customers as part of its regular engagement with UK businesses to help them understand how consumer habits are evolving.

Rob Wood, chief UK economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, says the biggest news is from S&P’s PMI data is the composite employment index rising above 50 for the first time since the 2024 budget.

double quotation markThe jobs balance rose to 50.5 from 48.9 in September, consistent with a 9K month-to-month payrolls gain in October. Solid growth is helping, probably alongside an easing drag from the payroll-tax hike.

…The steady recovery in jobs growth further undermines any case for waiting to hike rates. A November rate hike is a shoo-in, and we expect another rone in February. We are very close to adding a third hike in May or earlier. It’s a really close call, but at the margin, we hold off after weak consumer signals this morning. It would take little—small further energy price rises, a hawkish DMP—to push us to three hikes.

Some good news amid the doom and gloom this morning – UK business activity growth has accelerated to its fastest since February, helped by rebound in new orders, according to a survey published this morning.

The preliminary S&P Global UK composite purchasing managers’ index (PMI) rose to 53.1 in October, higher than forecast and up from 52.0 in September.

A number of businesses cited a boost to sales from AI investment spending and rising demand for technology services, according to the survey. However, it found there will still many reports of sales being affected by geopolitical uncertainty and weak consumer confidence. Weaker demand was evident in the construction and real estate sectors in particular, it found.

But Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said that the survey also showed that businesses were taking on additional workers for the first time since hiring fell after the autumn budget of 2024.

double quotation markThere are reports of paused spending due to a lack of clarity on domestic economic policy in the run up to the budget, meaning the promising economic picture from the latest PMIs should provide an encouraging base for further robust economic growth through the winter months, barring any adverse surprises to businesses in the tax and spending review.

Geopolitics, and notably the potential for conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine to add to energy market volatility, are, however, clearly still unsettling many businesses, and cost of living concerns and broader fiscal worries are being compounded by the shift to higher borrowing costs.

Price pressures remain worryingly elevated, not only making a rate hike from the Bank of England at its upcoming policy meeting a near certainty but also likely shortening the odds of further rate hikes into 2027.”

It is red across the board in the European stock market this morning, though the falls are not steep. The UK’s blue chip FTSE 100 index is down 0.4%, while the French Cac 40 is down 0.7%. The German Dax is down by 0.6%.

The Stoxx 600, which tracks the biggest companies across the continent, has fallen by 0.4%.

While less red tape will be welcome news for small businesses, the chancellor is still facing pressure from bigger companies in the UK for more support.

Earlier this month some of the UK’s biggest retailers and hospitality businesses, including Tesco, Costa Coffee and the Co-op, met John Healey to urge him to cut the cost of employing young people in his first budget.

Businesses have asked for a partial reversal of the surprise move by Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, who lowered the earnings threshold at which they start to pay national insurance contributions (Nics) from £9,100 to £5,000 a year. They argue the change contributed to the plunge in the number of high street jobs for young people and part-time workers and a rise in youth unemployment.

They want the Nics threshold raised to £6,000, arguing this would help create jobs and ease inflation pressures on high streets.

The UK government has promised it will “slash red tape” for businesses, in reforms it claims will save firms across the country £800m in administrative and tariff costs per year.

The changes will make compliance guidance clearer, simplify the UK’s corporate reporting requirements and extend import tariff suspensions on products favoured by businesses, it said.

It comes as pressure grows on prime minister Andy Burnham and chancellor John Healey to reduce the cost of doing business in the UK ahead of the budget next week.

The government has set itself a target of reducing the administrative burden of regulation on businesses by 25% by the end of the current parliament.

Burnham and business secretary Jonathan Reynolds are scheduled to meet with small business leaders at No 10 North today, where they are expected to accept recommendations from the Small Business Taskforce.

double quotation markIt’s not right that pointless bureaucracy gets in the way of people working hard to build something that matters to their high street.

So we’re getting government off their backs and giving businesses the breathing space to grow. Because when businesses succeed, they create good jobs, strengthen their communities and bring growth to every part of the country.”

double quotation markBritish firms are fed up with form-filling and pointless paperwork that eats into valuable time and money when they simply want to get on with running their businesses.

That is why we are cutting unnecessary bureaucracy and giving businesses the breathing space they need to invest, innovate and create good jobs.”

Rain Newton-Smith, chief executive of the Confederation of British Industry (CBI), said that the changes were a “welcome step towards giving smaller firms more time and headroom to focus on their businesses.”

double quotation markThe test now is delivery. Cutting unnecessary admin can free firms to invest, compete and grow – and business will want to see that ambition translated quickly into meaningful reductions in the burden they face.”

And pressure continues to build this morning, with oil prices rising again. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, is up 1% this morning to $114 a barrel – its highest level since May.

Richard Hunter, of the broker Interactive Investor, points out that oil is now up by about 60% since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran, and up around 90% in the year so far.

double quotation markWidespread reports that the US is considering renewed military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections rather than pursuing a diplomatic route was enough for the price to pop, after what many had considered would be a brief conflict is now in its eighth month.

Susannah Streeter, of the broker Wealth Club, says fears are rising that American and Israeli forces will be ordered to launch strikes on Iran’s energy infrastructure after the US mid-term elections.

double quotation markAt the same time, the attacks on Saudi Arabia’s facilities by Houthi rebels have intensified this week, and for ships attempting to cross the strait of Hormuz, it’s still a dangerous journey, with projectiles still be fired.

Ukraine’s bombardment of Russian diesel refineries is adding to supply concerns. The deteriorating situation is once again fanning inflation fears, with companies unlikely to keep absorbing higher energy and freight costs. The longer the conflicts rage, the greater the chance of higher prices becoming more embedded in the economy, and that’s why bets have increased on central banks hiking rates more rapidly.

Consumer confidence in the UK has fallen at the fastest rate outside the Covid pandemic since the 2016 Brexit vote as the escalating economic damage from the war in the Middle East hits Britain.

With less than a week before John Healey’s first budget, the latest barometer from the data company GfK indicated confidence plunged by 11 percentage points in October to -24 amid pressure on consumers from the rising cost of living.

Highlighting the challenge for Andy Burnham and his chancellor before the statement on Wednesday, GfK said its consumer confidence index last fell by this much in a single month in July 2016, following the shock leave result in the EU referendum.

The index – which has been closely tracked by the government and the Bank of England for early warning signs from the economy since the early 1970s – recorded its largest ever fall, of 25 points, in March 2020 just after the start of the first UK lockdown.

double quotation markRelentless cost-of-living pressures, against an international backdrop of unresolved regional conflicts that are themselves contributing to domestic inflation now at 3.5%, appear to have swept aside the nascent optimism we saw following the appointment of a new UK prime minister this summer.”

Economists are warning there could be more gloom ahead for retailers as they enter into the crucial final quarter of the year – which includes Christmas.

double quotation markOctober’s sharp fall in consumer confidence and the dip in retail sales volumes in September show that times are getting tougher for households just as the all-important festive period for retailers is just around the corner.

In itself, the 0.4% m/m fall in retail sales volumes in September (consensus -0.1%, CE 0.0%) isn’t bad as it followed a 0.7% m/m rise in August, which was revised up from the first estimate of 0.5% m/m. Admittedly, some of it was due to a 2.2% m/m rise in fuel sales as households topped up their tanks before fuel prices rose even further. They are unlikely to do the same in October. But equally, part of the 0.9% m/m fall in sales at clothing stores was due to the unusually mild weather limiting sales of the new autumn/winter ranges. Soft clothing sales also contributed to the 0.4% m/m drop in sales at supermarkets. Both may perform better in October. Either way, total sales rose by a decent 0.7% q/q in Q3 as a whole.

That all said, the plunge in the GfK measure of consumer confidence, from -13 in September to a six-month low of -24 in October, shows that rising fuel and utility prices, higher borrowing costs and the fear of tax rises in the budget are taking a bigger toll on households. On the face of it, that’s consistent with the annual growth rate of retail sales volumes slowing from 0.8% in September to well below 0%.

This supports our view that both real consumer spending and real GDP will grind to a halt in Q4 and Q1. And this fall in consumer confidence is also the kind of thing that makes the prime minister less likely to call an early election soon.

Jacqueline Windsor, head of retail at PwC UK, noted that fashion retailers had fared the worst in September, despite the warm weather.

double quotation markAlthough all other retail categories saw sales rise year-on-year, rising petrol prices meant that consumers had to divert more of their spending on filling up their cars – over 30% more than last September - meaning less to spend on other things.

So, while retail prices, and grocery prices in particular, have remained subdued thanks to industry competition and the delayed pass-through of cost increases due to the conflict in the Middle East, the higher-than-expected inflation reported earlier this week will inevitably translate into less in shoppers’ pockets in the critical run-up to Christmas.

With most retailers’ sales coming in the last three months of the year, the upcoming peak season remains on a knife edge. This time last year, uncertainty surrounding the late budget at the end of November held back spending in the preceding two months. While that makes this year’s comparisons easier, retailers will be hoping that anything announced by the Chancellor this year does not add further to their cost of doing business nor dent consumers’ sentiment, which already seems to have fallen from the highs at the end of summer.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: ‘An orchestra being gassed should be an alarm signal’: the musical activists targeted in Paris
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Kim Willsher in Paris
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
New World Orchestra’s musicians are shocked at French police targeting peaceful gathering with teargas

As riot police encircled Place de la République last week, lobbing teargas canisters to disperse demonstrators, the conductor Étienne Jarrier and his orchestra played on. They kept playing even after everyone else had disappeared and teargas was being fired into the central Paris square.

It was only when Jarrier noticed his musicians were being directly targeted that he ordered them to stop. “There were teargas canisters landing in the double bass and music stand cases, and starting fires the musicians had to stamp out,” he told the Guardian.

The Orchestre du Nouveau Monde (the ONM, or New World Orchestra) is used to accompanying protests. Co-founded by Jarrier in 2022, the Paris-based ensemble is made up of hundreds of young professional and amateur musicians, all volunteers and all committed to blend classical music and activism, particularly social and climate justice.

The orchestra describes itself as “anti-racist, anti-capitalist, feminist, environmentalist and committed to de-growth”, with the dual aim of linking artistic performance with activism and increasing awareness of classical music among the young rather than its traditional “white bourgeois and elderly” following.

In 2022, ONM played at the foot of a melting Alpine glacier; two years later it was outside the headquarters of the far-right Rassemblement National (RN), performing a parody of an anthem popular with Marshal Pétain’s Vichy regime that collaborated with the Nazis. Last year, it formed a welcoming committee outside a television station for the Eurosceptic RN leader Marine Le Pen, and played the EU anthem, Beethoven’s Ode to Joy.

“We’re very happy to play at demonstrations,” Jarrier, 25, said. “There are lots of anthems for social struggles in France, like the Marseillaise or the International or activist music of the last centuries, but it’s important to play music that appeals to new generations.”

For the recent protests, its repertoire has included The Hanging Tree from The Hunger Games, and the theme from Marvel’s The Avengers film. “Music from a superhero movie on a day of social struggle seemed appropriate” said the conductor.

Jarrier, whose late father was a photographer and whose mother is an archeologist, studied classical music and the clarinet until the age of 17, but is a self-taught conductor.

Photographs of last Saturday’s protests show Jarrier, baton raised, conducting the ONM against the backdrop of the 10-metre high bronze monument representing Marianne, symbol of the French republic, and a dense white cloud of teargas.

French security forces, including the CRS riot police, were unimpressed. The squadrons of police, often nicknamed Robocops, have been widely criticised for their aggressive policing of recent demonstrations, particularly their liberal use of stun grenades (that emit a deafening explosion), flash-balls, baton charges and teargas against protesters. Yet they seemed impotent to stop those looting shops and destroying public buildings.

On Saturday, Jarrier had invited musicians to join the orchestra at Place de la République, the starting point for the official demonstration by high-school students protesting a failing and unjust education system, and by unions angry with the government’s failure to address wider grievances.

“It was a day of what we call a convergence of struggles,” Jarrier said. “The orchestra is engaged politically in the fight, so our presence was necessary on such a day. We appealed to any musicians with an instrument who wanted to play to come to Place de la République before the official protest march starting at 1pm.

As between 400 and 500 musicians gathered in the square, orchestra members alerted the CRS that they would be present and performing, Jarrier said. “We asked them to let us know if they plan to charge or gas the square, and they said they would warn us,” he said.

“While we were rehearsing, a very happy crowd of people of all ages gathered around us. Then the teargas canisters started being thrown around the orchestra. Not directly at us at that point. After a while there was almost nobody there except us.

“Clearly the aim was to clear a peaceful crowd from the place, which is quite serious and something we’ve not seen before. But even when the square was empty all around us, the CRS continued to gas the orchestra. After 20 minutes we had no choice but to stop playing.”

“It was quite scary,” he said. “We’d reassured the musicians before the protest saying: ‘Don’t worry – they’re not going to use teargas or charge us when we’re peaceful.’”

As the musicians packed away instruments, the orchestra’s security volunteers formed a human chain between the musicians and police.

“We are very angry about what happened,” Jarrier said. “It’s an extremely serious shift in maintaining order; the [government] is not listening to demands and is responding not with politics but police.

“It’s trying to divert attention from a legitimate movement that demands better public services, better lives. By making this about violent police repression they divert attention from the real concerns. We are not the martyrs, but the image of an orchestra being gassed should be an alarm signal,” he said.

The French Ministry of Defence and the Paris police prefecture were asked to comment on the use of teargas at Place de la République, but did not respond.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.title: ‘Fighting an impossible fight is the only way to reclaim dignity’: Lee Chang-dong on class warfare and his searing Oscar contender
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.author: Rebecca Liu
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oc.text:
The auteur’s new film – a study of labour, capital and the fallout of redundancy – won the grand jury prize at Venice. Telling tales of the disenfranchised is ‘our moral responsibility’, he says

A quintessential 21st-century horror story: a private equity firm has set its sights on your company. That’s the premise behind director Lee Chang-dong’s new film, Possible Love, and the idea for it first came more than a decade ago, when mass layoffs resulted in a standoff that “fundamentally changed the Korean labour movement”.

In 2009, workers at Ssangyong Motors company protested against plans to lay off between 37 and 43% of the workforce, staging a historic 77-day strike and occupation of the factory that was eventually broken up by riot police. “Until that point in time in Korea, labourers’ rights were widely accepted,” Lee says, speaking through an interpreter in a central London hotel; “however, afterwards, the basic rights of labourers changed; to the public, they couldn’t be seen as more important than market profitability or corporate competitiveness.”

At the time, Lee shelved the project. “The more I examined the pain of these individuals” – after the violent crackdown on the Ssangyong Motors strike, there were several suicides, and reports of long-term mental health issues – “I constantly asked myself: am I worthy of telling this story? And if I am, how do I tell it? Do I stand close to the workers, or keep my distance?” Later he and his co-writer Oh Jung-mi, wrote “many different” scripts, including one with post-apocalyptic elements, before Oh suggested introducing a character who is a documentary film-maker, thereby finding a way to work in Lee’s ambivalence about his intentions.

The result is a sharply observed Russian doll of a film that places a narrative about “labour and its relationship to capital” within a broader story about the ethics of film-making, and the tensions and desires that emerge when a working-class couple collide with an astronomically wealthy one. It has, like many of Lee’s previous films, been received to great acclaim: it recently won the grand jury prize at Venice film festival, and has been hailed by critics as one of the best films of the year.

The film’s opening title shows the 10th commandment, “Thou shalt not covet”. You can already guess that it will be swiftly broken. Soon we see the depressed Ho-seok, who has been fired from his job at a metal factory, reprimanding his free-spirited wife Mi-ok for caring about her clothes. They’re on their way to a funeral of Ho-seok’s former colleague, who killed himself after being made redundant, and meet the ambitious film-maker Lee Ye-ji and her financier husband Sang-woo. They radiate the kind of glow afforded by wealth. After a stay at a luxury resort in Qatar made Ye-ji reflect on the nature of hidden labour, she’s making a film about the state of labour in Korea, and believes she’s found her ideal subjects; if only Ho-seok, who refuses to go to therapy let alone talk about his experiences in front of a camera, would agree.

Since his first feature in 1997, Lee, now 72, has made luminous yet unsparing films about disempowered people swept up in brutal economic and political circumstances: his protagonists include blue-collar workers, ex-prisoners, people with disabilities. In his previous film Burning, an adaptation of a Haruki Murakami short story, a poor writer battles for a woman’s affections with a wealthier rival. (Possible Love brings together two lead actors from Lee’s most acclaimed films; Secret Sunshine’s Jeon Do-yeon and Sul Kyung-gu who starred Peppermint Candy and Oasis.) Class tensions bristle throughout his work: now, however, he’s wondering whether we’ve outstripped the usefulness of the term.

“It’s difficult to use the word ‘class’ because it is so vast,” he says of the difference between the couples in Possible Love. He describes Sang-woo, who moves about the world with possessive ease, an allure and emptiness, as a “symbol of capital … It’s not even that Sang-woo is a wealthy man. It’s about how he is capable of moving and controlling a huge amount of capital. And that capital creates further wealth. It’s almost as if you can’t really grasp how much wealth it creates. It’s just something of a different dimension.” At the same time, “I didn’t want to show that the two couples belong to completely different worlds, because they do live in the same world.” It is, after all, the abstract financial machinations of people like Sang-woo that materially overturn the lives of people like Ho-seok. Making the characters interact together at restaurants, their homes, and on a charged summer holiday “was going to naturally bring out the tension, the hidden power difference between them. There is a gap that just cannot be crossed.”

The film exposes the audience to many different kinds of looking: we are shown Ye-ji’s documentary footage; a CCTV feed; newsreel-style clips of a violent police crackdown on a workers’ strike. Lee wanted to study the “issue of the gaze”; “the ethics of capturing and observing the lives and pain of others”. Ye-ji has a habit of holding her camera up at inappropriate moments, often to the discomfort of Mi-ok and Ho-seok’s young son, Cheol. I wonder if she’s supposed to be a sympathetic character. “Anyone who’s really hardworking, they tend to overdo it,” Lee says. He feels a “closeness” to her, “and cameras by their nature search for drama.” Can there ever be equality between a film-maker and their subject? “It’s very hard to be equal because the person holding the camera without even realising it is given power. And it’s a one-sided relationship.”

In his telling, Lee became a film-maker almost by accident. He was a writer in 1980s South Korea, then under a military government, feeling called to draw attention to human suffering: “That was our moral responsibility.” As the country moved towards democracy and into the new century, he felt that although the suffering still remained, “that moral responsibility among people in literature began to disappear. Literature that dealt with the close pains of reality were treated as if they were expired goods. I was disappointed with that change.” He took up screenwriting to try something new, before working as an assistant director, “because I almost wanted to punish myself in a way, make myself go through something very tough. I worked so hard at it that people around me were moved, and they said: ‘Oh, you should be a film-maker.’”

South Korean films today are known globally for their confronting depictions of capitalism, though unlike, say, Bong Joon-ho’s Parasite (which also features a class divide between two families) or Park Chan-wook’s No Other Choice (also about the misery of corporate layoffs), Lee’s characters are not schemers who attain pyrrhic, depraved victory against the system. We instead are often left to observe how they are marginalised by the world around them; we witness their small disappointments, the cruelties they endure, and how they strain to hold on to their hopes.

Yet his films also reveal the small but significant moments of solace and grace these characters find: in nature, other people, or their own willpower. Lee has previously described his films as stories about people taking on impossible fights against large, impenetrable entities. “However, despite that, I think the fight itself has meaning. I think these fights the individuals take on against the world is quite possibly the only way they are able to reclaim dignity. Regardless of your chances of winning, I think the fight itself is significant and meaningful.”

You could say that his latest film was made after a fight of sorts. Lee struggled to find domestic funding for the film, given the “structural crisis” facing the Korean industry, caused by the economic losses from a strict Covid 19 lockdown, and the rise of streaming services. Netflix stepped in to fund it, granting the film a theatrical release in some countries worldwide. “The character Ye-ji has a wealthy husband. She lives with someone who holds that capital but still tries her best to be independent,” Lee says. (Her husband, Sang-woo, somewhat disparagingly describes an independent film as a “film independent of capital”; “I thought it would be very amusing to have him say that line,” says Lee.) “I feel like she and I are in the same shoes. I am also dependent on capital to get my films made. You could say that I am also someone who is married to capital, but trying to protect my own voice, which I almost think is the fate of all film-makers.”

After its victory at Venice, there are already whispers about the Oscars; it is South Korea’s submission for best international feature. I ask what success means to him. “I’ve always made films wanting to connect with audiences. It’s always meaningful for me when my audiences accept the questions that I ask through my films and try to find their own answers. And hopefully that leads to a very small change in their lives.” It’s a fitting answer for a film-maker who has long portrayed the subtle acts of resistance people can mount against a hostile world; who finds in small changes, causes for hope.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: The young Americans choosing Y2K cars over shiny new SUVs: ‘I get so much crap from people’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Andrew Lawrence and photographs by Jordan Putt in Kennesaw, Georgia
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
People under 35 are hunting for no-frills rides they can pay for in cash and fix themselves – defying expectations to take on steep loans

Jack Price joined the Marines in fall 2021 knowing he would need a car to get around base and that he couldn’t afford a new one. A joyless, month-long search through dealer classifieds and Facebook Marketplace listings ended when his mother spotted a 2010 Volkswagen Jetta posted on her office listserv by a co-worker moving abroad. With just 60,000 miles (96,560km) on themeter, the car (a manual!) was mechanically sound, and the air conditioning, sunroof and Bluetooth radio worked too. At $6,000, it was a steal. Price paid in cash.

Five years on, the Jetta, which he called the Pewter Pebble, is still carting him from A to B in unassuming style. “I’ve completely driven it into the ground,” says the 30-year-old, who lives in Los Angeles. “All over bases, cross-country a couple times, not really lovingly. I get so much crap from people, but not people my age.”

For generations, buying a first new car has been a rite of passage in the US, the clearest sign of a young person responsibly striking out on their own. But younger millennials and gen Z are increasingly finding that path blocked. The average new vehicle costs more than $50,000, an alarming figure that reflects Americans’ insatiable appetite for progressively larger SUVs and pickups. Meanwhile, adults under 35 are disappearing from showroom floors, accounting for less than 10% of new vehicle registrations in 2024 – a new low.

According to the credit reporting agency Experian, the average monthly car payment in the US is $765 for a new car and $542 for a used one, with the loan terms now stretching to six, even seven, years. A record 21% of new-car buyers pay $1,000 or more a month, according to the autos research group Edmunds. And that’s before factoring in maintenance, fluctuating gas prices and the eye-watering insurance premiums often charged to drivers under 35.

For many young Americans already under the strain of student loans, high housing costs and an unforgiving labor market, buying a new car or even a newer used one is out of the question. Enter the Y2K car – the retro ride that has become a trendy romantic choice for some younger Americans. “There’s definitely a golden era of cars from the late 90s and early 2000s that people just really want all of a sudden,” says Charlie Spears, a service adviser at an independently owned repair shop in Atlanta who conducts prepurchase inspections of used cars on demand. “A lot of people just want something that’s not going to fail them.”

Y2K cars don’t encompass everything produced in that era. They are the ones that simply won’t die. Think wedge-shaped Honda Accords and slab-sided Toyota Camrys: dependable, hand-me-down transport that can last 150,000 miles or more with routine maintenance. (Price’s Jetta, which was built at the end of a model production run that began in 2005, just makes the cut.) They’re economical to run and relatively inexpensive to insure, owing to their drastically lower worth. Best of all, the purchase price is low enough to pay in cash. Even when buyers need a loan – at steep interest rates as modern cars have in effect become mortgage payments on wheels – they can pay it off in a fraction of the time it takes to finance a newer car.

The supply of these bargains is dwindling: used vehicles priced under $15,000, the sweet spot for Y2K cars, have shrunk from 21% of inventory a year ago to 15%, according to industry analysis from Cox Automotive – numbers that speak to the demand for affordable cars. “Part of the draw is the nostalgia factor – people wanting cars they grew up with,” says Consumer Reports’ autos expert Keith Barry. “An old car with the right music on is kind of the closest thing to a time machine.”

On social media, the Y2K car has emerged as an ironic status symbol – a marker of maturity, grit and lack of pretense. Defects – busted aircon, glitchy windows, bits and bobs that have failed, fallen off or been held on with gaffer tape – are simply treated as part of a Y2K car’s personality. “I don’t know what kind of disease that is in the brain,” says one TikTok creator, who has to pry open the fuel door of her 2003 Mitsubishi Outlander with a screwdriver. “But I don’t get frustrated. I’m like, ‘Oh, this is fun.’”

In a Y2K car that takes a lickin’ and keeps on tickin’, creature comforts are beside the point. For many, part of the appeal is the absence of dashboard infotainment displays and other screens that have replaced basic switches and knobs in newer cars, often in the name of cost-cutting. Automakers’ zeal to monetize in-car technology, sometimes charging extra to activate physically installed features such as heated seats and remote start, only reinforces young buyers’ doubts about the value of a new car.

At the same time, do-it-yourself repairs have become harder as cars grow more digitally complex and auto manufacturers cut off access to owners and even independent mechanics. Oftentimes, they require investing in specialty digital readers or computer software to diagnose problems, and bespoke tools for wrenching. Most car owners would sooner punt, take the car to the dealership and pay whatever the maintenance and repair costs – which, of course, is exactly the vertical integration that shareholder-bound manufacturers are after.

Hence the romance with Y2K cars: you can fix ‘em yourself, their old-school controls fall easily to hand, they’re tried and tested, seemingly built to last. They just have an aura of invincibility – never mind that their age makes them fundamentally more dangerous and susceptible to frequent repairs. “I’ve used my Jetta as if it were a truck,” Price says. “Transported trees in it, put my surfboard through the sunroof. I’ve done every single thing possible to thrash it beyond its abilities.”

Price’s passengers, however, don’t have much appreciation for Pewter Pebble’s quirks. Often while carpooling to US military installations, senior officers compelled to hold up the sagging headliner would ask him when he was trading in his beater for a new truck or SUV. It was a similar story when Price left the military last year and started chauffeuring Alex Vindman, the Iraq war veteran turned US Senate hopeful, on the campaign trail during Florida’s special election. “I drove him around a couple times in it, and he was like, ‘What is going on?’” Price says. “The fact that we expect folks who are getting paid, like, a grand a month to have a new car is nuts.”
