Sivanandan has thus already joined the 10 youngest 2400-rated players of all time, who include the new Russian star Roman Shogdzhiev, the world No 5, Nodirbek Abdusattorov, Argentina’s Faustino Oro, and Turkey’s Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus.

If Sivanandan wins her final round game against a 2034-rated opponent on Friday afternoon, which will be shown live on lichess, starting at 1pm BST, she will also achieve her third and final international master norm and with it a historic title, breaking Judit Polgar’s female world age record from 38 years ago and joining the 10 youngest IMs of all time.

Shogdzhiev, like Sivanandan, was born in 2015, and is clearly being groomed as the heir apparent to Soviet legends Mikhail Botvinnik, Anatoly Karpov and Garry Kasparov.

For several years now his team of coaches led by the experienced GM Evgeny Tomashevsky have organised periodic blitz tournaments in Moscow where the youngster could hone his speed skills against strong rivals.

Shogdzhiev’s final record-breaking IM norm was organised at a so-called norm factory in Serbia, but he has since then registered two of the three required grandmaster norms in the Asian Championship in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, and more recently in the Serbian League. Now he requires just one more norm and a 2500 rating to capture Abhimanyu Mishra’s world age record as the youngest ever grandmaster. He could easily do it before his 12th birthday in February 2027.

Pride of place in this week’s column would otherwise go to IM Richard Pert, who scored a career-best result when he defeated GM Jorden van Foreest, rated 2716 and No 24 in the world, in the Cheddleton Savills Catering v SuperChess Romania round three match in the European Club Cup in Budva, Montenegro.

Pert, 45, an ECF national chess coach, is on a roll, with a 6/6 total before Friday’s final round. Richard’s twin brother, Nicholas, is a grandmaster of long standing, and his children Max and Nina both have Fide titles.

The Dutchman, who famously won Tata Steel Wijk aan Zee in 2021 and played No 2 in the SuperChess team behind Abdusattorov, opened with the experimental 2…h6 and 4…a6 but was still comfortably level at move 24 when his blunder 24…Rd6??, instead of 24…Rd5, instantly lost a piece to 25 a4. He resigned immediately, as 25…Nd4 allows 26 Bb4 skewering Black’s rooks. Pert scored another speedy win in round five of the European Club Cup.

Cheddleton Savills Catering have been a team revelation, after an opening round in Budva saw two of England’s other teams defeated 6-0. Seeded only 16th, Cheddleton have won five of their six matches by wide margins and now face the Israeli champions Rishon LeZion, whose top board is the former world title challenger Boris Gelfand, in Friday’s final round, with an outside chance for a medal.

The London Chess Classic returns next month, from 25 November to 4 December. Full details on how to enter, and details on who is already competing, are here.

The US Championship at Saint Louis went to a rapid and blitz playoff on Thursday night after Fabiano Caruana, the world No 3 and defending champion, caught up with the world No 6, Wesley So, in the final round. So won the playoff 1.5-0.5. He stood better in both games, but Caruana narrowly escaped defeat in the first.

So had led by a point before round 11 and faced the tailender Samuel Sevian, who had a favourable lifetime score against the former Filipino and said after winning the game: “He is really good in setting tricks in shorter time controls, but in classical I kind of figure out his little ideas.”

Final leading US Championships scores: Open So (playoff winner) and Caruana 7/11, Jeffery Xiong and Grigory Oparin 6.5, Andy Woodward 6, Mishra, Levon Aronian and Awonder Liang 5.5. Hans Niemann finished joint 10th out of 12 with 4/11.

Women Rachael Li 8.5/11, Alice Lee 8, Irina Krush 7.5. The holder, Carissa Yip, finished equal seventh with 4.5. Li, 16, is the youngest first-time champion although Krush, who debuted at 11, was 14 when she won the first of her eight US titles in 1998.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Netanyahu orders ‘very extensive’ operation in West Bank after two Israeli soldiers killed
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Lorenzo Tondo and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Israel’s prime minister gives order after military says it thwarted ‘terror attack’ by two armed Palestinians

Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered the army to prepare for a “very extensive” operation in the occupied West Bank after two Israeli soldiers and two Palestinians were killed in an exchange of fire near a checkpoint in Hebron.

Netanyahu said the military would go house to house and demolish homes in an operation on a scale unseen in the occupied West Bank for decades, after the Israeli military said it had thwarted a “terror attack” by two armed Palestinians on Friday, amid heightened tensions before next week’s election.

According to the Israel Defense Forces, the two assailants opened fire on soldiers at a temporary checkpoint outside Hebron after failing to reach a nearby highway, where the Israeli military believes they had intended to attack civilians. According to a preliminary military investigation, the ensuing gunfight lasted more than 20 minutes, leaving five Israelis wounded, two of whom later succumbed to their injuries.

An AFP photographer who was en route to another assignment and witnessed the gun battle saw two Palestinian men armed with a handgun and an automatic rifle exchanging fire with Israeli forces.

Netanyahu’s office later said it had instructed security forces to immediately cordon off Hebron and prepare for a full closure of the West Bank starting on Friday.

After the shooting, the Israeli prime minister held an emergency meeting of his security cabinet and officials from top military and security agencies. He said Hamas was “planning a major attack aimed at murdering innocent civilians”.

During a visit to Hebron after the attack, Netanyahu later said Israeli forces would enter the neighbourhood of the attackers and displace its residents. He said the military would apply a model previously used in refugee camps in the northern West Bank.

A large-scale military operation named the “Iron Wall” launched in January 2025, forcibly displaced tens of thousands of people across several refugee camps, according to the UN rights office.

“We will evacuate the residents, we will go from house to house, we will also seize the weapons there, and all the terrorist infrastructure will be dealt with and destroyed,” Netanyahu said, according to his office.

Closures of the West Bank are becoming more common. Friday’s lockdown was the fourth time in the past month that Israel had imposed restrictions across the territory, shutting gates and checkpoints connecting Palestinian villages to major roads, which will remain open to Israeli drivers, including settlers, who can still travel through the area.

Bezalel Smotrich, the far-right Israeli finance minister who also holds a position within the defence ministry, called for a military campaign in the West Bank “exactly like in Gaza”. He said: “There is no other option but a comprehensive military campaign to dismantle the Palestinian Authority, collect weapons and eliminate terrorists. Exactly like in Gaza and Lebanon.”

Smotrich added: “In the next government this will be one of the first measures that we must demand and apply.”

Human rights groups warned that Netanyahu and his government could use the attack on Israeli soldiers to justify tougher measures against Palestinians and bolster their security credentials before the election.

“Every day in the West Bank is a dramatic day for the Palestinians,” Yariv Oppenheimer, the former director of Peace Now told Al Jazeera. “The Israeli army is getting into the Palestinian cities, the settlers are attacking Palestinians, and the situation is impossible.

“There will be house demolitions. We will see [a] curfew. We will see more soldiers … making arrests, and definitely we might see the settlers trying to target Palestinians in revenge for this attack, and trying to take advantage of this situation in order to escalate the situation even more.”

Voters go to the polls on Tuesday in an election that will help to determine whether Netanyahu secures another term as prime minister. The vote comes three years after the Hamas-led attacks on Israel that triggered the war in Gaza.

Israeli settlers are increasingly taking over Palestinian properties, and authorities have stepped up demolitions of homes lacking building permits, displacing families.

The campaign has intensified since the war in Gaza started in October 2023 amid accelerating land seizures and settlement expansion across the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers, whose violence has surged during the annual olive harvest.

On 16 October settlers attacked Palestinian villages, burning cars and trees and injuring a Washington Post photographer. The next day they attacked European diplomats, a French mayor and Palestinian olive pickers, injuring three people and damaging a diplomatic vehicle.

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.title: Ryu Murakami, cult Japanese author, dies aged 74
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.author: Ella Creamer
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.text:
The bestselling writer, known as Japan’s enfant terrible, explored the dark underbelly of Japanese society in more than 40 works of subversive fiction including Audition, later made into a landmark indie horror movie

Ryu Murakami, the cult Japanese author and film-maker whose subversive, blackly comic novels found millions of readers, has died aged 74. He died on 17 October at home, according to his Japanese publisher Gentosha.

Described as the enfant terrible of contemporary Japanese literature, Murakami incorporated violence, explicit drug use and sex into stories that offered a sharp-eyed critique of Japanese and American culture.

“It has been a huge privilege to bring many of Ryu Murakami’s strange, original and cinematic novels to an English-speaking audience,” said Adam Freudenheim, publisher and managing director at Pushkin Press, which, along with Bloomsbury, publishes Murakami’s works in translation in the UK.

Murakami was the son of two teachers, born in Sasebo, Nagasaki prefecture, in 1952. During high school, he joined a rock band as a drummer, and after participating in a rooftop protest was placed under a three-month house arrest. He published his first novel, Almost Transparent Blue, in 1976. The book, written while he was still a student, is narrated by a character called Ryū, and depicts the hedonistic lifestyle of a group of disillusioned, nihilistic young people. It won the Gunzo prize for new writers along with the Akutagawa prize, Japan’s most prestigious literary award.

Murakami was not related to his better-known namesake, Haruki. Ryu Murakami’s books are “edgier and angrier” wrote the journalist David Pilling in 2013. “If Haruki is the Beatles of Japanese literature, Ryu is its Rolling Stones”.

Murakami went on to write more than 40 novels and short story collections, including Coin Locker Babies, In the Miso Soup, Audition, Piercing and Popular Hits of the Showa Era. Most of his books have not yet been translated into English.

Many of his works have been adapted for screen, either by himself or other film-makers. The best-known is Audition, a 1999 feature film directed by Takashi Miike. The story follows a widower holding fake movie auditions in order to find a new girlfriend. Writing about the novel in the Guardian in 2009, Irvine Welsh described its prose as “elegiac and affecting, but it has the sharp, visceral feel of the butcher’s knife or surgeon’s scalpel”.

Murakami’s third novel, Coin Locker Babies, about children abandoned in storage lockers, won the Noma literary new face prize. The novel is “a surreal coming-of-age horror story that runs wildly through the heights of love and superstardom, and the lows of insanity and murder”, wrote Russell Thomas in the Guardian in 2020, selecting the novel as one of the best books set in Japan. “Murakami’s stories never shy away from shining a light on the darkest corners of society,” he added.

“All at Pushkin Press are saddened to hear of his death and extend our sympathies to his many readers around the world,” said Freudenheim.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.title: Being pro-Trump has been ‘easy radio’ for conservative hosts like Jesse Kelly. Those days are ending.
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.author: Jeremy Barr in Webster, Texas
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
Conservative media personalities who have long benefited from boosting the president will be forced to wrestle with the likely fallout of Republican losses in next month’s US midterm elections

Nothing lasts forever. Jesse Kelly knows his meteoric rise through conservative radio will end one day – just like Donald Trump’s power over the Republican party.

Every day, the 6ft 8in Kelly walks a tightrope between sycophancy and criticism of the US president: the same fine line many rightwing hosts have attempted to tread throughout Trump’s rise, fall, and then resurrection from the political graveyard after his 2020 presidential election defeat.

What Kelly, 45, does next will be telling. Conservative media hosts have achieved untold fame and fortune riding the Trump train. Yet as Trump enters the final two years of his presidency, these hosts must prepare for life after the train pulls into the station. More imminently, they will wrestle with the likely fallout of Republican losses in next month’s US midterm elections – and the question of how much blame to put on an unpopular president.

With a daily show syndicated by radio powerhouse Premiere Networks across more than 200 stations across the country, between 6pm and 9pm, Kelly is one of the most influential players in the medium. His broadcast follows a three-hour block by Fox News host Sean Hannity, long an eminence grise in conservative media.

“When he was the bee’s knees there for a while on the right, honestly, it was easy radio, easy podcasting, easy TV to just sit down and just powder Trump’s butt all day long,” Kelly said over lunch recently at a suburban Red Lobster in Webster, Texas, approximately 20 miles south-east of downtown Houston. “That’s what the audience wanted to hear.

“For a while, that was the case. But like any other politician, same for all of them, you don’t stay hot forever. It’s not possible. No matter what, we’re nearing the end of the Trump era because his last term’s almost over and people are going to start looking around for the next guy.”

In recent months, Kelly has gained even more attention for his willingness to criticize Trump for starting a war with Iran just months before an election he reckons will be “rough” for Republicans. “I think if you told Donald Trump that he’d still be stuck over there with $4-a-gallon gas a month before the election, I think he probably would’ve made a different call,” he said.

But these days, any criticism of Trump from a conservative media figure leads to questions like the one he got from a Twitter user named @Swanso45003Kyle recently: “Are you anti Trump now?”

Kelly is not anti-Trump. But he is prepared to upset those who are slavishly devoted to praising the president and ignoring his missteps.

“When Trump does something I don’t like, I’ll say it. And I’ll say it when he does stuff I like,” he said. Make no mistake: Kelly still spends most of his time bashing “commie” Democrats, referring to them on a recent show as “sick, evil and demonic”.

While Kelly said “a lot of people” in conservative media care about securing an invite to the White House, he claims to be uninterested in such an offer. Unless he approaches his daily show with candor and honesty, he worries listeners will think he’s a phony and turn the dial.

“I think a huge percentage of Trump’s supporters have always understood that Trump has flaws like any other human being has flaws,” said Kelly. There is “a tiny percentage who worship everything he says and does”, he added. “Those are just generally ridiculous and stupid human beings. But the large percentage of Trump supporters are not sheep.”

Michael Harrison, the founder of the talk radio-focused publication Talkers magazine, said the art of “positioning” is an extremely important skill in the industry – and one that conservative hosts will need to lean on when pondering a post-Trump political world. “Anybody who is in radio and who plans to be in radio for a very long time has got to – or eventually learns – that the carpet is going to be pulled out from you eventually, with switching circumstances and public opinion,” he said in an interview.

Talkshow hosts on the right are “all competing with each other”, added Harrison. “It’s a game of musical chairs, and right now that’s what the conservative element of news talk radio is facing. All of a sudden the game is changing, and it’s changing very rapidly, and they’ve got to figure out what their position is.

“And it’s got to be somewhere between their own deeply held beliefs or what the audience wants. It ultimately comes down to business. It ultimately comes down to what will get ratings, what will get clicks, what will get views and what will get advertising.”

Kelly was an unlikely candidate to host a nationally syndicated radio show. Born in Ohio, he went to high school – and a little bit of college – in Montana before joining the marines in 2000, serving in Iraq before being honorably discharged in 2004.

He lived in Arizona for a time and worked for a family-owned construction company. Then, fully embracing the Tea Party movement, he ran for Congress in Arizona in 2010 and nearly ousted incumbent Democratic representative Gabrielle Giffords.

“I just got out of the Marine Corps and got mad and decided to run for Congress,” he recalled. He tried again in a special election two years later, but lost again to a Democrat – something he says he is now thankful for. “It would suck to be in Congress.”

Not giving up on politics, he moved to Washington DC and worked in development for the conservative advocacy group Citizens United, but hated living there and left the job after a year. He says he then drove around the country looking for work, getting close to running out of money before eventually finding a job through Craigslist selling RVs in Texas.

After one of his tweets went viral, Kelly did a guest appearance on Houston-based conservative radio host Michael Berry’s show, and it was Berry who called him up – while he was in a Taco Bell drive-through – to introduce himself before ultimately suggesting he pursue radio as a career.

In 2018, he began hosting a one-hour, late-at-night show on KPRC 950 AM: an entry-level “prove it” gig in the radio business. Only three years later, in 2021, he got “the phone call everybody who does what I do wants” from Premiere Networks president Julie Talbott offering him a job.

“I don’t think it’s supposed to work out that way,” Kelly said of his quick rise in an interview.

Talbott suggested in a statement that Kelly’s non-traditional background “gives him a fresh perspective and an unfiltered style that stands out in today’s media landscape.” She added: “Over the past five years, we’ve had the opportunity to watch his audience and influence grow significantly, and that success is rooted in the trust he’s earned with listeners.”

For several years, he also hosted a nightly streaming show for rightwing online platform the First, though that arrangement recently ended. Kelly said he wants to focus fully on radio moving forward.

On a recent Monday afternoon, Kelly settled into his desk chair and prepared for his show. On the front of his large desk, he placed his car keys and his gun. “Unless I’ve gone through a metal detector, I have a weapon on me,” he said.

While Kelly has been encouraged to use a “show sheet”, listing segments and topics for the day, he feels better off the cuff, detecting a certain stiffness in his presentation when working from prepared lines. The same was true when campaign consultants told him to script speeches during his two runs for Congress. “I just would rather do it off the top of my head.”

Kelly doesn’t take the current success of his radio show for granted. “I’ll probably never fully understand why people love it the way they love it,” he said. But while he believes “the safest thing you can possibly do is everything Maga, all the time”, at least for the past decade, he has made the calculation that his market value depends on ideological consistency without predictability, as well as a heavy dose of personality and banter.

“In a lot of ways, in a lot of different places in life, you completely eliminate your voice as having any importance if you’re a given on anything,” he said. “You just get dismissed. You’re banked already.”

He hopes his audience – at least those who have not dropped him in favor of a more reliably pro-Trump host, or because they dislike one of his food opinions – will keep listening, even when they disagree. “Look, you’re never going to get 100% of a rightwing media audience,” said Kelly. “That’s not possible. But if there are 40%, and you can grab them and keep them, then you can have a long career that way.”

During a late September radio segment comparing Trump to a once-elite baseball player who has lost his home run power, Kelly acknowledged that his day, too, will come – possibly sooner rather than later.

“There will come when I don’t deliver for you when you tune in,” he told his listeners. “And that sucks. And when you think about that, especially when you’re doing OK – right now, the show is growing, doing great – when you think about that, you think, ‘No, it’s going to last forever!’ No, it won’t.”

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Experts cast doubt on Anthropic report detailing how AI has altered work at the company
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Ramin Skibba
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Anthropic claims AI will shift how work gets done and labor demand – but some experts are skeptical of the vision

Last year, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned that artificial intelligence could eliminate half of entry-level white-collar jobs and that in six months it would be writing 90% of code. Neither of those predictions came to pass.

Now, in a report Anthropic published on Thursday, the company said it was hiring fewer junior technical workers and that human attention has become the new “bottleneck” as it increasingly relies on its Claude AI agents.

Anthropic says AI has changed the way work gets done, and as a result, restructured employment at the company. The report suggests its changes foreshadow the future of work more broadly: as more companies adopt AI agents, software engineers could face a tougher job market while entry-level tech workers struggle to build necessary skills and experience.

“As AI diffuses and improves, the organization of work could shift,” Anthropic’s report reads before offering a potential future. “One possibility is single-person startups, each with a human founder steering swarms of agents to rake in billions in revenue.”

In its report, Anthropic touts its “deep adoption of AI”, which it claims resulted in “producing more code per person, closing more sales per rep, and processing more contracts”. By outsourcing some coding and sales-related tasks to AI agents, Anthropic said it raised productivity within a few months.

From May 2026 onwards, AI agents logged more work hours than human employees, the report said. Employees now spend about 22% of their time managing Claude agents, more than double the amount a year ago, based on Anthropic’s analysis of their chat summaries.

It also says since March 2025 – soon after the release of its agentic AI coding tool Claude Code – entry-level technical hires dropped from nearly 30% to 9%, and headcount dropped from about 21% to 14%. It attributes the shifts to AI usage, and described its workers as merely “a thin layer atop a growing contingent of AI agents”.

While the report provides a small glimpse of the inner workings of the AI heavyweight, some AI researchers are skeptical that it will herald big changes across companies or industries. Instead, they say the findings are likely Anthropic’s attempt to drive its valuation ahead of its initial public offering – similar to how SpaceX boasted about proposed space data centers to boost its market debut in June.

Anthropic’s claims seem to back some tech executives’ view that AI is behind recent waves of corporate layoffs, but research complicates that.

Morgan Frank, a Case Western Reserve University researcher on how AI and technological changes affect workers, recently posted a paper that’s in peer review showing that AI-exposed job markets deteriorated well before the arrival of ChatGPT in November 2022 and Claude a few months later. State unemployment claims reveal that job markets tanked starting at the beginning of 2022, months before ChatGPT’s release, according to the paper.

“It doesn’t appear that the launch of ChatGPT corresponds to any major increase in loss or worsening outcomes,” he said.

Frank said several factors could explain recent job losses, including cutting pandemic-era hires and “AI-washing”, where some bosses credit AI for layoffs they might have made anyway.

Julián Posada, a Yale social scientist, also questions Anthropic’s motives for publishing its report.

“It is written from the perspective of a company that wants to sell shares, a company that really wants people to invest in it,” said Posada, author of the book Platform Extractivism: Data Work and the People Powering Artificial Intelligence.

Unlike an economics study, the report lacked an independent assessment by outside auditors, Posada said. Its figures and graphs only tell part of the story, without revealing how Anthropic’s workers feel about their work or how they’re actually engaging with the models, he said.

Dylan Baker, lead research engineer at the non-profit Distributed AI Research Institute, said he was also curious about how Anthropic’s developers feel about the changes. Shifting some software development to AI, while hiring few entry-level workers and having the remaining engineers wrangle AI agents seems “shortsighted”, Baker said.

“That’s such a strange way to put it,” Baker said. “It fundamentally misunderstands how software is written, architected and designed. It’s such a social, interpersonal and human process.”

Anthropic’s report quotes an unnamed engineer, who described facing “an army of Claudes, with every one asking for my attention”. That doesn’t sound like a fruitful work environment, Baker said. “I wouldn’t think really thoughtful, well-designed products are coming out of that team.”

As generative AI products proliferate, a majority of Americans are wary of AI, with particular concerns about AI-related job losses, according to Pew Research Center. In its report, Anthropic suggests that tech employers should offer their workers stock ownership, posing this as a potential solution to rising concerns. “It is difficult to imagine a version of pro-worker AI adoption in which workers do not hold a financial stake in successful rollout,” it said.

Anthropic, which could debut on the stock market as soon as November, released its employment report one day after pledging to commit 5% of its shares to the “public good”, though it didn’t provide details. Critics noted that philanthropy has long doubled as a reputation builder used by tech titans like Bill Gates and Mark Zuckerberg.

But Anthropic, and its claims it’s improving how work gets done, could face tougher scrutiny as it nears its IPO. A draft of the company’s S-1 filing revealed that Anthropic had a $80bn net loss over the first half of this year, and that it received a junk credit rating in June. Considering Anthropic’s slowing revenue growth, investors now project a valuation of $1.5tn, down from earlier estimates of $2tn or more. At the same time, Anthropic’s cloud computing partner, CoreWeave, has become swamped in AI debt and its stock is plummeting, fueling concerns that the AI bubble may begin to deflate.

Regardless of when or whether the bubble pops, software engineers and other tech workers will surely be affected, Baker said. The question is how that will play out.

“My hope is that there is a reckoning, a reassessment or re-evaluation of how much this has always been about human work,” Baker said.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Crowded nest? How parents and their adult kids can live together in peace
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Rebecca Cope
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
With record numbers of adult children living at home with their parents, how can this arrangement work for everyone? Set ground rules from the off, respect each other’s privacy, and don’t revert to type, say the experts

Whether they are fresh out of university and looking for a job, have recently been made redundant, are saving to buy a home or newly divorced, it’s becoming increasingly common for adult children to live at home with their parents. According to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), 35% of men and 22% of women aged between 20 and 34 were living with their parents in 2025.

I speak from experience: my younger sister lived at home with my mother for two years while she did her PhD, and I moved home for almost three years after becoming a single mother postpartum. In both of our situations, it would have been good to have some practical advice to make it work, with tensions sometimes running high and arguments inevitable.

If parents and their adult children are going to coexist successfully, honest communication is essential from the outset. How long do children expect to stay? Will they contribute financially? Will they do any housework? Are guests allowed? Difficulties will arise if you aren’t clear about these boundaries from the off.

“You won’t be able to anticipate every point of tension in advance, but you might want to discuss typical frictions like noise and overnight guests,” says Anita Cleare, a parenting expert and author of How to Get Your Teenager Out of Their Bedroom. “Parents should aim for a balance between making adult children feel welcome and maintaining their own mental and financial wellbeing.”

Parenting expert Sue Atkins, whose grownup children have both lived with her for periods, recommends writing down everything you want to say first, so that you can stay focused – and, crucially, to pick your moment. “It’s all about your tone of voice and your attitude,” she says. “If you do it when you’re angry or frustrated, that’s the wrong time. I always say: ‘Strike when the iron is cold.’”

Both parents and adult children can fall into the trap of reverting to childhood dynamics. Parents find children annoying and untidy, and feel free to comment on their lifestyles (“You’re not going out in that?” “What time will you be back?” “That’s a waste of money,” etc), while children regress into teenagers, expecting Mum and Dad to do the laundry, housework and cooking.

“The biggest trap adult children fall into when returning to live with parents is to demand the rights of adulthood while still expecting to enjoy the privileges of a child,” says Cleare. “For example, expecting their parents to provide household comforts while insisting on sticking to their own separate daily schedule. Vice versa: now that your child is an adult, you don’t have the right to know where they are at all times, what they are doing or what they are thinking. Voicing your opinion on how they should be going about life differently will send you right back into parent-teenager dynamics.”

Instead, conceive of it as more of a housemate situation. “It can help to think of your adult child as a friend who is staying with you, rather than as your child,” says Cleare. “Parent-child dynamics have a power imbalance – parents tell children what to do (and children assert their power by not cooperating). Friendships tend to be more equal. Aim for discussion and collaboration rather than rigid rule-setting. Set your parameters, but then treat your adult child as a problem-solver by inviting their views and ideas.” For the adult child, they can also consider what being a good housemate means: chiefly, pulling their weight by doing chores without being asked.

If an adult child is moving back home after living away for some time – perhaps even in their own home – then they will have accumulated a lot of “stuff”.

Kate Edmondson, the founder of Home Edited, a professional organisation service, recommends first agreeing on where belongings will be stored and how much space is realistically available. “Ask them to go through their belongings and make decisions about what is genuinely worth storing,” she says. “Make sure they know what they have and where it is. Clearly labelled, categorised boxes make belongings much easier for them to access without having to pull apart an entire storage area. If you’re storing a larger volume, encourage them to keep their own simple inventory on their phone.”

While you might not agree on politics, what to watch on TV, or other hot topics, see this as an opportunity to spend quality time together.

“Build some new family traditions,” suggests Cleare. “Families are glued together by spending time together – whether that’s eating or cooking, watching TV or sport, or shopping. So try to find new ways to spend time doing things you all enjoy.”

There’s no reason you can’t view the experience as a positive one. “I think you have to see living together as a springboard, not a destination,” advises Atkins. “When you come through the other side, you may realise you gained a lot from it and are closer.”

Whether you are already in a relationship, or looking to date, there’s no denying that living with your parents puts a dampener on romance. Elinor Harvey, a psychotherapist at The Relationship Therapy Practice, says communication and boundaries are key.

“A family might agree that Friday night is the adult child’s night to go out and date, and that they can bring someone home afterwards,” she says. “Another family might be more flexible, but simply want advance notice if someone is coming back. There doesn’t have to be one set of ground rules that works for everyone. What matters is agreeing to the rules early and making sure everyone understands them.” It’s also important to remember that if the adult child’s parents are in a couple – whether with each other or a new partner – then they will want time alone for their relationship too.

If parents don’t want their child to bring anybody back, and that’s a deal-breaker for the adult child, the arrangement is simply not going to work.

If there’s one thing that adult children and parents are likely to fall out over, it’s privacy. After all, many have been living away from home – whether at university halls, in shared housing, or with an ex-partner – and won’t appreciate parents walking into their room without knocking. The same goes for asking about their whereabouts or who they are seeing – though it is always considerate for adult children to check in and offer a little reassurance, rather than turning up half-cut at 3am after a night out and waking everyone up.

“They’re adults now,” says Atkins. “You don’t just walk into their bedroom because they’re your children. You have to respect their personal space and remember that they may have been independent for years.”

As tempting as it is to try to swoop in and save adult children living at home in less than ideal circumstances, Cleare advises against playing the hero. “When adults move back home, it is often because something isn’t going right in their lives,” she says. “They might have lost their job or relationship, or be struggling to cope in some way. The temptation is for parents to see these issues as something their adult child needs our advice on and to overstep the mark.”

Instead, parents can try to boost their child’s confidence by taking an interest without meddling. “Be mindful not to rescue them – empower them,” says Atkins. “If it’s budgeting and money, you might say: ‘Can I give you a hand? This is how we do it.’ You’re helping them develop the skills to move forward rather than taking over. Don’t judge them or patronise them. Ask open-ended questions: ‘What can we do to support you?’ And use ‘I’ statements. Say: ‘I’m feeling … ’ rather than: ‘You always … ’”

When an adult child moves back in with a parent, it can cause undue pressure on household budgets, particularly for single parents. And as more than 38% of people who married in England and Wales in 1995 had divorced by 2015, according to the ONS, this is clearly an issue for many families.

Beverley Sayers, a mediator who works with the Family Mediation Council, has encountered parents who are struggling to support an adult child after a separation or divorce. “There’s an unrealistic idea that you don’t have to continue paying for children once they reach 18,” she says. “I often advise the young person to have a conversation with the parent they don’t live with and ask: ‘Can I have some funds to help with this situation so I can contribute to the household?’”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: France to deploy 70,000 police across country on Saturday to prevent unrest
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Jon Henley in Paris
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Move follows some of the worst street violence in years on the fringes of cost-of-living protests last weekend

France will deploy about 70,000 police around the country on Saturday as the government seeks to prevent more civil unrest after some of the worst street violence in years erupted on the fringes of cost-of-living protests last weekend.

The interior minister, Laurent Nunez, said on ⁠Friday ⁠the security forces would include elite units usually used for counter-terrorism operations and hostage rescues, adding that there had been social media calls for violence from “ultra-left” groups.

“We are not talking about ⁠a peaceful, friendly demonstration,” Nunez ​told reporters after a meeting of senior ministers and officials chaired by the president, Emmanuel Macron. “We ​are ​ready tomorrow ​to be ‌extremely firm ​and ​not tolerate anything.”

Macron and his government are struggling to get on top of a crisis that has caught it off guard six months before presidential elections to choose his successor. The government has admitted it “lost control” over widespread rioting on Saturday.

Largely peaceful demonstrations were hijacked by groups of determined rioters, degenerating into rampant violence and extensive looting in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and other cities. In Limoges, the town hall was set on fire and partly destroyed.

“We will be uncompromising with rioters, looters and all who commit violence,” Nunez said, adding that besides 10,000 more police, the operation would include water cannon, armoured vehicles, mounted police, helicopters and drones.

Demonstrations are expected in several other countries this weekend, triggered by a broader, continent-wide wave of discontent over declining public services, housing affordability, public sector budget cuts and the spiralling cost of living.

Protests over related grievances have been called for Saturday in Milan, Rome and Turin in Italy; in Vienna, Austria; and in Madrid, Barcelona and other cities in Spain, as well as in Lisbon and Porto in Portugal, Dublin in Ireland and Tirana in Albania.

Protests are expected across France on Saturday, although several cities have banned demonstrations or forced them to change their planned routes to protect shops and public buildings, and forecast heavy rain and high winds could dampen turnout.

The centres of Lyon and some other large cities will be off-limits to protesters, while authorities in Paris authorised a union march along a limited route in the east of the capital, between the Places de la Bastille and Nation, that will avoid the city centre.

But requests for rallies in Paris organised by France’s main student union, UNEF, and the gilets jaunes movement, whose nationwide protests rocked France in 2018 and which plans 600 small-scale events around France on Saturday, were refused.

UNEF said its rallies, which grew from high school protests last month against teacher shortages and dilapidated facilities, would go ahead regardless. Several of Paris’ best-known cultural institutions, including the Louvre, said they would close on Saturday.

Authorities in Marseille had also banned all protests, but announced on Friday that a union-organised demonstration would be allowed on an “exceptional basis”. It will be the only authorised protest in the southern Bouches-du-Rhone department.

Unionists and opposition leaders have criticised the government for refusing to allow more rallies on Saturday, a decision being challenged in court in several cities. Marylise Léon of the CFDT union federation accused Macron of an abuse of authority.

“It’s ​counterproductive because there is a lot ​of anger and a demand to be considered and to be listened to,” Léon, the CFDT’s general secretary, told TF1 TV. “It’s not for the president to decide who can legitimately protest.”

The radical left La France Insoumise party of Jean-Luc Mélenchon said the government had “crossed the lines that separate a democracy from an authoritarian and police state”, adding that the bans would only “generate more chaos”.

Adding to the tensions, the far-right leader Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner for next spring’s presidential elections, is due to host her National Rally (RN) party congress in Orléans, drawing thousands of supporters – and left-wing, anti-racist opponents.

Nunez was due to visit the city on Friday to “inspect the security arrangements” at the request of the prime minister’s office. The interior minister, Gérald Darmanin, said 217 people – half of them first-time offenders – had been jailed since Saturday.

On Thursday, Macron called for “the utmost severity” against “acts of delinquency”, saying gangs of rioters had been mainly responsible for the looting but the worst violence was caused by “ultra-left” groups seeking to “bring down the republic”.

Further stoking disquet, one person was killed and four others injured – including a 12-year-old girl – in ⁠a shooting in the town of Trappes, west of Paris, on Friday in an attack that police said could have been racially motivated.

https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.title: We asked real people what they’re wearing this fall – burgundy, secretly comfy pants and fierce boots
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.author: Lauren Gould
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.text:
I chased down people on weekdays, interrupting their brisk walks and lunch breaks to ask them to share details of their fall outfits

It’s October and New Yorkers have finally retired the breezy pants and linen button-downs required to brave stuffy subway stations. Like much of the US, we’re now tasked with expertly layering for autumn’s up-and-down weather while still looking put together for the workday.

You might also be staring down your closet’s sea of denim and bulky coats, wondering what to wear. Instead of consulting the runways or analyzing the latest fashion trends, I wandered through Manhattan’s financial district, which boasts millions of square feet in office space, to ask people about their outfits.

I chased down people on weekdays, interrupting their brisk walks and, most likely, their lunch breaks. Below, New Yorkers (and two visitors) share the details of their fall outfits. We couldn’t find exact matches for many of the items, so we linked to similar options, usually from the brands that they recommended.

“A good leather jacket is regrettably worth it.” Ruth Baron, Guardian senior newsletter editor

“Technically in-office days require business formal but on days when I know I won’t see another soul in the office, I feel I can get away with a comfy sweater and dark jeans that could possible pass for slacks. Working in New York City requires comfy shoes en route, so I opted for my chunky Uggs.” Bridget, political communications (and friend)

“I love pants that are presentable yet feel like pajama bottoms (no one’s the wiser).” Karen Yuan, Filter commissioning editor

“I jokingly say I dress like an angsty teen.” Michelle, writer and publicist

“Grown-up goth teen goes to the office (and maybe the tailor).” Jessica Machado, Guardian movement building and power editor

“I’m going for dark red, maroon, cherry (this fall).” Isabelle, Data Scientist

“This fall, I’m leaning into basic silhouettes with pops of color.” Lauren Gould, Filter editorial coordinator

“I like to feel free and flowing, but I don’t like to look like I’m wearing a trash bag.” Lisa, UX researcher

https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.title: Seth Meyers on Trump’s fixation on men’s bodies: ‘Why are you so weird?’
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.author: Guardian staff
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.text:
The late-night host discussed Trump’s ramblings at rallies and expressed disdain for a controversial Republican ad

Seth Meyers shared his horror at a much-criticised Republican campaign ad while also trying to understand why Donald Trump has become so fixated on men’s bodies of late.

The Late Night host said there had been “widespread bipartisan” outrage at a “despicable” new ad that has been causing controversy this week.

He started with footage of Trump at a rally, claiming the Democrats will undo all of the great work he has done if they were to triumph at next month’s midterms.

“All you’ve done is undo things!” Meyers responded, adding that “we had nice things” before Trump came in and ruined them.

Trump also claimed the midterms would be on 31 October before “a thing called November”, which Meyers said sounded like a book one would read to impress someone at a bar.

He also joked that if you said that after being pulled over by a cop, “they wouldn’t even give you a Breathalyser”.

Trump has been campaigning in deep red states but has been “unravelling” onstage, rambling again about not winning the Nobel peace prize while forgetting its name and calling it the Pulitzer.

“What other awards does this guy think he deserves?” Meyers asked before joking that he would expect a Tony as “I know so many Tonys.”

But on Wednesday he was “misfiring a lot” and made a bizarre sound that was “less like a president and more like a bullfrog”.

Trump has also seemingly developed “a bizarre fixation on men’s physiques” with Meyers playing a strange montage of the president describing men’s bodies. “The only issue he has left to campaign on is me likey what I see,” Meyers added.

Meyers said that Trump “sounds like a blindfolded bachelorette at a strip club” but he has “always valued surface over substance … he just knows marketing”.

There have been repeated references to men’s asses which Meyers shared with viewers before asking of Trump: “Why are you so weird?”

Meyers added: “No one cares if you can bounce a quarter off Jon Husted’s ass because thanks to inflation that quarter is worthless.”

Meyers joked that Trump sounds like “Samantha when she’s dating a new male model”, he said referencing the Sex and the City character. Yet with Texas candidate Ken Paxton, Trump has been “far less glowing”.

The Republicans are getting “desperate” and nowhere is that more obvious than in Ohio with candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, the “annoying tech billionaire that even Republicans hated when he ran in 2024”.

In his campaign for Ohio governor, he has been running “one of the slimiest and most disgusting ads in the history of politics” which uses the estranged mother of his opponent to claim she was lying about being sexually assaulted as a child.

“Have you ever seen a more insufferable prick in your life?” Meyers asked before saying the ad is “so clearly over the line” that even Republicans have been speaking out.

But instead, JD Vance has been attacking any Republicans who have called the ad out. “Is there no soul behind all that eyeliner?” Meyers asked.

Meyers added that the vice-president “revels in being an asshole but being an asshole has a cost”.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Mamdani loves Arsenal. He should challenge them to cut ties with the UAE over Sudan | Sasha Lezhnev and John Prendergast
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Sasha Lezhnev and John Prendergast
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
The New York mayor’s passion for the Gunners and human rights presents an opportunity to push back on the club’s lucrative UAE sponsorship

Like him or not, there is no doubt that New York mayor Zohran Mamdani’s passion for certain issues is electric, and that passion played a large part in him getting elected. But today, two of his biggest passions are on a collision course.

On one hand, Mamdani is now arguably the US’s most high-profile supporter of English Premier League champions Arsenal. A superfan since he was a child, he has put the Gunners into the American spotlight more than anyone since becoming mayor. The Empire State Building gleamed in Arsenal’s red and white when they won the Premier League title. He wrote an essay about what Arsenal’s championship means to him, talks about Arsenal at press conferences and interviews and inaugurated Thierry Henry Way near Times Square in honor of the Arsenal legend.

But another of Mamdani’s passions – standing up against genocide and for human rights – is now presenting a problem for the mayor’s Arsenal fandom. One prominent part of Arsenal’s current image is deeply disturbing, and it presents a major opportunity for Mamdani.

Arsenal’s chief sponsor is Emirates Airlines, owned by the Emirates Group, a state-owned Dubai-based holding company. Emirates is on the front of every jersey, and the team plays at Emirates Stadium in London. The United Arab Emirates has spent more than $1bn sponsoring the team, including expanding its contract through 2033 to more than $100m per season. Arsenal is the UAE’s second biggest sports investment globally.

The trouble is the UAE is also sponsoring a genocidal militia in Sudan, where war has created the world’s largest displacement crisis, with 14 million people, or a quarter of the country’s population, forced to flee their homes, and 21 million people facing acute hunger. The UAE has provided the militia, known as the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), with weapons and killer drones, according to numerous investigations. In fact, the UAE is the RSF’s biggest supplier of weapons and drones.

And therein lies the rub. The UAE is engaging in one of the world’s largest sportswashing campaigns in an attempt to clean up its image, including with Mamdani’s beloved Arsenal. The UAE’s sportswashing isn’t limited to the Gunners. We calculated that the UAE government has spent more than $5.2bn on sponsoring sports teams and leagues around the world, including Manchester City, the NBA champion New York Knicks (a team Mamdani also cheers for), the Emirates NBA Cup and Formula One. There are multiple other football, basketball, cycling, rugby, cricket and UAE-sponsored teams as well.

The good news is that Arsenal’s ownership isn’t blind to abusive sportswashing relationships. Last year, the club announced it was cutting its sleeve sponsor, Visit Rwanda, after the country’s invasion of the Democratic Republic of Congo and the humanitarian catastrophe that ensued as a result. More than 8 million people have been displaced from their homes, as Rwanda has invaded the DRC and commanded the deadly M23 militia that has tortured victims, engaged in extensive sexual violence and enlisted child soldiers. The Arsenal Supporters’ Trust weighed in on the issue, following campaign initiatives such as Gunners for Peace, and the owners changed course.

Now it’s time for Arsenal to tackle their bigger sportswashing sponsor, and Mamdani can play a key role. As one of the world’s most visible Arsenal fans, his voice would have an important impact on the club’s decision makers. The club’s owners are American, Josh and Stan Kroenke, and they have stood up in the past for human rights – for instance, calling for a lifetime ban on former Los Angeles Clippers owner Don Sterling for making racist remarks.

Mamdani could make the Kroenkes and the rest of the Arsenal board aware of the UAE’s sportswashing and call on them either publicly or privately to move on to another sponsor because of the genocidal militia the UAE is sponsoring in Sudan. The club is, after all, awash in cash after winning the league and reaching the final of the Champions League, earning $411m in total, a record for Arsenal. It is now reportedly the most profitable football club in England. So they don’t need the Emirati money.

Importantly, the UAE is not the only game in town for football sponsors – there are viable alternatives. Snapdragon, a Qualcomm tech company, pays approximately the same amount for sponsoring Manchester United as the Emirates pays Arsenal, and automaker Jeep and telecom company T-Mobile pay Juventus and Bayern Munich just a hair under.

Arsenal canceling the deal would also have a meaningful impact on the UAE and on the genocide unfolding in Sudan. The UAE is very sensitive to public image, and a cancelled Arsenal deal would be a major public relations blow. Mamdani’s intervention could have major human rights implications.

Mamdani is passionate about human rights, combating genocide and supporting his favorite team. Urging the club’s leadership to change its sponsor from the UAE would combine all three passions into one and potentially have a positive impact on the world’s deadliest humanitarian crisis. New Yorkers and Arsenal fans alike should encourage Mamdani to weigh in with the club on this important issue.

Sasha Lezhnev is Senior Policy Advisor at The Sentry, where John Prendergast is Co-Founder.

The small town in southern Ukraine has been the centre of an increasingly desperate humanitarian crisis under Russian occupation.

A data leak from Germany’s far-right German Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has revealed the extent of efforts by the party to court Donald Trump and other leading figures in the Maga movement, stretching back more than a decade.

The trove reveals the pains the AfD took in wooing the president, whom they saw from the beginning as a potential ally, with senior party officials agonising over the wording of an obsequious congratulatory telegram when he was elected in 2016, which included the wish that his “hopes as a person be fulfilled”.

The AfD became a home for anti-immigration voters after 1.2 million refugees arrived in Germany in 2015 and 2016. It entered the Bundestag, Germany’s parliament, in 2017 with 12.6% of the vote, came second in the February 2025 federal election with 20.8%, and now leads national polls at about 30%. In September it won 43.8% of the vote in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, and it is now trying to form Germany’s first far-right state government since the second world war.

Trump hailed the win in Saxony-Anhalt in a post on his Truth Social, concluding his message with a German version of his Make America Great Again acronym, “MGGA!!!”

Germany’s domestic intelligence agency monitors the party as a suspected rightwing extremist organisation, and state agencies classify five of its regional branches as confirmed extremist.

The leaked documents show AfD officials quickly moving to requests for support from the White House on policy issues when he first won the 2016 election.

Others show a burgeoning political courtship between senior figures including the AfD’s now leader Alice Weidel and key Trump ideologue Steve Bannon.

The data, provided to reporters by the transparency organisation Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets), covers more than 420,000 emails, along with documents and personnel records, from the party’s foundation in 2013 to the present, with most coming before 2019.

https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.title: The Narco Hack review – an epic tale of how detectives’ tech wizardry smashed a billion-euro drugs ring
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.author: Phil Harrison
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.text:
Human heroism is celebrated in profoundly personal ways in this extraordinary tale of a mind-boggling investigation into massive criminal organisations. It’s part The Wire, part The Imitation Game

We begin with the audio of a horrifying call made to the French police in 2020. Two men are driving home when their car is attacked. The police ask for the caller’s name as bullets ricochet around the vehicle. “Who cares what we’re called?” the man shouts. “I’m going to die!” Seconds later, his companion is dead. This killing (of a mechanic called Houcine Hakkar) was planned and discussed in detail on an app called Sky ECC. The police were at the tip of an enormous iceberg.

Showing modern law enforcement on screen can be a challenge: in the online era, it’s less cops and robbers; more zeros and ones. So it’s a surprise to be confronted with something as thrilling as The Narco Hack. This three-part documentary explores an extraordinary investigation by French, Belgian and Dutch police, during which they undermined several massive criminal organisations via methods at once impressively logical and completely mind-boggling by compromising Sky ECC’s encryption software.

Sky ECC was developed by a company called Sky Global, apparently with lawyers and journalists in mind. The app was designed to strip phones of all their normal features, leaving just itself. When the app was shut down, the phones deactivated. Oh, and the phones could be wiped remotely, which was a handy feature. “At Sky, they knew very well that it wasn’t going to be choirboys buying it,” says “Albert”, a drug dealer. “You weren’t going to be talking to your mum on Sky.” Thomas Herdman, who worked for the company, is interviewed and offers an unconvincing defence constructed around the idea that a luxury hotelier wouldn’t ask their guests how they could afford to stay at the hotel.

And so begins an epic tale of brave detective work and tech wizardry. This kind of material is undeniably hard to render visually – but while The Narco Hack does feature an awful lot of scrolling computer text and close-ups of smartphones being turned on, it also hears at length from the cops involved. From shrewd, single-minded prosecutor Johanna Brousse to eccentric cybercrime whiz “Bertillon” (his name is protected and he appears via a series of AI-rendered face-swaps), they’re an engaging bunch.

Furthermore, the investigation grips hard, and the stakes are extremely high. As Bertillon walks us through the decryption process (server locations, cryptographic keys: you’re glazing over already, aren’t you?), most viewers almost certainly won’t fully understand. However, what unfolds on the ground is approximately The Wire meets The Imitation Game. The various police jurisdictions involved aren’t singing from the same charge sheet – the Belgians want to stop the drugs and guns moving, while the French want to identify suspects and follow them.

Then there’s the issue of how much to reveal to their quarries. As the detectives realise they’re looking over the shoulders of drug kingpins, they also understand that if they act hastily, they’ll only land small fry. How much further could access take them? This dilemma is sharpened by the sheer horror of what is being revealed as indigestible chunks of gibberish text become comprehensible. Sexual torture. Skin flayed with scorching hot skillets. An innocuous-looking pink house in Serbia which turns out to contain meat grinders into which informants are fed. Surely, at some point, the police have to stop intelligence-gathering and start smashing down front doors?

Soon enough, they do. They uncover billions of euros (mainly laundered via cryptocurrency) and Dubai-resident drug lords calling themselves things like Saddam Hussein, Putin and Hitler. It’s hugely satisfying to witness but feels like a sisyphean task all the same. Underpinning everything is perhaps the crucial conversation of our era. About the thin line between innovation and crime. About who polices tech companies and how. And about where responsibility ultimately lies.

This documentary is specific in its field of interest but it’s more widely thought-provoking, prompting consideration of everything from social media companies that enable the creation of child sexual abuse material to AI companies and their laissez-faire attitude to intellectual and creative theft. Sky ECC is what happens when tech finds its ideal users and, for reasons of commercial expediency, simply shrugs its shoulders.

Still, there’s a very human heroism being celebrated here. The consequences of the hack were significant in all sorts of smaller, more profoundly personal ways too. In the wake of Houcine Hakkar’s horrible fate, there were mutterings about the unlikeliness of smoke without fire. In revealing the conversations around his killing, the hack unequivocally cleared his name. His murder had been a terrible mistake. The look on his sister’s face as she talks about her brother suggests that’s no small consolation.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Two ex-FBI officials charged with lying about investigation into Hunter Biden’s laptop
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Contents of laptop of Joe Biden’s son were part of a bizarre saga in the final weeks of 2020 presidential election

Two former FBI intelligence officials who specialized in foreign election interference were charged on Friday with making false statements about their roles in investigating the origins of Hunter Biden’s laptop in the run-up to the 2020 presidential election.

Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides surrendered on Friday and made their first appearance in federal court in Washington DC. Floris’s legal team expressed outrage at the development coming from the US Department of Justice, the parent agency of the FBI.

“Nikki Floris is a patriot. She served our nation as a dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years. Yet today, the [justice department] has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts. It’s no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election,” her attorneys said in a statement.

The case was filed 10 days before the 3 November midterm elections and marks the latest in a series of high-profile and politically charged investigative actions the justice department has undertaken in the run-up during the height of campaigning ahead of the vote.

The prosecution, a rare justice department criminal case against a former employee, revisits a tangled and bizarre saga that roiled the final weeks of the 2020 race, in which Joe Biden, Hunter Biden’s father, beat Donald Trump but Trump refused to accept the result and tried numerous ways to overturn it – which ended up in his second impeachment, accused of inciting an insurrection attempt on 6 January 2021, and criminal charges that were ultimately dismissed after Trump’s 2024 election victory.

Friday’s court proceedings also came amid a broader, backward-looking effort by the FBI director, Kash Patel, who before taking over the nation’s premier law enforcement agency was a harsh critic of it, to scrutinize high-profile episodes from the bureau’s recent past that for years have animated Trump’s conservative base.

The revelation of the laptop’s existence in October 2020 injected a thorny storyline in the race between Trump and Biden.

The laptop’s contents were publicized by the New York Post, which said it had obtained from Trump ally Rudy Giuliani a hard drive of a computer dropped off by Hunter Biden at a Wilmington, Delaware, repair shop. The laptop contained emails that appeared to show discussions of the younger Biden’s foreign business dealings.

The peculiar circumstances of the laptop’s discovery raised concerns among Democrats and former intelligence officials about the possibility of Russian disinformation, particularly when the Trump administration’s own intelligence community was assessing that Russia was attempting to interfere on Trump’s behalf in the election and as Giuliani had traveled abroad looking for dirt on the Bidens.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: Tinned mackerel, hand-crank radios and bags for poo: crisis-prepping guides around the world
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Ajit Niranjan
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
UK allies have long urged people to stockpile supplies for a crisis. How are people from France to Australia being advised to prepare?

The UK has told people to fill their pantries with food for three days in case of catastrophe, joining a host of countries urging citizens to ready themselves for core systems failing.

Such advice, once dismissed as the preserve of preppers, has become more common in government circles as climate breakdown worsens weather extremes and geopolitical tensions turn cyberattacks and sabotage into a regular occurrence. Even in countries with national strategic food stockpiles – a buffer the UK lacks – authorities have asked individuals to play their part in societal resilience.

What actions do Britain’s allies – from the US and Europe to India and Australia – recommend people take before disaster strikes?

France calls the first 72 hours a “decisive period” in which people should monitor TV and radio news for official updates, and keep an emergency kit close by in case they have to get out fast. In addition to the essentials, such as food, water, medicine and cash, the guidelines recommend filling the go-bag with photocopies of documents, spare sets of house and car keys, and even games to pass the time.

The strategy emphasises the need for solidarity and calls on people to be in close communication with loved ones, resist rumours and disinformation, and consider volunteering as a reservist or with civil protection organisations. Experts have warned that maintaining societal cohesion is crucial during crises.

As far back as the 1960s, households in West Germany were encouraged to stockpile 14 days of canned food – a target that few seem to have reached despite cold war tensions. About a decade ago, the recommendation fell to 10 days, and guidance issued last October said households should do this “where possible”, describing even three days’ worth of supplies as “a big help”. Almost half of Germans fail to meet this threshold, a YouGov poll for the German Press Agency found in January.

Guidelines from the Federal Office of Civil Protection and Disaster Assistance recommend stockpiling durable foods that are ready to eat, in case cookers stop working, and foods that have short cooking times, allowing fuel for a camping stove to last for more days in a blackout. The checklist of items also features a hand-crank or solar-powered radio, a paper list of important phone numbers, and a well-stocked medicine cabinet.

The US emergency readiness campaign, launched in 2003, recommends people “make a plan today”, noting that members of a family may not be together when disaster strikes. Its toolkit foresees people storing enough water for each person to have one gallon (3.8 litres) a day, both for drinking and sanitation, as well as items such as a whistle to call for help, a dust mask to filter contaminated air and plastic sheeting for shelter. Food supply advice varies between states, ranging from a few days in California to more than two weeks in Hawaii.

The guidance suggests families rethink the contents of the kit each year as their needs change. It also calls for storing supplies at home, at work and in the car.

Nordic countries have ramped up emergency preparations since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The Finnish advice describes home emergency supplies, including backup power and hygiene articles, as an “excellent basis” for many situations, while warning against hoarding. It recommends people have enough for at least three days and says these can help even when mundane obstacles such as illness keep one from going to the shops.

Secure silos of grain that make up Finland’s ample strategic reserve provide an extra layer of security, designed to feed the population for nine months if supply chains collapse or domestic production fails.

The Swedish advice, which is framed around conflict but also covers pandemics and extreme weather, says people can “contribute to collective preparedness” if they can manage on their own for at least one week. It includes specific tips such as growing berries on windowsills, freezing bottles of water, which can function as ice packs if freezers break and then be drunk once the ice melts, and, if the toilet won’t flush, disposing of excrement in plastic bags covered by sawdust.

The Norwegian guidelines, which are offered in 30 languages, also encourage people to be able to “fend for themselves” for at least a week when systems such as the internet, mobile phone networks and bank payments are down. The country is particularly reliant on electricity for home heating, and recommends people store warm clothes, sleeping bags and candles, and keep fireplaces and chimneys clean. “In a crisis or war, people must be prepared for the fact that not everything will work as normal,” it warns. “The help will first go to those who need it most.”

The Danish advice gives a sample three-day meal plan, which includes 500g crispbread, 300g of canned mackerel in tomato sauce, 300g of chickpeas and kidney beans, 500g each of pasta and groats, and 1.5kg of tinned vegetables, as well as 100g of nuts and some vegetable oil.

The Australian government can declare a national emergency but individual states and territories are mainly responsible for management. Most authorities recommend storing supplies to last three to seven days, though the New South Wales health service recommends planning for two weeks. Its “pantry list” recommends giving special consideration to family members with special needs, such as babies, pregnant women and those who are old or ill.

Its fire services also have detailed guidance on preparing for bushfires, ranging from trimming vegetation to wearing a wide-brimmed hat to protect the head from falling embers and respirator masks to avoid the worst of the smoke.

India’s disaster preparedness checklist, prepared by the National Centre for Disease Control, recommends finding out which hazards threaten your home and finding safe spots for each type of disaster. It calls for storing at least a three-day supply of water and food, prioritising products that require little cooking or refrigeration, while avoiding very salty or spicy ones.

The recommended emergency bag includes a battery-operated torch, chlorine tablets to purify water, a first aid book, and thick ropes. It recommends practising evacuation drills with all family members twice a year. The checklist also explicitly warns that the climate crisis is likely to lead to more frequent and severe disasters.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Officer who shot and killed Black toddler in Mississippi resigns from police force
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Adria R Walker
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Hunter Foster fired at vehicle during a shoplifting call at a Walmart, killing one-year-old Kohen Wiley

Hunter Foster, the Mississippi police officer who shot into a vehicle and killed one-year-old Kohen Wiley, has resigned from the Senatobia police department. Earlier this week, Mississippi’s attorney general, Lynn Fitch, announced that the shooting was “justified”.

The Senatobia board of aldermen accepted Foster’s resignation on 21 October and the resignation took effect immediately. Foster was placed on leave on 16 June, days after the 14 June shooting. Yesterday, the Mississippi department of public safety released body-camera and surveillance footage from the shooting, at a Walmart in Senatobia, during which the toddler died in his mother’s arms after being shot.

In the footage, Foster is seen running out of a Walmart with other officers after an employee said shoplifters were fleeing. Officials have alleged that Kohen’s mother and a friend stole diapers from the Walmart; neither woman has been charged.

Within seconds of leaving the store, Foster aimed his gun at a vehicle in which Kohen, his mother and another woman were. Three shots were fired, all from Foster’s gun, though several officers drew their guns. Foster hit and injured the driver of the vehicle, and killed Kohen.

At a press conference on Thursday, the prominent civil rights attorney Ben Crump, who is representing Kohen’s family, called for a federal investigation into the shooting. He is also calling for Foster to be decertified, which would prevent him from serving as a police officer anywhere else.

“The bullet that killed Kohen Wiley was not justified,” Crump said. “This decision sends a message that a Black baby boy, his life, is not as valuable as the white diapers that he is wrapped in.”

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: New Jersey Devils land Olympic hero Connor Hellebuyck in blockbuster trade with Winnipeg
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Connor Hellebuyck finally has a new home after the Winnipeg Jets granted the three-time Vezina Trophy-winning goaltender’s trade request in a deal that sent him to the New Jersey Devils on Friday.

The Devils sent center Dawson Mercer, goalie Nico Daws, prospect Alexander Command, forward Nick Bjugstad, a 2029 second-round pick and a 2027 seventh-rounder to Winnipeg for Hellebuyck.

The long-awaited blockbuster trade ends months of speculation, a failed bid to move the US Olympic gold medal-winner and 2024-25 NHL MVP in June, and the Jets’ suspension of Hellebuyck for failing to report to training camp in a standoff that required the involvement of the league and the Players’ Association.

The 33-year-old Hellebuyck, who backstopped the US to Olympic gold at the Milan-Cortina Games in February, leaves Winnipeg after spending his entire 11-year career there. Hellebuyck joins Jack Hughes, who scored in overtime of the final to defeat Canada, with the Devils and immediately puts them closer to being Stanley Cup contenders.

When training camp opened, new Devils general manager Sunny Mehta said he was very comfortable with the team’s goaltending situation. Since then, Daws and Jake Allen have combined for an .880 save percentage, which ranks 23rd among 32 teams.

It was not immediately clear how soon Hellebuyck might be ready to play for his new team. He has been skating in his home state of Michigan while trade talks were ongoing.

Hellebuyck has five seasons left on a seven-year contract with an annual salary cap hit of $8.5m.

He becomes the latest high-profile American to leave Canada for the United States. In June, Ottawa dealt captain Brady Tkachuk to the Florida Panthers, where he joined his brother Matthew. In December, the Vancouver Canucks traded star defenseman Quinn Hughes, a brother of Jack and teammate Luke, to the Minnesota Wild.

The process to trade Hellebuyck became messy, especially after the goalie went public with his request to leave Winnipeg in September. The Jets suspended the goalie for failing to report for camp in a disciplinary move that extended into the season, with Hellebuyck not getting paid.

The length of the suspension became an issue, with the league and union determining Hellebuyck would be allowed to rejoin the Jets on Friday. Instead, a move to New Jersey materialized ahead of Winnipeg hosting the outdoor Heritage Classic this weekend.

The post-Hellebuyck plans went into motion over the summer, with the Jets signing Stuart Skinner in free agency. Winnipeg claimed Clay Stevenson off waivers before the season began, and their combined .907 save percentage is seventh-best in the NHL.

The Jets were second-guessed for not dealing Hellebuyck in June, when teams had more options to prioritize salary cap space to make room to acquire the goalie. The Sabres were among the teams expressing interest in Hellebuyck and were preparing to package a deal that included swapping first-round draft picks – Buffalo had the No 4 selection and Winnipeg had the eighth.

The challenge for Winnipeg became finding a willing trade partner to acquire a goalie with a high price tag and a lengthy contract well after most teams had set their rosters and had little salary cap space to work with. Another question mark involved Hellebuyck’s age and track record of following regular-season success with a spotty playoff record.

After Hellebuyck went 9-8 in leading the Jets to the Western Conference finals in his playoff debut in 2018, he has gone 15-26 since, with the Jets advancing to the second round just twice in their next six playoff appearances. In four first-round exits, Hellebuyck had a combined 5-15 record.

The disparity between regular-season and postseason success was evident in 2024-25. Leading Winnipeg to the Presidents’ Trophy and winning the Hart Trophy as MVP, Hellebuyck recorded a career-best 47 wins, then went 6-7 in the playoffs as the Jets were eliminated by Dallas in the second round.

With a 345-208-55 regular-season record, Hellebuyck ranks 27th in career wins on the NHL list and fifth among US-born players. Among US-born goalies with 300 or more career starts, his .916 save percentage ranks fourth and his 2.58 goals-against average ranks sixth.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: US and Israel are warned against launching fresh strikes on Iran
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Multinational ‘anti-war bloc’ uses Istanbul summit to call for a diplomatic solution to Middle East crisis

Foreign ministers at a summit of eight European and Middle Eastern countries have urged the US and Israel not to renews their attacks on Iran, warning a fresh outbreak of fighting would spread conflict and push oil prices even higher.

The development of a new multinational “anti-war bloc” represents a challenge to the increasingly open plans by the US and Israel to relaunch strikes on Iran while talks on Tehran’s nuclear programme remain deadlocked.

The Turkish foreign minister, Hakan Fidan, joint convener of the summit in Istanbul, said: “Military intervention in Iran is not any kind of solution. We agreed that a new military attack would spread the war and the conflict in the region. All the countries around the table do not want the war to spread even more, once again.”

Ministers also demanded an end to the Houthi assaults on Saudi Arabia, and an immediate opening of the strait of Hormuz currently blockaded by Iranian ships and drones.
