Jean-Noël Barrot, the French foreign minister, said another war between Iran and the US would be bad for both sides, and only worsen rising oil prices, which have hit their highest level since May. Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, also urged both sides to embrace diplomacy.

The Istanbul meeting, an unprecedented gathering of regional and European leaders initiated by Turkey and Germany, represented a rare chance for European ministers to have any input into the crises afflicting the Middle East, including in Yemen, Palestine and Iran. They have largely been left as bystanders, apart from sending air force protection to Saudi Arabia as it tries to fend off Houthi drone and missile assaults on its airports and energy installations.

The Middle Eastern states were represented by Fidan, Egypt’s Badr Abdelatty, Pakistan’s Ishaq Dar and Saudi Arabia’s Faisal bin Farhan. Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia formed the Mecca defensive security pact in August, a grouping Egypt may join.

The European side was represented by Barrot, Miliband, Germany’s Johann Wadephul and Italy’s Antonio Tajani. The agenda covered the Palestinian issue, including settlement expansion, settler violence and the two-state solution, as well as security in the strait of Hormuz, Yemen and efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war and prevent spillover into the Black Sea.

Wadephul said: “We are united by the impact these deadlocked conflicts are having on the economy and security of our countries and by the will to seek new ways to bring about solutions.”

He made no criticism of the US but accused “the Houthis and Iran of blackmailing world trade and continuing to stranglehold global supplies of energy and fertiliser”.

“We are feeling the effects of the attacks on shipping routes and whether at the petrol pump or the supermarket,” he said. “Elsewhere there is threat of famine.”

Tajani said the aim of the meeting was to work for “de-escalation to guarantee freedom of navigation”.

“I do not believe the problem can be solved from a purely military standpoint,” he added. “If we want to reopen Hormuz, which is vital for our economies, we must promote dialogue and make Iran understand that this attitude cannot continue.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: As midterms loom, Trump and his allies try to change the subject
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Callum Jones
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Despite distraction and distortion, voters know what issues will be informing their votes in this election

This was originally published in The Stakes 2026, a newsletter about the midterm elections. Sign up to get it in your inbox

Elections too often get pigeonholed. The hot take, or simplistic analysis, would have it that just one issue – often the issue the source so happens to be most animated about – will decide the entire result.

Tens of millions of Americans will go to the polls next month. Will they be galvanized by affordability? Maybe it’s Iran. Or healthcare? Taxes, perhaps. Or crime.

It depends, of course, on whom you ask. The US electorate is not a monolith. Just as different voters are grappling with different pressures and realities, they have different priorities and concerns.

Take a look at our voter panel. For Justin Daniels, 45, in Detroit, Michigan, the most significant issue in this election is economic malaise. For Yajaira Martinez, 43, in Pharr, Texas, it’s labor. For Scott Akridge, 60, in Marietta, Georgia, it’s the administration’s brutal crackdown on immigration.

The challenge for any one party trying to win over such a sprawling country is whether it can address enough of these concerns, and obtain the trust of enough voters, to build a coalition.

Which makes the latest polling all the more disconcerting for Republicans, less than two weeks before election day.

The headline takeaways from the most recent Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos survey were damning enough: as my colleague Shrai Popat reported, most Americans think Donald Trump is using the US presidency to enrich himself, and his approval rating has fallen to a new low.

Beneath the surface, though, the numbers are yet more dismal for Republicans.

Presented with a dozen issues, from affordability and corruption to taxes and transgender issues, respondents were asked which of the two main parties they trust to do a better job of handling them. On all but one – crime – a greater share picked Democrats than Republicans.

On the economy, as the White House continues to hail a “new golden age”, Republicans have lost ground significantly over the past six months. While they commanded a one-point lead over Democrats in April, they are now nine points behind on the issue voters consistently rank as a top concern.

And on immigration, which Trump and his officials have put at the heart of his second presidency, the five-point Republican lead in April has reversed. Almost two years into the administration’s deadly and controversial crackdown, Democrats are now ahead by two points.

In Kansas, where voters have not sent a Democrat to the US Senate since 1932, the party’s candidate, Adam Hamilton, has been pledging to turn down the heat, and ignore partisan battles, amid rising political polarization. Some recent polls have put him ahead.

Midterm elections are almost always tough for Washington’s governing party. There is a conventional playbook for navigating this: senior figures fan out nationwide to reassure the people who backed them two years prior that they get it. They hear them. They’re on it. They just need more time.

The president is indeed fanning out across the country. This week alone, he was in Kansas on Monday and North Carolina on Tuesday, before South Carolina on Wednesday, Iowa on Thursday and Florida on Friday. Georgia and Michigan follow this weekend. JD Vance is on a cross-country tour of his own.

But this is where Trump and his allies depart from convention. Rather than acknowledge the golden age has yet to shine for much of the country – let alone concede that some of his priorities since taking office, like the beautification of Washington, or adding his name to the Kennedy Center, were not among the campaign promises his base had found so appealing in 2024 – Trump has opted for an altogether different response.

This summer, as questions over Iran, the cost of living and hardline anti-immigration policies loomed large, the most powerful elected officials in the US tried to stoke fears that communism was rife inside the Democratic party.

In September, the president dangled a $5,000 “Trump dividend” for every US citizen, a proposal that was widely criticized as a pre-election bribe.

Now, in the final stretch of the campaign, those questions very much remain. Rather than address them, Republicans appear to be resorting to a volatile mix of distraction and distortion.

Having spent much of the Iran war, which he launched in February, claiming it was about to end, the president is now pivoting to Ukraine – striking a stunning deal to buy Russian diesel, pausing some sanctions on Moscow and suggesting the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, should quit.

And as France was gripped by fresh unrest this weekend, Vance entered the chat. Demonstrations that began as student protests against crumbling schools and the soaring cost of living were, in fact, evidence of “western liberals” having “imported the third world” into their countries, according to the vice-president.

“And I hope Americans are paying attention. This is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country,” added Vance. Not to be outdone, Trump himself has used public appearances to echo such warnings in recent days, as my colleagues Joseph Gedeon and David Smith reported.

Many Americans are paying close attention – not to France, necessarily, but to the issues that dominate their daily lives. In November, we’ll find out whom Americans trust to address them.

The US politics team hosted a series of reader Q&As leading up to the midterms. In our final session, Guardian immigration reporters answered your questions about how ICE and Trump’s mass deportation agenda could shape election results. See our other conversations here:

Will the Iran war cost Trump in the US midterm elections? Your questions answered

Will Trump’s economy sink Republicans in the US midterm elections? Our reporters answered your questions

Mary Peltola’s campaign to represent Alaska in the US Senate has taken her to parts of the huge state’s interior that are inaccessible by road and on the frontlines of the cost-of-living crisis she hopes will make her the first Democrat to win the seat in nearly two decades.

She has been to towns where paper towels retail for $40, a half gallon of oat milk goes for $21 and the cost of a new freezer can be quadruple what it is in the state’s largest city, Anchorage, simply because it’s so complicated to get there. She’s heard of communities along the Arctic Ocean where power bills have climbed to $1,500 a month because they rely on generators for power and the Iran war has pushed the cost of diesel to new heights.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on Europe’s protests: the social contract has broken – and young people want solutions | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
An electoral supercycle over the next year may redefine the continent’s future. But what’s happening on the streets is shaping it, too

France sneezed, and Europe has again caught the cold. The wave of unrest which began with teenagers at a high school soon drew in hundreds of thousands of people nationwide and then spread across the continent. Protests have filled the streets in Lisbon and Madrid, and have ignited into violence in Milan, Brussels and Tirana as well as in French cities.

French authorities say they are deploying 70,000 officers on Saturday and are allowing only marches organised by unions. They blame hard-left militants as well as opportunistic young perpetrators for last weekend’s destruction and looting, when a minority hijacked largely peaceful protests. But with fuel prices set to rise further over the winter, the demands and participants broadening, and President Macron utterly failing to meet the moment, there is no sign of an end to the wider discontent and no speedy resolution in sight.

Europe is experiencing distinct movements, with distinct causes, demands and actors, which should not be elided. In France, crumbling and overcrowded schools were the touchpaper, with Greek protesters echoing their complaints about educational underfunding this week. In Spain and Portugal, housing is the central issue. German students are angered by the possible reintroduction of compulsory military service. But those involved see the commonalities, with some Italian demonstrators chanting in French.

Underlying all these is the breakdown of the social contract. A generation expect, with reason, to be worse off than their parents. They are understandably angry at inadequate education and job precarity, are struggling to rent places of their own well into their 20s, and are paying for pensions which they don’t believe that they will ever receive themselves, while the climate crisis haunts their futures. They see that governments worried about debt and fearful of the bond markets either cannot or will not offer them solutions. It might be more remarkable if they were happy with their lot, or confident that casting a vote at their next opportunity would fix it.

Meanwhile, increasing inequality means that they watch others grow wealthy, sometimes profiting directly from their misfortune, with flats and houses treated as financial instruments rather than homes.

This unrest also echoes the wave of gen Z protests seen around the world last year – with some of those on the streets in France, Italy and Germany even borrowing emblems used earlier from Morocco to Madagascar. The affordability crisis, heavy-handed security forces and the sense that ordinary people are being left behind while governments have no convincing answers for them were at work in those cases too.

In Europe, far-right parties, egged on by the Trump administration, are seeking to capitalise on the unrest through lies that immigrants and open borders are to blame, and that a strong hand is needed to restore order. Within the next year, four of the biggest states – Spain, France, Poland and Italy – will hold elections, threatening a radical rightwards shift that could fundamentally change the EU. Yet these parties do not have real answers to the questions raised by protesters, and a financial crisis in France might yet highlight Marine Le Pen’s economic weak spot and National Rally’s internal divisions. The future course of the continent is being shaped, for better or worse, on the streets as well as at the ballot box.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump says he ordered DoJ to file lawsuit to block Alaska Senate results certification
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Shrai Popat in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Trump justice department claims there could be ‘confusion’ about two Republicans on the ballot named Dan Sullivan

Donald Trump said he ordered the justice department to file a lawsuit to block the certification of Alaska’s US Senate results if the Republican incumbent on the ballot does not win.

The justice department claimed there could be “voter confusion” about the two Republican candidates on the ballot named Dan Sullivan, which it claims might influence the race’s outcome in favor of the Democratic nominee, Mary Peltola.

Alaska could determine control of the Senate, and polls suggest the Republican incumbent senator, Dan S Sullivan, is in a dead heat with Peltola, a former Democratic congresswoman. Another candidate named Daniel J Sullivan, a retired schoolteacher, is also running as a Republican and will appear on the November general election ballot.

The administration is asking for there to be a pause in certifying the vote in Alaska “pending an investigation” to determine whether votes that are cast for Dan J Sullivan were actually meant to be for the Republican incumbent.

The federal government argues in the complaint that “the sole purpose” of Dan J Sullivan’s of candidacy is to “benefit the Peltola campaign by reducing the number of votes for Senator Sullivan”.

As a result, “there is a substantial likelihood that a certification of the election will reflect an electoral process that lacked integrity”, it writes.

The state uses a ranked-choice voting system in their elections, under which the top four candidates from an open primary advance to the general election. Voters then rank candidates in order of preference, and votes can transfer to their next-ranked candidate as lower-placed contenders are eliminated.

The president and his allies have repeatedly claimed, without evidence, that Daniel J Sullivan – who is challenging the two-term incumbent – is an “impostor”.

Meanwhile, many Republicans across the country have accused the former teacher, who lives in Petersburg – a town of about 3,000 people in the southern part of Alaska – of being a Democratic plant in place to cannibalize votes from the Dan S Sullivan.

Trump has routinely disparaged the state’s voting system, adopted by voters in 2020, calling it a “scam” and encouraging Alaskans to support a state ballot measure to repeal it. The incumbent senator will appear on the 3 November ballot in Alaska with the words “(Registered Republican) Incumbent” next to his name to make it clearer for voters.

Voting rights experts say the basis for the lawsuit is thin given the fact that any meaningful investigation into voters’ preferences after they have voted would be practically impossible to conduct.

In June, the Alaska supreme court ruled that the Dan J Sullivan could remain on the ballot, despite the frustration it has caused the Trump administration and national Republicans hoping that the incumbent Sullivan can win against Peltola, a moderate Democrat, in their bitter fight for a Senate seat that could deliver Democrats a key victory in their path for control of the upper chamber of Congress.

The Trump administration’s targeting of Alaska’s Senate race is particularly consequential as Democrats have been making waves in flipping the red-leaning state.

Alaska’s Democrats believe circumstances have aligned for them to win a slew of competitive elections in the midterms, with the Senate seat being a top prize. If Peltola were to win the election next month, she would be the first Democrat to win the seat in nearly two decades.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Epstein-linked billionaire Glenn Dubin stepped down from Mount Sinai board earlier this year
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Johanna Berkman
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
The board change is the latest development for the renowned New York hospital plagued by revelations related to Jeffrey Epstein

Hedge fund billionaire Glenn Dubin, one of several Wall Street figures whose relationship with Jeffrey Epstein is facing scrutiny, has stepped down from the board of Mount Sinai hospital, according to sources close to the renowned New York institution.

The revelation follows news earlier this year that Mount Sinai, which has long ranked as a top medical provider in New York City, had reportedly formed a committee to review its longstanding ties to the late accused sex trafficker. The hospital features prominently in the Epstein files released by the Department of Justice, including an incident in which a Mount Sinai doctor appears to have operated on a young Russian woman inside Epstein’s Upper East Side townhouse after she got hurt during a stay on his Caribbean island.

Dubin, a founder of Highbridge Capital Management, who had financial connections to Epstein and previously referred to Epstein as a friend, served on Mount Sinai’s board of trustees since 2007 and was a vice-chair. His wife, Dr Eva Andersson-Dubin, who had once dated Epstein prior to her marriage, also stepped down earlier this year from the board of Mount Sinai’s Icahn School of Medicine.

The circumstances surrounding the Dubins’ departure from these Mount Sinai boards are not clear.

In a statement, Mount Sinai said: “The Dubins’ terms on the board of trustees ended this past spring, and they did not seek re-election.”

The hospital did not respond to questions about whether it had concluded its Epstein-related review or about the findings of the review, or about whether there was a link between the review and the Dubins’ decision.

A spokesperson for the Dubins did not respond to questions about their departure from the boards. In a statement, their spokesperson said: “Had they been aware of Epstein’s vile and unspeakable conduct, they would have cut off all ties long ago and certainly never allowed him to be in the presence of their children.”

The couple were still listed as members of the hospital’s “boards of trustees” in May 2025, in a journal marking the hospital’s 40th anniversary Crystal Party, a major fundraiser. In the journal marking the 41st annual Crystal Party, held this past May, neither of the Dubins’ names appeared on the “boards of trustees” list, which included those who were members as of 31 March 2026.

A 2019 report in the New York Times, published after Epstein’s arrest on sex-trafficking charges but before his death, said Dubin first met Epstein through his wife and had provided Epstein with financial advice earlier in their decades-long relationship. The newspaper also reported that Epstein had invested $10m in Dubin’s hedge fund, and that the two men continued to socialize in Palm Beach even after they “parted professional ways”.

At the time, a spokesperson for the Dubins said that they were “horrified” by allegations of Epstein’s sex trafficking. “The Dubins were loyal friends and mistakenly believed Mr Epstein, a person they had known for decades, had rehabilitated himself after his 2008 plea and deserved a second chance,” the spokesperson told the newspaper in July 2019.

Last month, the congressman Thomas Massie, a Republican from Kentucky, alleged on the floor of the House of Representatives that Glenn Dubin was one of 14 “Epstein co-conspirators” who ought to face investigation and possible prosecution. A spokesperson for Glenn Dubin did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment about Massie’s statement.

Massie also named Leon Black, another Wall Street billionaire tied to Epstein who also served on the board of Mount Sinai hospital.

“Perhaps hearing these names,” said Massie, “will shame the Department of Justice into delivering justice.”

Black has said he is the target of a political witch-hunt. Last month, Congress voted unanimously to hold Black in contempt for refusing to comply with subpoenas issued by the House committee on oversight, which demanded that he appear for a deposition and provide the committee with all his nondisclosure agreements. Black, who has denied having any knowledge of Epstein’s alleged crimes and has sued the House committee for allegedly overstepping its authority, served on Mount Sinai’s board of trustees from 2001 to 2012. He also served on the board of its Icahn School of Medicine through 2024. In 2000 Black and his wife endowed the Debra and Leon Black Professor of Pediatrics chair at Icahn; in 2005, they established Mount Sinai’s Black Family Stem Cell Institute.

Attorney Brad Karp has served on the Mount Sinai board since 2019. He was the longtime chairman of the Paul, Weiss law firm until he resigned from that position earlier this year after emails released in the Epstein files revealed extensive personal and business communications with Epstein. Paul, Weiss has said that Karp “regrets” his interactions with Epstein. Karp remains on Mount Sinai’s board.

According to the justice department files released in January, Epstein donated hundreds of thousands of dollars to Mount Sinai and its medical school in the years following his 2008 conviction on state charges. In 2019, in the wake of Epstein’s death in jail by suicide, the hospital said it was “contributing a sum equal to the donations we received from Mr Epstein and his foundation to a charity focused on preventing human trafficking and exploitation”.

Mount Sinai declined to answer questions about how much money it donated, and to whom.

The Epstein files indicate that Epstein’s donations to Mount Sinai gave him “VIP” status at the hospital. According to a report in the New York Times, Dr Jess Ting, an assistant professor of surgery at Mount Sinai, sewed 35 stitches into the forehead of a young Russian woman inside Epstein’s townhouse on Manhattan’s Upper East Side after the woman injured herself, in October of 2012, while riding an ATV on Epstein’s private island in the Caribbean. Alongside its article, the New York Times published an undated color photograph that appeared to show the surgeon performing the procedure in Epstein’s dining room.

In February 2013, four months after the procedure in his dining room, Epstein directed his accountant, Richard Kahn, to make out a check to Mount Sinai for $50,000 which, according to an email written by Ting, was “earmarked” for his research. When, four years later, Ting co-authored an article about an experiment related to “aggressive sporadic breast cancer” in Clinical Cancer Research, a peer-reviewed medical journal, the article’s acknowledgements noted that the research was supported by donations from, among others, “Jeffrey Epstein to JT”.

Tax records for the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai show Ting received $4.6m in compensation in 2019.

Mount Sinai did not respond to questions about whether Ting faced any consequences from the hospital for having apparently performed the procedure in Epstein’s home. Ting did not respond to questions from the Guardian.

The New York state department of health was asked to comment about the medical procedure apparently being performed in Epstein’s dining room and whether it was investigating the matter. In a statement, the department of health said:“While the department cannot discuss or provide details pertaining to active investigations, the allegations in recent media reports are deeply troubling and clearly warrant review. As regulator of New York state hospitals and diagnostic and treatment centers, the Department of Health holds all facilities accountable for the quality of care they provide to ensure the safety and wellbeing of all patients. The New York State Department of Health condemns any abuse that undermines patient trust and safety, including any predatory or unlawful behavior, and takes its responsibility to investigate allegations like this very seriously. We extend our support to all victims and survivors of medical misconduct, physical abuse, or sexual abuse and encourage any patient who believes they are a victim of misconduct to file a complaint.”

In 2010, the Dubins established Mount Sinai’s Dubin Breast Center, which is now a 15,000 sq ft facility inside Mount Sinai’s main campus on the Upper East Side. The center’s entrance on Fifth Avenue is marked by a large hot-pink awning with the words “Dubin Breast Center” imprinted on it in white.

The Epstein files reveal that Andersson-Dubin and Epstein communicated frequently about many topics, and that she reportedly served as Epstein’s “conduit” to Mount Sinai. In April of 2012, according to emails released by the justice department, Andersson-Dubin, at Epstein’s request, sought to help a young Russian woman attain a volunteer position at the Dubin Breast Center.

When Mount Sinai’s director of international personnel stated that the “volunteer tasks” that the “foreign national” was seeking to perform “potentially conflict with the duties designated for the union”, Andersson-Dubin wrote to Epstein that the young woman could “sit there and just look pretty … if that makes it better!! This woman … has something against Russian girls I think … ,” to which Epstein replied simply: “socialism.” Ultimately, after Andersson-Dubin made an appeal to the hospital, the volunteer position was approved.

A spokesperson for the Dubins did not respond to questions about the alleged incident. Mount Sinai declined to comment.

Celina Dubin, the Dubins’ daughter, was a student at the Icahn School of Medicine and is now an assistant professor of dermatology at Mount Sinai.

The daughters of two other billionaires linked to Epstein, both of whom have testified in Congress about their relationships with him, have also attended Mount Sinai’s medical school: Bill Gates’s daughter, who graduated in 2024 and is now a pediatric resident at the hospital, and US commerce secretary Howard Lutnick’s daughter, who is currently enrolled there.

Last month, the US district judge Jed Rakoff, who has presided over all the Epstein-victim class action lawsuits filed against banking institutions – suits which, to date, have yielded $438m in settlements – ruled that the newest of these, brought against FirstBank Puerto Rico by Boies Schiller Flexner and Edwards Henderson, could proceed.

According to that lawsuit, Epstein’s donations to Mount Sinai, which included at least $50,000 drawn from his Enhanced Education account at FirstBank Puerto Rico in June 2014, were “directly used to fund” his illegal activities. In addition, the lawsuit alleges, Mount Sinai was “linked to individuals known to have recruited for him”. The lawsuit does not specify the names of those linked to Mount Sinai who it alleges “recruited” for Epstein.

FirstBank said in a legal filing that while it provided “routine banking services” to Epstein, it did not violate anti-trafficking laws or knowingly facilitate his alleged crimes. The bank also said it filed a suspicious activity report (SAR) shortly after Epstein’s 2019 arrest.

A group of Mount Sinai employees, including female doctors, filed a separate federal employment discrimination lawsuit against Mount Sinai Health System, its Icahn School of Medicine, and various current and former male Mount Sinai officials in April 2019.

The lawsuit alleges, among other things, that one of the defendants, a Mount Sinai doctor, “regularly called women ‘bitches’ and ‘cunts’”. The case now awaits a ruling on a motion for summary judgment brought by Mount Sinai before the US district judge Vernon Broderick.

In a legal filing, Mount Sinai called the complaint “nothing less than a malicious instrument of character assassination” that was “rife with allegations that are immaterial and/or scandalous”. “The Epstein connection is what gets attention, but that kind of culture never has just one victim or kind of victim. When powerful institutions let their men mistreat women, it’s usually a feature, not a bug,” said Ann Olivarius, head of the McAllister Olivarius law firm, which filed the 2019 suit against Mount Sinai.

This past summer, outside of Mount Sinai’s annual Crystal Party fundraiser held at Chelsea Piers downtown, volunteers supporting Equity Now, an organization formed by the former Mount Sinai employees who sued the hospital, handed out fliers that featured photographs of its current and former Epstein-linked board members: Glenn Dubin, Brad Karp and Leon Black.

“WOULD YOU LET THESE MEN RUN YOUR PTA?” asked the text above the pictures. “SO WHY WERE THEY RUNNING MOUNT SINAI?”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Severe flooding in US west triggers rooftop rescues and evacuation orders
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
At least one injured after flooding in Four Corners region – which includes Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona and Utah

Severe flooding in the Four Corners region on Friday led to water rescues – some from rooftops – and impassable roads, with some residents being told to evacuate low-lying areas of Colorado and New Mexico and others advised to shelter in place until water levels go down.

It followed several busy days of flooding in the region that swamped dozens of homes in Utah. Earlier in the week, tornadoes blew off roofs, knocked trees on to houses and downed power lines in Arizona. At least one person was injured.

An unknown number of people were rescued overnight and continued to be rescued on Friday by New Mexico guard boats, helicopters and amphibious vehicles, Devin Neeley, a San Juan county spokesperson, said.

“We’re picking people off of roofs and pulling people out of houses that have 3 or 4ft (1-1.5 metres) of water in them, and there’s more water coming,” Neeley said.

Skies were clearing but the rivers continued to rise, with forecast crests surpassed, he added.

“This is serious. We’re still sending deputies as I speak to get people out of their homes right now. In fact, our sheriff is damn near going to lose his home today,” Neeley said.

About 600 households were told to evacuate in Farmington, where areas along the San Juan River were closed off, city spokesperson Gina Intoppa said.

Farmington is the biggest city in the Four Corners, the only place in the US where four states – Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona and Utah – come together.

National guard members also were deployed to assist with flooding in south-west Colorado. Rising waters prompted mandatory evacuations along four rivers, including the San Juan River through Pagosa Springs. The resort town famous for its riverside hot springs suffered flooding from a similar weather pattern a year ago.

“Please shelter in place, water levels are beginning to recede, but many roads are impassable and unsafe for travel,” the Archuleta county sheriff’s office posted online on Friday.

In nearby Rio Grande county, trailers at a campground were surrounded by high water and trucks were partially submerged in other areas.

Jared Polis, Colorado’s governor, had declared a disaster emergency in 11 counties in response to heavy rain and flooding in the south-west part of the state.

The city of Hurricane in far south-western Utah was cleaning up after declaring a state of emergency on Thursday. Reddish-brown flood water lapped into and about 80 homes in a neighborhood and 50 recreational vehicles in an RV park.

The flooding was not unexpected, just the latest from two months of heavy rain that ended a summer of drought. While parts of the south-west are rocky with little vegetation and are naturally prone to flash flooding, the recent rains have made flooding everywhere more likely, said Kate Abbott, a National Weather Service meteorologist in Grand Junction, Colorado.

“At this point we’re saturated and can’t take too much more without flooding,” Abbott said. “This is the third or fourth round of this kind of moisture we’ve seen in as many weeks.”

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: World and Olympic marathon champion Jepchirchir suspended after positive doping test
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Agence France-Presse
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
In a fresh hammer blow for Kenyan athletics, the women’s world marathon champion, Peres Jepchirchir, has been provisionally suspended for doping, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) announced on Friday.

The highly decorated 33-year-old Kenyan, who won Olympic gold in the Covid-delayed Tokyo Games in 2021, was suspended after an out-of-competition sample tested positive for the banned blood booster EPO.

The athlete is provisionally suspended while the case is investigated, while the AIU said Jepchirchir’s out-of-competition sample had been collected in Kenya before her recent Sydney Marathon victory.

More than 140 Kenyan athletes, including the women’s marathon world record-holder, Ruth Chepngetich, have been suspended or banned by the AIU since 2017.

Jepchirchir’s lauded career includes a world record in the half-marathon, while she is a four-time World Marathon Major winner, having captured the Sydney Marathon (2026), the London Marathon (2024), the Boston Marathon (2022) and the New York Marathon (2021).

The decision of World Athletics to award Nairobi the 2029 world championships is likely to increase the scrutiny of the east African nation’s anti-doping policies.

Barnabas Korir, Athletics Kenya’s youth development director and vice-president of the national Olympic committee, said he was left feeling shocked by the news of the suspension. “It’s a big disappointment coming soon after we were awarded the World Athletics Championship in 2029,” Korir told AFP. “We are in shock, especially in the calibre of Peres Jepchirchir after a stellar career. We don’t know what is happening with our athletes.”

Jepchirchir’s manager, Gianni Demadona, said she had tarnished her reputation. “When I learned from the AIU three days ago that she had been tested positive for EPO, I was confused and shocked,” Demadona said. “I can’t say anything because I was trusting her after 13 years working together that she was one of the most trustable athletes around. I was completely wrong. She spoiled her long and amazing career and she closes her career in the worst way.”

Kenya played host to a three-day visit from the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada) this month, with the body’s chief, Witold Banka, telling the country that it had to strive for zero tolerance on doping.

“Kenya proudly calls itself the home of champions. But for that home to remain respected and credible, it must also be clean,” Banka said. “That is why Kenya needs a strong culture of clean sport, zero tolerance for doping, and a more determined approach to preventing and fighting doping.”

Banka said that joint cooperation with Kenyan authorities would help lay the foundations for a cleaner sport. “Wada or Adak [Anti-Doping Agency of Kenya] alone cannot achieve its vision if we do not cooperate with those who have the power to go against those who are producing, smuggling and trafficking dangerous steroids to your athletes,” he said.

“We’ve found a common understanding and we are on the same track and there’s a clear goal within Kenya for zero tolerance for doping policy and it has to be established immediately with joint actions and a more aggressive approach to those who are destroying the image of the country and the reputation of the athletes.”

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: ‘Black October’: cybersecurity experts sound the alarm over new era of AI-enabled hacking
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Johana Bhuiyan
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
After discovery of severe bug in the PHP programming language, executives warn of ‘vulnerability tsunami’

Leaders in cybersecurity are sounding the alarm after the discovery of a major vulnerability this week. They are predicting that artificial intelligence tools will expose more fundamental weaknesses in global internet infrastructure in the months to come.

“I no longer think we’re going to be able to patch all bugs,” said Sam Altman on Thursday evening, joining the chorus of executives. In the midst of what’s being called “Black October”, for which researchers used AI to help identify critical flaws in a coding language that is used across millions of websites and may have been unpatched for years, tech executives are warning about the ways AI will be used both to identify and exploit security vulnerabilities at an unprecedented scale and pace.

The next few months will see a “vulnerability tsunami”, according to Jason Clinton, Anthropic’s deputy chief information security officer. “There won’t be enough time to patch critical infrastructure,” Clinton said in a post on X on Thursday evening. Marc Benioff, the Salesforce CEO, agreed and called it a “code red”.

AI is uniquely able to find and identify security flaws in a way and at a pace that will feel catastrophic because the security community will not be able to move quickly enough to address them, said Matthew Prince, the Cloudflare CEO. “It’s going to feel like the sky is falling. It’s going to feel like there’s nothing we can do.

“The next two years are going to be incredibly, incredibly, incredibly fraught with new tools that have infinite patience to go look for vulnerabilities across the Internet,” he wrote in a post on X.

While cybersecurity experts have been warning about a “vulnpocalypse”, or the ability for AI to more easily identify security bugs for months, it wasn’t until “Black October” that researchers were able to use AI to find a flaw as fundamental and critical as the one announced on 21 October.

Massive bugs were found in a programming language called PHP, which may have left the millions of websites that run on it vulnerable to hackers for years. Some experts estimated 70% of all the sites on the internet were at risk of hacking.

However, in the same way AI will be used to aid in identifying security vulnerabilities at an unprecedented pace, tech leaders worry it’ll also be used by malicious actors to exploit those bugs at an unprecedented pace.

After the vulnerabilities were announced, government and private websites across the US and UK temporarily took down their sites to patch the bugs. The US National Security Agency (NSA) issued an alert recommending any site that runs on PHP implement the patches immediately. Malicious cyberactors may seek to further exploit these bugs to access servers without authorization, the NSA said.

“Such an access vector could help attackers steal sensitive data, disrupt services or move deeper into a network,” the warning read.

In a post on X, Prince said CloudFlare, a security provider, had seen evidence of thousands of people trying to exploit the PHP flaws in the 10 hours before it was announced.

“That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now,” he wrote.

In a blogpost, researchers at AI security platform Wiz said that this was “among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history”.

“The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,” they wrote.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Mysterious ‘black triangles’ spotted over sensitive US site, new Pentagon UFO files reveal
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Richard Luscombe
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Unidentified object vanished suddenly and silently, anonymous senior military observers claim

Two senior military observers say they watched a mysterious black triangular object flying at an extraordinarily high speed over a sensitive site in the western US earlier this year, in the latest tranche of reported UFO sightings released on Friday by the Trump administration.

The unidentified object showed none of the characteristics of a conventional military aircraft, their report to the defense department said, and it vanished suddenly and silently within seconds, leaving no exhaust trail or other evidence of its existence.

The claimed sighting, by anonymous sources with “extensive operational experience working alongside government agencies”, occurred at a location that was redacted in the file made public on Friday.

The “unidentified anomalous phenomenon” (UAP), a term that has superseded UFO in military, governmental and scientific circles, resembled a delta-wing drone with a wingspan between nine and 15ft (2.75 to 4.5m), the observers recalled. They calculated its speed at 1,800mph.

Similar to hundreds of other reports released by the Pentagon since May as part of Donald Trump’s promise to bring transparency to decades of previously classified or secret documents relating to UFOs, many other details are vague, inconclusive or blacked out altogether.

While many previous accounts have been accompanied by real photographs or video footage of apparent sightings, the “black triangles” report features nine identical images of the same unidentified canyon with tiny, trilateral silhouettes crudely added to replicate the movement of the object the observers said they saw.

“This does indeed look like little more than a black triangle shape superimposed on a landscape background to illustrate the report. I don’t think it really adds anything substantive to the report itself,” said Greg Eghigian, professor of history and bioethics at Penn State University, and author of the 2024 book After the Flying Saucers Came: A Global History of the UFO Phenomenon.

After an early flurry, the Pentagon’s releases in the second Trump administration have become less frequent in recent months, and noticeably thinner since the US president declared in February that he was ordering full disclosure about the government’s knowledge of UFOs and the search for alien life beyond our planet.

The move followed allegations aired in Congress in 2023 by a former intelligence official that successive administrations engaged in a cover-up, and that the government had possession of crashed alien spacecraft.

Friday’s release contained fewer than 25 text documents, and no videos or images.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Macron condemns racism after one killed in ‘terrorist’ shooting near Paris
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Angelique Chrisafis in Paris
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Gunman opens fire from car in Trappes and Verrière, killing one and injuring five others, including a 12-year-old girl

Emmanuel Macron has condemned racism in French society after a gunman opened fire from a car west of Paris on Friday, killing one person, wounding a 12-year-old girl and injuring four others in what the president called a “racist terrorist attack”.

Macron arrived at the scene of the drive-by shooting in Trappes, a town west of Paris, on Friday night, saying he was deeply saddened by what he called the “premeditated” attack. The 12-year-old girl, who was shot eight times, is being treated in hospital.

“What happened today ​marks a turning point for our ⁠country; what happened today ​was ​a terrorist ​and racist attack,” ​Macron said.

He said the gunman had targeted people because of the colour of their skin. The president said racism had often become part of the “ambient discourse in France” and created “an atmosphere”. He said: “Don’t let this terrorist attack divide us.” He called for “respect and unity”, saying many French people would be scared and thinking “this could happen to me”.

Ali Rabeh, the leftwing mayor of Trappes, said that the gunman had set out by car on Friday morning “firing at random, wanting to cause a bloodbath” as he drove through the town and neighbouring La Verrière. The mayor called it “objectively a racist attack, probably Islamophobic”.

Rabeh, whose family has Moroccan roots, said: “The people targeted today could just as easily have been my mother, my brothers or my sisters-in-law.

“A 12-year-old girl is between life and death after being targeted by a volley of automatic gunfire in our country. Her crime was probably being of colour,” he added. “It’s probably one of the first attempts at a mass crime of Islamophobia and racism.”

Rabeh said everyone in France had a responsibility to bring “calm and harmony”. He called for a collective condemnation of rhetoric that “ideologically arms those capable of carrying out such acts”.

Anti-terrorism prosecutors are investigating whether the gunman targeted the “real or supposed race, ethnicity, nationality or religion” of the victims.

The 39-year-old suspect, who was stopped by police in his car, was named by France’s anti-terrorism prosecutor as Kevin T. He had driven through the towns of Trappes and La Verrière in Yvelines at about 10.30am on Friday. Over the course of 15 minutes, he repeatedly fired an automatic weapon, first at a petrol station, then a medical centre and a children’s playground.

The French public broadcaster reported that he shot dead a young black man, then targeted a woman wearing a headscarf, before shooting the 12-year-old girl, who was being treated for her eight gunshot wounds at a children’s hospital on Friday night. The prosecutor said in a statement on Friday night that the medical status of the five wounded victims was not stable. Rabeh said the man killed was “of African origin” and that another of the wounded was “of north African origin”.

Nicolas Dainville, the mayor of La Verrière, told Agence France-Presse that two of the wounded people in his town were cleaners of African origin attending to a school Friday on morning when the shooter got out of his car to open fire.

The prosecutor said that when the suspect was stopped by police in his car he was found with a sten gun – a British submachine gun used in the second world war – as well as teargas grenades. The man had also booby-trapped his home with gas canisters and electric wires connected to a timer, authorities said, adding that a member of his family was arrested and taken into custody for questioning.

“The investigations are ongoing, but it is clearly a terrorist crime. It is an extremely serious act,” the interior minister, Laurent Nunez, told reporters from ⁠Yvelines.

The ‌shooting comes at a moment of particular tension in France. Last Saturday saw one of the most violent days of unrest in years, which left public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted, and at least 2,400 people arrested in cities across the country. Renewed protests, over teacher shortages and crumbling buildings in high schools as well as the high cost of living, are expected on Saturday.

Marine Le Pen, the leader of the far-right anti-immigration the National Rally party, is polling highly ahead of next spring’s presidential election when Macron steps down.

After the Trappes attack, Fabien Roussel, a Communist candidate, wrote on social media that the far right was responsible for “racist hatred” in France.

Le Pen condemned what she called the “abject motive of racism” of the “barbaric act”.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Aaron Rodgers says NFL’s Paris game is safe despite PSG cancellation amid unrest
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Guardian sport and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
The NFL would have cancelled its first regular-season game in Paris, scheduled for Sunday, if the situation were unsafe, Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers said on Friday, referring to the recent protests in the French capital.

France experienced some of its worst urban unrest in years last weekend, prompting President Emmanuel Macron to tighten restrictions on protests on Thursday amid fears that demonstrations planned for Saturday could turn violent.

The unrest has already forced the postponement of Sunday’s Ligue 1 match between Paris Saint-Germain and Lyon, which has been moved to Monday night at the request of local police. Authorities cited security concerns and the strain on police resources over a weekend that will also see the NFL stage its first regular-season game in France.

The demonstrations have been driven by anger over the rising cost of living, deteriorating conditions in public schools and teacher shortages. Some estimates put the number of protesters who marched last weekend at 800,000.

The Steelers face the New Orleans Saints at the Stade de France in Saint-Denis on Sunday, around 10km from central Paris.

The four-time NFL MVP said he was confident the game would go ahead as planned.

“I definitely think that the NFL is alert to what’s going on,” he told a press conference on Friday.

“This game means a lot to the NFL. If it was unsafe, then I’m sure we wouldn’t be here.”

The NFL said last week that preparations were continuing as scheduled despite the unrest. “We continue to work closely with local authorities and partners on all operational and security matters,” the league said, adding that there had been “no disruption or impact at league sites”.

The game in Paris has been largely overshadowed by the nationwide protests, with new demonstrations planned for Saturday. The Steelers informed fans on Thursday that a “Steelers House” fan event in the Bastille neighbourhood would not go ahead.

The US state department issued a security alert on Thursday night, calling on its citizens to “avoid demonstrations and areas of unrest”.

“Americans in Paris for the NFL game on Sunday, October 25 should also exercise caution and be aware of their surroundings,” the state department added.

Many Americans and other foreign visitors have travelled to France to watch Sunday’s game despite the protests.

Fred Zelt, a 67-year-old Steelers fan at the NFL House set up in Paris, arrived in the French capital a week ago.

“We saw [last Saturday] a march of probably several hundred students. It was completely peaceful,” he told Reuters.

“Every place we’ve been seemed calm and normal to us. We now see shops boarding up windows.

“There are lots of people out. People are having a good time and we’re not overly worried.”

Fabian Bauer, a 28-year-old Saints fan, travelled from Germany with his parents.

“We had a long discussion about whether we should come here or not,” he said. “In the end, I informed myself, and most of the fans said it’s likely to be safe, especially on Sunday.

“It’s not as bad as one might have thought. The shop windows are a bit damaged.”

The NFL pop-up store in Paris will be closed on Saturday, the league said on Friday.

Monika Allen, a 56-year-old Steelers fan, was on her way to the shop on Friday to buy “more Steelers clothes”, saying she “didn’t prepare for the cold and the wind”.

The unrest is not the only thing that has disrupted the build-up to the game, with Storm Austen hitting parts of the country. Météo-France, the national weather agency, has issued orange alerts for much of the country’s north-west, including the Paris region.

The Steelers landed in France on Friday morning. They were due to practise at the Stade de France before holding a press conference.

They eventually cancelled their training session because of bad weather, and the press conference was moved to their hotel in Paris.

The Saints have been practising this week in Versailles after arriving in France on Monday.

“Due to elevated wind and rain conditions, in accordance with local authorities, there will not be a media viewing portion during today’s Saints practice,” the Saints said in a statement.

“NFL Experience Paris presented by Wilson is closed for the rest of today due to adverse weather. Please do not attend the site,” the NFL said in a statement.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: NWSL drops controversial criteria around ‘Rodman Rule’ in settlement with NWSLPA
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Ella Brockway
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
The NWSL and the NWSL Players Association have reached a settlement to drop the restrictive criteria around the controversial High Impact Player (HIP) rule, allowing any player to earn the league’s highest salaries.

The NWSL introduced the rule late last year, allowing teams to spend an additional $1m above the salary cap to sign star players. Players with the designation had to meet one of eight criteria, ranging from US national team minutes and Ballon d’Or recognition to NWSL Best XI honors to media lists, including the Guardian’s Top 100 and a ranking that ordered athletes by marketability.

The NWSLPA opposed the mechanism and filed a grievance, arguing that the classification of players was a violation of federal labor law and the existing collective bargaining agreement. About 100 players had qualified for the designation based on the criteria – a total that, at the time the rule was introduced, included the likes of Trinity Rodman and Sophia Wilson but would have excluded such players as two-time NWSL MVP Sam Kerr and US star Catarina Macario.

Under the settlement, which was announced Friday, the eligibility criteria were eliminated. Beginning 1 January 2027, clubs will be able to designate any player as a High Impact Player, so long as their salary equals at least 12% of the base salary cap. The league can also set a limit on the number of HIP players per club.

The two sides settled six grievances in total, including one over the rejection of a contract proposal between the Washington Spirit and Rodman. Another involved the league’s footwear policy, which had dictated what brands players could wear during games.

“This settlement is certainly evidence of the NWSLPA’s strength and commitment to enforcing the terms of the Collective Bargaining Agreement,” NWSLPA director Meghann Burke told ESPN, which was the first to report news of the settlement.

“Disagreements are a natural part of any mature labor relationship, particularly in a league that is growing and evolving as quickly as ours,” NWSL executive vice-president Bill Ordower said in a statement. “What matters is how you work through them. This agreement gives the players, clubs and league greater clarity and certainty moving forward, while protecting the integrity and competitive balance that is fundamental to the NWSL.”

The initial version of the HIP Rule was introduced by the league last December. It allowed teams to spend $1m above the salary cap – for the 2026 season, set at $3.7m – to keep star players amid a wave of talent departing for Europe, where teams are not bound by salary caps.

The rule was ratified by the league’s board of governors and went into effect on 1 July. It became known informally as the “Rodman Rule” because its introduction coincided with the Washington Spirit star’s prolonged contract saga this past offseason.

Rodman had received lucrative offers from teams in Europe that the Spirit could not have matched under the NWSL’s salary cap rules. In November, before the HIP rule was introduced, the Spirit attempted to re-sign Rodman to a deal that would have averaged more than $1m annually, but NWSL commissioner Jessica Berman blocked the offer and said it violated the league’s rules because of its backloaded structure. The NWSLPA filed a grievance on Rodman’s behalf, calling the refusal a “flagrant violation” of player free agency rights.

Weeks later, the league introduced the HIP rule. Rodman re-signed with the Spirit in January on a record deal worth more than $2m annually.

The union grievance over the initial refusal of Rodman’s contract remained open after she signed the new contract. While teams are not required to disclose who is signed using the HIP mechanism, several players who would have been eligible under the criteria have since been signed or re-signed by teams in the league, including Denver’s Lindsey Heaps, Orlando’s Barbra Banda and Gotham’s Rose Lavelle.

The league will still have the ability to reject contracts for salary cap circumvention, but it must notify the union of the decision and provide an explanation within 72 hours. The league will also be required to provide salary cap and revenue updates to its clubs throughout the year.

The settlement also addressed the league’s footwear policy. Throughout this season, some players have received warnings and fines for wearing cleats from brands that were not official sponsors. The league will now honor pre-existing endorsement deals for most players and withdraw previous fines.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: ‘A different kid’: from karting to F1 champion-elect, Antonelli’s ability has always stood out
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Giles Richards in Austin
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
With first drivers’ title all but secure, a friendlier champion would be hard to find, but Italian’s eight wins this season speak to his focus

Even as Kimi Antonelli may be world champion-elect, it is sometimes hard to equate the young man who has driven with such exceptional skill and no little verve to touching distance of an historic first Formula One title with the smiling, wide-eyed kid with tousled hair who still almost looks out of place in the F1 paddock. Yet what has become clear in this extraordinary season is that Antonelli’s talent and his personable, endearing character are inextricably entwined.

Whether the Italian seals his place as F1’s youngest world champion, at 20 years old, at this Sunday’s US Grand Prix in Austin or the next round in Mexico or even beyond that is moot – that he will do so is all but assured and for all that he is still in only his second season in the sport, a more rounded, well-liked champion than the Mercedes driver would be hard to find.

Engage with Antonelli and it is almost impossible not to still see the three-year-old child who insisted on taking to his father Marco’s knee to try out the racing simulator the former driver had brought home. Marco would control the pedals and his son the wheel with an irrepressible enthusiasm that could barely be contained and is still there in every dart, feint and incisive pass he makes today.

Pictures from his childhood in Bologna, a couple of hours’ drive from where his father runs a racing team in San Marino, show whenever Antonelli has a wheel in his hands there is a smile on his face and his eyes alight. His joy is clear and it is a passion that has run clearly through his career. From going karting at the age of five, a meteoric rise through the ranks, being taken on as a Mercedes junior driver aged 12, then making his debut for the team in 2025 after a whirlwind of three years moving from F4, to Formula Regional and then F2.

The faith Mercedes placed in him, not least in that he was stepping into the shoes of the departing seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton, was huge, yet the team principal Toto Wolff had no doubts as to his talent and his character.

“In the past, there was the opinion in F1 that in order to be winning, you need to be an asshole, you need to be ruthless and opportunistic,” he observed this season as Antonelli made a stunning start with five wins on the trot and the entire world was paying attention to the kid who, for many, had come from nowhere. “I don’t think that Kimi is that. It’s just down to driving faster than the others, and being a nice person also.” It is an opinion often echoed by those close to the young Italian. Gwen Lagrue, the talent scout who led Mercedes’ junior driver programme, remembers more than just his remarkable talent from their early encounters.

“With Kimi, I saw almost from day one that I was dealing with a different kid,” Lagrue said. “First, what impressed me, well, amazed me, was his natural presence. He was already having such an impact on everyone in the paddock, you noticed this kid has something different than the others. Everyone liked Kimi, everyone was hugging him. He was like the Kimi you see today when he was 11. He was so passionate about what he was doing, about racing, about F1, everything.”

At the heart of this engaging character it seems is a grounded and emotionally rich relationship with his family. While he was supported in following his racing dreams, he was told unequivocally that if he was to kart on a weekend, school must follow on a Monday until he graduated. He duly did so, completing his maturità school exams just after coming third – his first podium – at the Canadian GP last year.

“Which driver has done the A-levels or the baccalaureate? Name me one that has finished school. No one,” Wolff observed pointedly of his prodigy. The role of his family has clearly been crucial. His father as guide, mentor and, both have admitted, stern taskmaster at times, whom Antonelli has described as his “rock”. But there is also clearly a hugely important relationship with his mother, Veronica, and younger sister Maggie.

“My dad is always going to give me his point of view, he’s going to give me advice and then if I decide to listen, good, but if I don’t decide to listen, it’s OK as well,” he said. “We always have a strong relationship but this is the same with my mum and my sister. The way I am I don’t think I could cope with having a bad relationship with my family member, it’s something that I would really struggle to cope with, that’s why I couldn’t see myself, you know, just taking distance from them.”

Intriguingly, racing was not a direction his father had initially wanted him to go in. Marco had been a quick sportscar driver and almost signed as works driver for two German touring car teams but was unlucky in not getting a shot. “I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation,” he said. “At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport.”

However, having decided to let him pursue the dream, Marco has been there ever since. He is at the track on many weekends and clearly the pair share an easy, close bond with echoes of the one Hamilton shared with his father, Anthony, in his early years. In Hungary, the race after he had risked receiving a penalty for exceeding track limits on his way to a brilliant win in Belgium, Antonelli laughingly recalled his father’s reaction: “He said: ‘Congrats, but …’ Always a but … ‘If I see you doing another track limit for nothing, I’m gonna stretch your neck like a chicken.’”

Antonelli’s boyish honesty has been as engaging as his talent. Wolff has noted his ability to switch into a “race mode”, a zone where he is wholly focused on the task, where he has a daring, aggressive driving style, pushing to the limit and past it, on occasion, but which he always learns from. “We had to teach him instead of always being at 110%, just be at 100%,” Lagrue said which, as Wolff has remarked, is a trait he would rather indulge than having to “take a stick to a donkey”.

Yet alongside that verve Antonelli has shown a maturity beyond his years belied by his character when out of the “zone”. He has displayed the judgment of a veteran while being able to manage the endless adjustments of touch and feel of the car and its balance – especially of these fiendishly complex modern rides – such that he, like many of the greats, has made it look easy.

Watching him do so this season has been a pleasure not least because he is a driver who has taken such untrammelled and infectious joy in doing so. A feeling perhaps summed up by his father, who told La Gazzetta dello Sport just after his son turned 20: “I hope he remains who he is, sweet and generous, and continues to do what he loves for as long as possible.”

Before his extraordinary victory from 19th on the grid at the Italian GP, Antonelli said he wanted to win the championship but that it was important for him to do so by being himself. The latter he can consider a job most admirably well done. The former is only a matter of time.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Indiana police officer arrested for using Flock cameras to search wife
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Marina Dunbar
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Justin Craig charged with official misconduct and fraud, after searching plates of wife and ‘previous acquaintance’

An Indiana police officer has been arrested on allegations that he misused Flock cameras hundreds of times in a case involving his wife and a previous acquaintance of hers.

Georgetown police department officer Justin Craig was charged with official misconduct and two counts of fraud. Documents show that he searched his wife’s license plate more than 80 times and that of a “previous acquaintance” of hers nearly 250 times, the news outlet WLKY reported.

The documents say Craig’s searches started in January and continued up to July.

A reporter from the Washington Post triggered the investigation, the documents show, after he called the Georgetown police chief with the tip.

An internal review by the Georgetown police found that the searches Craig conducted on the Flock system were unrelated to any police investigations, and he had intentionally mislabeled those searches to make them appear justified.

The searches had been labeled with subjects including traffic infractions, narcotics, assault/battery, theft and stolen vehicles.

Flock’s cameras are automated license plate readers (ALPRs), which take pictures of vehicle license plates so police and security companies can log the movement of cars in a given area. There are about 120,000 Flock cameras across the US, which conduct roughly 2bn scans monthly.

Flock, the company behind the tech, provides cameras and software to more than 4,800 law enforcement agencies and nearly 1,000 businesses. Flock says it intends for its technology to aid criminal investigations, but it has come under increasing bipartisan backlash over alleged privacy violations and data-sharing.

There have been multiple reports of police officers across several US states who have allegedly misused or abused the technology. That includes officers who have been accused of using the cameras to stalk former romantic partners and to track down individuals seeking abortions.

The network the cameras feed in to is also frequently utilized by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), whose aggressive tactics under the second Trump administration have drawn nationwide criticism.

After Craig’s arrest, his attorney, Matthew Lemme, released the following statement to multiple news outlets: “Flock sells this same technology to cities, homeowners associations, and shopping malls. When public criticism of it came, the response was to put it on the shoulders of individual police officers. The conduct alleged does not violate any law or department policy.”

The statement continued: “If the public or police agencies believe it should, the answer is to write that law or policy. Having that public conversation about privacy and practice is appropriate. Charging officers before it has even started is not. Officer Craig will file a motion to dismiss the charges against him.”

In August, Flock’s CEO announced the company would be taking steps to curb police abuses of its tech by mandating that law enforcement agencies switch on features that could help audit the way individual officers use its tracking capabilities.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Skye Blakely caps remarkable injury comeback with world gymnastics all-around title
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Guardian sport
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Skye Blakely completed a sensational comeback from a ruptured achilles tendon to win the women’s all-around title at the world gymnastics championships in Rotterdam on Friday, claiming the biggest individual prize in the sport outside the Olympics.

The 21-year-old American scored 55.733 points across four apparatus to finish ahead of Russia’s Liudmila Roshchina (55.199), with China’s Ke Qinqin taking bronze (55.032).

Blakely’s triumph came little more than two years after her Olympic ambitions were shattered when she ruptured her right achilles during floor exercise training, just two days before the US trials for the 2024 Paris Games. The injury required surgery and ended a season in which she had finished runner-up to Simone Biles at the national championships.

It was the second major setback of her career after she tore an elbow ligament while warming up for the Tokyo Olympic trials.

“I already cried, but it just means the world to me,” Blakely said after qualifying at the Rotterdam Ahoy arena. “Knowing how much I’ve been through – two major surgeries, a lot of hardships, ups and downs.”

Blakely entered Friday’s final as the second-ranked qualifier and delivered under pressure, producing assured routines on uneven bars and balance beam before protecting a lead of more than a point on floor exercise.

Her 14.200 on beam, an apparatus that had caused problems during the Americans’ silver-medal finish behind China in Wednesday’s team competition, gave her a commanding advantage heading into the final rotation. A misty-eyed Blakely became overwhelmed by emotion after completing her floor routine, then wrapped herself in an American flag once the result was confirmed.

Algeria’s Kaylia Nemour, the leading qualifier, finished fourth after a mistake on her opening vault forced her to perform a less difficult attempt. She recovered with an outstanding performance on uneven bars but missed bronze by just 0.034 points. Fellow American Claire Pease finished seventh after falling from the balance beam.

Blakely, a University of Florida junior, became the first American to win the world all-around crown since Biles in 2023, extending a US streak of podium finishes at every Olympics and world championships since 2003.

Competition continues on Saturday with the first apparatus finals. Blakely and Pease are set to compete in the women’s vault and uneven bars finals, while Fred Richard will contest the men’s floor exercise and Patrick Hoopes the pommel horse.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Dallas Cowboys cheerleaders unionize after years of fighting for fair pay
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Guardian sport
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
The Dallas Cowboys cheerleaders have unionized after years of advocating for fair pay and better wages.

The Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders Association (DCCA) was voluntarily recognized by the Cowboys as the collective bargaining representative for the cheerleading squad, according to a Friday news release. The recognition came after “meaningful discussion” between the Cowboys organization and the DCCA, and the parties are set to begin collective bargaining.

“The Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders are an esteemed part of the Cowboys organization, deeply respected for the talent and dedication they exhibit,” the DCCA said in a statement. “They remain one of the most sought-after opportunities for talented dancers worldwide.”

Established in 1961, one year after the football team played its inaugural season in the NFL, the Cowboys cheerleaders are among the most recognizable dance groups in the world. They are showcased in a Netflix series, America’s Sweethearts: Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders, which released its third season in June. The show has offered a glimpse into the lives of the squad members, many of whom hold full-time jobs in addition to being cheerleaders, and shed light on their years of fighting for fair pay.

In 2018, cheerleader Erica Wilkins filed a federal fair wage lawsuit against the Cowboys, who are the NFL’s most valuable franchise at $17bn, per Forbes. Wilkins claimed she averaged $15,000 during her seasons with Dallas and said she made less money than the team’s male mascot.

The Netflix series’ second season followed contract negotiations for the 36-member team – including threats of a walkout – and ended with the squad receiving a 400% pay raise, increasing the hourly rate for some members from $15 per hour for the 2024 season to $75 per hour. One squad member told the New York Times that while the new contract increased wages for game day appearances, it did not provide health insurance.

The Cowboys cheerleaders are not the first in the NFL to form a union. In 1995, the National Labor Relations Board ruled that the Buffalo Bills cheerleaders could unionize. The Buffalo Jills, as they were known, joined the National Football League Cheerleaders Association. The union was short-lived and the Jills squad disbanded in 2014.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Enciso rescues point in storm for Ipswich to deny Nottingham Forest
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: John Brewin at Portman Road
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Amid a Suffolk squall, winds whipping in, a constant drum of rain, an encounter full of half-chances, mistakes and questions. Do Ipswich have the stones to deal with the big league this time? Perhaps so. How long can Nottingham Forest’s dip sustain before their president, Evangelos Marinakis, takes his usual course of action. Perhaps not much longer.

Ipswich’s Gary O’Neil should be the happier manager, Forest creating the cleaner opportunities, only for familiar failings to count against them. A first-half exchange of goals, both owing much to defensive laxness, determined the result.

A long time since 1978, that year’s FA Cup winners taking on the First Division champions. So many shifting sands since, Ipswich’s aim is to establish themselves as Forest have in the Premier League. Liam Delap’s presence in the Forest ranks, the striker barracked on every touch, served as a reminder of the failed mission of two seasons ago.

Not that Forest or their manager can be presumptive. Oliver Glasner’s team had collected five points from seven matches, a single win. A record of starting slow only to flourish at previous clubs has offered protection, though Forest’s ownership is not like others. Wednesday was the anniversary of Sean Dyche’s appointment. That tenure lasted just 100 days. At Portman Road Glasner reached 40.

The return of Morgan Gibbs-White, missing against Arsenal, was welcome as perhaps was playing away from the City Ground, where form continues to be rotten, whoever the manager. Forest kicked off as lowest scorers in the division, no side had drawn a blank more often.

Their drought did not take long to break. Early stages had seen both teams’ No 10s to the fore, Julio Enciso firing wide, Gibbs-White creating forcing an early chance for Delap to miss the target. Ipswich’s soft centre had been exposed and Neco Williams’s goal came via an overlap and a looping cross from Daniel Muñoz, the player Glasner brought with him from Crystal Palace. Williams glided in unmarked, his low finish true.

Another Forest goal appeared the likelier though Gibbs-White cutting inside and booming his shot wide drew a response from Ipswich. Home fans, previously exasperated, were lifted by Jaden Philogene forcing a save from Matz Sels and then Enciso dancing through red shirts to force another. Pushing onwards left gaps, only Leif Davis’s goalline intervention stopped Gibbs-White’s goalbound shot.

The equaliser came via the collective loss of concentration characteristic of Forest’s 11 October defeat at Crystal Palace. Jair Cunha gallivanted forward, adrenaline coursing, his touch eventually betraying him. Dara O’Shea’s clearance was poorly dealt with by Nikola Milenkovic, the resulting back-pass even more slack. It was left to Enciso to exhibit calm.

Forest failing to claim rewards on offer from the first half told a familiar story. So too are repeated refereeing controversies, and attendant howls of conspiracy among their supporters. How the officials, led by Thomas Bramall the referee, did not view Issa Diop’s clattering of James McAtee, clean through, as a foul defied belief. More understandable, if still highly debatable, was the verdict via video assistant that McAtee had lost possession as the collision came. Diop’s yellow card and a resultant free-kick that came to naught were little consolation.

Injustice, though, did fuel Forest, both Williams and Murillo firing in shots among a flurry of chances. Murillo missed a far easier chance when granted a free header from a corner, before Davis made another last-ditch intervention when Dan Ndoye, in open space, had beaten Christian Walton.

That asked the staying power from Ipswich that brought wins from Sunderland, Crystal Palace and Fulham. So far, they have been the soft touch under Gary O’Neil as they became in Kieran McKenna’s survival attempt.

That asked the staying power from Ipswich that brought wins from Sunderland, Crystal Palace and Fulham. So far, they have not been the soft touch under Gary O’Neil as they became in Kieran McKenna’s survival attempt.

Delap leapt highest to seize on a mistake by Abdoul Ouatarra, only to head wide. More jeers, more following when a barrelling run was followed by a shot wide. Williams’ night came to an end after an awkward fall among a flurry of late substitutions

One of the arrivals, Callum Hudson-Odoi, as eight minutes of injury-time were added, received the time and space to do far better than fire wide. The story of the night for Forest and of their season.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Father who killed Oregon school shooter speaks out for first time: ‘I have to go in’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Dani Anguiano
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Kaylub Giamanco recounts the day he confronted the Silver Rail elementary school shooter, who killed three boys and one teacher

The Oregon father hailed as a hero for stopping a school shooting last week spoke for the first time about the incident, describing his experience and how he told a 911 operator: “I have to go in. People are going to die.”

Kaylub Giamanco, a 36-year-old carpenter, has received national attention and praise for stopping the bloodshed at Silver Rail elementary in Bend, Oregon, where his children attend school.

He fatally shot Griffin J John II, a 16-year-old former student at the school, who broke in and shot six people, killing Megan Lambert, a 25-year-old teacher, and three children, including five-year-old Rhoam Summer.

In an interview with Oregon Public Broadcasting (OPB), his first since the 15 October shooting, he recounted that day. He told reporters that he was only in the area because he had decided to return home and eat lunch with his wife rather than the meal he brought to work that day.
