https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Rosanna Greenstreet
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
The beauty entrepreneur on why she wears three wedding rings, her fear of running out of HRT, and what put her off being a midwife

Born in Liverpool, Caroline Hirons, 57, moved to London at 17. In 1997, she joined the Aveda counter in Harvey Nichols and went on to train as an aesthetician. She started a blog in 2010 and, 10 years later, published her first book, which won the nonfiction lifestyle prize at the British Book Awards in 2021. In 2022, she launched the Skin Rocks app and skincare line. Her new book is Skin Rules: Expert Advice That You Can Trust. She is separated with four children, and lives in London.

What is the trait you most deplore in yourself? I can be a tad impatient, and my team would say that’s an understatement.

What is the trait you most deplore in others? I have a long list: misogyny, homophobia, rudeness, greed, arrogance, ignorance.

Aside from a property, what’s the most expensive thing you’ve bought? I do like a handbag. The brand begins with H and ends with èrmes.

What is your most treasured possession? My trio of wedding rings I wear every day – my mum’s, my grandmother’s, mine. I’m separated, but still have the ring because it gave me my kids.

Who is your celebrity crush? Colin Farrell – and I hope he reads this. I hear he likes an older woman.

What do you most dislike about your appearance? I strongly advocate looking at what we like about our appearance rather than what we don’t like.

Who would play you in the film of your life? Queen Latifah, and the menopause years would be played by Denzel Washington.

What is your most unappealing habit? Interrupting people. I have ADHD and I sometimes have to physically bite my tongue and cover my mouth because my instinct is to join in.

What did you want to be when you were growing up? A midwife. And then I had a baby and thought, sod that.

What is the worst thing anyone’s said to you? “I’m very sorry but your mother has passed.”

Have you ever said ‘I love you’ and not meant it? No, I’m very tight with “I love you”.

Which living person do you most despise, and why? So that I can still travel, I would say the majority of old white male politicians.

If you could edit your past, what would you change? In the words of Helen Mirren, I’d tell more people to fuck off.

What do you consider your greatest achievement? Leaving school at 15 and going on to found and run two multimillion-pound businesses.

What keeps you awake at night? Nothing. I’m old, tired and on progesterone so I can sleep.

What is the most important lesson life has taught you? That it’s fucking short. Don’t have any fear. Crack on.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Verse from Qu’ran inspired US man to leap on runaway school bus and halt it
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Ebro Ahmed, who acted after driver’s medical emergency, said he hopes incident will show Eritreans ‘in a good way’

A man who hopped on to a school bus full of terrified children that was careering down a Minnesota street after its driver had a medical emergency and manually halted it says he was motivated to act by a Qu’ran verse about how saving one life is equivalent to saving all of humanity.

“I’m a numbers guy, and those numbers make sense to me,” Ebro Ahmed, 27, said on Friday during an interview about his actions four days earlier in front of his family’s convenience store in Saint Paul, Minnesota. “I didn’t do it for me. It was selflessness in the name of God.”

In a dramatic sequence of events captured on surveillance video by the shop, Ahmed was kicking a soccer ball and scrolling on his cellphone during a break outside his family’s Ya Bricks Snacks and Tobacco store on Monday afternoon when he noticed a yellow school bus passing by with its door flung open.

Ahmed said he deduced something was wrong when he saw the bus driver with foam coming out of his mouth, which can be a symptom of a seizure. He recalled instinctively sprinting to the bus; leaping through the door; and tossing his phone and glasses at two girls in the front to free his hands.

His first thought was to see if he could somehow shift the bus into park. But, with frightened boys and girls screaming all around him, Ahmed said he pulled the emergency brake on the bus, bringing the vehicle to a stop without anyone onboard or on the street being injured.

A statement from Saint Paul’s public school district on Friday confirmed there had been a medical emergency on the bus outside Ahmed’s family store that day that required paramedics to respond. Another bus came to pick up the 19 students onboard and bring them home, the district said.

Meanwhile, the driver was resting at home after being brought to a hospital and discharged.

The National Safety Council estimates that about 20.3 million children ride school buses across the US daily – a number large enough for driver-related emergencies to occasionally occur.

When such emergencies do happen, quick-thinking and -acting bystanders can often help avert disaster.

The local news outlet KTSP obtained and published the surveillance video of Ahmed running on to the runaway bus. That footage went viral alongside an interview that the station did with Ahmed, in which he credited the medical TV drama Grey’s Anatomy with teaching him “what to do in situations that you could never see yourself in”.

Ahmed elaborated with the Guardian on Friday, saying the Qu’ran verse declaring that “whoever saves a life, it will be as if they saved all of humanity” also entered his mind at the moment he decided to intervene on Monday.

Furthermore, he mentioned how challenging it had been for his parents – who are immigrants from the east African country of Eritrea – to run a store in Saint Paul during the mass deportation campaign pursued by Donald Trump during his second presidency.

Ahmed, who said he was US-born, added that business at the store had dropped ever since federal immigration agents at the forefront of that campaign descended on Saint Paul and nearby Minneapolis as part of what the Trump administration dubbed Operation Metro.

But Ahmed described a welcome sense of relief taking the opportunity to – as he called it – portray Eritreans and represent Eritreans and east Africans “in a good way”.

He alluded to a local marketing and media company donating $1,000 to him as a token of appreciation for his bus heroics – a presentation which involved a Superman performer and a novelty check.

Ahmed said he had been invited to speak on at least one panel, and a city council member had contacted him to congratulate him. An uncle in Europe did, too, after learning of what Ahmed had done on the news.

Perhaps most meaningful to Ahmed, he said, was seeing his story trend among Eritrean circles.

“It makes me proud to be able to represent them in a good way,” Ahmed remarked.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Tom Kean had everything going for him. Then the Republican New Jersey congressman disappeared
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ariana Baio in New Jersey
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Even with a multimillion-dollar war chest, the US representative faces a stiff fight for his seat from Democrat Rebecca Bennett

The Republican congressman had a war chest of more than $2.4m in February, an endorsement from Donald Trump and a district whose lines were redrawn in 2022 to benefit his party. He was an established political figure with widespread name recognition, thanks to his father’s stint as a well-regarded governor of New Jersey.

Kean, 58, was not seen in Congress, or public, for more than three months and missed 100 votes without explanation – as Trump’s war on Iran piled pressure on the US economy, and the president threatened fresh tariffs on global imports.

Democrats meanwhile selected a moderate, Rebecca Bennett, to challenge Kean for his seat. Kean, who resurfaced at the end of June, is now in the midst of a tight race in one of the wealthiest districts in the nation.

In an ominous sign for Republicans, the closely watched Cook Political Report moved New Jersey’s seventh congressional district from “toss-up” to “lean Democrat” last month.

Most Republicans fighting for re-election while aligned with Trump are grappling with the impact of the president’s growing unpopularity. His war with Iran has driven the cost of fuel and groceries up, angering the voters who were promised lower prices under his administration.

But Kean has also endured months of discourse – and national headlines – over his prolonged absence, and reserved public appearances. When he returned at the end of June, the congressman said he had been hospitalized for depression.

“I think mental health issues aside, which are serious ... I don’t think he handled the issue very well,” said Albie, a New Jersey voter attending a No Kings protest in New Providence last weekend.

Mike Johnson, the Republican speaker of the House of Representatives, appeared to agree in August. “You know, if it were me, I would have done it a little sooner,” he told the New York Times of Kean’s reluctance to explain his absence.

Johnson, like many, is sympathetic to Kean’s health condition, which affects millions of Americans.

Since his return, Kean has been accused of avoiding the media spotlight. His campaign denied a New York Times reporter entry to an event attended by other media outlets in August; he refused to take questions from reporters after participating in a livestreamed debate against Bennett, his Democratic opponent.

The Guardian sent two emails to Kean’s campaign requesting an interview, or the opportunity to attend a campaign event. They went unanswered.

Harrison Neely, Kean’s campaign manager, did not respond to an initial text message containing the same requests earlier this week. He did, however, respond to a second message asking for a brief interview on Thursday.

“I think the narrative that congressman Kean doesn’t engage with the press is simply false,” said Neely, adding that the campaign prefers to communicate with voters directly. (On Thursday, New York Magazine published an article saying its multiple requests for an interview went ignored.)

Kean does give interviews, mostly to local reporters, and the campaign has invited local outlets to cover events. Neely said the campaign most recently challenged Bennett to a debate on WRNJ, a local radio station. However, the Bennett campaign declined to participate.

“So you know, I think it’s basically fair to say that congressman Kean does more local press engagements than any sitting member of the New Jersey delegation,” Neely said.

Bennett, a political newcomer, is cautiously optimistic that she can flip a battleground district in New Jersey for the Democrats in next month’s midterm.

“We’re going to do everything we can for the next 16 days to flip the seat, but we are feeling good about where we are,” Bennett told reporters after a meet-and-greet with voters in Basking Ridge last Sunday. “We’re seeing a ton of momentum and enthusiasm on the ground.”

Bennett, 39, is a former Navy helicopter pilot and aircraft commander. She’s also a former executive at an online healthcare company.

Democrats in the state are hopeful her moderate stance can appeal to the district’s voters, especially because many 2024 Trump voters have expressed discontent with the economy.

Bennett said she often hears “deeply frustrated” voters bring up Kean’s willingness to let Trump unleash his agenda, such as voting for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, continuing the war with Iran or not doing enough to stop Trump from halting funding for the Gateway Hudson Tunnel Project between New Jersey and New York.

“I understand the challenges that we’re facing because my family is dealing with them too,” said Bennett. “My oldest kid’s in public school. My youngest is in daycare. And so when we talk about the cost-of-living crisis we’re dealing with, this is not abstract talking points on a page – this is my life.”

But nothing is certain in New Jersey’s seventh congressional district, which has seesawed between Republican and Democratic representatives since 2018. The district voted for Trump by a slim majority in 2024, and also elected Mikie Sherrill – its Democratic governor – in 2025.

The Congressional Leadership Fund – the Super Pac dedicated to helping House Republicans – and the Safety and Affordability Pac, affiliated with Trump, have reportedly canceled remaining funding for Kean’s district.

When asked about the pulled funding by the New Jersey Globe, Kean dismissed concerns, pointing to $6.2m in funding from the National Republican Congressional Committee.

Neely also expressed confidence. “If you take a step back and look at the facts, Republicans have outspent Democrats in this district to this point,” he said. “Our campaign is fully funded down the home stretch, and will be matching the Bennett campaign dollar for dollar on the airwaves.”

As Kean’s campaign pushed back against the claim he doesn’t engage with the media, before reaching Neely by phone this week, the Guardian spent time driving around the district one weekend earlier this month.

There appeared to be something in the air: a lack of Tom Kean Jr lawn signs in the Trump-friendly Bedminster area, and an autumnal breeze that appeared more present than his campaign.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘It was so magical’: the 33-year-old who made history swimming the length of California
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Lois Beckett in Los Angeles
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Ultra-endurance swimmer Catherine Breed navigated waves, wildlife and pollution to become the first person to swim from state’s northern-most tip to Mexico border

Nearly four months ago, Catherine Breed, a 33-year-old from the San Francisco Bay Area, set out to become the first person to swim the entire coastline of California – from its northern-most tip to the border with Mexico. She and her support team prepared for encounters with sharks and storms. They hadn’t anticipated completing the marathon swim during a year of historic super El Niño weather.

But after dodging hurricanes, wildlife and 8ft waves in an unusually volatile Pacific Ocean, Breed finally celebrated the end of her journey on a beach in San Diego on Monday.

Breed joins a group of elite ultra-endurance swimmers who continue to set new records for long-distance swims, including swimming the entire coastlines of Ireland and Iceland and one side of New Zealand’s North Island – all journeys of close to 1,000 miles (1,600km).

Breed spoke to the Guardian this week about living onboard the Catalyst, the sailboat that accompanied her, her physical and mental preparations for her 111-day swim, and what she thought about while spending more than 15 weeks in the water. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

On your website, you talk about the desire to be part of “an elite group of humans who have been the first to accomplish a monumental feat”. What does that feel like now that you’ve done it?

It is a little bit of an out-of-body experience. Like, I know I’m the one who did it, but there are parts of me where I feel like I’m along with the audience, watching this thing happen. I think I’m still trying to grasp what I’ve done.

How did you get the idea to swim the full length of California, which no one has ever done before?

Other people showed me that the model was possible. Ross Edgley swam around Great Britain. Sean Conway and Jasmine Harrison swam the length of Britain. [In 2022] I did a swim down the California coast from the Golden Gate Bridge to Half Moon Bay, and it made me realize how much fun I had during that, and I was like: I want to try to do this with the coast.

In college, my coach used to say you only get so many energy units per day. Overthinking or excessive thinking or negative thinking – that can take some of that energy you have. During these marathon swims, I try to keep my thoughts very focused on the task at hand. Coaching myself to get to the next 30 minutes, coaching myself to do the next 2 miles, and kind of like celebrating those little moments. When the conditions were really rough, there was a lot of thought around my technique, because I really had to adjust how I was swimming to not wreck my shoulders in the big waves.

I had earplugs on, so I couldn’t hear the crew. But one thing I could hear very clearly was dolphins. And so there were many occasions where I would hear the dolphins before the crew could see them. And I would look up and I’d be like, you guys, incoming, there’s dolphins.

At points, you were swimming through 6-8ft waves, which you have described as feeling like you were in a washing machine. What is it like to swim in those conditions?

If I’m swimming into the swell, it feels like you’re swimming up a hill. But if it’s behind me, then it’s actually very fun because it feels like I’m surfing. So it really depended on the conditions. When you’ve got a lot of wind and a lot of swell, the waves can crash on you from the back or the side or the front. And it does take a lot of effort to keep my body in the right position. One day a wave picked me up, and I landed on my butt.

I’ve been marathon swimming for 10 years. I grew up swimming, I grew up sailing. So my whole life has been in the ocean. So those moments, they’re difficult, but I’m comfortable. I surf a lot. And so I think surfers are comfortable with waves and they understand kind of just wave mechanics and moving with the ocean.

I think the challenging part of the swell was not so much as swimming, but that there’s no chance of recovery [with living on a boat]. Getting ready to swim is really hard – like you’re trying to make breakfast and you’re falling over, your coffee’s spilling. Even putting my wetsuit on is a challenge in itself.

Yes. Many days. [She laughs.] But for myself, I committed to this goal, and my team committed to being part of it. And so, the days I didn’t want to get in it, it didn’t matter what my emotions were, because this project is bigger than just me.

You swam the English Channel in 2018 and the North Channel crossing between north Ireland and Scotland in 2019. How was preparing for this California challenge different from preparing for those classic marathon swims?

For my other swims, I did follow English Channel rules: it was just one cap, bathing suit, goggles. So that preparation required a lot of cold adaptation, and spending hours in the San Francisco Bay being comfortable to be in those conditions for a long time. In California, I’m wearing a wetsuit, so I didn’t have to focus so much on the cold training. I focused more on putting on muscle, and ensuring my body composition was going to benefit me for the swim. So the training was a little less swimming than my other marathon swims, and more time in the gym.

Swimming down in San Diego by the Imperial Beach and Tijuana River and knowing about the sewage pollution crisis [where billions of gallons of raw sewage and toxic chemicals flow from the river into the ocean] – that was probably the most nerve-wracking, because, though we were 3 miles offshore and I was taking prophylactic antibiotics, I still was so scared about my health. And then, you know, any moments that the team spotted a shark fin.

The team just says: “Shark!” And within five seconds – definitely less than 10 seconds – I’m out of the water. Then we observe the situation. And if we see the shark again, then we were just done for the day. That only happened once in four months. So it really was the most insignificant part of the trip.

Our biggest shark deterrent is the fact that I was swimming right next to a 52ft sailboat. And on the other side of me, I had a tender in the water. Ultimately, the sharks just really weren’t interested in me.

You’ve spoken out on your social media accounts about the assumption that sharks are the biggest threats to your swim. Why do you think that’s the wrong focus?

The pollution definitely made me more uncomfortable than any shark sightings ever did. It’s so interesting how people focus so much on sharks when sharks have been in the water with humans for a really long time. We’re so concerned about them, but we should be more concerned about what damage we’re causing to our planet and our home.

Outside populated cities like San Diego and Los Angeles, we saw trash and plastic pollution every day, all day. It was astounding. I think we picked up over 10 Mylar balloons in one day. I had no idea there were that many in the ocean.

You did not plan to do this swim during a year of extreme super El Niño weather, but that’s what happened. How did that change your experience?

The California coastal current historically goes north to south. That’s why we picked the direction. But with the super El Niño, all of the tropical storms and hurricanes that happened this year, instead we were fighting this insane current that is pushing against us. We had to do a lot of problem-solving and pivoting to make forward progress: some of our sections, we did the opposite way. [Breed swam some daily segments of the journey backwards, south to north, allowing her to go with the current, rather than against it.]

You were swimming down the coast during a summer of massive tropical storms in the Pacific, with giant waves that have wrecked havoc on southern California’s beaches. How did you handle that?

We had some days where we knew there was going to be really bad weather, and so we just didn’t even go out that day. I can think of four or five days where we started to swim – for example, during Hurricane Rachel, we were supposed to be able to swim until 2.30pm. But then the wind went from about 10 knots to 25 knots (11mph to 29mph) in about seven minutes. And so the team was like: we’ve got to get out. We need to get to harbor.

I’ve had manta rays swim around me. In Morro Bay, a humpback whale and her calf swam right next to me. I could see them diving. It was so magical. In Santa Barbara, a pod of bottlenose dolphins came and played with us for about 10 minutes. It really felt like the ocean was welcoming us.

From Humboldt [county] all the way to Point Concepción, we probably saw anywhere from five to 10 whales a day. I think the most we saw on a day maybe was like 50. We would have whales come swim right under the boat.

No, it’s not lonely. It’s absolutely the opposite of a solo expedition. It requires a huge team and it requires a team that I literally trust with my life. Yes, I was in the water for four to five hours a day by myself. But when I got out, I was surrounded by just this incredible team of women. And through the difficult, through the tough, we still found moments to connect with laughter and just bring some lightness to the whole swim.

https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.title: Forget the Live Aid image, Africa is only a broken continent in the minds of the west | Moky Makura
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.author: Moky Makura
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.text:
Innovators and business leaders are driving progress across the continent-wide, but the ‘visibility gap’ prevents the rest of the world from truly seeing it

Thirty years ago, shortly after South Africa emerged from apartheid, I left London for Johannesburg in search of a better life. Not long afterwards, a friend who was preparing to visit from the UK called with an intriguing question: do they have ATMs in South Africa?

After I picked myself off the floor, I explained that not only did South Africa have ATMs, but in many respects its banking system was far more advanced than the one I had left behind in Britain. She was surprised and – dare I say – delighted that she wouldn’t have to lug a wad of cash around South Africa after all.

That moment has stayed with me far longer than it should, because I’ve witnessed too many moments where the continent has persistently surprised and delighted the uninitiated. That’s because, for much of the world, the image of Africa still owes more to Live Aid’s legacy than to the reality.

A study we commissioned by social psychologist Dr Adam Hahn at the University of Bath helps explain why. When people in Britain and the US think about Africa, they disproportionately associate it with economic and political dysfunction, harsh environments and a lack of modernity and culture. Those associations affect whether they want to visit the continent, buy its products or engage with its culture. In their minds, Africa remains a place that is broken, dependent, lacking in agency and apparently in ATMs, too.

Britain may have more ATM’s and higher conventional bank-account ownership, but it was Africa that pioneered one of the biggest innovations in modern finance: mobile money. Kenya showed that millions of people could, in effect leapfrog traditional banking altogether, using their phones to store, send and receive money. Today, sub-Saharan Africa remains the centre of the global mobile-money revolution. And when it comes to new money, Nigeria now ranks third in the world for cryptocurrency adoption, while Britain ranks 17th.

Global investors have noticed the continent’s leadership when it comes to finance and are moving in. We have produced a surprisingly high number of fintech “unicorns” – privately owned startups valued at more than $1bn (£760). Nigeria alone has Flutterwave, OPay, Moniepoint and Interswitch. Investors are not putting billions into African financial technology out of charity; they are backing the entrepreneurs who are not waiting for help to create viable, profitable solutions.

One of those is Aliko Dangote, Africa’s richest man, who has been all over the global media for the world-class refinery he built in Nigeria. The $20bn Dangote refinery is the largest single-train refinery in the world, built in a country that, despite being Africa’s biggest oil producer, spent decades exporting crude oil only to import much of its refined fuel.

Dangote is exceptional in his wealth, the scale of his ambition and visibility he has garnered. But he is not exceptional in spirit. There are thousands of smaller “Dangotes” on the continent: entrepreneurs who see a gap, build something to fill it and, in doing so, move their country forward.

Take Siny Samba, a Senegalese entrepreneur who launched an infant food brand after wondering why virtually all the baby food in her country was imported. She started in her kitchen with banana and millet and in 2018 launched Le Lionceau, creating new markets for local farmers and women’s cooperatives.

In Tanzania, Diana Orembe looked at fruit and vegetables being thrown away and saw fish food. Her company, NovFeed, turns that waste into affordable feed in the agriculture sector and has worked with at least 200 farmers.

In Maiduguri, northern Nigeria, Mustapha Abubakar Gajibo started by converting petrol-powered tricycles to electric. Today his company, African Motor Works, designs and builds electric vehicles, producing about 200 units a month.

Samba, Orembe, Gajibo and thousands like them who are contributing to their countries’ growth, will probably never make international headlines. And that may be one of Africa’s most overlooked challenges: not the absence of progress, but the lack of visibility.

Development experts talk endlessly about Africa’s many gaps – the infrastructure gap, financing gap, skills gap – but perhaps the most consequential gap is the visibility gap: the distance between the Africa today (the one that surprises and delights) and the Africa the world imagines.

Addressing the visibility gap is why the Opportunity Africa initiative was started earlier this year. Its mandate; to make the continent’s progress impossible to overlook by spotlighting the many people – such as Samba, Orembe and Gajibo – the places, the policies and the initiatives moving Africa forward.

Places such as Rwanda, which has rebuilt its reputation around innovation, tourism and digital government. Ethiopia has transformed its agricultural sector and sharply reduced its dependence on imported wheat. Kenya now generates up to 91% of its electricity from renewable sources.

Then there are the policies, the unglamorous government decisions that rarely make headlines: Benin keeping more of its cashews for local processing; Namibia requiring more of its lithium to be processed at home; and Zambia removing fees from state education.

And progress is happening continent-wide through ambitious initiatives. Fifty countries have ratified the African Continental Free Trade Area, making it easier for African businesses to trade with each other. A pan-African payments system now lets them settle transactions in local currencies. And 38 countries have joined the single African air transport market, helping create 108 new intra-African routes since 2022.

And this is just the tip of the iceberg. If my friend was surprised by South Africa 30 years ago, imagine what else has changed and progressed. Through the recent Correct the Map campaign led by Togo, we challenged the world to see Africa differently – quite literally. Now we are asking the world to see us as we truly are.

The #NotWaiting campaign is where you will find the proof point: stories of a continent already building, solving, producing and moving forward.

“I think the people that thought a week ago Barca would thrash us will keep thinking the same thing. I don’t think just for the Paris game, or Madrid’s [4-1 win against] Leipzig, they will change their way of thinking,” said Mourinho, keen to point out he’s been in charge for only a few months whereas that Hansi Flick fella has been at Barca since 2024.

“People look at us like a finished product, but finished products in football are difficult because they are never finished... but they look at us like we’re in an advanced phase of the process,” continued Mourinho, really warming to the task now.

“We’ve been working for three months, out of that you can take pre-season when the players were arriving [back from the World Cup], and the recent international break, then we’ve been together a month-and-a-half, two months...

“This is the start of a product, we’re in an initial phase where the coach is learning, analysing, bit by bit defining paths, the players are learning about the coach... comparing a team in this state [to more established sides], I think is unfair.”

But now some defiance when asked about Barcelona winger Lamine Yamal. The 19-year-old Spain international is in sublime form and hopes to win the Ballon d’Or award on Monday.

“He’s a great player and great players you respect,” added Mourinho. One thing is respecting, another thing is to change plans, structures, forgetting your own essence. That we will not do, neither for him or any other player of great quality we face.”
