Other voter concerns have prevailed but return of Congress likely to see renewed focus on late sex offender’s activities

As US voters head to the polls for crucial and fraught midterm elections, some survivors’ advocates in the Jeffrey Epstein investigation have expressed concern that the scandal could recede into the background.

Political experts believe, however, the Epstein issue is not going away permanently and that many voters can balance day-to-day concerns such as affordability and AI with the scandal involving the late financier and accused sex trafficker whose social circle was widespread among America’s elite.

“My greatest concern is not that the public will forget Jeffrey Epstein, but that the politicians and institutions responsible for accountability will use the chaos of world events as an excuse to move on,” said Spencer Kuvin of Goldlaw, who has represented multiple Epstein survivors.

Kuvin added: “Wars, economic crises and political controversies may dominate the headlines, but they do not erase the suffering of the victims or the unanswered questions about how Epstein and his powerful associates were allowed to operate for decades.

“Justice should not have an expiration date, and it certainly should not be dictated by the news cycle. We cannot allow the Epstein scandal to become yesterday’s news simply because today’s headlines are more urgent.”

Kuvin called for the US government to continue releasing Epstein files – which many have said were excluded from allegedly incomplete disclosures – and for Congress to demand accountability.

“It has been disappointing to have seen attention diverted from Jeffrey Epstein in the past year,” said Jennifer Freeman of Marsh Law, who represents numerous Epstein survivors in litigation surrounding his sexual abuse of teenage girls.

Freeman, however, expressed optimism about the long-term prospects of justice for survivors, saying: “While public attention may have shifted from the Epstein case, given the electoral cycle, I am confident it will command concentration and accountability shortly again.”

Freeman noted that she was continuing to pursue a lawsuit against the US government for alleged negligence “in repeatedly, for decades, dropping the ball on investigating and prosecuting Epstein”. She is also litigating a class-action lawsuit against his estate related to his collection and production of child sex abuse images.

Political experts said that Epstein might get less attention from campaigning politicians and voters, but that it was probably a temporary dip, not a permanent drop-off.

“It really does feel like everything is on fire. I think people can care about several things at once, but what’s directly affecting their lives tends to take priority,” Brittany Martinez, a Republican strategist who works as acting director of Principles First, said. “When they’re worried about gas prices, living costs and whether their government is working for them, that can push Epstein out of the immediate conversation.

“I don’t think the questions or the demand for answers have gone away; they’re just competing for attention. So I’d expect to hear less about it for stretches, rather than see it disappear altogether.”

“There’s just something every day with Trump,” said Shawn Donahue, clinical associate professor in the University at Buffalo’s department of political science.

For Donahue, timing also plays a key role. The US Congress has been in recess and without members on the House floor, so there’s not any discussion of the Epstein Files Transparency Act’s proposed new iteration. This bill, the Epstein Files Transparency Act II, seeks to address what advocates have said are shortfalls in the present EFTA – such as an absence of enforcement mechanisms.

“It kind of feels like whenever Congress comes back into session, this probably starts to become more of an issue again, and especially if Democrats are looking at being in control of one or maybe both chambers of Congress,” Donahue said.

Should Democrats win the house, as polls project, Donahue expects they will swiftly “put Republicans on the spot” with Epstein. “Democrats are ready to start on the investigation from day one.”

For Julie Roginsky, who co-founded the non-profit Lift Our Voices and pursued a sexual harassment lawsuit against the former Fox News CEO Roger Ailes, the significance of Epstein among voters has not gone away.

“I think Epstein is part of the reason that Trump’s numbers are at record lows. I think it’s something that was one of the issues where even Maga Republicans broke with him,” Roginsky said. “I think that if Democrats do get control of at least one house of Congress this year, then starting next year, you’re going to see a lot more conversation about survivors and about Epstein.”

Congressional supporters of survivors said they would keep fighting for truth and justice.

“This is bigger than a moment. It’s a reckoning, and Americans are ready to have this conversation about power, abuse, and who gets protected,” the Democratic New Mexico representative Teresa Leger Fernández said in a statement. “Of course, Americans will vote with their pocketbooks. They’re worried about groceries, gas, and making rent. But they won’t forget that this president was Epstein’s friend and tried to hide the truth from them.

“The survivors have fought for decades to be heard. Our responsibility is to keep fighting alongside them, get the truth out, and hold those responsible accountable. That responsibility doesn’t disappear when the headlines change.”

The Massachusetts Democratic representative Ayanna Pressley said in a statement: “Justice for survivors of Epstein’s abuse has been a prominent issue amongst the electorate because people of conscience see through the cover-ups of the Trump Administration and demand accountability – that won’t change no matter how much they try to flood the zone and distract us.”

Pressley and fellow representatives Leger Fernández and Deborah Ross recently introduced legislation to address survivors’ financial burdens.

The New Mexico Democratic senator Ben Ray Luján similarly commented that whatever might be unfolding, he would keep pushing for the files to be released in full despite the Department of Justice insisting they have released all Epstein investigative files required under the law.

“We cannot lose sight of the need to release the full Epstein files, hold those responsible accountable, and ensure survivors receive the justice they deserve,” Luján said.

Asked for comment, the White House insisted Trump had advocated for survivors.

“Just as President Trump has said, he’s been totally exonerated on anything relating to Epstein. And by releasing thousands of pages of documents, cooperating with the House Oversight Committee’s subpoena request, signing the Epstein Files Transparency Act, and calling for more investigations into Epstein’s Democrat friends, President Trump has done more for Epstein’s victims than anyone before him,” the White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement.

The statement then claimed that several Democrats had yet to explain why they were soliciting money and meetings from Epstein after he was a convicted sex offender.

As for the Department of Justice, the department maintains they have complied with disclosure requirements under the original EFTA. They also rejected claims by New Mexico’s attorney general, Raúl Torrez, that the justice department had not been helping the state’s investigation.

“The Epstein Files Transparency Act does not require, and the protective orders in place in the Southern District of New York do not permit, disclosure of victim-identifying information carte blanche, and New Mexico has provided no lawful basis to justify such sweeping disclosures,” the department said in a statement. “Protecting victim privacy remains a top priority for the Department, and neither [legal] requests nor a desire to cooperate outweighs that privacy. DOJ remains available to assist New Mexico’s investigation consistent with the law and binding court orders.”

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: NFL shutters Paris fan experience as protests overshadow first France game
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
The NFL closed its “NFL House” in Paris on Saturday as the city braced for street protests with a heavy police presence and storefronts boarded up.

The league announced the closure to fans on Saturday morning through its “OnePass” app, a day after saying its pop-up NFL shop would also be shut on Saturday – in both cases citing “potential accessibility issues”.

Security concerns have overshadowed the NFL’s debut in Paris. The New Orleans Saints will play the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday at Stade de France in the league’s first regular-season game in France.

Also on Saturday, the Saints announced that “Saints House has been postponed until Sunday.”

Events planned for Saturday at NFL House included “French Athletes in Football” and “From the Field to the Community”.

“I was looking forward to just checking out some of the installations they had – they were going to have the Lombardi Trophy,” fan Nick Paiva said.

Major museums, including the Louvre and the Musée d’Orsay, were closed on Saturday, though tourists lined up to enter Notre Dame Cathedral. French authorities were intent on preventing a repeat of recent violent unrest.

The disorder has also disrupted French football, with Sunday’s Ligue 1 match between Paris Saint-Germain and Lyon postponed until Monday at the request of local police, who cited security concerns and the strain on resources.

The US state department issued a security alert this week cautioning “Americans in Paris for the NFL game” to “exercise caution and be aware of their surroundings” because of protests.

NFL commissioner Roger Goodell said this week that preparations had been made in consultation with US and French authorities. Street protests, he said, “are not unusual in France”.

Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers said on Friday that he was confident the game would go ahead as planned. “I definitely think that the NFL is alert to what’s going on,” the four-time MVP said. “This game means a lot to the NFL. If it was unsafe, then I’m sure we wouldn’t be here.”

On Friday, French president Emmanuel Macron met Goodell, Saints owner Gayle Benson and Steelers owner Art Rooney II at the Élysée Palace to “discuss Sunday’s game and the long-term future of the NFL in Paris”.

The NFL said on Friday that its pop-up shop in the city center would be closed on Saturday but that fans could use an alternative shop at Stade de France, north of the city in Saint-Denis.

A weekend event for Steelers fans was canceled on Thursday because of security concerns.

Paiva, an American who lives in France, wanted to visit NFL House, where his French partner could learn more about the sport.

He had also expected to participate in the league’s “Hail Mary over the Seine” activation, in which fans try to throw a football across the famed waterway near Notre Dame. Despite having registered, Paiva was told at the site that he also needed to have reserved a time slot.

“That was not communicated very well,” he said after being turned away. “C’est comme ça – it’s the way it is.”

French teenager Oskar Le Gall, wearing a Bryce Young jersey, was able to give it a shot. His throw came up a little short. A worker on the other side stayed busy scooping balls out of the river with a long pole fitted with a net.

Le Gall, who is from Brittany, said “the atmosphere of the NFL in Paris is amazing”, noting that French sports leagues and teams typically do not promote themselves as extensively.

Le Gall and his brother were keeping an eye on the planned route of Saturday’s protests.

“It doesn’t feel calm and good to be a tourist in Paris,” he said. “It’s not good for the NFL.”

At one point during the Hail Mary event, 11 national police vans with their emergency lights flashing drove past on the street above as a fan prepared to throw a ball.

Steelers fan Monika Allen was able to avoid any protests thanks to advice posted in fan-led Facebook groups.

“The fans are doing a good job keeping each other informed of where to be and where not to be,” Allen said near the Hail Mary event.

Her cousin, Viktor Toth, was wearing her black Terry Bradshaw Steelers jersey.

“We’re not worried,” she said. “My cousin is Hungarian, so he knows that the protests happen regularly in Paris.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Tens of thousands of Lula supporters rally on eve of Brazilian election runoff
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro and Tiago Rogero in Belo Horizonte
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Nearly 159 million people to head to polls on Sunday in battle between leftwing incumbent and Flávio Bolsonaro

Tens of thousands of supporters of Brazil’s leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, have streamed on to Rio’s most famous beach for a giant protest they hope will propel him towards a historic election fightback against his far-right rival, Flávio Bolsonaro.

Nearly 159m Brazilians will vote in the election’s runoff on Sunday, with the pair tied in the polls after Bolsonaro won the first round on 4 October by 47% to 45%.

On Saturday, under a fierce sun, red-clad crowds packed the 2.5-mile Copacabana beach in an attempt to help Lula clinch a dramatic and unprecedented comeback. Never since the return of democracy to Brazil in the 1980s has the first-round loser managed to bounce back.

Josias Silva, a 61-year-old truck driver, voiced confidence that his 80-year-old president would win a fourth non-consecutive term. He carried a homemade sign to the carnival-like procession reading: “Lula re-elected. Tomorrow will be a new day.”

“The people have woken up,” Silva said of the large pro-Lula street protests that have swept Brazil since the leftist’s first-round defeat, many led by students.

“Young people know we need this victory because otherwise we will have dictatorship again – and we don’t want dictatorship. We don’t want hatred. We don’t want guns. We want a country of love,” added Silva, celebrating the large number of people who came to witness one of the final presidential campaign rallies in Lula’s storied 50-year political career.

“There’s never been a demonstration like this one. This is the biggest protest in the history of Brazil. And we are going to win tomorrow with more than 60% of the votes,” Silva claimed.

Polls suggest a far tighter margin and most analysts see Bolsonaro, whose father, Jair Bolsonaro, was president from 2019 to 2022, as the slight favourite, having sold himself to voters as someone who will tackle chronic levels of violent crime with an iron fist.

However, in recent days Lula has appeared to regain the initiative and climb in the polls, amid a succession of scandals involving his rightwing foe. Last week the Brazilian magazine Piauí claimed that at the height of Brazil’s 2020 coronavirus outbreak, Flávio Bolsonaro attended a boat party attended by sex workers and vaccine lobbyists hoping to strike a deal with the government of his father.

Some experts speculate a Lula comeback may be possible. At the Copacabana rally, activists unfurled an enormous yellow and green banner declaring: “WE ARE GOING TO TURN THIS AROUND!”

“I’m super excited. Lula’s going to win,” said Marta Moraes, a 59-year-old restaurateur, as she joined Saturday’s demo.

Moraes said the election was not about left versus right. “We’ve nothing against the right … what we’re against is Bolsonarismo,” she said, tears filling her eyes as she recalled how Flávio Bolsonaro’s father botched the response to Covid during his chaotic 2019-2022 administration.

“I lost four members of my family because of Bolsonaro’s neglect,” Moraes said.

Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after he lost the 2022 election to Lula. Many Brazilian democrats fear he will be released – and could even return to government – if his son wins. Reports in the Brazilian press suggest several of Bolsonaro’s fellow plotters – who are now in prison or hiding in exile – may be given top military and police jobs in a Bolsonaro administration.

Cammy Marinho, a 49-year-old DJ and activist, said: “I’m here to prevent democracy becoming extinct – which is what the Bolsonaro family wants”.

Marinho said she had spent the past fortnight fighting to persuade people who voted for Bolsonaro, or did not vote in the first round, to back Lula.

“It’s non-stop work: in the bakery, in the supermarket, on the underground – whenever you feel there is an opening to talk to someone and show to them the reality, everything that Lula has done and is doing for the people and everything that this [Bolsonaro] family has done against the people,” she said.

Many marchers were part of the so-called “Lula’s Army” – a 10 million-member WhatsApp group that was created after the first round in the hope of turning the election around.

“Being a soldier in Lula’s army … means fighting for Brazilian democracy. This isn’t a normal election,” said Isabella Gaze, 64, a retired teacher and one of the group’s members.

“They constantly claim Lula is corrupt. But the truth is that they represent the most rotten and worst part of Brazilian politics. This is what we are fighting against now,” Gaze said of the Bolsonaros.

Many of the faces on Copacabana beach were teenagers, including 14-year-old Heitor Lopes da Silva. Silva had come from the city of Duque de Caxias in his wheelchair, with a placard that said: “Lula, I’m a person with a disability and I’m here to support you.”

“My whole life I’ve believed Lula was a good president. [Bolsonaro] represents the destruction of Brazil …. he represents sadness and death,” he said of the Bolsonaro-era Covid catastrophe.

Large crowds of Bolsonaro supporters also hit the streets, including in Belo Horizonte, the capital of Minas Gerais state, which has Brazil’s second-largest electorate after São Paulo, and is a key bellwether. No presidential candidate has ever won the presidency without securing Minas Gerais, where Bolsonaro led by just under 5% in the first round.

Thousands of Bolsonaristas gathered to see their candidate in a palm-lined plaza called Praça da Liberdade. To the booming sound of AI-generated funk carioca tracks praising Bolsonaro, a sea of supporters dressed in Brazil’s yellow football jersey waved Brazilian flags – and many of the United States too.

“The US is a great nation. Who wouldn’t want to be aligned with them?” said 56-year-old cosmetics entrepreneur Marcos Antonio, holding a flag that merged the emblems of both countries.

“I don’t want an alliance with Cuba or Venezuela. I want to move forward,” Antonio added. When reminded that Venezuela was currently aligned with the US after Donald Trump’s January invasion, he said: “True. But for now, a fully right-wing government hasn’t been installed yet. It’s in transition.”

Antonio Carlos Costa Jr, the 59-year-old owner of a shooting club, complained: “Lula did nothing for the country.”

Jair Bolsonaro relaxed gun ownership and buying laws – which security experts agree ended up diverting many firearms to criminal gangs – whereas Lula tightened regulations once again. “Jair Bolsonaro simply gave citizens the right to defend themselves, and his son will do the same,” said Costa Jr.

Lula supporters scoff at the idea that Bolsonaro, who has a history of well-documented ties with members of Rio’s paramilitary “militia” groups, could rid Brazil of criminality.

“If we vote the militias into power, we will be living in a dictatorship,” said Erika Cavalcante, 43, an architect who came to the march with a sign reading: “Don’t let the mobsters win.”

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Tottenham stun Chelsea for second league win in a week as Cole Palmer is sent off
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Jacob Steinberg at Stamford Bridge
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
There were times when Roberto De Zerbi’s frustration threatened to boil over. The Tottenham manager cut a tense figure in his technical area. He bounced around for 90 minutes and let out blasts of fury whenever he saw something that displeased him, but in the end he was able to celebrate leading Spurs to their first win at Stamford Bridge since 2018.

It was not a pretty game. It was not a good game. The breakthrough was a comedy own goal from Mike Penders. The young Belgian goalkeeper, deputising for the injured Emi Martínez, was culpable when Spurs went ahead, flapping at a corner from the excellent Mateus Fernandes and punching the ball into his own net.

Xabi Alonso, who saw his side lose at home for the first time this season, could argue there was an element of fortune to the result. But this was one of Chelsea’s worst performances since appointing the Spaniard in the summer. They were caught out at both ends. Penders’ inexperience proved costly and Chelsea struggled without João Pedro leading the line. It was strange that Alonso did not start Danny Welbeck.

Chelsea were blunt and knew they were beaten when Cole Palmer was sent off shortly after the own goal. Mathys Tel soon made it 2-0 to clinch a second consecutive win for Spurs and lift them into 12th place.

If Spurs were to improve on their dismal record in this fixture then they would have to take care of Chelsea’s fast starts under Alonso. The absence of João Pedro helped on that front, forcing Alonso to modify his attack, and the opening exchanges were muted. Both sides lacked someone to hold the ball up and the closest either went to scoring an early goal came when an error from Fernandes led to Antonin Kinsky pushing a shot from Palmer away.

Chelsea never adjusted to their 4-2-4 system. The experiment with Palmer and Morgan Rogers as false 9s left them without an obvious outlet. Pedro Neto was not receiving the ball in good positions on the right and Geovany Quenda, making his first start since joining from Sporting Lisbon, was tentative on the left.

Spurs built confidence, their midfield of Fernandes, Sandro Tonali and James Maddison outplaying and outnumbering Moisés Caicedo and Jordan Henderson. As ever the challenge was finding a clinical touch. There was not enough conviction to Spurs. Mohammed Kudus and Tonali sent hopeful efforts off target. Tel wasted opportunities to run at Josh Acheampong and Omar Marmoush failed to take the best chance of the first half, pinging a shot too close to Penders from Andy Robertson’s cutback.

Marmoush, preferred to Dominic Solanke as Spurs’ No 9, buzzed around but was often gobbled up by Maxence Lacroix and Levi Colwill. But it was a similar story at the other end. Kinsky saved from Henderson after giving the ball away but Chelsea created little before half-time.

• Spurs gained just their second away win in 35 attempts against Chelsea in the Premier League (D11 L22) and their first since April 2018 (3-1).

• Spurs have beaten Chelsea in all competitions at Stamford Bridge while keeping a clean sheet for the first time since December 1986 (also 2-0).

• Chelsea’s Mike Penders (21yrs 85d) is the second-youngest goalkeeper to score an own goal (pictured) in the Premier League, after Illan Meslier (20yrs 354d) for Leeds against Wolves in February 2021.

• Cole Palmer’s sending-off was the 100th red card Chelsea have been shown in the Premier League (excluding rescinded cards), becoming the third team to reach this milestone after Everton (113) and Arsenal (110).

Spurs were comfortable. Too comfortable? Their luck was out at the start of the second half. Maddison, who was a doubt before the game, had played well before making way for Conor Gallagher. Not that there was a response from Chelsea. Fernandes, the best player on the pitch, was running the game for Spurs.

Chelsea played in random bursts, Neto testing Kinsky, and a flurry of changes followed. Solanke and Pedro Porro for Marmoush and Robertson were positive moves from Spurs, while the home fans were happy to see Estêvão come on for Quenda.

Estêvão was soon involved, bursting in from the right and shooting into the side netting. The temperature had risen, Chelsea fired up after a clash between Palmer and Fernandes led to some aggro between the benches. But with the quality so low it was fitting that the opening goal arrived in farcical circumstances.

Austin MacPhee, Chelsea’s set-piece coach, was busy telling four home players to stay high when Spurs won a corner in the 77th minute. The box emptied out, Fernandes delivered from the left and Penders got his angles horribly wrong. The 21-year-old, who struggled in the air when Chelsea beat Leeds in the Carabao Cup last month, was thrown by a challenge from Jan Paul van Hecke and watched in horror when his weak punch spun into his empty net to give Spurs a shock lead.

Chelsea were still coming to their senses when any hope of a comeback disappeared. Palmer, on a booking after his row with Fernandes, could have no complaints when he received a second yellow for a lunge on Gallagher. It was Chelsea’s first red card of the season and came a day after Alonso had spoken about emotional control helping his side improve their disciplinary record.

Not here. Down to 10 men, Chelsea faded. It was over when Tel skipped in from the left and clinched the points for Spurs with a crisp low shot from 20 yards.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Six Flags to reopen Goliath rollercoaster – but now with seatbelts after recent rider death
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem fell from ride earlier this month, spurring amusement park to temporarily shut it down

Six Flags will install seatbelts on its Goliath rollercoaster in Georgia, after a rider plummeted to his death earlier this month.

Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, a 42-year-old father and educator, was thrown from his seat on the Goliath, a coaster that plunges riders down 165ft, before a second drop of 180ft. On his way down, he collided with the ride’s other cars.

Georgia authorities have launched a probe into Kariem’s death. The gruesome fall prompted the park to temporarily close the Goliath and eight rides at five other parks.

“What happened has deeply affected all of us at Six Flags. Safety has always been fundamental to the experience we provide for our guests,” the theme park’s CEO, John Reilly, wrote on Friday.

Seatbelts will also be added to coasters with a similar restraint, he announced, although an exact list remains unclear. The Goliath features a lap bar that locks over a rider’s waist, a design from Bolliger & Mabillard.

The park has also commissioned an independent review of the safety procedures for all of its attractions.

“I know trust is earned through actions and not words,” Reilly said. “We will continue to communicate about our progress and hold ourselves accountable to our commitments to you.”

The Six Flags Over Georgia fatal incident comes as the theme park is being sued over alleged bodily harm from its X2 ride at Magic Mountain. A recent CNN investigation uncovered a long history of brain injuries and at least two deaths linked to the ride.

A group of past riders who say they sustained brain injuries on X2 has accused the park of having a defective coaster and negligence for allowing its continued operation, according to court documents.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Valkyries hold off Dream comeback to win Game 4 and level WNBA finals at 2-2
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Gabby Williams scored 17 points and Golden State played stellar defense to beat the Atlanta Dream 67-62 on Saturday and even the WNBA finals at 2-2.

The Valkyries stymied Atlanta star Angel Reese, holding her to just eight points. She had dominated the previous two games, averaging 25.5 points and 14 rebounds in the Dream victories. Reese struggled in Game 4, missing 10 of her 12 shots, including a few layups in the fourth quarter, after having double-doubles in each of the first three games.

In the US, the series will air on NBC, USA Network and CNBC, with all games streaming on Peacock. In the UK, it will be carried by Sky Sports. In Australia, fans can watch through WNBA League Pass, with selected coverage also available through ESPN.

Atlanta trimmed a 16-point halftime deficit to 61-55 midway through the fourth quarter, bringing fans in the sellout crowd of over 17,000 to their feet. Golden State answered with a three-pointer by Veronica Burton to briefly silence them.

The Dream then scored seven of the next nine points, including a three-point play by Rhyne Howard with 28 seconds left to get within 66-62.

Burton then made the first of two free throws a second later and Atlanta couldn’t convert on the other end.

Howard finished with 19 points for Atlanta, who shot just 33.3% overall and four for 23 from three-point range.

Golden State players had said between the 26-point Game 3 loss and Game 4 that they were confident they could win on Saturday and just needed to be more physical and play harder. They showed that grit on both ends of the court.

Defensively, they challenged Atlanta shots led by Kiah Stokes and limited the Dream to few second-chance opportunities. Stokes finished with three blocks and now has a WNBA finals record of 14 in the four games, surpassing the old record of 12 by Brittney Griner and Sylvia Fowles.

Offensively, they limited turnovers, which had led to easy points for Atlanta in their two victories. The Valkyries also crashed the offensive boards, rebounding their own misses to give themselves more chances to score. Stokes had eight offensive rebounds of her 16 total.

Coach Natalie Nakase also made a change in the starting lineup, inserting Tiffany Hayes and Kaila Charles for Kayla Thornton and Cecilia Zandalasini. While the Valkyries got off to a slow start again in the early afternoon tip-off with the Atlanta Hawks playing their home opener at night, when Thornton and Zandalasini entered the game they paid immediate dividends.

The two helped a key first-quarter run that gave Golden State their first lead since the third quarter of Game 2. Atlanta got within 24-20 on Reese’s basket – her lone one of the first half – but the Valkyries responded with an 18-6 run to close the half.

The 42-26 deficit at the break was the largest that the Dream had faced all play-offs.

Atlanta had dominated the third quarter in the WNBA finals, outscoring Golden State 60-35 in the first three games. The Valkyries wouldn’t let them do that in Game 4.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.title: Barack Obama to rally for Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan before key US Senate race – US politics live
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.author: Cecilia Nowell
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.text:
The former Democratic president is showing major support in Detroit for the progressive Michigan candidate in final days before US midterm elections

Good afternoon and welcome to a rare weekend edition of the Guardian’s US politics live blog.

We are coming to you live as US midterm elections draw closer and candidates are jockeying fiercely to win the hearts, minds and votes of the American people.

As part of progressive Abdul El-Sayed’s effort to do just that, he’s added Democratic star power to his rally lineup tonight in Detroit: former president Barack Obama will take the stage and offer his support to the Senate hopeful.

This rally falls on the first day of Michigan’s in-person early voting period and 10 days before election day.

Abdul El-Sayed, a doctor and former Wayne county health director, ran on Medicare for All and a refusal to take corporate Pac money, and was backed by Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

He made opposition to US military aid to Israel and criticism of its conduct in Gaza central to his campaign, and has described Israel’s actions there as genocide. Aipac and its allies as a result spent a record-breaking $30m trying to stop him, according to AdImpact.

Barack Obama’s presence matters most in Detroit, where Black residents make up more than three-quarters of the population and where he is still highly popular.

Kamala Harris, the first Black and south Asian vice-president, campaigned with El-Sayed last month, and Obama phoned him after the primary.

Hundreds of Michiganders have gathered outside Cass Technical High School in Detroit, Michigan, where former president Barack Obama will stump for Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed at a rally slated to begin in about an hour.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Additional 178 cases of measles reported by US health authorities amid outbreak
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Jessica Glenza
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 4,588 cases across the country, more than double the tally in 2025

Federal health authorities reported an additional 178 cases of measles in the US this week, as the vaccine-preventable illness continues to sicken people across at least 43 outbreaks.

The new data reported by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) comes as experts criticize the agency for lack of transparency, and as health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr takes steps to further upend US vaccine infrastructure.

The CDC reported 4,588 cases of measles across the country in 2026 as of Friday – more than double the tally for 2025. Pennsylvania alone reported 1,338 cases on the same day. The CDC also reported large outbreaks in South Carolina and Utah, both of which are reporting more than 500 cases.

In spite of rising measles numbers, official tallies represent an undercount of the disease. Measles is widely regarded as one of the most contagious diseases known to medicine. Its most common symptoms – rash, runny nose, fever and cough – may not immediately send the infected to a doctor.

Measles sends one in five unvaccinated people who become infected to the hospital, and one to three people in 1,000 die of disease-related complications. The measles vaccine is 97% effective at preventing the disease. Vaccine side effects include injection-site soreness and low-grade fever. The measles vaccine has been a focal point of anti-vaccine activism for decades.

In Pennsylvania, which has had the worst outbreak in the nation for months, state authorities have reported five measles-associated deaths and are investigating a sixth. The CDC has reported three measles deaths nationally, but has refused to say where the third death took place, obscuring whether it is counting a death in Pennsylvania or elsewhere.

Kennedy reportedly asked senior CDC officials in September to remove a measles death from the official tally after he questioned whether the disease contributed to the death, according to Reuters.

In addition to criticism of how the CDC has tallied measles deaths, Health and Human Services (HHS) this week announced changes to vaccine injury reporting systems. A proposal will allow doctors to bill for reporting suspected vaccine injuries, among other changes.

The “vaccine adverse event reporting system”, or VAERS, has been a long-time fixation of the anti-vaccine movement. The system has proved useful for researchers tracking rare vaccine safety issues. However, it has also become a source of misinformation for anti-vaccine activists, who point to VAERS to make claims, however unfounded, about safety.

All vaccines have risks – a fact acknowledged by vaccinologists. Before Kennedy’s appointment to the health department, an expert panel considered each vaccine change individually to decide whether benefits outweigh risks. Kennedy fired all 17 sitting members of that board. He replaced them with members with whom he ideologically aligned. A court blocked the members’ appointment in March.

In his time as secretary, Kennedy also misleadingly claimed children get more than 90 vaccine doses; linked vaccines to autism in spite of extensive evidence to the contrary; directed the CDC to remove claims that vaccines do not cause autism from its website; claimed the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine contains “aborted fetal debris”; and stated that vitamin A and cod liver oil may help children with measles, which leading physicians described as misleading.

https://www.theguardian.com/law/2026/oct.title: ICC prosecutor says court making ‘significant progress’ despite US sanctions
https://www.theguardian.com/law/2026/oct.author: Julian Borger Senior international correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/law/2026/oct.text:
Nazhat Shameem Khan claims some staff are facing ‘banking difficulties’ but their work is unaffected

The deputy prosecutor of the international criminal court has said new US sanctions are beginning to take effect on its staff but insisted they have not hindered the court’s work.

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, announced the sanctions this month, accusing the ICC – a frequent target of the Trump administration – of being a “rogue court” and declaring: “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC.”

Nazhat Shameem Khan, who is co-running the office pending the appointment of a new chief prosecutor, said the court was so far continuing its work.

She said the Gaza war investigation and others had made “significant progress” since war crimes arrest warrants were issued in November 2024 for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and his former defence minister, Yoav Galant. Further applications from the prosecutor were being kept secret by order of the court, she said.

Some ICC staff had however encountered banking problems, she said, even though the US sanctions on the court were not due to take effect until six months from 9 October, the date of their announcement. She said the banks were “over-complying” to minimise risk while there was uncertainty over the ultimate scope of the measures.

“These are sanctions imposed on the institutions and, in principle, our individual members should not be impacted directly,” the Fijian deputy prosecutor said in an interview with the Guardian. “But again, what I am hearing from members of our staff is that some of them are experiencing difficulties in banking.”

The court is working on insulating itself from sanctions imposed by a hostile administration in Washington. It has switched its software from Microsoft to European ​alternatives, and is negotiating with relevant service providers over banking and health insurance.

“All the investigations across all situations continue. We haven’t made any decision based on the sanctions to reduce our capability or reduce our output,” Khan said, acknowledging that it was impossible to anticipate the full impact of sanctions when they officially took effect.

The new sanctions target the whole institution of the ICC, but the US first targeted 13 ICC staff in February 2025. Khan was one of them, so is accustomed to dealing with sanctions, which affect aspects of everyday life.

“Life without a credit card is inconvenient. It’s amazing how many things now we cannot do around the world, particularly in relation to travel, without a credit card,” she said, but added that her inconvenience was put into perspective when she visited refugee camps or sites of mass atrocities.

“We see the faces of our victims for whom sanctions and credit cards are completely irrelevant. They just want justice.”

American sanctions are not the only disruption to the ICC prosecutors’ work. Formal investigations began in late November 2024 into allegations of sexual harassment against the former chief prosecutor, Karim Khan. The British jurist (who is no relation to the deputy prosecutor) denied the charges. He was removed in July this year after a vote by member states.

No further charges over the Gaza war have been announced since late 2024. Khan insisted that investigative work on the Israel-Palestine file had only gone quiet because of the court’s ruling earlier this year that all charges and applications for warrants should be kept secret until the judges decide they can be made public.

“Even if we reach a stage of the investigations where it might be imminent, we may not discuss it publicly,” she said. “And so while there might be an appearance that nothing is happening, I can assure you that there’s significant progress in that particular situation as well as others.”

When announcing the sanctions, Rubio gave the ICC a six-month grace period “to negotiate and present a solution to address our concerns” but it is unclear what would satisfy the Trump administration, which has exhibited a longstanding hostility towards the court.

Rubio claimed, without evidence, this month that “globalist ‘experts’ an ocean away” wanted the ICC to prosecute US citizens. Khan said it was unclear who and what Rubio had in mind.

“It is possible that there is a mistaken belief on the part of those who are concerned that we are pursuing Americans, but we certainly haven’t brought any Americans before the court,” she said. “If his reference is to Afghanistan, then in fact the priority for the investigation is in relation to offences committed specifically against women, girls and other vulnerable groups by the Taliban and by the Islamic State Khorasan in Afghanistan.”

This month, four arrest warrants were unsealed by the ICC pretrial chamber against members of the Taliban on charges of gender persecution.

The court registrar for the ICC is in negotiation with the EU over blocking the US sanctions or protecting the court in other ways. There has been support for the court, and on Thursday, the European parliament awarded its Sakharov prize for freedom of thought to the court and its officials.

Khan said the support was “a very important message that the staff at the court need to hear”, as were pledges from other countries to continue to contribute towards the ICC’s costs.

“I think that the fact that there is so much attention on us is a reflection of how relevant we are,” Khan said. “This is a court that provides an avenue of justice for victims who have nowhere else to go, who really want to cut past politics and want their voices to be heard.”

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Hundreds of thousands march across France in protests over schools and policing
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Angelique Chrisafis in Paris
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Almost 1,000 arrested as police charge crowd in Paris and teargas used to stop protesters reaching other city centres

Hundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday in largely peaceful protests to support schoolchildren’s demands for more teachers and repairs to dilapidated buildings, as Emmanuel Macron faces a social and political crisis in his final months as president.

In Paris, at least 110,000 people marched along the eastern edge of the city, according to government estimates. They supported high schoolers but also complained of the high cost of living and the government’s heavy policing, saying riot police had been sent to target school protesters over the past month, instead of the government offering political solutions.

The mood in Paris on Saturday afternoon was peaceful and lighthearted, with brass bands playing and children and grandchildren present. Some people carried banners critical of the government’s policing, saying: “Oppression breeds rebellion” and “The right to protest”.

But at the end of the Paris demonstration, at Porte de Vincennes on the city’s eastern edge, different groups of masked men dressed in black emerged who had not appeared to have taken part in the peaceful march. Some groups of masked men threw glass bottles and stones at police, who responded with teargas, water cannon and stun grenades. A bin was set alight and fireworks were set off towards police.

Riot police also charged a larger crowd of protesters at the end of the Paris march, using batons against them.

Police fired teargas to prevent protesters in Lyon, Lille, Montpellier, Nantes and Toulouse from reaching city centres. In Marseille, some bin fires were lit amid clashes with police. At least two people were seriously injured, one in Clermont-Ferrand and another in Toulouse, who reportedly had fingers blown off.

The government estimated that at least 400,000 people had marched across France. Trade unions estimated the number at double that. The interior ministry said there had been almost 1,000 arrests.

Laurent Nuñez, the interior minister, said that at various street marches across France there were what he called “high-risk groups” who “broke away from the main body and sought to commit acts of violence”.

More than 70,000 police were on the streets of French cities, with shops boarded up and many museums closed. The government had feared a repeat of last Saturday, when, despite peaceful protests taking place, France saw one of the most violent days of unrest in years, with public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted and at least 2,700 people arrested in cities across the country.

At Saturday’s protests, there was widespread anger at Macron for banning non-union demonstrations that his government deemed “illegitimate” and for keeping all protesters away from city centres.

At the Paris march, Nadège, a 43-year-old communications worker, said she had been teargassed last weekend at a peaceful demonstration. “I’m out again peacefully today to support everyone who is brave enough to demonstrate. It does take courage. People are afraid now. We have to keep our rights alive … In France, it’s our legal right to protest in the street and I’m here to defend that.”

A 21-year-old student from a Paris science faculty that is now blockaded by demonstrators said: “We feel in France that we are increasingly living in an authoritarian regime that is trying to stop our democratic right to protest in the street.”

The radical left presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who took part in the Paris rally, said Macron must “give in” and address France’s social malaise or face repeated protests. “Given the current situation, I think he will come to understand that this will happen again every week,” Mélenchon said.

The government has been facing a crisis since the start of high school demonstrations in mid-September, when children aged between 15 and 18 began protesting against staff shortages at their schools, leaking and crumbling buildings, and a lack of chairs in overcrowded classrooms. It grew into the biggest youth movement in years, with trade unions, teachers and parents joining. Police investigations are under way after some children and protesters were maimed and injured by explosive police weaponry.

At Saturday’s march there were some people dressed in yellow vests who had taken part in the gilets jaunes anti-government protests of 2018 and 2019. Standing amid demonstrators, Jérôme Rodrigues, a key figure from the gilets jaunes protest, said: “Today the government is afraid; that is why they are pushing demonstrators to the edge of the city, away from places of power. It’s not police shields that will provide an answer to French people struggling and unable to make ends meet.” He said it was likely that demonstrations would continue.

Pierre, 60, a retired banking consultant, said he was demonstrating in support of school students. “I have an eight-year-old granddaughter. I want her to have a brighter future than the sombre times we are facing today. There is a complete refusal by the government to listen to people’s demands.”

Jesse, 40, a charity worker from the north of Paris, carrying a sign saying “Free Hugs”, said: “I’m so angry. I’m here to support schoolchildren’s demands for better conditions. I’m so proud of them, and we have to stand together.”

She said: “I know I’m not going to war by coming out to demonstrate peacefully. But at times it really does feel like a war … This is the first time I’ve prepared so carefully for a peaceful march, wearing old clothes in case they are gassed or torn.”

In Orléans, thousands shouting anti-fascist slogans marched against a congress held by Marine Le Pen’s far-right anti-immigration National Rally party. Protesters criticised Le Pen, a frontrunner in next year’s presidential election, as well as Macron, who steps down from power next year. “Macron, resign. Le Pen in prison,” the crowd shouted.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2.text:
🏎️ Updates from Austin; start 10pm BST, 4pm local 🏎️ Giles Richards’ preview | Mail Philip

The slippery surface flag – my second flag ID failure of the week, after failing to recognise Oman’s on the streets of Windsor, ready for a state visit, as I was en route to Legoland – is showing at turn one.

“The cards have fallen for him but he has been relentless,” Brundle says of Antonelli.

Martin Brundle is suggesting that drivers will need to “take some time off the table” because of track limits, and that the bouncing Giles referred to earlier can be enough to kybosh a lap.

Ted Kravitz is at Ferrari, saying that it really has to be their pole, given what is at stake for them here. The company president is among the dignitaries in Austin; a quarter of all Ferraris are sold in the US; they have brought an upgrade that seems to be working; they have the FP hat-trick.

Simon Lazenby wonders if drivers should go for a safe, early lap, before pushing later, but Naomi Schiff points out that some of them are doing fine: just stick within the limits.

Davidson then runs us through Hamilton’s FP3 best, which is the fastest legal lap anyone has had all weekend.

Anthony Davidson, right on cue on Sky, starts a track limits sequence – and the second driver he shows going over a white line is Antonelli.

One feature of free practice generally, referred to in that snippet from Reuters’ FP3 report, has been drivers having times deleted for breaching track limits. If Antonelli had had one weakness this season, then that has been it.

Twenty minutes to go. It is warm – 30C – and sunny in Austin, while the UK recovers from Storm Austen (no relation) and Storm Boelo.

double quotation markThe seven-time world ⁠champion had trailed ⁠Leclerc a ​day earlier, complaining about the bumps and the setup direction of his upgraded car, but he seemed to have ⁠got it back to what he wanted.

The 41-year-old lapped in a best time of 1min 34.893sec, 0.168 quicker than his Red ⁠Bull rival Max Verstappen and 0.234 faster than Leclerc, to complete the Ferrari practice ​sweep before Saturday’s qualifying, with ‌the team chasing a first ‌pole of 2026.

“Ferrari looks to be very strong. They have some nice upgrades, ‌and Red Bull. It looks to me like Ferrari might be the team to beat this weekend,” said the McLaren team principal, Zak Brown.

Leclerc would have been top, had he not had his best lap deleted for exceeding track limits at turn nine, while Hamilton also had to take evasive action on a late ‌fast lap to avoid Gabriel Bortoleto’s slow Audi ahead of him. Reuters

How did people fare in practice? Friday was a good day for Charles Leclerc. As our Giles Richards wrote:

double quotation markIn first practice at the Circuit of the Americas, Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc topped the timesheets from Verstappen, with Lando Norris third for McLaren and Russell and Antonelli in fourth and fifth. Ferrari had brought their final swathe of upgrades to the race and on the early showing they had found some extra pace.

In the afternoon running Leclerc was once more on top, four hundredths clear of Antonelli in second. Verstappen was in third, from Hamilton in fourth.

One man has had to take the rough with the smooth almost all season. George Russell has endured a frustrating 2026, which was supposed to be his year. As the Associated Press reports:

double quotation markMany thought Russell [would be winning a maiden title] when the season started in Australia. Russell won his eighth career victory in a new generation Mercedes that was the class of the field.

Instead, the British driver heads into the final stretch of the season far behind his teammate, and fending off mounting frustration, and hoping he can somehow pick off a win or two to send him into a better 2027.

double quotation mark“It’s been a season that has very much tested my character and resilience,” Russell said this week.

“I’ve had to look at myself in the mirror numerous times and think: ‘How do I want to bounce back from these blows?’ Do I just want to give up and accept the misfortune or the poor performances, or do I want to try to rectify things, make the most of it and control everything I can control.”

Russell said he’s capable of doing that. “I intend to be here for many, many, many years to come, and you can’t give up when you’re being kicked to the floor. You’ve got to bounce back. I can at least be proud that I’ve given it my all in that regard.”

Antonelli is a happy bunny, with Mercedes posting social footage on social media of their kid on a rollercoaster, but not all the rides at the Circuit of the Americas have been smooth, as our man in Austin reports:

double quotation markGoing into the weekend, however, the circuit has drawn unusually severe criticism from drivers. The race was first held in 2012 and the circuit has a contract until 2034. It has become hugely popular, with sold-out crowds, but the track has come under intense scrutiny.

It is built on marshland and the bumps caused by the ground beneath the track have been condemned as potentially harmful, with the uneven surface forcing impacts into the base of the drivers’ spines.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull’s four-time world champion, said: “The bumps are unacceptable. Over time they’ve been grinding a little bit here and there but it’s just putting a plaster on the big problem. You need to really fully open up the track. That costs a lot of money and time but that’s the only way to get rid of it because these bumps are not natural and they are out of control.”

Forty-five minutes to the off. How has Antonelli built that lead? Well, as our graph shows, he burst out of the traps, overtaking George Russell with his second consecutive victory in Japan in race three and only briefly looking as if he could be hauled back. Russell won in Austria, with Antonelli third, then second at Silverstone, with the Italian out of the points. But the 20-year-old was soon back in command.

Newsflash: Kimi Antonelli is going to win the world drivers’ championship. Oddsflash: he is unlikely to do so this weekend.

You probably know the maths roughly, so here it is exactly. With six races left, Antonelli leads George Russell by 102 points and Lewis Hamilton by 111, and if he leads everyone by at least 125 after Sunday then that will be that. He would be guaranteed to have had more race wins should he go pointless for the rest of the campaign while a rival swept the board and levelled the points up.

But to stand a chance of reaching that 125-point advantage, he has to win in Austin. He then needs Russell to get no more than the two points for ninth place, and Hamilton to get no more than the 10 points for fifth place. No one seems to be offering odds on Antonelli pulling it off, but Russell is a 1-9 shot to be in the top 10, and 1-3 to be in the top six; somewhere between those two lie the odds on him making the top eight, while Hamilton – 1-7 to make the top six, 8-5 for top three – looks to be a shade of odds-on for fourth.

Antonelli himself is only second favourite for the race, behind Max Verstappen, and that status is questionable: Antonelli has not stood on the top step in the past three races. The Dutchman has won two GPs in a row, as well.

But if we knew what was going to happen we wouldn’t be watching. Never underestimate Russell’s 2026 susceptibility to misfortune, for instance.

So, join me from what is 3.15pm in Austin and 4.15pm eastern time – and 9.15pm in the UK, for Guardian sport’s last BST blog of 2026 – for the buildup to qualifying, which starts on the hour.

In the meantime, Giles Richards has been looking at the make-up of the (fairly) soon-to-be champion:

double quotation markAt the heart of this engaging character it seems is a grounded and emotionally rich relationship with his family. While he was supported in following his racing dreams, he was told unequivocally that if he was to kart on a weekend, school must follow on a Monday until he graduated. He duly did so, completing his maturità school exams just after coming third – his first podium – at the Canadian GP last year.

“Which driver has done the A-levels or the baccalaureate? Name me one that has finished school. No one,” Wolff observed pointedly of his prodigy. The role of his family has clearly been crucial. His father as guide, mentor and, both have admitted, stern taskmaster at times, whom Antonelli has described as his “rock”. But there is also clearly a hugely important relationship with his mother, Veronica, and younger sister Maggie.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Nashville SC seal first MLS Supporters’ Shield with 2-0 win over CF Montreal
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Nashville SC scored twice in the second half to claim the Supporters’ Shield as the top team in MLS with a 2-0 win at CF Montreal on Saturday.

The win allowed Nashville (21-3-7, 70 points) to stretch their unbeaten streak to seven games (5-0-2).

Montreal (6-18-7, 25 points) have just one win in their past 11 games (1-8-2) and have been officially eliminated from playoff contention.

Sam Surridge buried his own rebound to give Nashville a 1-0 lead in the 52nd minute. Montreal goalkeeper Samsy Keita, the 17-year-old homegrown player making his MLS debut, denied Surridge’s header from the right side of the goal area off a cross from Reed Baker-Whiting. The rebound went right to Surridge, who easily put it into the far side for his team-leading 18th goal of the season.

Hany Mukhtar made it 2-0 in the 76th minute. He intercepted defender Brayan Vera’s clearing attempt outside the box, was first to it as it rolled inside the box and then hit a shot that deflected off Keita and into the net from the top right corner of the goal area.

Mukhtar nearly tied Surridge atop the Nashville scoring charts with an attempt inside the box in the 80th minute, but Keita got his hands up to deflect it away.

Keita was tested early in the first half, coming off his line to the penalty spot to deny Surridge an opportunity late in the second minute.

That was all either side would generate offensively in a slow start, with just one shot attempted between the two teams through the first 18 minutes.

Montreal started to find their game as the half progressed but couldn’t convert.

Vera’s header off a corner from the left side in the 21st minute just missed the far post. Ten minutes later, Nashville goalkeeper Brian Schwake easily snared a free kick off the foot of Alexis Sanchez and 90 seconds later got in front of an opportunity from Hennadii Synchuk.

In the 33rd minute, Dante Sealy came down the left side on a rush but sent the ball over the net.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: New York archdiocese finalizing $800m settlement with clergy sex abuse survivors
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Eric Berger in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Agreement with more than 1,300 victims of clergy members and lay leaders would resolve long legal fight

The Catholic archdiocese of New York is finalizing a settlement for at least $800m with more than 1,300 people who said they were sexually abused by clergy members and lay leaders, according to one of the plaintiff’s attorneys.

The agreement would resolve a long legal fight, as well as reportedly reduce the risk of the diocese going bankrupt.

While the parties have not reached a final deal, just a few details remain, according to attorney Paul Mones, who represents some of the plaintiffs.

“It gives closure to people, many of whom are in their 60s, 70s and even into their 80s,” Mones said in a phone interview on Saturday. “That is a significant matter in terms of closing the emotional door – or trying to – because it’s never going to be closed, but [it] at least gives some measure of justice to people who were terribly wronged.”

In 2006, the New York state court of appeals refused to waive a statute of limitations concerning allegations that Catholic priests committed sexual abuse in the 1960s, 1970s and 1980s, the New York Times reported.

The state then in 2019 passed the Child Victims Act, which allowed sexual abuse survivors to bring civil lawsuits against abusers until the plaintiff turned 55. Afterwards, thousands of people filed lawsuits against the archdiocese, the Boy Scouts and Jeffrey Epstein, among others.

Then, in 2025, the archdiocese of New York started trying to raise $300m to pay 1,300 survivors of clergy abuse. The New York Roman Catholic district sold off assets and cut costs to settle the claims; in New Orleans, the archdiocese declared bankruptcy amid similar scandals.

The New York survivors can now either enter into an agreement with the archdiocese in which each receives $250,000, or fill out a form detailing what happened and participate in an allocation procedure that will determine how much money they receive, Mones explained.

In an email to priests, which was shared with the New York Times, the New York archbishop, Ronald A Hicks, said: “We are on the verge of being able to, please God, bring some measure of healing and reconciliation to all victim-survivors.”

While the settlement would resolve the claims in New York, the Catholic church faces lawsuits concerning alleged sexual abuse in other states.

Chicago attorneys filed a half dozen lawsuits this month against the city’s archdiocese alleging that the institution knew its priests were running a sex ring at a parish and did not stop it, according to WTTW News. In Baltimore, the archdiocese is in mediation with sexual abuse survivors, WBAL reported.

Mones said that he is representing alleged survivors of sexual abuse in lawsuits against archdioceses across the country, including Buffalo, San Diego and San Francisco.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Man detained at Georgia immigration detention center dies as hunger strike continues
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: José Olivares in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Death inside Folkston facility comes as officials allegedly threaten hunger strikers there with force-feeding

An immigrant detained at a sprawling detention center complex in Georgia died on Friday, local and federal officials confirmed, after the facility has already faced national scrutiny for its response to an ongoing hunger strike inside.

The death inside the D Ray James facility in Folkston, Georgia, comes as federal immigration officials and private contractors are allegedly threatening hunger strikers there with force-feeding, a detained hunger striker, his wife, attorneys and advocates all said this week. Detainees are refusing food to protest prolonged captivity and bad conditions.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on Saturday confirmed the death inside the facility, which is adjacent to the Folkston ICE processing center. Together, both facilities make up a large detention complex. GEO Group, the private prison company that runs the facilities under contract for the federal government, referred all questions to ICE.

The Georgia bureau of investigation (GBI), a state law enforcement agency, confirmed in an email that the local sheriff’s office requested the GBI conduct an “in-custody death investigation” at the D Ray facility, the Guardian can reveal. ICE and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), its umbrella agency, did not respond to requests for comment about the death or the hunger strike.

“This was a preventable tragedy,” said Azadeh Shahshahani, the legal and advocacy director for Project South, a social justice organization based in Georgia. “We hold ICE and the private prison corporation fully responsible for any harm that migrants suffer at Folkston. We call for an immediate independent investigation into this tragic death and for accountability. Folkston must be shut down immediately.”

The man, Luis Sandoval, was 48 and from El Salvador, ICE said in its statement, adding that at about 1.46am on Friday, facility staff found Sandoval with a ligature around his neck. He was pronounced dead less than an hour later.

Sandoval was arrested by ICE officials earlier this month, and transferred to the Folkston facility on 8 October. In its press release, the agency said Sandoval had prior convictions for aggravated assault and other crimes, and that his death was under investigation.

It was unknown on Saturday whether Sandoval had participated in the hunger strike. The GBI said it could not share more details because of its active investigation.

Sandoval is the 60th person to die in ICE custody since the start of the second Trump administration, as ICE continues with its aggressive anti-immigrant crackdown.

Austin Kocher, president of Relevant Research, which studies the immigration enforcement system, and who is a research fellow at American University, said that this year, there have been an average of one death every 10 days in the custody of ICE. That figure includes people dying in detention centers or in nearby hospitals while still in the custody of ICE.

“Even in the past, there has not been such an overt dehumanization and overt view that migrants’ lives are expendable,” Kocher added. “I worry that that tone [from the Trump administration] has a tendency towards neglect and viewing migrants as disposable.”

Tens of thousands of people have been arrested and detained by ICE, leading to prolonged detention, as immigrants and asylum seekers fight their cases, and the agency has been stepping up its offensive in recent months despite a less showy presence on the streets.

One man currently in the Georgia detention center is Andrei Gerdiukov, a Russian asylum seeker who is participating in the hunger strike.

Nearly three weeks ago, Gerdiukov and dozens of others launched a hunger strike to demand their legal cases be processed more quickly through the US immigration system and to protest the conditions of their confinement. The hunger strikers were placed in solitary confinement, according to Gerdiukov and attorneys.

“I feel tired, I feel dizzy. Every move, it is hard,” Gerdiukov said in an interview by phone on Saturday from detention. “They threatened us that they were going to force-feed us.” He had heard about the death but did not know Sandoval.

Gerdiukov and his wife, Polina Chertushkina, came to the US from Russia to seek asylum after they faced persecution for their opposition to the war in Ukraine, Chertushkina said. Their cases are ongoing, but as the couple were driving through Florida this February, they were pulled over and detained by immigration officials. Chertushkina was released, but Gerdiukov was taken to Folkston eight months ago.

“I am so worried about him, I don’t know what to do,” Chertushkina said about the force-feeding threats, speaking on Saturday by phone. Chertushkina is asking lawmakers to assist her husband.

At least 12 hunger strikers are still participating, despite the threats of force-feeding, Gerdiukov said, adding that several had been fainting.

On Friday, the hunger strikers were moved to a nearby unit, where medical officials “wearing combat boots” took their vital signs, raising fears of imminent force-feeding, Gerdiukov said.

It was not clear on Saturday whether or when the authorities intended to use force-feeding.

The process to force-feed hunger strikers is secretive, with court records often sealed.

A judge has to approve the procedure, and then detention guards restrain a hunger striker while medical staff push tubing up the nose and down the throat to pump nutritional liquid into the stomach. Medical ethicists and human rights organizations have called the practice torture.

ICE generally says in court filings that force-feeding is necessary to maintain “good order” in detention centers as well as to keep detainees alive.

“On the one hand, they’re trying to force-feed people [to keep them alive],” Kocher said. “And yet at the same time, in that same [Folkston] facility, you have someone who died and possibly was able to kill themselves.”

The Guardian has been tracking force-feeding cases nationwide. From January 2025 through August 2026, ICE sought court permission to force-feed at least 19 detained hunger strikers. One Afghan man was force-fed for nearly six months. A Kurdish man was force-fed for nearly eight months.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Kimi Antonelli seizes F1 US GP pole and chance to seal first world title
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Giles Richards at the Circuit of the Americas
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
Kimi Antonelli claimed pole position for the US Grand Prix with a hugely impressive lap for Mercedes at the Circuit of the Americas. In beating Red Bull’s Max Verstappen into second place, Antonelli did exactly what was required to give him the chance to close out his first world championship title this weekend.

Isack Hadjar did well to secure third for Red Bull, with Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton in fourth and fifth for Ferrari, and Antonelli’s Mercedes teammate George Russell in sixth.

Antonelli’s first pole since the Belgian GP in July could not have been better timed as he attempts to take his first title. The Italian has a 102-point lead over Russell and needs to be 125 points in front after this race. To take the title he must win on Sunday and have Russell finish outside the top eight, with Hamilton outside the top four. The win certainly looks to be a strong prospect but he still needs his rivals to stumble on Sunday.

He can only do his best and knows that even should the title not be secured here, on this form it will surely be done and dusted by the next round in Mexico.

“We got pole, so we’ll try to win tomorrow,” Antonelli said. “Max has been very quick and did an incredible job in qualifying so it’s not going to be easy. Hopefully we’ll be leading into turn one and we’ll try to set the pace, even though it’s going to be very tight. Very happy with qualifying today, Q3 was very tough with the wind, gusty, unpredictable but happy to stick it on pole.”

It is another striking achievement from the Italian, not least because the Mercedes upgrades applied in Malaysia have made the car more of a handful to drive. Indeed, Russell was a full four-tenths off his teammate, and it was a strong return to form for Antonelli as he looks to become the youngest F1 world champion at just 20 years old.

He was flawless for the lap that proved unbeatable in the Texas sunshine but it was a performance by which Mercedes, too, will be buoyed given they were hoping to extract the maximum from their recent upgrades which had not delivered as expected on their opening salvos in Malaysia and Singapore. With the team having found a way to exploit them, Antonelli gave a reminder of just what a formidable opponent he is.

His engineer, Pete Bonnington, admitted it was somewhat unexpected given both the team’s work on their upgrades and the form of the recently resurgent Red Bull, with Verstappen taking pole and the win at the last two rounds. A sentiment echoed by the beaming Antonelli.

“It was unexpected, we felt it would be close but it was a good surprise,” he said. “I am happy because we have been working very hard on this package and since Singapore we have taken a big step further. The team have done a tremendous job and finally we are seeing the results.”

For the first runs in Q3 in what had been a tightly contested session, with both Red Bull and Ferrari looking to be very much in the mix, it was Antonelli who set the pace. He put in a blistering lap with a time of 1minute 34.035seconds, almost two-tenths up on Verstappen, with the Italian hooking up what was one of his very best laps of the weekend.

On the final runs Verstappen gave his all but could not improve and, although Antonelli too could not go quicker, he had done enough. His time was not bettered and a somewhat unexpected pole was secured with no little style. “Yes man, it’s good to be back,” he said.

For Antonelli, in a season of milestones, including eight wins, his first pole in Austin is his seventh of the season and the first for Mercedes here since Valtteri Bottas last took the top spot in 2019, from which he went on to win – a feat Antonelli will hope to emulate.

The Italian looked very much at his best and has given himself the chance to potentially finish the job. But as Verstappen observed, if not here on Sunday, then at the next round or the round after. The hard yards are over.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Barack Obama rallies Michigan crowd for El-Sayed, saying he’s ‘fighting for real change’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Joseph Gedeon in Detroit, Michigan
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Former president speaks to rapturous crowd of thousands in support of Democrat Abdul El-Sayed for US Senate

Barack Obama told a Detroit crowd on Saturday that Abdul El-Sayed was “fighting for change, real change, that will get money out of politics and put money in your pocket”, as he threw his weight behind the Democratic Senate candidate and the rest of the ticket on the first day of early voting in Michigan.

Obama said in front of thousands of onlookers at Cass technical high school in Detroit that El-Sayed would “finish the job we started with the Affordable Care Act and guarantee quality, affordable healthcare to every single American”.

The former president headlined the rally for El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for US Senate, and secretary of state Jocelyn Benson, the party’s candidate for governor, at an evening event to “get out the vote”.

He accused Donald Trump of “enriching himself and his family”, and said the administration had set a “culture … at the top” of taking favors. “Never seen a president so intent on selling favors like this,” he said.

The rally came on the first day of Michigan’s early voting period, with the general election on 3 November. It was also Obama’s first weekend of in-person campaigning during the midterms, which started in Cleveland, Ohio, earlier in the day to stump for the former Ohio senator Sherrod Brown and Democratic nominee for governor Amy Acton earlier in the weekend. He issued similarly scathing remarks aimed at the White House and the GOP.

The Detroit stop is Obama’s first public show of support for El-Sayed, who emerged from a bitter August primary in which the former president stayed on the sidelines. El-Sayed, a doctor and former Wayne county health official, beat the moderate congresswoman Haley Stevens who was riding on the backing of the Democratic establishment and pro-Israel organizations.

Obama was on the offensive against the administration, mocking the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, as “laser-focused” on the “jawline and testosterone levels of our troops”, asking: “How much time do you think this man spends in front of the mirror every day?”

On tariffs, Obama said Trump was toughest on “that well-known evil empire”, referring to Canada, a few minutes’ drive from Detroit across the bridge. “These are the people who gave us Martin Short and maple syrup,” he said.

Questions had hung over whether Obama would back El-Sayed at all. El-Sayed, a champion of Medicare for All, had at one point called the Affordable Care Act, Obama’s signature domestic achievement, an incremental fix. The two men spoke by phone after the primary, and El-Sayed has since called Obama a mentor figure.

El-Sayed has the most ground to make up in Wayne county, where Detroit is the county seat, after Stevens beat him there by about 51% to 45% in the August primaries. Obama last campaigned in Detroit – which is more than three-quarters Black – in October 2024 for Kamala Harris, and Harris herself appeared with El-Sayed in Detroit last month.

Republicans have not held a Michigan Senate seat in 25 years, but the party sees the seat as one of its better pickup chances nationwide. El-Sayed faces Mike Rogers, a former congressman endorsed by Donald Trump who lost a 2024 Senate matchup against Democratic senator Elissa Slotkin by less than half a percentage point. The Cook Political Report rates this race a toss-up.

Slotkin, a featured speaker at the rally, told the crowd that “Michigan believes in electing fighters”. And when it came to any disagreements she may have with El-Sayed, she said: “It’s OK because we agree on so much more.”

“We’re putting a check and balance on Donald Trump in the White House,” she said.

A Marist poll of likely voters statewide conducted in mid-October put El-Sayed at 50% and Rogers at 48%, within the margin of error. RealClearPolitics’s average had El-Sayed ahead by about 2.6 points in a similar timeframe.

Trump has attacked El-Sayed throughout the campaign, calling him a “jihadist”, pointing to his middle name and alleging that he had ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, which El-Sayed strongly denies, and has created one of the most viral moments of the year. El-Sayed has also faced a barrage of criticism from the establishment wing of the Democratic party over his appearances with leftwing streamer Hasan Piker.

Trump is due in the state himself on Sunday, when he will hold a rally for Michigan Republicans in Port Huron, on the Canadian border. The city said it will be the first presidential visit to St Clair county.

If elected, El-Sayed would be the first Muslim and first Egyptian American in the US Senate. Benson faces the Republican congressman John James; a James win would make him Michigan’s first Black governor.

Turning to the disagreements between them, Obama acknowledged that some people had pointed out that El-Sayed “didn’t like some things you did as president”. “We are not going to agree on every detail of every issue,” he said. “You know who else doesn’t agree with everything I do? Michelle Obama.”

“We share those values of making sure everybody gets a fair shot in this society,” Obama said, “and that the system’s not just run for those at the top.”

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Alonso urges Cole Palmer ‘to learn’ from red card in Chelsea’s defeat to Spurs
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Jacob Steinberg at Stamford Bridge
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Xabi Alonso said that Cole Palmer must learn from his red card during Chelsea’s shock 2-0 defeat to Tottenham, who claimed their first win at Stamford Bridge since 2018 thanks to an own goal from Mike Penders and a late effort from Mathys Tel.

Spurs, who had won on one of their previous 34 trips to west London, were already 1-0 up when Palmer earned a second yellow card for catching Conor Gallagher with a late tackle. The playmaker could have been sent off earlier – his first booking came during a clash with Mateus Fernandes – and Alonso agreed that this could be an important lesson for the 24-year-old.
