He’s currently engaged in a war of words with Live Nation over gig ticket prices (he is proud that Bleachers’ tickets are “as low as they can physically possibly be”). “Live Nation keep missing the point, because every time I say something, they’ll call my people and say: “Let’s have a meeting.’ You don’t get it, I don’t want to fucking talk to you people, I want to make it clear that I’m not fucking OK with you turning the most sacred thing into the world into some weird free-market piece of shit … the idea that if you’re rich, any ticket you want is yours at any time and if you’re not, you have to go through this demoralising online experience where you get whacked and kicked and fucked around.”

When I meet him, his social media channels are filled with abuse from commenters angry that a Jewish artist has made a point of saying “free Palestine” onstage at Bleachers shows: he points out that he was saying it long before the recent Ed Sheeran/Macklemore controversy blew up but says he has “felt way more emboldened to say it now, because it’s not in any way a strange, uncomfortable or controversial thing to say, it’s a deeply human thing to say. If you think it is [controversial] you’re lost in some other sauce that is so crazy. They’re going to let some fucking promoter tell me what I can say? Don’t book me. I’ll play for free outside. [Ed Sheeran] missed a massive, beautiful opportunity there: just cancel the whole fucking tour, then play for free outside each venue, raise a bunch of money, rather than let a fucking billionaire tell you what to do. The reason it’s not an anomaly or niche issue is because we all live in a world where billionaires are constantly telling us what to do. So stand the fuck up.”

Of course you could argue that Antonoff has more freedom to be unguarded than the artists he works with. Bleachers enjoy a curious kind of success – their albums sell respectably rather than astronomically and they’ve never come “even close”, Antonoff points out, to having a huge crossover hit. Yet they are capable of filling out Madison Square Garden with an audience that Antonoff says aren’t there to see “that producer’s band”. His own celebrity is largely by proxy, thanks to the company he keeps in the recording studio – his 2023 wedding to actor Margaret Qualley took place amid a scrum of fans and paparazzi, but that seemed to have less to do with the bride and groom than the fact that Taylor Swift was in attendance.

Recently, the gossip pages have been alive, first with his former partner Lena Dunham’s memoir Famesick, which suggested that one of the reasons their romance floundered was because Antonoff was more invested in shepherding Lorde through her Difficult Second Album than their relationship, and latterly with news of his marriage’s collapse. That came as a surprise given that Bleachers had released an album thick with loving peans to Qualley and to marriage a matter of weeks before their split was announced: one of them, You and Forever, even came with a video starring the couple together.

Antonoff thus currently finds himself on tour, singing songs about a relationship that’s now over. When I mention it, he first interrupts me – “Oh, I can imagine what you’re going to say: it’s bizarre” – then clarifies my point: “Songs which I wrote recently,” he nods. “I obviously was really worried about this specific thing, I sat long and hard with it and thought: ‘If I change the setlist …’ and in my gut there was a unanimous jury that said, ‘No, this is the deal. The deal I’ve made with my audience is that I’m going to tell you honestly how I feel and I’m going to risk at any moment having to stand behind it for fucking ever.’

“Anyone could relate to the terrible sadness and pain, but there’s a great power to it also,” he says. “It’s actually been really beautiful. I mean, for people to come together, to know what I write a song about, to know how that must feel for me now, to know what that song means to you as an audience member, to just hold it all and sort of celebrate. I don’t rewrite the past, I have no shame about the things I’ve said. My life has been dedicated to making it impossible for me to rewrite the past, because I’m standing there, singing about how I felt during the good times, so when the bad times hit I can’t look myself in the mirror and pretend that those times didn’t exist. I would rather live through something publicly than even escape it privately.”

After we speak, on stage at Colorado’s Red Rocks Amphitheatre, there is indeed a fraught emotional charge to Bleachers’ performances of Dirty Wedding Dress and You and Forever. Antonoff follows the latter by playing I Wanna Get Better alone on acoustic guitar. The audience – who, as he promised, are an odd combination of twentysomething women, middle-aged couples and a smattering of grizzled Deadheads in tie-dye T-shirts, none of whom look as if they’re there to see Taylor Swift’s producer in the flesh – bellow along, so loudly that they’re in danger of drowning him out entirely. For a moment, in the spotlight, Jack Antonoff does not need figuring out.

Bleachers are touring the UK and Ireland, 23 November to 4 December; tour starts Kingston upon Thames. Their album Everyone for Ten Minutes is out now.

https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/o.title: Lara Croft is 30! We look at the video game icon’s biggest blunders
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/o.author: Ellie Gibson
https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/o.text:
We all know the highlights of the tomb raider’s storied career – but what about the lowlights? We dig deep to unearth the archaeologist’s less glorious moments

Happy birthday, Lara! This month marks 30 years since Ms Croft first swan-dived into our lives with her unique blend of athletic prowess, archaeological expertise and giant knockers. More than 100 million Tomb Raider games have been sold since. We all remember the good times: the bold design and sheer playability of the original titles; the establishment of Lara as a 90s icon, embodying both lads’ mag culture and girl power; the way she made games cool, even appearing on the cover of the Face. We’ve had blockbuster movies, big budget reboots, and shiny reissues. And who could forget the time we got to powerwash her house?

But no one gets to 30 without a few skeletons in the closet – or in Lara’s case, butlers in the freezer. So here’s a look at the darker parts of her past.

Lara’s image has been used to hawk a multitude of products over the years, from cereal and soft drinks to reasonably priced Spanish hatchbacks. Low points include the 1999 promo for a German women’s magazine in which Lara tells us what she really, really wants isn’t the Dagger of Xian or the MacGuffin of Atlantis, but a big meringuey wedding dress.

See also the weird Dreamcast advert where Lara talks about the console as if it’s a jar of anti-ageing moisturiser. This led an entire generation of women to try reducing the appearance of fine lines by rubbing Sega hardware on their faces. Because she’s worth it? Let’s hope the money was.

Back in 1996, no one predicted how successful this quiet game about a posh archaeologist made by a small team in Derby would be. But once publisher Eidos realised it was in possession of a goose that laid golden eggs, it launched an intensive battery farming operation. Core Design was forced to churn out a new Tomb Raider title every year.

Four games in, the developers had had enough. In 1999 they decided to bury Lara under a collapsing pyramid at the end of The Last Revelation. News of her demise was tucked away towards the end of the design document, the Core team having taken a punt that their publisher overlords wouldn’t bother reading that far.

They were correct. The Eidos execs were furious when they learned of Lara’s fate, but it was too late to change the game’s ending. Instead they put pressure on Core to find a narrative workaround so they could squeeze out one last PS1 adventure. The result was Tomb Raider: Chronicles, which begins with a memorial service for Lara and continues in a series of flashbacks. It is rubbish.

Lara’s first PS2 outing, The Angel of Darkness, was released in 2003. It was aiming for mature and edgy, but landed slap bang in the middle of dull and depressing.

The game missed the point of what players loved about Tomb Raider – the thrill of exploring exotic locations and abandoned temples. No one asked to wander around a gloomy version of Paris that could pass for Croydon, talking to sex workers and pawn shop owners while dressed in double denim.

It didn’t help that the game was full of bugs and had awful controls. A terrible new strength mechanic forced the player to build up Lara’s muscle before she could perform previously simple tasks, like moving a crate.

To top it all off, a secondary protagonist was introduced: tiresome edgelord Kurtis Trent, whose toxic masculinity ruined the party for everyone. Which brings us to…

Another key appeal of the original Tomb Raiders was the feeling of being a solo adventurer exploring a strange world, never knowing when the eerie silence would be shattered by the snarl of a hungry wolf. No one ever wished Lara was accompanied by a bloke in a padded gilet saying: “Hey, I wonder if that rusty key we found will fit in this rusty lock?”

But when Crystal Dynamics took over from Core in the 00s, they decided Lara needed some annoying sidekicks. The worst offender is Jonah, who makes his debut in the 2013 reboot. Not only is he feckless and mansplainy, he actively creates work for Lara by being an absolute liability. Over the course of their adventures he gets trapped, tortured, stabbed, kidnapped, knocked unconscious, shipwrecked, buried in an avalanche, caught in a tsunami, falsely declared dead, and almost killed in a plane crash. Ironically, the only calamity that doesn’t befall Jonah is being swallowed by a whale. A shame.

None of the Tomb Raider films are stellar – although many middle-aged women have a soft spot for the first Angelina Jolie outing, in which our hero dispatches an army of goons without having to leave the house, or even get out of her pyjamas.

The follow-up, The Cradle of Life, is absolute twaddle. Philip French called it “repetitive and curiously inert”. The BBC’s Nev Pierce went further: “Incoherent, dumb and stupefyingly bland … It’s as though they wanted to make a terrible film.”

Pierce went on to describe Lara as a “pumped-up Judith Chalmers”, which points to a missed casting opportunity – who wouldn’t want to watch the affable host of Wish You Were Here…? scale Angkor Wat with a grappling hook?

Although Chalmers never got the chance, plenty of other women were cast in the role of real-life Lara over the years. They included model Nell McAndrew, who donned the turquoise tank top to promote Tomb Raider III.

Things went tits up when she also appeared in Playboy magazine, the game’s logo proudly displayed on the cover alongside the words: “LARA CROFT NUDE.”

Core Design sued, unhappy that the video game character they had endowed with comically enormous breasts was being sexualised. They won – a judge ordered stickers be applied to 20,000 copies of the magazine, covering up the offending logo. It is not known how badly this affected sales among the Playboy readers eager to catch an illicit glimpse of unlicensed intellectual property.

The 2013 Tomb Raider reboot was solid and polished. However, its creators failed to understand Lara’s appeal as a strong, enigmatic main character, particularly for female gamers.

Art director Brian Horton talked about wanting to make players “care for” Lara. He said her torturous experiences and ripped clothing would show “beauty and vulnerability”, suggesting this was “sexy in its own way”.

The controversy really kicked off after a trailer was released showing a man pinning Lara against a wall and groping her. Executive producer Ron Rosenberg said the sexual assault would make players want to “protect” the game’s protagonist, and “root for her in a way you wouldn’t root for a male character”. This focus on the male gaze and demotion of Lara to damsel in distress represented a staggering failure to read the room, and to notice there were women in it.

There’s no doubt that Lara has endured some dark times over the last three decades. In fact, she’s had it harder than any other veteran video game character. No one ever suggested Solid Snake would have more appeal if he sported a gigantic pair of testicles, or insisted on giving Mario daddy issues. (Although, as annoying sidekicks go, Sonic the Hedgehog’s mate Tails gives Jonah a run for his gold rings.)

Yet here she is, still standing, with another adventure arriving next year. Perhaps this one will tell Lara’s true origin story: how she rose to prominence not because of her prominent chest, or past traumas, but because she was the cool, enigmatic star of a bloody great game.

Lara Croft remains a leading icon of gaming culture, despite the repeated failure of sexist developers and unimaginative marketing teams to understand her power. As someone born after she was created might say, that’s why Lara Croft is the GOAT – not just the greatest of all tomb raiders, but the greatest of all time.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.title: ‘Brilliant James’ helped return Trump to the White House. Can he conquer the midterms?
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.author: David Smith in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
James Blair’s data-driven approach delivered victory in 2024 but president’s unpopularity and idiosyncratic style do not bode well this time

They are both young, bald and fathers of four. They are also the brains behind Donald Trump. But while Stephen Miller is infamous as the US president’s ideological enforcer, James Blair could, in the words of Time magazine, “be the most important person in Donald Trump’s Washington you’ve never heard of”.

That imbalance is deceptive, however. Blair has sufficiently impressed Trump to earn the nickname “Brilliant James”. And a well-positioned source told the Guardian: “I would say that James is probably twice, five times, 10 times more effective than Stephen Miller.”

Blair, 37, is a data-driven political operative who played a key role in Trump’s historic comeback to win the 2024 presidential election. He became a White House deputy chief of staff, working with Congress to pass the president’s signature “One Big Beautiful Bill Act”. Now he faces his stiffest challenge yet: helping Republicans hold the House of Representatives and Senate in the next month’s midterm elections.

A tight-knit circle of Florida loyalists, strategists and political fixers has become central to Trump’s political operation, with his Mar-a-Lago club serving as a centre of political power. Blair, born in Tampa, is a Florida man. His father was a small-businessman who worked in printing; his mother was a homemaker. He has three older brothers and a younger sister.

Blair cut his political teeth in the partisan pressure cooker of Florida politics. He graduated from Florida State University with a bachelor’s degree in finance and, in 2013, founded the political consulting firm Rapid Loop Consulting. At 22, he was interviewed for a policy and fundraising position under Richard Corcoran, then a powerbroker and future speaker of the Florida house of representatives. Corcoran recalls being instantly struck by the young applicant’s intellect and unusual composure.

Corcoran hired Blair, making him his go-to staffer throughout the Florida state legislature. Blair developed a reputation for working around the clock, combining ruthless efficiency with an easygoing, personal charm among colleagues.

Corcoran, now president of the New College of Florida in Sarasota, said: “James Blair is one of the finest young men I’ve ever met. He’s an A-plus in almost every category. He was tremendously discreet. He worked around the clock. He was extremely bright.”

He added: “James is a great hang. He’s very personable. Every single legislator that worked with him – he worked with all of them because he was my go-to guy – will tell you that James Blair is one heck of a great guy.”

By 2018, Blair was serving as senior adviser to the gubernatorial campaign of Republican Ron DeSantis and joined his administration as deputy chief of staff, where he forged his defining alliance with political strategist Susie Wiles, now Trump’s chief of staff.

Chris Whipple, author of The Gatekeepers: How the White House Chiefs of Staff Define Every Presidency, said: “He is clearly one of Susie Wiles’s favourite people, one of her so-called junkyard dogs. She thinks very highly of him. That’s a pretty strong bond.”

Sensing turbulence ahead, Blair resigned from DeSantis’s office in 2019, only weeks before DeSantis turned against Wiles, ousting her from his political committee and helping engineer her expulsion from Trump’s political operation. Wiles returned to Trump’s camp the following year, running his Florida re-election effort and bringing in Blair. Trump ultimately lost the election to Joe Biden.

Wiles hired Blair again for Trump’s improbable bid to regain the White House. In March 2024, Blair became political director of Trump’s presidential campaign, helping shape its voter-targeting and get-out-the-vote strategy. Larry Jacobs, director of the Center for the Study of Politics and Governance at the University of Minnesota, observes that Blair quickly established himself as Trump’s “political brain”, utilising data, polling and voter modelling to dictate strategy.

Blair’s core contribution to the 2024 campaign was his radical willingness to discard Washington’s conventional wisdom. While traditional operations rely on costly brick-and-mortar field offices and heavy television advertising, Blair argued that broadcast television was losing influence to digital-first strategies, taking the bold step of both closing field offices and outsourcing get-out-the-vote operations to independent super political action committees (Pacs).

“Washington is filled with folks who make their living from consulting, and Blair came in with a whole new approach and, frankly, hurt the bottom line for a lot of consultants,” said Jacobs. “He took a lot of abuse, but the president’s comfortable win was read as a confirmation of Blair’s data-driven approach.”

A Republican strategist, who did not wish to be named, added: “The thing about James is that, when he believes something is right, he’s willing to be attacked for it. He will pursue a strategy he thinks is right even if it’s unpopular in the Beltway.”

Roger Stone, a longtime political operative based in Florida, argues that Trump’s core strategy team – comprising Wiles, Blair, consultant Chris LaCivita and pollster Tony Fabrizio – deserve huge credit for orchestrating the greatest political comeback since Richard Nixon in 1968.

“People don’t understand that political strategy is a data-based science,” said Stone. “It takes a certain skill not only to interpret sophisticated polling data, but also to use the numbers and put them into action. This is something I think James excels at. Blair is among a handful of those who really understand how to interpret and implement the data.”

Sean Spicer, a former White House press secretary, agrees. “He made a lot of big good decisions that resulted in a win,” Spicer commented. “He’s fairly data driven but, like a lot of things in politics, you’ve got to have a good sense of judgment where the data guides you 80% of the way and then 20% is judgment on timing and on tone.”

After Trump’s second inauguration, Blair entered the White House as a deputy chief of staff, bringing political affairs, intergovernmental affairs and legislative affairs under his control, giving him an unusually broad portfolio.

Stone describes Blair’s working style as “intense, blunt, extraordinarily organised” and fueled by “incredible” energy levels. Spicer said: “He’s a guy’s guy. You can joke around with him. He doesn’t take himself too seriously, but he knows his stuff. He puts his head down and gets the job done.”

Blair, a quieter figure than Miller, has maintained a far lower profile. It took a while for Trump to fully appreciate his talents. The president told a holiday reception last year: “I’d hear from other people he’s a total political genius, but I didn’t see it. And you know what? He’s not quiet. He’s incredible – the job you’ve done, thank you, James.”

Blair is equally complimentary about his boss. In a phone interview, he said that Trump “is the most patriotic person of anyone you know. He loves America and he wants it to do well. He’s willing to make hard decisions.”

As the 2026 midterms approached, Blair stepped away from the White House to take charge of the political action committee Maga Inc, taking the lead in the effort to preserve Republican control of Congress. By the end of August, it had $415m in the bank.

But Blair is acutely aware of the economic headwinds facing the party. Whipple recalls a candid conversation with Blair in December regarding the midterm outlook. “Blair said essentially that it doesn’t matter what we do about [Jeffrey] Epstein or any of the other problems we have. If we don’t do something about affordability, we are fucked. And so here we are.”

Whipple added: “He’s a smart, savvy political operative who understands that Trump should have been talking about affordability and gas prices ... but he also understands the nature of the beast, that Trump is going to talk about whatever he wants to. He’s a smart political operative but he’s also a realist.”

As election day approaches, Blair’s data models have run headlong into the realities of midterm politics. Trump is not on the ballot, making voters who are less likely to turn out in midterm elections notoriously difficult to mobilise compared with a presidential cycle.

Blair acknowledged this: “Yes, it’s harder. Being a challenger is easier in some ways than being the incumbent party. That’s borne out by the entire history of the midterms. And of course with President Trump on the ballot, we historically do much better.”

Asked whether he is adopting the same strategy as in 2024, Blair replied: “There are elements that are similar. Low-propensity voters are the bread and butter of our coalition and they’re even harder to turn out in a midterm year.”

He added: “President Trump built a historic coalition and movement that is uniquely powerful and at the same time hasn’t been entirely transferable to other Republicans. We are all trying to change that, and nobody more than him, as evidenced by him pouring his energy, sweat and treasure into the midterms.”

But Republicans have been forced to engage in tactical retreats. Jacobs notes that in Minnesota, national Republican groups under Blair’s influence refused to put major funding behind the Senate candidate Michele Tafoya, despite close polls. “Blair’s fingerprints were all over it,” Jacobs said. “The data doesn’t support it. Yes, the polls show her close, but close is not winning. They’re now in the business of trying to cut their losses rather than pick up wins.”

Even more damaging has been the apparent failure, at least in the short term, of the congressional redistricting push personally championed by Trump and Blair, in Texas and elsewhere. The strategy relied on replicating 2024 gains among Latino voters – gains that look set to erode amid anger over inflation and hardline immigration crackdowns.

Blair’s political headaches grew earlier this month when it was revealed that he and LaCivita travelled to Republika Srpska, a self-governing region of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The New York Times reported that the pair received substantial payments to advise the regional government before local elections.

Trump distanced himself from both men, describing them as “outside consultants” in a 7 October Truth Social post and warning that if he found a ‌conflict of interest, he would “terminate them, immediately!”.

Senior White House officials questioned why Blair was taking on lucrative work overseas when he was supposed to be overseeing the final stretch of the Republican campaign, Reuters reported. For Trump, the bigger concern was that Blair’s outside ​work distracted him from his political responsibilities.

Blair responded defensively to the mounting criticism, issuing a rare public statement. “All of this mudslinging is ridiculous, and counterproductive,” he insisted. “President Trump and me are focused on helping Republicans win in November. Every other Republican should be doing the same.”

On Thursday, Blair tweeted that he and LaCivita were donating their full fee to the future Trump presidential library. He wrote: “I love the President and am eternally grateful for the opportunities he has provided me. Contributing to the preservation of his legacy of greatness is my honor!”

The setback came as little surprise to those who believe Blair had been riding for a fall. One source who worked closely with Blair for many years said: “He’s an arrogant asshole who always thinks he’s the smartest guy in the room. His arrogance will result in the worst Republican election result for 20 years.

“James is a mercenary. He will go to the person with the most money,” they added. “If success is measured by how much money there is in your bank account, James is a winner.”

That view is passionately rejected by Blair. “A quick look at my professional history proves I’ve worked for both well-funded candidates and those with few resources and helped them succeed,” he said. “I work for candidates whose cause I believe in. I work intensely hard, and I don’t apologise for that.”

Spicer also pushed back against claims that Blair is in politics for personal enrichment. “I find it kind of bullshit, to be honest with you,” he said. “The guy works his tail off. That’s an undeniable fact.

“He was a government salaried employee making $170,000 a year. Just after winning the 2024 election, the guy could have hit the speaker circuit and made a heck of a lot more money.”

Trump had said Blair was expected to return to the White House after the midterms, describing his departure as a “short” leave of absence. But the source who worked with Blair for years predicted: “There’s no way he’s returning to the White House. James won’t go to work for JD Vance in 2028, because he thinks he will lose. He will present himself as Marco Rubio’s campaign manager in six years.”

In the meantime, on 3 November voters will determine whether Blair can defy the odds again. If the results are as catastrophic for Republicans as opinion polls suggest, he could face the wrath of a capricious president, looking for a scapegoat. “Brilliant James” could find himself with a less desirable nickname.

For Rick Wilson, a Florida-based political strategist and co-founder of the anti-Trump Lincoln Project, no amount of data modelling can overcome the fundamental flaw at the heart of Trump’s political machine. “It’s hard for the Republicans, including smart kids like Blair, to convert on that stuff right now because they don’t have a steady hand at the tiller,” he said. “Trump is crazy, and he’s gonna act crazy, and he’s gonna be crazy – all day long, every day, and no one’s going to turn that around.

“James Blair can be a raging political genius, and it’s not going to change that Donald Trump is an insane person.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump administration has pushed off 13% of Americans enrolled in food stamps
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Eric Berger
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Stakeholders concerned more people at risk of food insecurity after One Big Beautiful Act took effect

Enrollment in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (Snap) has decreased significantly over the past year in the US following restrictions imposed by the Trump administration, which has forced more people to seek help from food banks or go hungry, stakeholders say.

The number of people who receive food stamps has dropped from 41.6 million in July 2025, before the One Big Beautiful Act took effect, to 36.5 million in June 2026, a 13% decrease, according to the latest data from the US Department of Agriculture, which administers the program.

While Donald Trump and other Republicans have said the changes incentivize people to find jobs, elected officials, non-profit leaders and people with food insecurity say the changes simply make it harder for Americans to feed their families.

“There is always going to be a percentage of our communities who we need to help – we have to accept that – and so, once we accept it, it is easy to just move forward and do the right thing, which is to provide resources to people who need them,” said Rhona Kamar, founder and executive director of Feed Louisville, a non-profit that aims to reduce hunger and food waste.

The Trump administration’s changes to Snap will reduce spending by about $187bn over 10 years, the congressional budget office projected.

Previously, only able-bodied people between ages 18 and 54 who did not have dependents under 18 had to meet a requirement that they work a minimum of 20 hours per week or only get benefits for a maximum of three months over three years.

Under Trump, the rules now state that people from ages 18 to 64 who do not have a dependent under 14 had to perform paid or volunteer work for at least 20 hours weekly.

The One Big Beautiful Act also stated that starting October, states had to cover 75% of the Snap administrative costs, whereas before they had to cover half.

The changes have affected some states more than others. In Arizona, the number of people enrolled in Snap dropped by 50% between July 2025 and June 2026; Kentucky experienced a 6% decrease.

“I am concerned more people are going hungry in my state because of changes to” Snap, “impacting children and the elderly”, Kentucky governor, Andy Beshear, a Democrat who leads the predominantly Republican state, stated in a letter this month to Brooke Rollins, the US agriculture secretary.

But Trump and Rollins described the reduction in Snap recipients as a positive.

“Democrats don’t love” the decrease, Rollins said at a farming festival in August in Minnesota. “But for those of us that love work and celebrate work and want people to work and not be on food stamps, it’s a pretty big win when we move 5 million people off of food stamps.”

Critics of the changes point out that despite Trump’s promises, grocery and gas prices have increased during his second term, making it harder for families to afford necessities.

“If people were getting paid enough, they would not be on the Snap program,” said Gina Plata-Nino, director of Snap at the Food Research and Action Center, a non-profit that supports anti-hunger programs.

The Food Bank Council of Michigan operates a helpline where staff answer residents’ questions about applying for Snap and accessing local food programs. The organization started getting more than three times as many calls daily after the Snap changes took effect. This week, they had to temporarily suspend the helpline because of the high call volume.

The changes have also affected Feed Louisville, which receives surplus food from restaurants and farmers and uses those ingredients to prepare meals for partner organizations. Unused items go to the agencies too.

“We have always had enough food around,” Kamar said. “But now what we are seeing is every day the shelves are empty at the end of the day, so every bit of food that comes into our kitchen every day goes right back out to the community at the end of the day.”

The decrease in Snap enrollment has also affected schools’ ability to provide free meals to students. If at least 25% of a student body are recipients of Snap or some other public benefits, the school can participate in the Community Eligibility Provision (Cep) program and use federal funds to provide free breakfast and lunch to all students without needing household applications.

But because fewer students are enrolled in Snap, that has made it harder for schools to serve those free meals to students who need them, the Washington Post reported this week. In Houston independent school district, 26 schools that previously provided free meals to all students under Cep are no longer eligible for the program, according to the Post.

Anti-hunger advocates also say that the employment data does not support the argument that more people have found jobs or seen their wages increase and thus no longer need food stamps. The United States added 776,000 non-farm jobs between January 2025 and September 2026. During the last 20 months of Joe Biden’s presidency, the country added 2.6 million non-farm jobs, according to Factcheck.org.

“We don’t have the data to suggest that there are more jobs suddenly out there. We just know fewer people are getting benefits,” said Sheril Kirshenbaum, Food Bank Council of Michigan’s chief external relations officer.

“The number of individuals receiving benefits is constantly changing and is not representative of any one policy,” the spokesperson stated in an email to the Guardian.

It could soon become even harder for people struggling with food insecurity. States will now have to pay for most of the Snap administrative costs while also preparing for an October 2027 change that will require states to pay for some of Snap benefit costs if their payment error rate is above 6%, which according to the USDA, is not a measure of fraud. (Paradoxically, states that had error rates above 13% received a delay in implementation of the requirement.)

States will now be having to pay more for existing work while also finding funding for extra work to reduce the error rate, said Joseph Llobrera, senior director of research for the food assistance team at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities.

That could mean longer processing times and people who need assistance having to wait longer to get it, Kirshenbaum said.

The USDA spokesperson did not respond to a question about concerns that the Snap changes have forced some Americans to go hungry.

A Louisville woman, Sandra Scott, 58, has been homeless most of her life and said that until she started receiving Snap benefits four years ago, she ate at “soup kitchens or wherever I could, but for the most part, like on the weekends, there really was not anywhere to go”.

Scott has had six back surgeries and struggled with mental illness. She became addicted to methamphetamines but got sober two years ago and now lives in a subsidized apartment. She is working to obtain her emergency responder certificate and volunteers with The Table, a non-profit restaurant that uses a pay-what-you-can model.

Asked what she would say to members of the Trump administration about the Snap changes, Scott said: “Why don’t you walk in one of our shoes, somebody in the community that doesn’t have anything, that wasn’t born into money or doesn’t have a job because it’s so hard to find or [who] can’t find affordable housing because it’s too high?”

Ines and Ross shared a high sex drive, but things calmed down a bit after their daughter was born

double quotation markOur desire hasn’t diminished, but I’m content with a cuddly, loving shag these days

Ross and I had been dating for four months when I asked if he wanted children. I’d memorised a script, but I was so anxious I was visibly shaking as I asked him. It felt so vulnerable, and what if he said no? I’d have to end the relationship.

That year, I went through three rounds of egg freezing after being told my anti-Müllerian hormone levels were so low I might never be able to have a baby. I met Ross just before starting the first round, but I didn’t tell him because I didn’t want to scare him off. It also played on my mind that Ross was 28 and I was 36.

After Ross reassured me he did want children, he hugged me and said: “This is inappropriate, but I have a boner.” He called it a romance boner.

Six months after that, we decided to start trying. The fertility doctor told us we were having too much sex. Apparently having sex every other day gives the sperm time to properly develop, but we’d been doing it four or five times a day: once before work, when we got home from work, before dinner and again before bed. I’d never been with anyone whose sex drive was as high as mine.

After we miscarried our first child, sex became less about experimentation and more about comfort. And now we have a 10-month-old daughter, we just don’t have the energy to do it like we used to. Rather than four times a day, we have sex four times a week, and it’s more vanilla. But our desire hasn’t diminished, and I’m content with a cuddly, loving shag these days. We still hold hands and touch feet while we sleep.

Although there are some days when we joke that we’re more like workmates now we’re a team getting things done, we’re just as close as we always have been – it’s just a different kind of closeness.

Seeing how wonderful he is with our daughter has made me love him even more. I say to her: “I picked your dad wisely.”

double quotation markIt became a game to make Ines orgasm as many times as possible – I get a lot of pleasure from her pleasure

On our first date, Ines made a joke about being older, but it wasn’t an issue for me. We were just two people who were very compatible and had a lot of common interests. But the age gap probably sped up the process of having a child. When Ines told me she had frozen her eggs and I was welcome to leave if that wasn’t what I wanted, I gave her a big hug and said I’d love to stay.

On our second date, I baked Ines a red velvet cake and she opened the door in a bathrobe. The sex was amazing – the best I’d ever had. I came more than 10 times that night. It became a game to make Ines orgasm as many times as possible – I get a lot of pleasure from her pleasure. Although her drive was higher than mine at the start, mine increased to match hers because the sex was so good.

Although we were too sad to have sex after the miscarriage, we were still very open to each other. We got married soon after, which was a helpful distraction, and slowly our sex life returned to normal. When we first had sex after our daughter was born, we took it slowly because I was afraid of hurting Ines. Now we’re parents, we don’t have time for two-hour oral sex. It has gone from a marathon to a sprint, but it’s always very intimate. We’re often too tired, and it feels too weird to have sex with the baby in the room, so we have to be more sneaky, making the most of the time when she’s asleep.

I stopped initiating sex to take the pressure off Ines; so she doesn’t feel as if she’s letting me down by not wanting sex. Looking after our daughter is our priority. Although we love sex, we don’t owe it to each other. I’ve made it clear that, despite letting Ines take the lead, I still desire her. There’s intimacy outside sex too – dancing in the kitchen to our wedding song, or taking the baby out when one of us needs a rest. Names have been changed

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Influencers have taken over my city. If you can’t beat ’em, join ’em | Dave Schilling
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Dave Schilling
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
I can’t say I’m enjoying my new gig as a would-be creator. But these days, I don’t have much choice

Reels, as they call them. Where I say things, with one of those obnoxiously tiny microphones with the fuzzy head on top. I remember when microphones were gigantic tubular monstrosities that you couldn’t accidentally swallow without a pretty substantial effort and a handful of God-given talent.

Why am I making Reels? Because if I don’t, I’ll die in obscurity, penniless and alone. The global creative industry revolves around video content on social media, forcing even a mildly attractive middle-aged divorced parent to try to be a star just to pay the bills.

If I can turn into a well-compensated influencer by peddling my complaints about the new Burbank airport terminal, I will. I can either try to swim in the fetid pool of the attention economy or get eaten by a shark who posts TikToks about carb-conscious dieting.

In fact, I really, really don’t. I feel what gen Z might refer to as cringe whenever I open up CapCut and try to cobble together a coherent thesis while my head floats in front of a green screen.

It’s so easy to squirt a Reel out, and the medium so thoroughly demands the aesthetic feel rough, that it’s almost like a mockery of the idea of creation. My Uber Eats order didn’t include the Diet Coke I ordered? Let me do a Reel about how mad I am. Too much air in my bag of potato chips? Better make a Reel. The Dodgers lost? Reel time.

I miss the days when making a thing and sharing it with the world was hard. It doesn’t even have to be good. Just tasty enough for the Pac-Man monster that is the algorithm.

It being so simple to make a Reel is why thousands of people are doing it, and getting rich in the process. Influencers are everywhere, especially in big cities such as Los Angeles.

They wander around, consumed with a thirst for “hidden gem” restaurants to film in front of, or elaborate cocktails to try. They film explainer videos about your laundromat because it used to be owned by a mob boss or has a ghost living there. Since I started trying to be an influencer, I’ve filmed content while next to someone else also filming content a few yards away.

This is what I imagine the California Gold Rush was like – starving maniacs with greed in their eyes sifting around for something to change their lives. But swap out Levi’s jeans and a floppy hat for Alo workout gear and On Running sneakers.

Food influencing alone has become a massive industry that can make or break the success of a restaurant, or worse, make it so insufferable to try to eat there that normal people stay home so as not to end up an unpaid extra in someone’s vlog.

Some places, such as the fancy-pants Hotel du Cap-Eden-Roc in Antibes, are fighting back against the Night of the Living Dead invasion of content prospectors. The hotel has banned photoshoots to combat guests who have allegedly booked lunch reservations, then skipped the meal to take pictures in expensive clothes. Instead of functioning businesses tasked with serving paying customers, some places have devolved into mere backdrops for someone’s Robin Leach fantasy.

Look, I’ve on more than one occasion gone to the Sunset Tower hotel in West Hollywood with the explicit purpose of taking a bunch of photos for Instagram. I’ll do it again, too.

But what I will not do is not have the decency to sit down for a burger and a martini first. The Tower Bar is one of the most popular influencer traps in the city. The last time I was there, there were no cameras around, but it felt like there were. The Tower Bar has tried to limit photography for years, but no amount of begging has stopped patrons from snapping and ’gramming when they can.

Maybe a part of me wishes there were cameras around at the Sunset Tower. I wouldn’t be making Reels if part of me didn’t have the same thirst as the rest of the would-be influencers that haunt our major metropolitan areas.

That need is inside of me, even if I’m partially repulsed by it. My sense of modesty is a voice in my head, but it’s actually a quiet one that gets drowned out whenever I get a dopamine hit from a like on IG. If it feels good, why stop?

But it’s not just that it feels good. It is, as I said earlier, a way to make ends meet. It is a career path that, unlike almost every other one, isn’t shrinking faster than Lizzo’s album sales.

As social media video platforms such as Instagram Reels and YouTube gain more and more ubiquitousness in our lives, and as ad dollars migrate to those platforms from places that emphasize the written word, ignoring these opportunities starts to seem like a losing fight.

Restaurants can litigate and scribble rules on menus. Hotels can ban photoshoots. But this is the equivalent of banning breathing. I fear that society is now built for influencers, or more modestly, the entertainment industry is.

I might be too late to make money from influencer posting. I’m also probably too old for it. But if I didn’t, I would just be sitting around in a rapidly contracting room full of old writers typing away while the walls of their professional lives close in on them.

We used to make movies in this town. You’d see a film crew or two in every neighborhood. Studio backlots would be buzzing with activity.

The lunch spots where Hollywood movers and shakers used to dine are now the real backlots. The cameras are in our pockets. The sets are the mundane slop of everyday life. And the cast of characters is staring back at you in the mirror.

Nikola Jokić scored eight of his 35 points in overtime and finished with 15 rebounds and 10 assists, and the short-handed Denver Nuggets rallied from 23 points down to beat the New Orleans Pelicans 141-135 on Saturday night.

Jokić had his 199th career triple-double in the regular season, second to Russell Westbrook, who retired with 209.

Sections of the Nuggets home crowd booed the team when they went into half-time 73-57 down. After the game, Jokić made his displeasure clear.

“We got booed at our first home game, and I think those fans who booed us, they don’t need to come anymore,” Jokić said. “If you guys follow us, you know that we never quit and we’ve come back from much worse situations. So, if they ask me, they are not welcome anymore.”

Jamal Murray scored 42 points and rookie Trevon Brazille had seven of his 17 points in overtime in his home debut for Denver, which took an early lead in overtime. His corner three-pointer with 1:25 left in overtime gave the Nuggets a 133-129 lead.

Denver played without Cam Johnson (ankle) and Alpha Diallo (sprained wrist) and continued to be without Julian Strawther and Spencer Jones.

Trey Murphy III led New Orleans with 26 points, Dejounte Murray had 22 points and Derik Queen and Zion Williamson scored 17 each. The Pelicans have dropped their first three games under first-year coach Jamahl Mosley.

New Orleans shot 65.9% in the first half and led by 23. Denver rallied to cut it to 16, and Jokić and Murray combined to score 22 of the Nuggets’ 32 points in the third quarter but the Pelicans extended the lead to 19 heading into the fourth.

Denver erased the deficit on three-pointers from Murray and Jokić, a reverse dunk from Aaron Gordon, and then had a chance to go ahead with 17 seconds left but Murray made two of three free throws to tie it.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Glitch in Chelsea’s coding costs Alonso while resurgent Spurs are all systems go | Barney Ronay
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Barney Ronay at Stamford Bridge
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Home side broke the game open with some unique corner routines, but a goalkeeping error ruined the plan

There was an odd interlude at Stamford Bridge with 76 minutes gone and the score still 0-0, one of those moments where suddenly your brain seems to be on inside out, like trying to walk the wrong way down an escalator.

Tottenham had a corner on the left-hand side, in a game that had felt to that point like an extended practice session, a refinement of systems, the football equivalent of watching two middle-aged men methodically emptying the dishwasher, adding salt, descaling the hoses, tutting over knives incorrectly slotted, cups in the wrong row.

Fittingly it took a glitch in the coding to break this game open. Austin MacPhee, Chelsea’s set-piece coach, was, as ever, up on his touchline semaphoring his instructions. Except this time he was ordering Chelsea players out of their own box. Get upfield. We need fewer people defending. We must, for some reason, vacate that space and initiate some kind of counterattack chess game.

This had already happened at another corner on 52 minutes. On that occasion 10 players were arranged in various upfield positions, leaving just a small gaggle in the box doing the actual try-to-score stuff. The ball landed in one of the huge vacant spaces. Everyone cheered.

Who started this habit? It seems like one of those things that just happens and you don’t know how or why, like driverless cars, or Howard Webb suddenly having his own ref-based TV show. But it was decisive here.

The second corner came howling in right through that vacated area. Again it looked strange, not least on a wet, blustery day, the kind of day where the rain just seems to want to get inside the neck of your coat, up your trouser turn-ups, in your pockets. The ball kept travelling, right through all that open space. At which point Mike Penders punched it into his own net.

MacPhee came to Chelsea in the summer after the club activated his release clause at Aston Villa, the most remarkable part of which is that the bloke who waves at corners actually has a release clause (fee: undisclosed). Here his response to the goal was to walk pensively down the touchline, stroking his chin. Hmm, yes, need to log this. Look at the data on that.

To be fair, this was a goalkeeping mistake by Penders, a random variable. Although not really if you zoom out. Penders is not best equipped to deal with no protection, with rain, wind and a soaking ball. Penders is good with his feet, famous for stepping out to play centre-half sometimes at Strasbourg. Maybe he should have been waved upfield by MacPhee to mark the counterattack. Anything but this in fact.

MacPhee’s gambit, now safely in the data bank as Counter-Bluff Own Goal No 34, did at least open up the game. A few minutes later Cole Palmer was sent off for a second yellow after a foul on Conor Gallagher. And on 87 minutes Mathys Tel scored a lovely goal, surging upfield and shooting low inside the near post, signal for Roberto De Zerbi to invade the pitch in a strange capering run, cramped over at the waist, cackling provocatively, like a stylised martial arts pose. Enter: Haemorrhoid Warrior.

Until that point the entire afternoon had felt like an overload of systems-ball. Sometimes games like this are described as a fascinating tactical battle. This was something else, a dull tactical battle. At times in the first half the Stamford Bridge crowd got to watch a press being baited when there was no press, just a bait. Essentially, just people standing around.

By the end two things had happened. First, Chelsea were terrible. Maybe this is still a structural thing. After the years of wild overspend this has now become a high-speed talent trading house, new faces, old faces, faces you didn’t know were there, all simultaneously coming and going. End result: Chelsea had no cutting edge at all here in the absence of João Pedro, an entire system thrown by the lack of a focal point in attack. Danny Welbeck stayed on the bench for whatever reason.

Xabi Alonso played Palmer and Morgan Rogers in a strange, liminal forward role, ghost tens, nonexistent nines. There has been a lot of talk about the freedom Alonso likes to give his attack, the hard positional stuff reserved for the block behind. Sometimes freedom’s just another word for standing around in the rain, not sure which run to make.

Chelsea were static all game, lacking in edge, fire or urgency. There was even something a little sad in the crowd reaction on 69 minutes as Palmer earned his first yellow card, signal for a bust-up between the benches, basically a load of men in puffer jackets jostling and prancing. The home crowd leapt up, absolutely delighted to see some kind of edge finally. This is what they like here. In the end people just want to feel something.

Instead Chelsea had kicked off this London derby in cold systems-ball mode, and never got the engine hot. Forty minutes in Palmer had touched the ball eight times, Chelsea were on 27 per cent possession at home to Spurs, and the only real element of tension was the sight of Alonso’s weirdly inadequate golfing blouson steadily saturating with rainwater. Not his only misjudgment of the afternoon.

The second thing, Tottenham were good. Allowed to dominate the ball, and with Mateus Fernandes very good in deep midfield, this turned into their best result of the season, and a huge tick for the manager, who clearly loved every second.

De Zerbi is a funny concept. Wild, passionate, heart on his sleeve. But also obsessed with patterns and systems. He’s basically wildly excited about maths. But he was great to watch here. On the hour mark something complex happened in his team’s movements. Someone stood in the wrong space. A chance to swarm-press was passed up.

In response De Zerbi leapt in the air and let out a strange baying noise, the sound of an alpaca being garrotted. Moments later, Omar Marmoush passed straight to a Chelsea player and De Zerbi didn’t even flinch. We see things you’ll never see.

For a while James Maddison seemed to be playing a different game to everyone else, one where you’re allowed to make forward passes, carry the ball and make the game up in front of you a little. With 49 minutes gone he sat down in the centre-circle, his game done, which will be a concern. But this was still an excellent afternoon for De Zerbi’s Spurs; albeit one that turned on a missed punch and a moment of unnecessary helicopter coaching.

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: US military gives Elon Musk’s SpaceX access to sensitive tracking data
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Tom Perkins
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
This gives the company an advantage in tracking objects in orbit, raising national security concerns and fears of greater control over the space industry

The US military has given Elon Musk’s SpaceX access to restricted space tracking data, raising a new round of questions about whether the Trump administration is attempting to hand over traffic control in Earth’s orbit to a controversial donor.

The access also raises new national security questions, industry observers say.

The move comes after Musk’s Doge in 2025 fired many of the federal government’s nascent space traffic control program’s staff, and the administration has twice attempted to financially gut the department, called the Traffic Coordination System for Space (Traccs).

The moves were widely viewed in the industry as an attempt by Musk to privatize space traffic control. The defense department has now granted SpaceX access to its most precise data on potential collisions among satellites and other space objects, which will give Musk’s companies an advantage over competition that offers a similar service.

SpaceX and the Space Force signed the new contract. The commercial US space market is expected to grow to a value of nearly $2tn in value over the next decade, and the unprecedented access to military data appears to be another step toward Musk asserting monopoly control over commercial space activity more broadly, said Cole Donovan, a former Traccs employee now with the Stand Up for Science non-profit.

“It’s making a company the de facto source for space traffic coordination within the US,” Donovan added. “It’s like giving a trucking company control of all the traffic lights, which they can switch to red whenever it’s their competition’s turn to go.”

Traccs manages thousands of satellites, debris and spacecraft, and helps prevent up to 50,000 near-collisions, called conjunctions, daily.

SpaceX and Space Force did not respond to requests for comment from the Guardian, but in a statement to Breaking Defense acknowledged the move.

“The Space Force is engaging with several companies to exchange commercial data sources for access to sections of the controlled, unclassified information, high accuracy catalogue, where it provides benefit to the US government,” a spokesperson told the outlet.

SpaceX has been expanding its power over launch and other space services, while growing closer links with the US government. Multiple industry observers have said since the Trump administration took over that they fear a “vendor lock” scenario in which the government is overly reliant on SpaceX because it has such immense influence and is so technologically advanced.

The first Trump administration established Traccs to take over commercial space traffic control from the defense department. But Traccs has never been fully funded or staffed, and has struggled to take root. The latest move by the military comes at a crossroads for Traccs as the administration, Congress, and industry debate what to do next.

The administration in fiscal year 2026 tried to largely defund the $65m program during the budgetary process, but Congress re-inserted the funding. The administration has again proposed slashing the budget to nearly zero in fiscal year 2027, but the House again reinserted the funding.

Several employees of commercial space companies have told the Guardian since early 2025 that there is wide support in the industry for Traccs because it would level the playing field. But the administration’s apparent move to privatize and consolidate power with a Trump ally is consistent with its broader approach to governance, Donovan said.

However, a former National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) official who spoke on the condition of anonymity said SpaceX has largely been “remarkably responsive to space safety concerns” and they do not fault Starlink for stepping into a space that the government has failed to adequately address.

“My greater disappointment is with the government’s failure to fulfil its responsibility to establish a coherent space governance framework that provides guidance, transparency, and a level playing field for all operators,” the official said.

Musk’s growing lower Earth orbit empire includes a massive satellite constellation belonging to Starlink, a broadband internet company that is a subsidiary of SpaceX. It operates about 11,000 satellites in orbit, and could have as many as 20,000 in the coming years.

For the first time, the Space Force has given a commercial company “enhanced” access to the US Space Command’s most detailed, secure version of its High Accuracy Catalog (Hac) of on-orbit objects.

This includes Vector Covariance Messages (VCMs) made up of tracking data collected from military sensors, telescopes and radars on the ground that track the paths of satellites and other space objects in lower orbit that are down to about 10cm (3.93in) in size. The military largely uses the radars and data for monitoring other countries’ satellite positions, but it is also utilized to track commercial spacecraft and objects to avoid collisions.

The latter is part of the responsibility that the military no longer wants, and was supposed to hand off to Traccs, Donovan said. Instead, SpaceX has been given access to the data. The VCM data is valuable to Starlink because the company uses its own “Stargaze” system to track other satellites and space objects. Stargaze is made up of thousands of cameras and radars mounted on Starlink satellites. It can only see objects that are down to about a half meter in size, and is not as accurate as the military’s system.

The military “radar data is an extremely valuable tool to supplement Stargaze,” Breaking Defense quoted a SpaceX employee stating during an industry conference.

The government is receiving something in return for the data – access to Stargaze cameras and sensors. “The more observations and data that [the military] has, the better,” Donovan said.

However, the VCM data is designated as “controlled unclassified information” and has been closely held by the military because it could expose the limits of defense capabilities. The defense department has also wanted to prevent the reverse engineering of satellite sensors it uses to monitor other nations’ defense satellites, observers say.

In terms of ethical conflicts, the access is another example of the Trump administration rewarding a donor with business opportunities with the federal government, said Craig Holman, Capitol Hill lobbyist for Public Citizen, a government accountability non-profit.

“Elon Musk has bought his way into the favor of President Trump and with it, unlimited riches and lucrative government contracts in the space industry,” Holman added. “[His] political investment is paying off very, very handsomely – as was intended.”

https://www.theguardian.com/media/ng-int.author: Ed Pilkington
https://www.theguardian.com/media/ng-int.text:
Joanna Coles and Michael Wolff spend most of their days thinking about the president’s follies for their podcast, Inside Trump’s Head. Someone’s gotta do it

For a couple of journalists who spend such an inordinate amount of time sloshing around the putrid inner recesses of Donald Trump’s mind, they come across as remarkably chipper.

Michael Wolff, chronicler of the 45th and 47th president, and Joanna Coles, chief creative and content officer of the Daily Beast, are just about to record the 168th episode of their runaway podcast, Inside Trump’s Head. Now in its 15th month, the thrice-weekly show is attracting an expanding audience as it digs down into Trump’s unique blend of megalomania, narcissism and insatiable lust for fame.

We are sitting in Coles’s office on the fifth floor of the IAC building, the shiplike Frank Gehry structure in Manhattan where the Daily Beast is headquartered. Coles, dressed sharply as you would expect from a former mentor on Project Runway in snakeskin shoes, jeans and white jacket, is having her trademark shock of white hair groomed for camera.

Wolff, who has styled himself more in the mould of a country gentleman in sumptuous brown corduroy suit (of which more later), seizes on the hair arranging to unleash his own trademark: the Wolff monologue.

“I don’t have any hair,” he laments. “I used to. You should see the author photo of my first book – I looked like a 70s porn star, heavy moustache and heavy hair. All gone now …”

The pair are fond of ending each other’s sentences. And they bicker a lot, like those long-married couples in When Harry Met Sally. “Do be quiet!” Coles snaps at him in a mock schoolma’am’s voice. “She really was a kind of pest,” he snipes back, recalling the early days of their friendship.

In the fickle world of Trump-focused media, the Daily Beast’s podcast seems to be enjoying an enduring appeal. Since its launch in August 2025, its audience in audio form has tripled to 1.5m downloads a month, while it now exceeds 5m monthly full-episode views on YouTube. The lion’s share of its supporters are in the US, but it also has a healthy following in Canada, the UK and Australia.

Part cod psychology, part celebrity gossip, part Shakespearean tragedy, the podcast leads us to places that more traditional Trump reporting rarely goes. The title is indicative. As Coles puts it, “we go deep into the dark matter inside Trump’s head”.

The 168th episode, whose recording I attend, takes in Trump’s belligerent UN general assembly speech happening that day and his later fawning reception of China’s President Xi Jinping. But it is fair to say that fans of the podcast don’t come to it for geopolitical analysis.

An average episode will delve into such matters as: the defenestration of senior women in his administration, including the short-lived press secretary Katie Zacharia and ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle; Trump’s weight (they call him the “all-you-can-eat president”); Melania’s mysterious disappearing act (Wolff and the first lady have form, having locked horns in a long-running legal dispute); and the outsized role of executive assistant Natalie Harp, whom Wolff flagged as an issue well before the White House correspondents’ pack.

They have also tackled the portentous question: does the president wear diapers? “There was no odor that surrounded him,” Wolff revealed in one show, drawing on his olfactory reporting skills from when he trailed after Trump during the 2024 presidential campaign.

There is no mincing of words in the pod, no on-the-one-hand-this-on-the-other-hand-that. Coles brings the sharpness of her Fleet Street training to bear in analysing Trump, as well as her skills as a forensic interviewer well-versed in the seamier side of celebrity lifestyles. Wolff can inject the observations of a book and magazine writer and the knowledge he gained from the extraordinary access given to him at the start of the era, when he was invited to spend weeks inside the first Trump White House.

His language on the podcast is spicy. Wolff has variously described Trump on air as “that fat fucker” and a “fucking asshole”, while Coles likes to highlight what she is convinced is the president’s declining mental faculties.

Trump’s top team returns fire with equal gusto. Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, has on umpteen occasions slammed Wolff as “a lying sack of shit” and a “fraud”, while Coles is a “retard” and a “blithering idiot”.

Faced with such blowback, the duo are unapologetic about their choice of subjects or words, dismissing Cheung’s attacks as “performative”. “We talk how people talk, about their friends, about their bosses,” Coles says. “We are not trying to put a glass wall between us and politicians, we’re trying to understand them as people.”

Trump has often claimed that he has made a fortune for the “fake news” media, and such bragging would appear fair comment when it comes to Inside Trump’s Head. Coles estimates that a third of the Daily Beast’s content and traffic is entirely dependent on him.

As for Wolff, Trump has been a veritable cash cow. According to Forbes, Wolff made $13m just in the first year of Fire and Fury. Will he say exactly how much he has profited from all four books?

Coles, true to form, finishes his sentence. “Well, you have made a lot of money,” she says. “There’s your 18th-century mansion in Amagansett.”

“What about your hand-sewn Savile Row suit, it’s Anderson & Sheppard isn’t it?” she presses, referring to that sumptuous brown corduroy affair he is sporting.

Wolff silently concurs. A bespoke Anderson & Sheppard suit, as worn by King Charles and Daniel Craig, can easily set you back $9,000.

The podcast’s unashamed technique of examining Trump in the round, with all his personal flaws and foibles, is not without its critics. The New York Times columnist Frank Bruni last month wrote an opinion piece that berated media outlets that focus on Trump’s appearance rather than on the damage he is doing to the world. Though he didn’t mention the podcast, Bruni did mention “cankles”, a Daily Beast favourite.

When I raise the Bruni argument – that what matters is Trump’s anti-democratic actions not his inner psychology – it sparks off another Wolff monologue.

“Trump is the most unique politician anyone has come across,” he says. “He’s so unique no political reporter can cover him. That’s our conceit: to probe what the traditional media is not covering. They cover Trump as they would an ordinary politician, and his politics as an ordinary function of cause and effect. But Trump is completely outside of the familiar ecosystem of the presidency.”

He’s only half done. “You can analyse Trump’s policies all you like, but what he is doing has nothing to do with policy. It has everything to do with himself, with his self-aggrandizement. To understand him, you have to look at his character, how this guy thinks, what are his fundamental motivations.”

The seeds of Inside Trump’s Head can be traced back to the start of Wolff’s decade-long engagement with its subject. The two men had some contact in the early 2000s when Wolff was writing a media column for New York magazine, but it was not until May 2016 that he and Trump went head-to-head.

In the course of an interview during Trump’s first White House bid, Wolff asked him why he was running for president. Trump replied: “To be the most famous man in the world.”

Wolff recalls: “I thought at that moment, my God! This is going to be a trip.”

Ever since that exchange Wolff has been on an epic voyage of discovery to get to the bottom of Trump’s bottomless desire for fame. “It’s not just a character flaw that he craves all this attention. It has become Trump’s strategy. ‘How do I stay the most famous person in the world?’ That is literally the question he asks himself when he wakes up every day.”

Trump’s attention-seeking is one of the central themes of the four books that Wolff has written about him – starting with the bestseller Fire and Fury that took readers into the chaos of Trump 1.0, and most recently last year’s All or Nothing that marked his return to office. It is also what inspired Coles to create Inside Trump’s Head as part of her plan to reinvigorate the Daily Beast after Barry Diller, the billionaire chairof IAC, invited her and Ben Sherwood to take over its helm in 2024.

Coles and Wolff have been friends for 25 years, after she left her West Yorkshire roots and relocated as a Guardian reporter from London to New York. It was Wolff who gave her a leg up into American media, helping her leave the Times of London to which she had defected and secure an editing job at New York magazine.

(This seems a reasonable moment to make a full personal disclosure. I have been friends with Coles since we worked together in the Guardian newsroom in London in the 1990s. I have also known Wolff since I myself moved to New York for the Guardian in 2006, and I have on occasion written about him. The last time I did so I reported on the Trump-related interviews he conducted with Jeffrey Epstein, during which Wolff gave the convicted sex offender PR advice on how to handle the scandal spiraling around him. Wolff emailed me having read the piece. “Jesus, Ed, you’re a nitwit,” he said.)

The Coles-Wolff friendship hasn’t always been easy. They’ve had intermittent feuds along the way, in which they have avoided speaking to each other for a couple of years, though neither can remember why. “I feud with a lot of people,” Wolff concedes.

I wonder what price the two of them are paying for what they are doing. There are many journalists who have covered Trump for the past 10 years, myself included, who know only too well the toll it takes on one’s mental health, repeatedly grappling with his lies and darkness. But few have devoted themselves to the task as round-the-clock as they have. In one podcast, Wolff admits: “There are very few conversations I ever have that are not about Donald Trump.”

“Good question,” Wolff says. “I would fall back on that, as a writer, to get this story, to get this character, is once in a lifetime. You have the opportunity to have a voice in history. You don’t walk away from this so readily.”

“I’m British, so I don’t even think about my mental health,” Coles quips in that schoolma’am’s voice. She carries on: “We are at a pivotal moment for the global world order. Growing up in Europe, in the shadow of the second world war, you had tremendous confidence in America as an ally. All that is changing because of one man. I would feel depressed if I weren’t trying to understand this as much as I can.”

With the midterm elections fast approaching, the tone and focus of the podcast is inevitably shifting towards Lame Duck Trump. Aren’t they worried that we are nearing the end of this extraordinary epoch, of the “government of one” as they like to frame it, and the journalistic riches it brings?

Coles puts on a brave face. “We are interested in people and power. Whatever comes next will be interesting, because Trump has blown off the doors and allowed us to see inside the mechanics of power, and you can’t put the doors back on.”

The last question I direct to Wolff. Having sacrificed (at great personal gain) 10 years of his life to Trump, can he see the US, the world, ever recovering from this trauma? Will we ever be post-Trump?

“We’re going to get to the other side of this, yes,” he says, beginning his final monologue. “I absolutely believe that the unique Donald Trump will not come again. When he leaves, everyone is going to sigh with relief, even the Republicans.”

“It’s a fascinating thing. Nobody, except his fanbase, likes this guy. I mean, Trump is a fat fuck, even to those closest to him.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Bird flu outbreak at Utah mink farm sparks concerns about government response
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Eric Berger
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
State veterinarian attempted to get help from federal government but was told USDA didn’t regulate mink farms

An outbreak of bird flu at a mink farm in Utah – and the response from its owner and regulators – have sparked concerns from infectious disease experts about the Trump administration’s ability to manage such viruses.

While the mink becoming sick is unlikely to produce a “tidal wave of human infections”, an apparent lack of transparency from government officials about the infections is very troubling, said Jennifer Nuzzo, an epidemiology professor and director of the pandemic center at Brown University School of Public Health.

“No animal or human will be protected from the toll of this virus through secrecy,” Nuzzo said in a phone interview on Saturday. “The risk is greatest among people who have exposure to sick animals. If that is not you, I think you can take this off your worry list, [but] it does not abdicate the government of its responsibility to try to prevent a pandemic.”

For two months, an outbreak of bird flu has spread at a farm about an hour from Salt Lake City that raises thousands of mink for their fur, ProPublica reported earlier this week.

A state veterinarian, Amanda Price, handled the response and tried to get help from the US Department of Agriculture (USDA), but the federal officials told her that they didn’t regulate mink or have a vaccine approved for the animal, according to ProPublica, which obtained messages through the state’s public records law.

Federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) officials spoke with Utah health department staff but did not communicate with Price, the outlet further reported.

In other countries where such outbreaks have occurred, the government has ordered farms to kill their mink. Veterinarians told ProPublica that is what the Utah farm owners should already have done.

This is not the first outbreak in recent times at a Utah fur farm. During the Covid-19 pandemic, nearly 10,000 mink in Utah died from the coronavirus and quarantines were implemented at nine farms.

The virus was likely transmitted to the animals from infected workers, according to a report in the journal Emerging Infectious Diseases.

Mink are very susceptible to infection with several viruses that also infect humans, according to a report from the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America.

“The scenario I’m worried about is this one: workers who are exposed to these animals will get sick, and some of them might die, and that is awful because we potentially could prevent that through thinking about protecting farm workers with a vaccine, like other countries are using,” Nuzzo said.

The virus could infect humans and become a pandemic if it were to combine with an influenza virus, “a worry that grows with the onset of each human flu season when there are more influenza viruses in circulation”, Nuzzo said.

“I cannot tell you what the probability of that is. It could be zero,” she added.

In Utah, a fur trade representative told Price that culling the mink at C&T Fenn Farms would kill the business and the industry, ProPublica reported.

But Tom Peacock, an avian influenza researcher at the Pirbright Institute, told the news organization that in such situations, depopulation – ie, culling the mink – typically happens quickly and the fact that it didn’t in this case is “very concerning”.

Officials reportedly also did not monitor the farm workers for symptoms, despite CDC guidance to do so. ProPublica found two people who worked at the farm, one of whom had a red eye. The federal health agency urges testing for that symptom.

Price and the Utah department of agriculture and food did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The farm owner, Chad Fenn, told the news organization that the worker had dust in his eye and that the state health department did not recommend testing.

Nuzzo worries about how, she said, during Donald Trump’s second term, the federal government appears to be doing less monitoring of farms for such potential viruses than previous administrations.

Shortly after Trump took office, his administration fired federal employees who were responding to a bird flu outbreak among dairy cows.

Nuzzo said federal officials used to hold regular calls with disease experts such as her to “keep us informed about what they were doing”. That no longer happens, she said.

“I found them quite useful because it allowed us to push them and say, ‘Well, what about this?’, and to interrogate some of the ideas,” Nuzzo said. “A lot is lost when that doesn’t happen … It might mean that things are going on that people don’t see or know about. It might also be that actions don’t get the scrutiny they deserve.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.title: FDR made it a blue bastion – now it’s Trump’s stronghold in California. Is it forever lost?
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.author: Dani Anguiano in Shasta county
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
Shasta has embraced the Maga movement with gusto – can Democrats ever win back the rural, working-class voters they once relied upon?

A crucial election was approaching and the country was desperate. Despite promises that economic conditions were improving, nearly a quarter of the US was out of work as voters headed to the polls in 1932.

It was the darkest time since the civil war, a period so dire that in California’s capital people fought each other for work. In early 1931, a crowd of 200 men scuffled over a handful of temporary jobs moving back-breaking loads of granite, the Sacramento Bee reported.

That same newspaper urged its readers to find odd jobs to save fellow citizens from hunger and homelessness. Those who had already lost shelter set up along the banks of the Sacramento River, as unhoused people would do decades later, and were, in some cases, near starvation, according to the Bee.

The situation was often even worse in the remote and rural communities further up north, where opportunities were fewer and relief was slower. In Shasta county, which stretches from the northernmost reaches of the Central Valley to the state’s dense forests, residents were struggling.

Shasta had been founded in 1850, as hundreds of thousands flocked to California in search of gold. The region became a productive center for gold mining, with newcomers scouring creeks and boring through mountains in search of the precious metal. It was a place of opportunity, a soon to be railroad hub that offered jobs in copper mining, agriculture and the timber industries.

In one mountain town, a group of jobless men were accused of setting a blaze with the aim of being hired to extinguish it.

Desperate people returned to the green hills that once yielded fortunes, hoping to find a bit of gold again. “Not getting rich, but I dug out $18.90 last month,” one young man told a reporter in 1931. “I eat, and that beats being jobless and hungry.”
