Franklin Delano Roosevelt promised hope and help. He traveled to 41 states during his campaign, making a point to visit small towns and rural areas. When he stopped in Redding, the Shasta county seat, in September 1932, businesses closed and classes ended early so that everyone could see the New York governor’s remarks.

“I am not making this trip a political one. I am making it to learn the conditions and needs of every section of the United States,” he told a crowd of several thousand from the back of a train. “We are not making this fight against the Republican party but against Republican leadership which has brought the country to its present condition.”

His message resonated. Despite Republican insistence that the party would carry California, the state went, as one newspaper declared, “Democratic and progressive with a vengeance”. That was especially true in Shasta, where just over 72% of voters backed Roosevelt.

Nearly a century later, it’s an election result that is difficult to imagine. Shasta is the de facto Maga capital of California, and a center of the US election denial movement. Roughly two-thirds of voters supported Donald Trump in 2016, 2020 and 2024. They took his political philosophy and ran with it, electing officials who promoted falsehoods about stolen elections and frequently clashed with the state.

During the pandemic, the area drew national attention for its hostility to Covid restrictions. The years that followed brought more turmoil that touched all corners of public life, documented in headline after headline – a journalist assaulted while covering a meeting of local conservative groups, a protester who faced jail time for holding a sign calling for the resignation of an elected official during a public meeting.

For more than a year, the Guardian has explored the political transformation that unfolded here over the 20th century. The story that emerged through conversations with longtime residents, historians, and political experts is one of a community that dramatically veered right amid the collapse of its major industries and became a hotbed for radical conservative politics.

And it’s a chapter in the story of the Democratic party. Shasta can be seen as a case study for how the Democrats have struggled to regain a crucial pillar of the base they once relied upon – rural America – even as they appear on track to win back crucial seats this midterm election.

The small settlement of Cottonwood is perhaps best known for its rugged western beauty, nearby fish hatchery and rightwing militia. It is a place of wide open spaces with sprawling cattle ranches and pristine views of the junction of the Sierra Nevada and Cascades.

Even in a deeply Republican county, the community stands apart for its conservatism. Along the roads, underneath majestic oaks, are old signs for measure B, a controversial ballot initiative voters approved in June that would end nearly all voting by mail while requiring voter ID and a hand count. The effort put the county in yet another legal battle with the state – a judge blocked the measure from taking effect as the litigation moves ahead.

A few miles away, inside a packed home office not far from the Sacramento River, Pat Carr has assembled a sort of museum showcasing a mostly forgotten history. Old photos of local luminaries with Democratic presidents line the walls, along with letters from White House officials and even a supreme court justice.

The documents paint a portrait of a deep blue region built by Democratic policies.

“When I try to explain that to people here now, they’re going, ‘You’ve got to be kidding me. It couldn’t have been like that’,” Carr, 82, said sitting in front of a table crowded with memorabilia. “Those of us that remember a heyday, we’re almost all dead.”

In the 20th century, Shasta residents played crucial roles in state and federal politics. They chaired California’s Democratic party, helped bring major infrastructure projects to the region, and they served in John F Kennedy’s administration.

Carr knows the history well – it was his family’s. In a photo of Roosevelt’s Redding visit, FDR stands alongside Carr’s grandfather, Francis. Carr’s father and cousin managed Kennedy’s Northern California campaign, and his uncle was the undersecretary of the interior department under Kennedy.

“The money was flowing out of Washington into the north state, and the guys that were getting it done were all Democrats,” Carr recalls.

The Shasta Dam is a 600ft tall monument to that era. Constructed with 15m tons of concrete, with a reservoir capable of holding back some 4.5m acre-feet of dark green water, the dam has helped make California an agricultural powerhouse as the keystone of the Central Valley Project.

It sends vast quantities of water from the state’s far north to more arid sections of the Central Valley for farming, and generates enough electricity to power as many as 710,000 homes. The federal government, which manages it, considers the dam critical infrastructure at a level just below the White House and the Pentagon, a tour guide said on a September morning.

During its construction amid the Great Depression and through the second world war, it provided thousands of badly needed jobs.

Roosevelt came to the White House with broad support and implemented an ambitious agenda that over his first term helped build a powerful coalition of labor unions, African Americans, the working class, liberal professionals and white southerners that became the backbone of his party.

Mere months after he took office, there were work camps established in Shasta county through the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC).

The president’s administration put millions of Americans to work through programs such as the CCC, which enlisted jobless young men to build campgrounds, cut firelines and construct fire lookouts.

The agencies he created worked in virtually every county in the US, helped bring power to vast swaths of the country, and established much of the local infrastructure we now know. Redding, the largest city in the area, received federal dollars to build a fire station, post office, bridge and veterans memorial building.

“That won over the hearts of millions of ordinary people,” said Richard Walker, a professor emeritus at UC Berkeley and the director of the Living New Deal research project. “They felt that the government cared. Critically, they felt they participated. They were helping their own community, whether it was fixing streets and sidewalks or planting trees or building schools.”

The county had scored the most significant investment in the form of the dam, one of the largest public works projects of the era and one of the most important hydroelectric facilities in the world at the time, Walker said.

Most of California’s water is located in the north, while 80% of the demand lies in the central and southern regions of the state. For decades, California had sought a solution to the imbalance and the winter flooding of valley communities. The state couldn’t afford to finance the project during the depression, but after lobbying from prominent Californians including Francis Carr, Roosevelt’s administration funded it.

“Things are more optimistic than ever before in [the] Central Valley. We are delighted with prospects of immediate work,” state senator John B McColl said in 1937 before construction began.

It employed almost 5,000 people at one time – bringing new residents. Construction was under way 24 hours a day, seven days a week, and was considered so vital that some workers received draft deferments during the second world war. The dam translated into enduring Democratic loyalty, said Bob Mulholland, a veteran Democratic strategist and longtime resident of northern California.

“I think there was a certain amount of that commitment or thanks for years, from the workers themselves and the kids, to FDR and the Democrats,” Mulholland said in an interview with the Guardian in 2025 shortly before his death.

The war brought significant growth in the timber industry, as did surging demand for housing in the years that followed. It was an era of opportunity and expansion in this part of the state, with ample jobs in the mills and unions for wide swaths of workers from loggers to retail clerks to bartenders. It echoed what was happening across the US.

“After the war, the United States experienced the greatest economic boom in human history and moreover, even as inequality was declining, the rich were still getting richer,” said historian Harvey Kaye, a professor emeritus of democracy and justice at the University of Wisconsin-Green Bay. “Everyone was doing better.”

By 1948, when Diane Kinyon was born, Shasta was one of California’s bluest counties and an important part of its Democratic base. Kinyon’s family had migrated to the area in the 1860s and for generations worked in the industries that helped build and feed California, from the railroad to ranching and logging.

Her parents were “diehard Democrats”, she said. Her father, a union man, was employed by the county road department, working his way up after starting as a mechanic, and also owned a pizza shop with her mother. Her father emphasized the importance of unions to Kinyon who later who spent decades as a union organizer.

“We knew we were union. We knew we were Democrats, and we knew what that meant was that you help people,” she recalled. “But I think on the other side, [those were Republican] values too. They just financially had a different way to get there.”

In the 1960s, the construction of Interstate 5, the nearly 1,400-mile (about 2,253km) highway that runs from Mexico to Canada, opened up the county, and brought more tourists, Kinyon recalled. Road work, along with reservoir projects, offered even more jobs.

The region’s extractive industries created challenges over the years – pollution from the mining industry damaged crops, seeped into waterways and poisoned fish.

Still, a sense of hope hung over the region, along with near constant smoke from wood waste burners at the mills, recalled Pat Carr and his brother Jeff, a farmer and retired teacher. It was a sweet wood smell rather than the acrid wildfire smoke California frequently endures today.

The industry was in full swing in 1960, when Kennedy ran for president, and Shasta was still a Democratic powerhouse.

Kennedy visited the area twice, following the same trail as Harry Truman in 1948, he said on one visit. He spoke in Redding in 1960, praising the Shasta Dam and telling the crowd “water is key to the American future” and that “this valley shows what can be done”.

Shasta went on to have some of the highest support for Kennedy of any county in the state. And James Kennedy Carr, the Carr brothers’ uncle, became the undersecretary of the department of the interior.

While the US benefited from the legacy of the New Deal, major changes would soon alter the Democratic party and fracture the coalition Roosevelt built. The successes of the civil rights movement and the Democrats’ support of landmark legislation resulted in many white southerners beginning to abandon the party. Lyndon Johnson was the last Democratic presidential candidate to attract support from a majority of white Americans.

Meanwhile, conservatives and the corporate elite began what historian Kaye describes as a class war and crusade against the achievements of the “long age of Roosevelt”.

Business groups touted “free enterprise” in an effort to disempower unions and reduce government regulation, while corporations moved operations to the US south and abroad to cut costs and skirt regulations, Kaye has argued. Jimmy Carter embraced deregulation and austerity measures, Kaye said, and his policies ultimately weakened unions.

“The Democratic party basically turned its back on the working class,” Kaye said. “Republicans benefited from the Democrats abandoning the FDR tradition and the age of Roosevelt that had made them the majority party of the people from the early 1930s right through the early 70s.”

Shasta remained reliably blue for a little longer, but trouble was on the horizon. Mills had begun closing. For decades, wood products had been one of the top manufactured goods in the country, and far northern California was a key hub. The industry argued it was being hamstrung by increased regulation and environmental laws. But, Walker countered, by the late 70s the region had cut much of its prime timber and was being out-competed by new technology and production in Canada and the southern US.

Jeff Carr, 66, was a teenager at the time, and remembers the closures, and the hardship that followed. Instead of heading to the mills after graduating, people his age went into the military and some left town to attend college. Shasta was founded on extractive industries, he said, and it appeared it had largely used them up.

In November 1980, after nearly 50 years of almost uninterrupted support for Democrats, Shasta county, like the rest of California, backed Ronald Reagan for president. Voters also ousted the area’s long serving congressman Bizz Johnson in favor of a Republican.

It was a seismic shift, Jeff Carr recalled. And it echoed a change taking place across California.

“There’s one story here: California has gone to hell for Democrats,” Michael Berman, a Democratic consultant, told the Los Angeles Times in 1986. “Young people are registering Republican. And from what they’ve had to choose – between Jimmy Carter and Walter Mondale or Ronald Reagan – it’s not been a tough choice.”

The trend would ultimately reverse in much of the state, but in parts of California’s interior, including Shasta county, it proved a lasting change. Some locals began voting Republican and stayed aligned with the party. Meanwhile, a surge of new residents arrived from southern California, eager to escape to the more affordable north, and they leaned conservative. At the same time, there was an expansion in churches, including ultra conservative worship houses. Simpson University, an evangelical college, arrived in Redding in 1989.

Shasta was becoming more solidly conservative while the influx increased property values and drove up costs at a time when mills that had been critical to the economy were declining. The shift was shocking.

“None of us really saw that coming. I chalk it up to being complacent, being overly self-assured,” said Frank Treadway, a lifelong Shasta resident and Democratic organizer.

It manifested in countless ways. Treadway, 84, saw it in his coffee and tea shop where newly arrived conservatives would make a point to loudly discuss religion and politics, knowing he was active in the party. Jeff Carr heard it on ranches and job sites that suddenly rang with the endless soundtrack of conservative talk radio.

“With that fusion of religious fervor, it made politics extremely personal and a part of people’s fabric,” Carr said. “That’s when we began to see it: a real divide and the inability to meet on common-ground issues.”

A battle over wildlife highlighted the disintegration of this common ground. Even decades on, some Shasta residents shudder at mention of the spotted owl. Kinyon does not mince words: “The spotted owl screwed us.”

The timber industry had been in steep decline locally, but the federal government’s decision to list the northern spotted owl, which relies on old growth and mature forests for nesting, as a threatened species dealt another blow as the protection significantly restricted logging. The industry pushed a self-serving narrative, Walker argued, pinning the blame for its downturn on environmentalists who wanted to protect the small percentage of old-growth trees that remained.

While it was Republican George HW Bush’s administration that added the raptor to the list, following lawsuits, the Democratic party largely supported the proposal. It would become the source of years of resentment and further diminish the party’s popularity in the area.

“Not everybody is with me on the spotted owl situation,” Kinyon said. “As a Democrat I thought: we’re making a mistake.”

By the end of the century, California had turned into a blue bastion, while Shasta hardly resembled the community Roosevelt, Truman and Kennedy had visited decades before. The population had exploded, but the Democratic base had collapsed.

The transformation is emblematic of what happened throughout rural America as the loss of key industries drove economic decline, Walker said. These communities needed something akin to the New Deal, government intervention and investment to keep them viable and improved schools to allow students to better compete in changing labor markets. It never came – not from Democratic or Republican administrations.

“The government stopped caring. You’ve got very little government aid to workers whose factories were closing, whose lumber mills were closing, whose mines were closing. The basic foundation of their lives were shrinking,” he said.

On a sweltering afternoon in June 2016, Donald Trump stood before a crowd of thousands of supporters in Redding and promised a transformation.

“We are going to bring jobs back to this country. We need our jobs. We’re going to make it very expensive for companies to fire everybody and leave,” he said in front of a plane adorned with his name at the Redding airport. “You know, your area has lost one in three manufacturing jobs over a fairly short period of time. That’s a lot of manufacturing jobs.”

For Shasta, home to 180,000 people and now one of California’s most conservative counties, Trump’s words brought hope. He received more than 64% of the county’s votes that year and 65% in 2020. And Trump did deliver change here, but not the kind he had promised.

His refusal to admit he lost the 2020 presidential contest, coupled with the pandemic, ushered in an era of political extremism that reshaped public life in this region.

The latest shift began even before the election, amid a swell of outrage over California’s covid restrictions. There was growing discontent across the US during the pandemic, as seen in unruly school board meetings and city council sessions, but in Shasta it was particularly severe.

Some viewed the state’s strict rules as missteps and overreach, and further evidence that California’s Democratic leaders were out of touch with rural communities. The restrictions reinforced a feeling that had been building in past decades – that the region had been forgotten by Sacramento.

Many residents were aggrieved at what they saw as a sudden and lengthy intrusion into their daily lives. Photos of the state’s governor at a dinner party at the upscale French Laundry while the state was urging people to avoid such gatherings fueled further outrage.

The frustration over the pandemic and the state’s Democratic supermajority in the capitol intensified anger at the government and deepened allegiance to Trump. In Shasta, it also brought together disaffected residents and broad political groups including militia members, anti-vaxxers and secessionists. Reverge Anselmo, a Connecticut heir with a years-long grudge against the county, poured money into the growing anti-establishment movement. He also backed an effort to recall moderate Republican supervisors accused of not doing enough to push back against state pandemic rules.

Leonard Moty, a former police chief who had served on the board for years, suddenly found himself not conservative enough for the political moment. Trent Copland, a retired teacher whose family settled in the county in the 1860s, was friends with Moty and considered him a reasonable Republican. They had clashing political beliefs, Copland recalled, but when Moty faced a recall election, he rushed to help.

In the end, Moty lost his seat, and the recall handed control of the county’s governing body to a deeply conservative majority aligned with the anti-establishment movement. It set off years of dysfunction.

In the following five years, local politics would be defined by animosity, with Democrats and moderate Republicans pitted against ultra conservatives. Public meetings have seen little meaningful conversation and instead verbal sparring and even arrests.

Jenny O’Connell Nowain, a former pre-school teacher with no criminal history, was detained and charged for silently protesting against an official who had alleged without evidence that elections in the community were being manipulated.

Visiting Shasta county in recent years, one might come away with the impression that fraudulent elections are the most pressing local issue.

“Now the big deal is election fraud, and there’s not a shred of proof that election fraud has ever taken place,’ said Copland. “But that doesn’t seem to matter. The facts don’t matter.”

Still, a small but visible group of local residents has insisted local races are compromised. Some elected officials have supported those claims, arguing without evidence there has been widespread interference in local contests. They’ve unsuccessfully sought to implement a hand-count system, a method considered too costly and error-prone for complex US elections but embraced by those who mistrust the integrity of the country’s voting.

Last year, Shasta appointed Clint Curtis, a self-described election integrity advocate with no experience, to oversee its voting. Curtis accused his predecessors of interfering with elections – even though Republicans consistently win the county – and recently announced plans to hire a disgraced election clerk from Colorado for a job.

Longtime residents like Kinyon are frustrated by the significant time and resources officials have invested in trying to solve a problem that doesn’t exist while the area faces significant challenges.

Shasta county has one of the highest suicide rates in the state and high overdose rates. There is a severe lack of economic opportunity, residents say. Bethel, a conservative megachurch with about 11,000 members, plays a significant role in the local economy. The church’s school of supernatural ministry, which has been called a “Christian Hogwarts”, has attracted thousands of students and visitors, some of whom have stayed and started businesses.

The area relies heavily on federal funding – not in the form of massive infrastructure projects that once employed thousands – but through grants and social services.

Rural California is expected to take a significant hit with the Trump administration’s cuts to those grants and services, including about $1tn from Medicaid over 10 years. Last year, the head of Shasta’s largest healthcare provider warned the changes to Medicaid would have “crippling” impacts in a county where the local Medicaid provider serves nearly a third of the population.

It will take time for the full effect of the budget reductions to be seen, but they will have repercussions in the region for years to come. Experts have warned a new fund allocating $50bn for rural health is too small to offset the adverse effects.

Democrats have said they will reverse the cuts if they are victorious in the midterms.

Because of a redistricting effort undertaken in response to Trump’s push for gerrymandering in Texas, the region is poised to have its first Democratic representative in Congress in nearly 50 years.

Among conservatives, the redistricting measure, called Prop 50, has only fueled resentment against the California governor, Gavin Newsom, and intensified feelings that rural areas are not getting fair representation. Just over 70% of Shasta voters opposed it. But others celebrated the development, and are excited to have an experienced new congressman.

“I believe one of the best advocates that the North State will have gained is Jared Huffman,” Jeff Carr said, referring to the lawmaker slated to represent the region in January. He pointed to Huffman’s role as the top Democrat on the House natural resources committee and advocacy for farmers.

Local Democrats hope the party will be moved to invest more into organizing in the county. “We as Democrats [have looked] at Shasta county as a place where we gotta reduce our losses, not as a place we can win,” Mulholland said last year.

The California Democratic party concentrates resources in close races, meaning conservative rural areas receive relatively little support. Kinyon has long believed that if the state party invested more into local races, Democrats here could rally more voters.

In the meantime, local Democrats are focused on the same sentiment Kinyon recalled from her childhood; community building and advocacy with food and clothing drives and support groups for immigrants.

“I think we’re making meaningful progress in Shasta county in the ways that we find people need help,” she said. “Those are the things that we work on here.”

Jeff Carr serves on the local Democratic central committee, alongside Kinyon, and says the local party is trying to aid people at risk of losing food, health and housing benefits under recent federal cuts.

More support from the state party wouldn’t necessarily change the outcome of races right away, but it would help improve the conversation, argued Francie Sullivan, one of the few Democrats to ever serve on Shasta’s governing board.

But what the region needs, like similar areas across America, is massive investment, Walker said, to create thriving communities. Joe Biden’s administration backed some significant rural projects, but Democrats have largely been poor communicators and failed to articulate what they were doing, he added.

“People in the rural areas like Shasta county have no idea what Biden was trying to do for them … They don’t think the government helps them,” he said. “There’s a lot of money that flows into Shasta county from the richer areas, but nobody trumpets it. They need more, and they don’t get it. And I understand their despair.”

“If we don’t get a new New Deal of some kind it’ll continue,” he said. “The rural areas will continue to wallow in the mire of Magaism, and we’re going to be stuck with this horrible government. It’s a tragedy. It’s just a long, slow tragedy.”

Back in Pat Carr’s office, he and his brother pondered what it might take to turn things around in Shasta. Residents have previously lobbied the state to open a new university campus here, which would have a tremendous impact, Jeff Carr said. The region needs a change of perspective and a vision for its future economically, he said.

“There are other places that I could be that would be easier and the like. It’s well beyond family loyalty,” Pat Carr said from his property in Cottonwood, as the sun shone brightly over Lassen Peak framed in the window behind him. “I feel a duty almost to be here.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.title: How to build a police state | William Wheeler
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.author: William Wheeler
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-i.text:
To understand where Trump is trying to take the US, we should look to the authoritarian playbook of his favorite ally: El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele

One afternoon last year, Donald Trump welcomed “a friend” to the White House – El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele, the world’s most popular authoritarian. “I knew him as a very young man,” the US president said before the cameras. “He’s done a fantastic job. Mr President, it’s an honor to have you.”

Since March 2022, when gangs in El Salvador murdered 87 people over a weekend, Bukele has maintained a state of emergency in which key civil liberties are suspended and 2% of the adult population has been jailed – about 100,000 people, at least half of whom are probably not gang members, say local rights groups. The narrative of “the Bukele miracle” – that he swiftly dismantled fearsome gangs and restored order – has made him an icon across Latin America, where a new host of rightwing leaders have sought to replicate his heavy-handed tactics. And in the US, Bukele’s overnight success as a strongman has made him a hero of the American right.

“We know that you have a crime problem and a terrorism problem that you need help with,” Bukele said to Trump in their Oval Office meeting in April 2025. “And we actually turned the murder capital of the world into the safest country in the western hemisphere. Sometimes they say that we imprisoned thousands. I like to say that we actually liberated millions.”

“Who gave him that line?” Trump asked his assembled advisers. “Do you think I can use that?”

Bukele didn’t declare a dictatorship on day one. He built toward it incrementally, each step framed in the language of anti-corruption, public safety or efficiency. Before the coup came the “training exercise”: the population became inured to the sight of troops in the streets, as military and police rehearsed tactics for laying siege to communities across the country, deploying brutal methods of detention and incarceration. Then, suddenly, the “emergency” arrived: due process was gone, replaced by a new legal regime in which a host of domestic opponents could disappear into the gulags as “terrorists”. In the process, Bukele swept past constitutional term limits to unchecked, seemingly limitless power.

In the months after their meeting, Trump launched federal crackdowns on Democratic-leaning cities using tactics eerily reminiscent of those Bukele pioneered to build his police state – a central feature of what commentators have called a “rolling coup”. Masked agents in unmarked vans, kidnapping people into an opaque and growing detention network, reminded congressman Jim McGovern of stories from families he had met in El Salvador, he told the Guardian. “We’ve seen this movie before,” he said.

While Trump’s own authoritarian playbook has often been compared to those of leaders in places such as Turkey and Hungary – where institutions were captured slowly, over decades – the place we should really be looking to understand where the US might be headed is the country of Trump’s favorite foreign ally. And to understand how far along we are in that playbook, Trump’s policies must be viewed sequentially: their underlying coherence only emerges when you zoom out.

After four years reporting on the police state El Salvador has become, and on Trump’s ties to Bukele, I believe Trump may be trying to take the United States down the same path. Although his crime and immigration crackdowns on US cities don’t attract the headlines they once did, Trump has refused to rule out declaring a “national emergency” as the midterm elections approach, with all of the ominous implications inherent in the threat. What happened in El Salvador, set alongside Trump’s recent moves, shows why we need to start paying attention now.

Bukele’s chameleon-like trajectory shows how a police state can be assembled piece by piece, in plain sight. A rich playboy and college dropout, Bukele had previously run his family’s PR firm before entering politics at age 30. His flair for marketing and hyperslick command of social media would propel him from small-town mayor to the presidency.

Bukele broke with his leftist party in 2017 and ran for president as a reformer – a blank screen on which a country fed up with corruption and violence could project its hopes. In 2019, he was elected the youngest leader in Latin America and immediately began to ingratiate himself to Trump.

From Bukele’s first days in office, he promoted himself as a crimefighter, announcing a plan to take the fight to the country’s notorious gangs (“terrorists” under Salvadoran law). He deployed cops and soldiers to gang neighborhoods, normalizing their presence, while beginning Doge-style layoffs to purge the old guard, replacing the leaders of institutions with loyalists. Long before the March 2022 gang rampage that would justify it, he was building the foundations of his future police state.

The pandemic provided an unforeseen opportunity to scale up the experiment. In March 2020, Bukele asked El Salvador’s congress to authorize a state of emergency, which he then used to implement a draconian quarantine. Security forces encircled entire cities, detaining about 16,000 people in a matter of months and funneling them into “containment centers” that functioned as de facto jails. Three times, the supreme court issued rulings to end the practice, which Bukele publicly defied.

Cops and soldiers detained people for trivial violations to meet exacting quotas, using excessive force and beatings, incarcerating people in degrading conditions without access to adequate food, water and medical treatment. But it was just the beginning. Security forces were conducting simultaneous sieges across the country and practicing tactics out of use since the country’s 1979-92 civil war. According to two former Salvadoran security officials familiar with the operation, the Covid-era detentions were a training exercise for a much larger scale of mass repression still ahead. The quarantine was used to conduct “territorial control tests”, as one put it, to gauge how the general population would respond to repression – and its capacity for resistance. It was, in the words of the second source, “a laboratory of instilling fear”.

Another harbinger of what was to come was Bukele’s wishlist for a massive arsenal of surveillance technology. When the opposition-controlled legislature refused to sign off on a $109m loan request to buy the gear, in February 2020, he summoned thousands of supporters to surround Congress then stormed inside with armed troops, threatening to disband it.

After his party won a legislative supermajority in spring 2021 elections, Bukele quickly purged sources of opposition, firing the attorney general (who had been investigating Bukele’s inner circle for corruption) and the constitutional chamber judges (who had opposed his pandemic crackdown), and replacing them with allies. Critics denounced a “self-coup”. The new supermajority dismissed all judges over 60 years old while the reshuffled court unconstitutionally appointed 168 new judges – and then began amending the constitution and gerrymandering the country.

Help in that decisive electoral victory, however, had come from a surprising source: Bukele’s government had cut a secret deal with the leaders of the very gangs he claimed to be fighting. In exchange for money and power, they had agreed to reduce homicides and turn out voters for Bukele’s party in the midterms, according to US prosecutors and journalistic investigations (Bukele has denied this). Between July 2021 and February 2022, the government secretly released several prominent gang leaders.

Such pacts tend to produce more bloodshed, since they give gangs an incentive to escalate violence. Indeed, what came next offered the perfect pretext for a crackdown.

In March 2022, gangs killed 87 people, mostly civilians. In the middle of the killing spree, lawmakers met to approve the first of over a dozen decrees that would overhaul the country’s security architecture and civil rights laws, making it easier to arrest broad swathes of the population and hold them in legal limbo: anyone accused of “association” with a gang member in effect became a “terrorist”. The new state of emergency was initially authorized for one month. More than four years later, it’s still in effect.

Bukele’s crackdown has claimed union leaders, students, activists and journalists. A leaked police report shows that about 43,000 gang members are still at large. Zaira Navas, a former police inspector general now with the human rights organization Cristosal, believes gang members make up less than 30% of those captured, she told the Guardian, and that this was part of a deliberate “policy of terror” targeting poor neighborhoods and strongholds of opposition as the “internal enemy.” The cumulative effect: a population too frightened to dissent. Reports of torture in police custody have been extensively documented, including waterboarding, electric-shock and strangulation.

Mass trials accelerated sharply this year in El Salvador, and the fate of hundreds of defendants at a time now often rests on one or two anonymous cooperating witnesses who have struck deals with prosecutors. According to Navas, authorities found some of these witnesses by coercing imprisoned gang members. Prosecutors hand them lists of names to memorize, she said, whether or not they know the people on them.

Violence has indeed fallen in what’s now the world’s most incarcerated country (although the actual murder rate may be closer to twice what the official figures purport). Accordingly, Bukele remains popular in many quarters. Nonetheless, it is hard to draw the line between genuine approval and self-censorship: a majority of respondents tell pollsters they approve of the state of exception; a majority also says they are being more careful about what they say about it (with 48% believing they could end up in jail for criticizing the president or government).

Throughout Trump’s exile from power, Bukele stayed close to Maga, spending more than $1.5m to lobby Maga figures such as Donald Trump Jr., senator Ted Cruz, then senator Marco Rubio, senator Mike Lee, representative Lauren Boebert, and former representative Matt Gaetz, according to Mother Jones. In time, Bukele emerged as a Maga luminary himself – the poster boy for strongman solutions.

“President Nayib Bukele saved El Salvador,” Tucker Carlson posted after one of several interviews with Bukele. “He may have the blueprint for saving the world.”

Bukele’s blueprint happens to mirror a different one: the sequential architecture for consolidating power outlined in the Heritage Foundation’s Project 2025 report, which would become Trump 2.0’s policy roadmap. We can’t know that the report took inspiration from El Salvador. But the Heritage Foundation lavished praise on Bukele as early as 2019, and Project 2025 was drafted over the first year of his state of emergency. Much of what Project 2025 proposes is what Bukele had by then accomplished: turning tens of thousands of civil service positions into political appointments; increasing the president’s control over the levers of justice; deploying the military domestically; crippling unions; targeting media.

In February 2024, Bukele won an election marred by irregularities. Weeks later, he was given a hero’s welcome as a keynote speaker at the Conservative Political Action Conference outside Washington DC, where he echoed Trump’s rhetoric about carnage in Democrat-run cities and called on the next US president to follow his example and do “whatever it takes” to defeat “dark forces” already taking over the country.

At the June 2024 inauguration for Bukele’s new term, the surprise came from the White House: the Biden administration, concerned that a wave of migrants from Central America could wreck his campaign, sent a rare high-level delegation to attend – to critics, a crushing echo of Washington’s cold war support for Central American strongmen.

Bukele rolled out the red carpet – not for Joe Biden’s representatives, who were snubbed, but for Maga VIP’s.

Sharing the red carpet were Tucker Carlson and six members of US Congress, including Gaetz, who called Bukele “an inspiration to the western world”, and soon founded the El Salvador caucus in US Congress to “vindicate the choices President Bukele has made” and import his “good ideas”.

In the years since, Bukele has continued to rewrite the rules of the game. In February 2025, he cut public funding to political parties, leaving the opposition in disarray. In July 2025, his legislature in effect moved up elections and abolished term limits altogether, meaning he is “virtually guaranteed another term”, writes El País, which would bring his total time in power to 14 years.

Upon taking office in 2025, Trump’s second call to a foreign leader as president was to Bukele. Weeks later, Marco Rubio traveled to El Salvador to broker a migration agreement: Bukele offered to accept deportees of any nationality, and even imprison US citizens. Bukele asked for something in return: the MS-13 leaders in US custody. Weeks later, Rubio promised to hand over the gang leaders, some of them protected US informants who had told investigators about the gang’s secret dealings with Bukele’s government.

In March 2025, Trump secretly deported the first MS-13 leader, who was expected to testify in US court about Bukele’s secret dealings with the gang. Prosecutors later sought to drop narcoterrorism charges and deport other gang leaders (one warned a judge in a handwritten note that he “will be tortured and desposed of as it happen’d to another who was deported”). Deported along with the first gang leader were more than 200 alleged members of the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua, who were incarcerated in Bukele’s new Terrorism Confinement Center (Cecot), and allegedly tortured and sexually abused.

Among them was Salvadoran Kilmar Ábrego García, husband to a US citizen and father of three. A court had explicitly ordered he not be deported – and evidence that he was a gang member was thin to nonexistent – but the White House resisted a subsequent supreme court ruling to facilitate his return, threatening a constitutional crisis. Ábrego García’s deportation was “a test of their ability to do this to anyone”, as Ezra Klein put it: “If they can get you on a plane, they can hustle you beyond our laws and leave you in the grips of the kind of gulags they wish they had here.”

In April 2025, Bukele was greeted as a guest of honor in the Oval Office. “Mr President,” Bukele told Trump before the cameras, “you have 350 million people to liberate. But to liberate 350 million people, you have to imprison some.”

That June, Trump began launching federal raids in Democrat-leaning cities led by Immigration and Customs Enforcement. According to the Brennan Center for Justice, ICE and CBP had $118bn left unspent from the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act as of April 2026. Then the Secure America Act added $65bn more, bringing their available funds to $183bn. The $70bn package alone exceeds the budgets of all other federal law enforcement agencies combined. Meanwhile, Trump’s 2026 budget proposed cutting the FBI, ATF and DEA. Journalist Radley Balko argues the money is flowing to the agencies Trump sees as most loyal, and concludes he is “attempting to build his own paramilitary force”. In response to ICE increasing its spending on weapons by 700%, Wisconsin state senator Chris Larson warned that “the President is building an army to attack his own country”.

In crackdowns in cities such as Los Angeles, Portland, Chicago, Minneapolis, Memphis, Washington DC and elsewhere, the structure of these federal raids mirrored those carried out by Salvadoran forces: arrests for trivial offenses in order to meet quotas; the deployment, or attempted deployment, of parts of the military on domestic soil; and the cruel and degrading treatment of detainees (propagandized on social media).

At one of the largest ICE camps in the country, in Texas, human rights groups collected accounts from detainees describing officers who crushed men’s testicles, stomped on them, and beat them while handcuffed. Three men died there in six weeks; one death ICE attributed first to “medical distress”, then to a suicide attempt, before the medical examiner ruled it a homicide. Thirty-six Texas state house Democrats have cited “numerous credible reports of torture, killing, and inhumane treatment” and demanded an investigation. As historian Andrea Pitzer said in the New York Times, “the point isn’t that they hide it. The point is to instill terror on the society as a whole.” Brutality on the streets and secrecy in the camps work together: “the goal is always to use one group as an example of what can happen to everybody.”

And the crackdown has expanded beyond immigrants. Summoning hundreds of top military brass from around the world to an unprecedented gathering at a Virginia military base in late September 2025, Trump suggested he would soon deploy the troops to use US cities as “training grounds” for the “war from within”.

Trump signed an order that same month designating “antifa”, a term used to describe a loose constellation of leftwing groups with no central leadership, as a domestic terror threat. Days later, he signed a memorandum, the National Security Presidential Memorandum 7 (NSPM-7), which ordered federal authorities to develop a strategy to disrupt groups purportedly engaged in “domestic terrorism and organized political violence”. The memo asserted that “common threads animating this violent conduct include anti-Americanism, anti-capitalism, and anti-Christianity”.

NPSM-7 is “the signature policy document of this administration”, a former senior US official who worked in Central America under Biden told me – and a powerful echo of Bukele’s use of gangs as terrorists. “It’s exactly the same road map, down to the language of war used against his own people.”

In effect, Trump’s Antifa orders conjure “an imagined leftwing conspiracy” to “criminalize opposition”, according to the Brennan Center for Justice. “Buying a sandwich for an activist, allowing a protester to crash on your couch, or briefly lending a computer to print pamphlets critical of government policy could all potentially be considered material support” for terrorism. Soon thereafter the FBI organized a 10-agency Joint Mission Center to prosecute the targets of that order.

Prosecutions of Antifa as domestic terrorists have already begun. In June and July 2026, nine people were sentenced to between 30 and 100 years in prison over a 4 July 2025 protest at a Texas ICE detention center where one of them shot and wounded a police officer. Six people who never fired a weapon got 50 years each; a man who was never at the protest got 30 for moving a box of zines.

As crackdowns spread to Minnesota last winter, federal agents outnumbering the state’s two largest police forces combined faced protesters armed with snowballs. In January, immigration agents shot and killed two US citizens – a poet and mother of three, and an ICU nurse for veterans. Outcry peaked in Minneapolis, but the administration did not appear to have abandoned its plans, according to recent New York Times reporting, only to have delayed them. Behind the scenes, Trump’s team was debating suspending habeas corpus for unauthorized immigrants – a fundamental check on state power – while Vance and Miller continued pushing to invoke the Insurrection Act on US streets.

Former House Democratic leader Richard Gephardt and former senator Timothy Wirth argue that the US is in the middle of a “rolling coup,” designed to ensure Trump never loses an election. Many of the individual actions, they acknowledge, “may each appear legal or at least arguably so”. The danger, they argue, is in the pattern. “The first job of any coup is to make the recognition of it seem premature. That is the trap. By the time recognition is no longer premature, the moment to resist has already passed.”

That does not make El Salvador a postcard from some inevitable American future, of course. The US’s institutions and political opposition are stronger than El Salvador’s. Trump also lacks a credible public security threat like Bukele had in the gangs, said Steven Levitsky, a Harvard professor of government and co-author of the book How Democracies Die.

The crises that the Trump administration has tried to invoke to suspend democracy – from the supposed threat of Antifa to the Charlie Kirk killing – “so far, they haven’t worked,” he said.

I called Gephardt, the former Democratic House majority leader, a founder of Keep Our Republic, a bipartisan coalition to protect the US electoral process and the rule of law. In his view, 2020 proved that Trump and his team are unwilling to accept losing an election. While that effort was a “clown car”, he thinks that the president’s cronies are far better prepared today.

A new 45-day ICE surge in California has prompted local leaders to warn that these raids will be used to suppress voter turnout. Gephardt also worries that Trump has set the stage to claim that China or Iran has interfered with election integrity, seize voting machines and ballots in targeted state or cities, and invoke secret executive orders that long predate Trump – “a loaded revolver that’s been on the table for 70 years”, in Gephardt’s words – that he believes Stephen Miller is leading the effort to adapt. Those orders, as one government document notes, “are designed “to implement extraordinary presidential authority in response to extraordinary situations”.

Two months ago, conservative host Wayne Allyn Root told Trump he had the right to declare a national security emergency for elections. Trump’s reply: “Let me just say stranger things have happened. I’ll leave it at that.”

Trump might also call a red-state governor like Texas’s Greg Abbott, as he put pressure on Georgia in 2020, and insist that Democratic House winners were elected through fraud and that Abbott must intervene;; in a close midterm, flipping five or 10 seats could decide control of the House. Gephardt’s group, Keep Our Republic, is prepared to file lawsuits in every state should Trump launch such an effort.

The last resort: if Democrats retake the House, Mike Johnson remains speaker until the new House convenes at noon on 3 January. That morning he could fire the nonpartisan clerk of the House and install a loyalist who would refuse to accept the certifications of Democratic winners. While most experts believe this is not legally viable, it is the method that worries Gephardt most, because there’s some uncertainty about whether this could be resolved by a court.

Working against democracy, says Gephardt, is an alliance of ideologues and the tech industry. Trump is less the architect than a salesman fronting for people who want authoritarian rule and regard citizens with contempt.

What stands in the way? First, the courts. The administration has cowed the House and made gains with the supreme court, but the lower federal and state courts remain independent, and he believes that the combination of the courts and the people are democracy’s only hope.

Gephardt puts his faith in ordinary citizens, but if they take to the streets, they may hand the administration a pretext to invoke the Insurrection Act. Authoritarians rule through fear, he warns, and “they’ve got the guns”.

“We are in the test of whether or not the institutions and ultimately the people can maintain self-governance,” he said. “We are still working with this experiment, but it’s fragile … And we are on the brink of losing it.”

William Wheeler, a freelance journalist, is the author of State of War: MS-13 and El Salvador‘s World of Violence. His reporting in El Salvador was supported by the Fund for Investigative Journalism, the Pulitzer Center on Crisis Reporting, and Freelance Investigative Reporters and Editors (Fire)

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: ‘A hidden tradition’: Benjamin Moser wants you to know Jewish anti-Zionism is not new
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Aaron Gell
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
The writer rarely questioned the tenets of liberal Zionism growing up. Now he embraces anti-Zionism with the fervor of a new convert

In 1987, the Israeli human rights attorney Felicia Langer was paying a visit to the Neve Tirza women’s prison when a client named Siham shared some disturbing news: the prisoners held there had recently been sprayed with a chemical agent that left them writhing on the floor. Langer grabbed a tissue that had been exposed to the substance – a piece of evidence, perhaps, in a future legal case. Then, on impulse, she lifted it to her face and inhaled deeply. Her hope, she wrote later, was that doing so might enable a doctor to identify the toxin.

This anecdote appears in Anti-Zionism: A Jewish History, by Benjamin Moser. In it, the Pulitzer prize-winning author profiles a dozen Jews who actively opposed Zionism, before and after the establishment of Israel – from Aaron Samuel Tamares, a Polish rabbi who began inveighing against Jewish nationalism in the late 19th century; to British diplomat Edwin Montagu, who sought to derail the 1917 Balfour declaration promising a Jewish state in Palestine; to Israeli “new historian” Avi Shlaim – figures he sees as part of “a hidden tradition … of people who, though long dismissed and despised, were ultimately proven right”. Along the way, he seeks to dismantle the Zionist “fairytale,” as he puts it, piece by piece.

Langer’s heedless act made her ill but failed to provide the evidence she’d hoped for. It serves as a haunting analogy, however, for Moser’s own work of historical inquiry-slash-self-purification. Having been raised on what he considers a false narrative of the Israel-Palestine conflict, and therefore at risk of moral complicity in an apparent genocide, Moser now proposes to expose himself and his readers to a counter-narrative, however uncomfortable – Siham’s tissue as written history.

Of course, Zionism is a complex and multilayered subject, more hotly contested today than ever before. Where some see a movement of liberation and self-preservation, a principled, heroic response to centuries of oppression and near annihilation, others see a ruthless campaign of land theft, violent dispossession and genocide. Moser, having been raised with the former analysis, now embraces the latter with the defiant fervor of a new convert.

When asked during a recent interview in Brooklyn what had changed his mind, the author replied with characteristic brashness: “I didn’t understand the settler-colonialist element – that a group of foreigners sponsored by imperialist powers with bayonets had come into this country that was 95% to 97% non-Jewish and just said: ‘Everybody, fuck off.’”

This is not, to be clear, the consensus view (early Zionist immigrants to Palestine were mostly unarmed refugees fleeing pogroms). And anti-Zionism occasionally indulges in a similarly essentializing style. While the book is, as its subtitle has it, a work of history, it is also an impassioned act of soul-searching and, in places, a blunt polemic. This makes for an awkward combination, one that sometimes sacrifices objectivity on the altar of moral catharsis. Asked by Piers Morgan to respond to a critic who’d faulted his book for being overly simplistic, Moser cheerfully embraced the assessment: “I do think it’s black and white!” he declared of the Israel-Palestine conflict.

Anti-Zionism appears at a difficult juncture for the pro-Palestine movement, in which polarizing rhetoric and recrimination have become increasingly commonplace as Israel’s killing in Gaza continues. (See, for example, the UK Green Party’s declaration that Zionism is racism, the jeering of New York mayor Zohran Mamdani for attending a 7 October vigil and an increasing willingness to defend the massacre of 1,200 people in southern Israel as a legitimate response to oppression.) For some, even to suggest that not all Zionists favor ethnic cleansing, Jewish supremacy and the obstruction of Palestinian self-determination smacks of equivocation in the face of mass murder.

Moser’s book has given rise to considerable pushback for embodying that vehemence. Critics in the New Yorker, the New York Times and other influential outlets have taken issue with his portrayal of Zionism as fundamentally malevolent – and Palestinians as essentially blameless – and some have made note of factual inaccuracies.

The author seems unfazed, chalking up the critical reviews to politics. “A lot of the people who are coming for me now, who are they? They’re liberal Zionists,” he insisted. “Because what I say is: the whole thing from the very beginning was rubbish. It was a terrible idea. Israel is not something with problems. It is a problem.”

The grandson of Holocaust survivors, Moser, a lanky 50-year-old, was raised in the Reform tradition in Houston, Texas, and rarely questioned the basic tenets of liberal Zionism: that the establishment of a Jewish state in Palestine was a meritorious answer to centuries of victimization, that Israel represented a stronghold of democracy surrounded by hostile neighbors and that Arab recalcitrance was the primary obstacle to a peaceful two-state solution. “The idea of rebuilding a persecuted people in the land from which, millennia before, they had been exiled,” he writes in Anti-Zionism, “appealed to my sense of romance, and of justice … And so, though I was dis’appointed by Israel, Zionism remained, in my mind, something pure.”

A turning point occurred in the summer of 2016, when Moser accepted an invitation to speak about his acclaimed biography of the Brazilian novelist Clarice Lispector at the Palestine festival of literature. PalFest, as it’s known, is not simply a literary event; attendees tour the West Bank, meet Palestinian counterparts and absorb the grim brutality of the occupation up close. While walking down an eerily quiet street in Hebron, a West Bank city where Palestinians must contend with severe restrictions on their movement and constant settler abuse, Moser found himself overwhelmed by what seemed to him a terrible injustice. (The writer Ta-Nehisi Coates, in his recent book The Message, described a similar awakening in Hebron.) “I’m from Houston,” Moser said, but “I could walk down the street in this city where people whose families have lived there for thousands or hundreds of years were literally not allowed.”

Aside from detailing the experience in a 2021 Substack post, Moser largely kept his growing misgivings about Israel to himself until last year, when he published a fiery personal essay in the inaugural issue of Equator magazine, a bracing attempt to reconcile the Zionism of his youth with the grotesque civilian suffering imposed on Gaza in the wake of Hamas’s 7 October assault. The piece prompted “a huge reaction, probably more than anything I’ve ever written, all positive”, Moser said. It will be anthologized in the forthcoming edition of The Best American Essays.

“I thought, we have to write about how Jews are not on board with this,” he told me. In the essay Moser reserves special vitriol for American Jewish leaders, who as he puts it, “were happy to sacrifice our civil liberties, our free press, our judiciary, our foreign relations, to sustain the killing” in Gaza.

To tell the stories of these 12 apostates, and do so with such obvious affection – he calls such figures “the moral aristocracy of Jewish people” – is in some fundamental sense to join their circle, and to thereby knowingly invite the same calumny that rained upon each one in turn.

Moser has a lot to lose. He achieved wunderkind status in his early 30s with his Lispector biography, and was then offered the career-making opportunity to become the authorized biographer of intellectual titan Susan Sontag, a project he pursued with great zeal, conducting hundreds of interviews and nabbing the Pulitzer for the resulting 800-plus page monolith. More recently he published The Upside Down World, a collection of essays on Rembrandt, Vermeer and other Dutch masters. He has, to all appearances, won the literary lottery: when not traveling the world to research his books, he lives in the Netherlands and with his partner, Dutch novelist Arthur Japin, occasionally decamping to a charming tumbledown country house in southwestern France.

Why then take the risk of swatting at the most polarizing of geopolitical hornets nests?

“I think that at a time of genocide, you can either sit on the sidelines and exempt yourself from criticism and think that makes you feel safe,” he said, “or you can, as they say in Brazil, give your face to be beaten.”

The first blow came from the New Yorker, to which Moser has contributed a handful of pieces. Isaac Chotiner, who plainly shares Moser’s queasiness around Israel’s wanton destruction of Gaza, wrote a review of the book that was blistering, to say the least, deeming Moser’s “approach to facts … slovenly to the point of reckless”.

Chotiner focuses his critique on the book’s treatment of what Moser calls the “third rail” of Holocaust studies – the ways in which Zionist leaders found ways to cooperate with the Third Reich. “Did the Zionist movement benefit from the Holocaust?” Moser asked during our interview. “A lot of historians disagree, and a lot agree. I have my viewpoint, which I make very clear.”

Moser introduces this idea by outlining the shockingly anti-Jewish views of several prominent Zionists, including the movement’s founder, Theodor Herzl, who predicted that “The antisemites will become our most dependable friends,” and himself showed a penchant for classic antisemitic tropes, deploying a 17th-century antisemitic slur, “Mauschel,” to describe Jewish anti-Zionists. “We are a nation of hagglers and crooks,” Herzl wrote, “because Mauschel proliferates and plays stock market tricks.”

But Chotiner makes a compelling case that Moser’s attachment to this theme leads him to misrepresent several important facts. In particular, Moser’s book points to several articles in the Zionist press that appear to whitewash Nazi atrocities or advocate Jewish compliance, which Chotiner demonstrates do no such thing when presented with more context.

One can grant the validity of such objections, however, while also acknowledging the virtue of Moser’s larger project: a searching, vivid frontal assault on an ideology that is now fueling one of the greatest atrocities of our time. “It’s just like, people are getting killed every day,” Moser said with a long sigh. “And they want to fight with you about your footnotes. Then they want to attack you personally and try to destroy your career. But I 100% stand by my book. People can criticize me for whatever they want, but they can’t criticize me for not making myself clear.”

A few months ago, Moser visited Berlin to attend his niece’s batmitzvah. There, he visited the former home of his grandparents and paused to contemplate the Stolpersteine, the commemorative brass “stumbling stones”, dedicated to their memory. Before immigrating to the US, his grandfather, Franz Egon Moses, had spent time in Mandatory Palestine. Moses’s volume of Herzl’s Zionist Writings is now in Moser’s library. Had he lived, Moses might well reject his grandson’s turn toward anti-Zionism. But maybe not.

“I hope they’d be proud of me,” Moser said of his ancestors, growing somber. “People didn’t stand up for them. People shut up. They took their kids to school and went shopping, just like all these people are doing now. I don’t want to be that kind of person.” Briefly removing his glasses, Moser gave his eyes a quick wipe. “Those aren’t the people I respect.”

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.title: Stephen Fry: ‘Sherlock Holmes altered the course of my whole life’
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.author: Stephen Fry
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.text:
Nearly a hundred years after Arthur Conan Doyle’s last Sherlock Holmes story, the writer and broadcaster unravels the mystery of the detective’s enduring appeal

It has become quite the fashion for contemporary writers to have a go at reinventing past classics. We’ve seen it done with imperishable literary heroes like Bond, Jeeves, Poirot and Winnie-the-Pooh. This is a relatively new phenomenon. But not in the case of Sherlock Holmes, where the practice is almost as old as the man himself.

Sherlock Holmes was the conception of Arthur Conan Doyle, a Scottish doctor down on his luck who had turned his hand to fiction to make up for a worrying lack of success in attracting patients to his surgery. Conan Doyle could never have guessed that the first Sherlock Holmes story he wrote, A Study in Scarlet, published in the 1887 issue of Beeton’s Christmas Annual, would in a few years propel him and the characters he created to literary fame. The personalities and characteristics of Holmes and Watson became as familiar to late Victorians as their own friends and families. The readership was worldwide and spread across all ages and classes.

Conan Doyle himself – frustrated by the burdensome discomfort of what he felt had become something of a millstone around his neck – killed off his creation by having Holmes apparently plummet to his death in Switzerland’s Reichenbach Falls, pulling his arch-enemy Moriarty down with him into the roaring cataract. The public outcry was swift and over­whelming. Grown men and women wept openly, black armbands were adopted, and a host of angry readers wrote abusive letters to Conan Doyle’s publishers, to the Strand magazine and to Conan Doyle himself. He grudgingly bowed to public pressure and unearthed a story set before Holmes’s plunge into the abyss – The Hound of the Baskervilles. But only after the clamour still refused to subside did he at last bring his hero back to life in The Return of Sherlock Holmes, presaging a new stream of short stories and a full-length novel, The Valley of Fear. He was to continue writing Sherlock Holmes adventures right up until 1927, although he never set a story later than the eve of the first world war.

During his lifetime, stage productions (he collaborated on the first himself) and silent films were produced, and after his death in 1930 the great post-Conan Doyle Holmesian caravan began to rumble into full life.

Now, you should know that the Sherlock Holmes body of work written by Arthur Conan Doyle himself is called by Sherlockians “the Canon” (coincidentally and happily an anagram of Conan). The Canon comprises four full-length novels and five collections of short stories.

In all, 60 canonical stories. How many have been written since? I don’t believe it is possible to count. I know I have written one myself. Conan Doyle’s son Adrian Conan Doyle, along with the great Golden Age mystery writer John Dickson Carr, wrote a collection of new stories under the title The Exploits of Sherlock Holmes. After that, the stampede was on, in all media, of course. The Hollywood films starring Basil Rathbone as Holmes and Nigel Bruce as Watson began in 1939 with the canonical The Hound of the Baskervilles, but soon began to move the pair into all kinds of modern settings. By the 1940s, they were doing their bit for the homeland by pitting themselves against the Nazis. The Conan Doyle Estate was open to allowing and authorising such variations, which soon became an established and legitimised part of the whole Sherlock Holmes enterprise. Between 2014 and 2023 Holmes emerged from copyright and entered the public domain.

Most Sherlockians I have come across will, like me, cite Jeremy Brett as their favourite Holmes, but one feels there will always be a new kind of Sherlock for every age. I had the honour of playing Sherlock’s brother Mycroft in Guy Ritchie’s Sherlock Holmes: A Game of Shadows, with Robert Downey Jr and Jude Law as Holmes and Watson, and the pleasure of reading the entire Canon for Audible. Along with the publication of my own Holmes pastiche, these were the completion of some kind of a lifelong dream. The closing of a very strange circle.

I can say without the slightest fear of exaggeration that Sherlock Holmes altered and determined the whole course of my life. Let me explain.

I had been entranced by the Sherlock Holmes stories from the earliest age. I read and reread the entire corpus of stories avidly and before long I had joined, as their youngest member to date, the august Sherlock Holmes Society of London. This eccentrically aristocratic institution had Lord Gore-Booth as chair and the Marquess of Donegal as editor of its magazine, the Sherlock Holmes Journal. I managed to get permission from my housemaster to leave school one weekend, travel by train to London and attend a society meeting, at which I was scheduled to read a paper. The subject of my disquisition? Well, I had noticed with excitement one day the parallels between Sherlock Holmes’s description of Professor James Moriarty (“He is extremely tall and thin, his forehead domes out in a white curve, and his two eyes are deeply sunken in his head”) and TS Eliot’s description of Macavity the Mystery Cat (“his eyes are sunken in. His brow is deeply lined with thought, his head is highly domed”). The society was being very kind in letting me address them on this topic: any fool could see that Eliot had based his Macavity entirely on Moriarty, it was hardly news. I thought I had discovered a great literary secret. At any rate, the event went well, but the sequel did not.

I stayed in London, sitting in cinemas from dawn till midnight and watching any number of films. By the time I came to and hopped on a train back to school, a full three days later than had been agreed and sanctioned, I found that I had been officially declared missing. My parents and the police were informed, and the hunt was on. The fat was truly in the fire, my number finally up. The school expelled me. That expulsion led to other expulsions and disasters, which culminated in my landing in prison; I shan’t go into too much detail: Moab Is My Washpot, the first volume of my autobiography, is also happily still in print, and the full story can be read there.

Anyway, all these ructions finally got me thinking straight and determining to change my ways and try for Cambridge, the university on which I had always set my heart. I did get there, where I met my friend Hugh Laurie and found myself set on the course of writing and performing which has filled my life ever since. None of which could have happened without that Sherlock Holmes Society evening and its cascade of consequences back in the early 70s.

But I still haven’t quite addressed the most pertinent question. Why? Why do these characters – Holmes, Watson, Mrs Hudson and Mycroft (along with that hapless cast of professional bunglers, sceptics and sincere admirers from Scotland Yard) – seem to attract reinvention and retelling so much more than any other fictional creations? And why the Game? How did that arise? The Game, I should explain, is what Sherlockians call the tradition of Holmesian scholarship that makes the very serious and straight-faced assumption that Holmes and Watson were real and that they actually did live at 221B Baker Street and that everything Watson writes about (although he makes plenty of mistakes in consistency and continuity) truly did historically happen.

But I repeat: why? This doesn’t happen with Poirot, Father Brown or Lord Peter Wimsey. What’s so special about the denizens of Baker Street?

Well, one can begin by making the surely undeniable statement that Sherlock Holmes is one of the most fully realised and enduring fictional characters ever created. Very quickly, his complex and rounded personality, the details of his intellect, his manners, his dress, his habits, his appetites, techniques and methods combined to create a place for him in the public consciousness of a kind that had never before been experienced in literature.

Holmes’s world is also vivid and tangible. Everyone who has read even a handful of stories will have their own clear picture of the Baker Street rooms, the fireplace, the test tubes, the violin case, the pipe rack, the fog at the window … we all have our images, reaffirmed or modified by countless films and television adaptations certainly, but unmistakably real. So real, indeed, that even as the stories were still being written and published, tens of thousands around the world behaved as if Holmes and Watson truly lived and breathed. From as far as Japan and South America came letters addressed to 221B Baker Street begging for Holmes’s assistance. Some even wrote to Buckingham Palace and Downing Street to urge the king and prime minister to award Sherlock Holmes a knighthood.

But there is, I think, another reason for the astonishing connection that Holmes made with the public on his arrival and that he continues to make in all the multiplicity of his incarnations today. And that is need. The world needed him in 1887 and the world needs him now.

With the great rise in literacy from the middle of the 19th century onwards, it perhaps seems inevitable that a new kind of fiction should arise that tried to solve the puzzle of the lately arrived Big City – most especially the biggest by far in the world, London. The daunting size of the metropolis was something quite new in human history. Society was transforming itself from a knowable hierarchy into a bewildering network. It could be seen structurally as like a great web, interlinked and complex, mastered only by those sensitive enough to understand, touch, feel and identify every node and every twitch on the filament. In fact, by a Sherlock Holmes.

And after Holmes, of course, ten thousand more detectives sprang up, all with their own USPs, their own special ways of clearing up mystery and caging the monsters. But so, too, did a strange breed of 20th-century heroes who offered a similar promise of bringing light and order to the darkness and chaos of modernity, but in their case without bothering to think much. I mean, of course, the comic book and film superheroes. Our infantile side (and there was never an age in our history that so encouraged and coddled our inner child as the present) seems to have embraced magic, flying, invisibility, X-ray vision and all kinds of impossible superpowers. It seems to me fair to suggest that Superman and Batman, unlikely as it may seem, follow in the great detective’s footsteps and owe him their being. He was surely the first caped crusader, for all that his cape was constructed of good tweed. They, like him, answered a need.

Why so many have moved from valuing the real and achievable powers that Holmes exhibits – achieved through his own self-training, study and practice – to valuing imaginary, unearned, randomly achieved magical superpowers is another question. But fortunately the appetite for Holmes and real deductive talent is undiminished, too. We can have both kinds of hero, after all. On television alone, for every Superman and Deadpool, there has always been – as well as a new Sherlock for each new generation – a Columbo, a Monk or a Ludwig reaffirming the power of the Sherlockian method and re‑establishing the primacy of mind over mayhem. Holmes’s cigar ash, footprints and almost invisible telltale particles are the forerunners of the crime lab’s mitochondrial DNA, epithelial particles and microfibres, and his magnifying glass gives way to today’s scanning electron microscope. But the principles are quite unchanged. Which is why he is the presiding spirit behind every CSI operative and why the modern Scotland Yard criminal database (the Home Office Large Major Enquiry System) has initials that spell out the name HOLMES.

Like London and the wider human world, the world of Holmes and Watson is a work in progress, capable of being modernised and made over in countless ways, but always, underneath it all, entirely its noble and magnificent self.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: The WNBA finals are a basketball wonderland – unless you’re part of the Maga machine
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Andrew Lawrence at State Farm Arena
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
The Dream and Valkyries are tied at 2-2 after four absorbing games. Many in America would rather we revisited the national anthem debate

When Tyler Perry leading lady Crystal Renee took center stage at State Farm Arena to sing the national anthem before the Atlanta Dream’s WNBA finals clash with the Golden State Valkyries on Saturday afternoon, a smattering of photographers, game officials and event security took their familiar places around her as the capacity crowd stood for the flag. As soon as the lights went back up, the teams returned to the floor to resume their shootarounds. Anyone genuinely invested in the finals would have been unfazed by them briefly stepping away – if they remembered it at all after the Valkyries’ 67-62 win tied the series at two games apiece. But for many watching the game, basketball is beside the point.

Seven years ago, Jay-Z declared that the culture had “moved past kneeling” and similar national anthem protests, seemingly sounding the death knell for an era of sports activism that had helped raise awareness of racial disparities as a broader social movement gathered force. The line cemented his partnership with the NFL as the league bowed to political pressure to crack down on anthem protests, with other major US sports eventually following the NFL’s lead. But rightwing media and politicians never got the memo. They’re still making sports a battleground for patriotism, with basketball as the war’s chief casualty.

Credit OutKick, Fox’s renegade sports arm, for providing the spark that reignited the right’s outrage machine. They tipped off the WNBA finals by making a story out of Atlanta and Golden State leaving the court during the national anthem, then amplified the indignation aimed at LeBron James for appearing to practice his golf swing during the anthem at a Philadelphia 76ers game that same week.

That was all the scene-setting Donald Trump needed. “You know the NFL did that for a while and they stopped because people stopped watching games. I think you should do the same thing with women’s basketball,” Trump said. In a Truth Social post, he called James a “disgrace” and demanded he “apologize to all of those Great American Warriors and Heroes who died for the American Flag, and all that our Country stands for!”

Basketball has grown accustomed to this kind of punching down from the White House and the familiar cycle of provocation and outrage, especially when the administration’s poll numbers are dragging. James dismissed Trump’s diss as a sign of a “slow news day at the office” and the WNBA declined to engage, beyond noting that players haven’t been on court for the anthem for years now. Meanwhile, the Dream and Valkyries have been too preoccupied with winning their first championship to really enter the chat.

“For me, it’s staying off social media. It’s just going inward with our teammates and staff,” said veteran Golden State center Kiah Stokes, who helped drive her team’s victory with her stout defense of Atlanta star Angel Reese. “Staying together. That’s been one of our keys all season.”

But no matter how hard the WNBA resists the urge to clap back, no matter how valiantly it tries to keep the spotlight on basketball, there will always be someone on the right looking to steal it for their grievance grift. As OutKick and Trump reheated the stale anthem controversy, former NBA player turned Maga wannabe Enes Kanter Freedom was making a grand show of his latest appearance at a WNBA game, asking for special security arrangements so he could watch Game 3 of the finals from a courtside seat. The Dream offered to accommodate Kanter Freedom – who has disrupted WNBA games in the past – with a fully stocked suite, courtesy of the team and State Farm. But Kanter Freedom refused and beat a retreat with his camera crew.

Jennifer Sey, the red-pilled former US gymnastics champion, has attended this year’s finals in her anti-trans athletic gear – and her efforts to incite a reaction from the W’s progressives went largely unnoticed, too.

It is unfortunate that these finals have become a microcosm of the WNBA season, a tug-of-war between a basketball product that has never been better and a political class desperate to bend it to its own agenda. But the longer the right keeps up its fight, the more it gives its game away – exposing the hypocrisy beneath its moral posturing.
