We’ve seen how urgently conservative culture warriors believe women need protecting when the alleged assailant isn’t transgender. “Cornell’s a fine school,” Trump said in response to the university’s handling of a student’s gang-rape allegations. “I’m sure they’ll do what’s right.” We’ve seen how much this administration cares about its great American heroes as it sends them into an open-ended conflict, keeps sailors at sea for record stretches and downplays casualties, injuries and damage to US assets in the war with Iran – all while slashing veterans’ jobs across the federal government.

We know why basketball makes such a ripe target for attacks from Maga’s crusaders of the American way: the game’s politics lean left, its players are well-traveled, culturally sensitive and have no qualms about dunking on trolls. And we know why the WNBA, in particular, gets under the right’s skin: it is so Black and queer, and its players have set the tone for political protest in American sports. The Dream, specifically, helped usher Raphael Warnock, the Atlanta pastor who delivers sermons from Martin Luther King Jr’s pulpit, into the US Senate.

We see the play Kanter Freedom is trying to run by seeking out an altercation with a player in front of Atlanta’s largely African American crowd, and the statement Sey hopes to make by swanning around queer-friendly Ballhalla in her statementware. We see how closely these grifters actually follow women’s sports. That much was clear again in a recent episode of The Georgia Gang, Atlanta’s long-running political TV roundtable, when the talk turned to the hometown team’s WNBA finals berth. “Go Sophie Cunningham, she my’s girl not Angel Reese,” said panelist Phil Kent, a conservative consultant – a contrarian move that also betrayed his refusal to appreciate the absorbing WNBA finals matchup we are being treated to: Maga It girl Cunningham and her Indiana Fever crashed out in the first round. When others at the roundtable praised Reese’s selection as defensive player of the year, Kent doubled down (“I question that”) – and the clip has since drawn a torrent of criticism. “These white men are so broken,” said one Twitter user. “It’s never been about basketball.”

The Valkyries enter Game 5 with momentum on their side (“Block out the noise and understand the gameplan” was coach Natalie Nakase’s recipe for victory on Monday), but how the rest of the series unfolds is anyone’s guess. Will Stokes keep holding Reese in check? Will the Dream be forced back into their rinky-dink home arena for Game 6? Will the series go the distance and break more ratings records? The storylines are almost too juicy – the last thing anyone on the right will want to talk about.

Taking a closer look at the United team, Leny Yoro is back after his midweek suspension. Before it, he looked, finally, to have established himself in the first XI and, though he’s a centre-back, I expect he’ll play right-back today, with Ayden Heaven, back in after illness, taking the spot in the centre next to Harry Maguire. That’s because he’d never previously played left-back until forced to fill the spot away to Atletico – one of various things that so exercised Martinez. But now that you don’t ask, I’d probably stick him there again, to get Yoro into his position – he’s actually done better on the left of the two than on the right – and so Digo dalot can play on his natural side. Reports from Old Trafford, broadcast by Sky, advise us that Bruno Fernandes has been dropped by Michael Carrick.

We don’t know if it’s for consistent poor form or midweek insubordination – it could be either or both – but either way, it’s a shame it’s come to this. Ultimately, United have broken Bruno, who’s dedicated his career to elevating a club that has consistently let him down, and though he was out of line in what he said after Como, it didn’t come out of nothing, well earned though his omission is.

An egg walks into a kitchen looking unhappy, so a chef asks what’s up. “It’s the spurtles,” he says. “They beat me.”

“What about the forks?” ventures the chef; “Yes, they beat me too,” comes back the response, so there’s a pause while the chef considers.

“Have you thought about hanging out with Manchester United?” he eventually offers. They don’t beat anyone.”

It’s now almost two months since United won a league game, and that against promoted Ipswich – who now sit five places above them in the table. They did also manage a victory over Sabah, Champions League debutants, but otherwise, their start to the season has been miserable beyond conception, even by their august standards, and is rapidly getting worse. Already, it looks like yet another manager is toast, and this time, perhaps for the first time, there’s no sense of where they could go next.

Just three weeks ago, a home game against Bournemouth was as close to a gimme as possible – even for them. Since then, though, consecutive home wins over Sturm Graz, Sunderland and Milan with eight goals scored and none conceded have flipped the Cherries’ mood and they arrive at Old Trafford with Marco Rose ensconced and the club on a buzz. They’ll fancy this, and really who wouldn’t?

If that was the extent of our afternoon, it’d be plenty, but happily for us, it’s not even close. At Anfield, Liverpool – who’ve also won three on the spin in uplifting fashion – entertain Brighton, already three points clear of third with a game in hand. They’ll know a top-five spot is theirs for the taking and the way they’re playing, who knows what else?

Those two matches will be our focus, but we’ll also be updating from from KC where Hull, who might just be running out of form after a brilliant start, face Brentford while, at Selhurst, Palace meet Newcastle, struggling badly after a promising start under Matthias Jaissle. Or, in other words, this is going to be a lot of fun.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Jessica Glenza
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Man accused of shooting teen, who was driving to a party, has also been linked to shooting of a vehicle days earlier

A man accused in the shooting death of a Missouri teen has been charged in a second shooting incident – both of which involve firing into cars on the highway.

Alyssa Wilson, 17, was shot and killed as she drove down Interstate 170 in Overland, Missouri, on 14 October. The teen was on her way to a Halloween party at St Louis Zoo, called Boo at the Zoo, when a suspect fired a single shot into the back of Wilson’s Buick Encore.

The shot struck Wilson in the back, incapacitated her, and sent her crashing into a concrete highway median, according to prosecutors. She was pronounced dead at Barnes-Jewish Hospital.

The suspected shooter, Willie James Herndon, 43, of Texas, had no known relationship to the teen.

“Alyssa was 17, excited about her life, excited about her future,” her father Robert Hickman said, as state charges were announced. “She had 60 days until she turned 18, and we were getting ready to take our first family vacation together to go to Disney for her to see her favorite person in the world, Princess Tiana, and unfortunately, she’s not going to get to do that any more. This was a senseless act.”

Now, federal court documents show that Herndon has been charged in a second shooting incident, this one just a few days earlier.

On 11 October, St Louis metropolitan police received a report that a vehicle was shot just after exiting Interstate 55 in Missouri. Surveillance footage captured a white SUV fleeing the scene – a vehicle that matched the appearance of Herndon’s Buick Enclave.

A shell casing was also recovered from the scene. Prosecutors said they were conducting ballistics tests to determine if it was fired from the same weapon that killed Wilson.

In a federal criminal complaint, prosecutors lay out how they tracked what appeared to be Herndon’s Buick Enclave from the first shooting incident on 11 October, then the scene of Wilson’s death on 14 October, to a Days Inn in Caseyville, Illinois 16 October.

There, prosecutors approached Herndon’s wife Taiya Herndon, 45, and were speaking to her when Herndon “emerged” from the hotel room and began to flee. As he was arrested, he was “screaming words about a shooting”, prosecutors said.

Inside the Days Inn hotel room, prosecutors said they found a ABC-15 rifle “in plain view”, ammunition that matched the kind used in Wilson’s shooting, a receipt from a gas station near the scene of Wilson’s death on Interstate 170, two license plates and handwritten notes describing police vehicles Herndon believed were tracking him.

Federal prosecutors in Illinois have charged Herndon with being a felon in possession of a firearm. He has separately been charged with first-degree murder and armed criminal action in St Louis county, Missouri. His federal public defender did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: A child of Japanese incarceration’s call to arms: ‘The lessons of Manzanar have never been more urgent’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Andrew Gumbel in Lone Pine, California
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
How a rebuilt, historic California baseball diamond embodies ‘the contradictions in America’s legacy’

When Dan Kwong first dreamed of staging baseball games at the Japanese American concentration camp where his family was held captive during the second world war, he thought of it as an exercise in living history, an eye-catching way to convey the trauma of 120,000 men, women and children who were locked up in the wake of the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor.

Baseball was a passion for Kwong, a 71-year-old performance artist from Los Angeles. He knew that the wartime internees had played the game not just as a distraction from their predicament, but as a quiet expression of their loyalty to the United States. He wanted to stage an event that would cast the game as an act of resistance, and teach new generations about the damage governments do when they strip a whole segment of the population of their constitutional rights.

That, though, was before the second Trump administration brought its own wave of detention camps and mass arrests and made the treatment of Japanese Americans in the 1940s relevant in ways Kwong found both shocking and impossible to ignore.

“It’s not a cautionary tale any more,” Kwong said. “Now it’s a call to arms.”

That rebellious spirit was on full display last weekend as Kwong’s project came to fruition. After years of painstaking work to restore the old dirt field at Manzanar, the camp in California’s eastern Sierra mountains where his mother and aunt were once confined, hundreds of people watched a double-header featuring players from California’s Japanese American baseball league.

The players donned 1940s-era baseball uniforms, gloves and catcher’s helmets, smashed balls into the sagebrush beyond the outfield, and struggled all day with the unusual way the ball bounced and skittered across the grassless field. Kwong, who moves with the athleticism of a much younger man, took the field himself, first for the Li’l Tokio Giants, his team for the past 54 years, and then in an all-star game pitting southern California against the north.

The crowd, many of them holding up Japanese-style paper parasols as protection against the unforgiving high desert sun, cheered his every appearance.

Kwong also made sure that the racial animus of the 1940s and its modern-day revival stayed uppermost in people’s minds. In a speech delivered between the two games, he connected Donald Trump’s “Make America Great Again” movement with what he called the “premise of domination and supremacy” that had made different groups of immigrants and citizens of color vulnerable to scapegoating and criminalization in the past.

“It is a version of America frozen in time within Manzanar’s fences and here on its baseball field,” he said, still in his team uniform. “When we run its dusty base paths and sit in its sunbaked bleachers, for a few hours the past is unfrozen. And in that thaw, we may face the contradictions embedded in America’s legacy: our welcoming arms and our bigoted rejections, our highest aspirations and our lowest debasements, our cruelty and our kindness, our generosity and our greed.”

His was far from the only outspoken voice. “We gather at a time when the lessons of Manzanar have never been more urgent,” the chief executive of the Japanese American National Museum in Los Angeles, Ann Burroughs, said. “The racism, xenophobia and cruelty that made what happened here possible are once again unfolding before our eyes. So many of the laws that were used to discriminate against your families and people of color over hundreds of years of history in this country are now being used again.”

As the ceremonial portion of the day reached its climax, actors in 1940s clothing appeared on the field carrying suitcases, symbolizing the arrival of hundreds of families, most from LA, in the spring of 1942.

The plaintive voice of Nobuko Miyamoto, a celebrated Japanese American singer with a lifelong commitment to civil rights, sang of the Manzanar prisoners’ despair at being behind bars when they had done nothing wrong. “When will it ever stop?” she sang, to audible sobs from the spectators, many of whom grew up with stories about the camp from their parents and grandparents.

At least five men in their 90s or older had been in Manzanar themselves. Among them was Masayoshi Morioka, who first arrived as a nine-year-old and whose grandson Mason was now playing for southern California in the all-star game.

“Gramps, I’m going to Manzanar,” Morioka remembered his grandson announcing.

“Whatever for?” he asked. When Mason told him it was for a game, he vowed: “I have to go, for the last time in my lifetime.”

For years, Kwong’s baseball project seemed like a charmingly impossible dream. The field was neglected and overgrown, the work promised to be time-consuming and expensive, and the National Park Service, which maintains the site as a historical monument, had reservations about allowing an outsider to oversee it and bring in large crowds once he was done.

Kwong, though, never wavered. He raised the funds and won over the park rangers. For the past three years, he has made the 225-mile (360km) drive from LA as often as possible – sometimes accompanied by volunteers, sometimes alone – to clear the foliage and tumbleweeds, smooth out the rough terrain, excavate the outfield posts, erect a fence and bleachers, and build an announcer’s booth.

He first staged a game at Manzanar in 2024, but the public was not allowed in and he called it his “soft opening”. A year later, a federal government shutdown scuppered his plans to roll out a grander event. Then, this spring, a powerful windstorm knocked down the fence and forced him to build a new, stronger one.

The park service imposed a flurry of restrictions. He had to arrange offsite parking and a shuttle bus for his spectators, and was told after the announcer’s booth was already half-built that it did not meet government building safety standards. At the games, the announcers – now seated at a simple table beneath an awning – read a lengthy legal disclaimer and warned players they’d have to pause every time a car passed the field, which happened every few minutes.

The outspoken politics of the event also appeared to cause official nervousness – understandable, perhaps, since the National Park Service has itself been in the Trump administration’s crosshairs, losing 25% of its workforce as a result of sweeping cuts. The site superintendent, Jeremy Scheier, was not present during the speeches, and Kwong said he’d been told to be careful about what he said as a volunteer at a government site.

Manzanar was the first of 10 camps set up to house the Japanese American population of the western United States – the largest mass incarceration in US history, according to the Manzanar Baseball Project website. The site had once been thriving farmland, filled with apple and pear trees, only to turn arid after the city of LA bought up vast tracts of farmland across the Owens valley and drained the water to spur its own development in the early years of the 20th century.

By the time the government requisitioned the site and erected barracks-like structures to house arriving families, the area was best known as a filming location for B-movie westerns and the occasional blockbuster, including Gunga Din, for which the producers – three years before the internment – built a vast military encampment in the shadow of Mount Whitney, a few miles south of Manzanar.

Baseball and softball had been a big part of Japanese American life in California, and they continued in the camps, with some teams surviving intact and continuing to play each other as they had before the war, while others sprang up fresh with names like the ManzaKnights and, among the women’s teams, the Dusty Chicks.

The leagues became so strong that the authorities allowed teams to travel from concentration camp to concentration camp to play each other. As one Manzanar prisoner, Takeo Suo, put it: “Putting on a baseball uniform was like wearing the American flag.”

Kwong, who was born 10 years after the war, developed his own baseball obsession through his father, who came to the US from China. He also grew up with a mother who told him stories about Manzanar, including her experience making camouflage netting for the war effort, which inspired a later career as a tapestry artist. In homage to her, Kwong set up a do-it-yourself camouflage netting project behind the bleachers of the restored baseball field.

Throughout his project, he has managed to count on many others – volunteers, teammates, a Hollywood prop shop that provided the vintage equipment, a seamstress from Connecticut who specializes in vintage sportswear, a veteran of the farm-workers’ movement and the 1960s student protests at Berkeley who donated the labor and material to finish the fence, and several professional baseball teams who kicked in financial contributions.

Still, it has remained essentially a one-man operation. In the days leading up to the grand opening, Kwong’s modest rooms at the 18th Street Arts Center in Santa Monica, where he is an artist-in-residence, were crammed with Manzanar-themed baseball hats, vintage baseball uniforms and piles of paperwork relating to insurance, security, legal waivers and other unglamorous aspects of staging an unorthodox event. One night, he stayed up until 2am just to steam the creases out of the team jerseys.

“It’s been pretty hectic and I’m a little run down,” he said four days before the event. “And now I’m supposed to play baseball? I’m so not ready.”

The games themselves turned out to be the least of his worries. The crowd greeted him like a superstar: “No 12 on the field, but No 1 in our hearts”, the announcer called him. He played a tight first base, brought in a run with a single, and came around to score with the grace of a man half his age.

As the day wound down, Kwong was still flitting on and off the field, taking care of everything from the live stream and his elderly guests to water supplies and a bout of obon folk dancing that closed out the day. He didn’t want to talk about how he was feeling, but he did allude to the “indestructible nature of the human spirit” that the Manzanar experience inspired in its prisoners.

“They created beautiful gardens, exquisite art and music,” he said, “and, oh yeah, they played some hellified good baseball … We still do.”

https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.title: ‘There’s nothing interesting about me – and no interest in me’: how Larry David’s new biography nearly didn’t happen
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.author: Darren Richman
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.text:
He point-blank refused, begged the author not to talk to people who knew him … and eventually relented. Making the first authorised biography of the Seinfeld and Curb creator was no mean feat

Emperor of Nothing: The Making of Larry David might be the most begrudgingly authorised biography ever written. The story of how author Blake J Harris convinced the comedy titan to “tolerate” him begins, of all places, at Fox News.

It was 2020 and Harris’s second book, The History of the Future: Oculus, Facebook, and the Revolution That Swept Virtual Reality, had been published the previous year. Palmer Luckey, the Oculus founder, was “fired for being a Trump supporter” and Harris, anything but a Trump fan, simply reported the facts. Speaking on the phone from his home in Colorado, he explains: “My book ended up doing well because I was all over rightwing media, as they loved having me on. I was the liberal journalist who exposed the truth about how conservatives were treated in Silicon Valley.”

Glenn Beck was one of several rightwing commentators who gave Harris a television platform that helped his book to succeed. He even asked if the author would consider writing his biography. Harris politely declined but started to ponder whether there was a public figure he would like to spend years of his life researching and writing about. One day, while taking a shower, he started to think about the way Seinfeld and Curb Your Enthusiasm had shaped his sense of humour, formative years, his entire worldview. Harris had an epiphany – he would write about the man behind them, Larry David.

Harris had written a lengthy piece for ESPN to mark the finale, at the end of 2015, of The League, a sitcom written and directed by Jeff Schaffer. Schaffer was a Seinfeld writer who would become David’s chief collaborator as Curb Your Enthusiasm wore on. Schaffer liked Harris’s proposal because he felt there should be a biography of his mentor, arguably the most significant comedy writer in American television history. He was also aware that his boss would be reticent given David was the man whom comedy writer Alan Zweibel once described as: “The only person I know who has buyer’s remorse before he buys something.”

Emails flew back and forth in August 2020, with the potential subject informing the potential author that this was a bad idea. In one, reproduced in the prologue of Emperor of Nothing, the subtext is clear – curb your enthusiasm: “There are far better ways to spend your time. There’s nothing interesting about me and there’s no interest in me. That’s not being modest. It’s the truth. So why the book? My parents are dead, so now we’re only left with my kids and my wife to read it. I don’t think three books is making it to the bestsellers’ list. Surely there are better subjects that would welcome a biography.”

Harris was not deterred. He enlisted David’s friends and explained to his hero that this would not be a conventional biography, but rather David as “the protagonist in an ensemble story”. Eventually, to appease his friends in a way his Curb Your Enthusiasm alter ego rarely would, David sent Harris a five-word email: “Oh Jesus. If we must.”

When Harris was eventually introduced to his idol, he had what he considers one of the greatest ideas of his life: a ploy George Costanza (the scheming Seinfeld character modelled on David) could be proud of. He decided to focus on a shared interest: “I really wanted to make a good impression with Larry and show him I’m someone he can just shoot the shit with … I’m not a typical stiff journalist who’s going to make his life difficult … So, I suggested for that first conversation … the only topic I want to talk about is the New York Yankees.” (David is a lifelong fan.)

Steering clear of the work in that initial chat proved an inspired move, even if, six years on, David recently told Harris: “I agreed to do the book, but I immediately regretted it.” Those regrets will be his alone: what started with a conversation about baseball is a 576-page tome that captures the spirit of the comedy great in ways that suggest Harris understands the Davidian shtick so well that this is the closest we will get to a Larry David memoir. Take the story of David’s birth, which reads as a glorious tribute to the late Richard Lewis, his best friend and collaborator: “On 29 June 1947, at Brooklyn Jewish hospital, a remarkable little boy was brought into the world. This boy – who’d prove to be special in so many ways – would by the age of thirty become one of the most influential comedians of his era. Three days later, at that same hospital, another little boy was born. That boy’s name was Larry David.”

The author spoke to friends, family, colleagues and neighbours as he attempted to forensically trace a journey that began in Brooklyn, encompassed years of struggle on the standup circuit and would ultimately produce two of the greatest television comedies in the history of the medium. Few people manage to produce a work of such quality once; to do it twice is almost unprecedented.

The book is especially compelling when covering David’s lean years (a period that stretched into his early 40s). It explains how he found himself picking out potential spots in the street for when he would inevitably become homeless, despite being viewed as the “comedian’s comedian” by his peers. His talent was never in doubt, only his temperament. Harris is skilled at drawing parallels between the art and the life, just as Seinfeld and Curb were at their best when blending fact and fiction. We learn about our hero giggling uncontrollably at a piano recital when confronted with a Pez dispenser, quitting his job at Saturday Night Live in a fit of pique on a Friday only to walk back in the following Monday as though nothing had happened, and taking part in a masturbation contest. All this would become material during the Seinfeld years: Jerry ruins George’s girlfriend’s recital by making Elaine laugh with Pez; George screams at his boss and storms out, then acts as though nothing has happened when he realises the financial implications; and The Contest, in which the four main actors have a wager to determine who can go the longest without indulging in onanism, won David an Emmy. In 2009, The Contest was No 1 in TV Guide’s Top 100 Episodes of All Time.

Indeed, every funny life experience in those early years would invariably find its way into a David sitcom. The urgency of the writing and our awareness of the greatness to come ensures Harris’s biography rattles along like a thriller, but one which, rather than heading inexorably towards a crime scene, instead leads to some of the greatest art of the past century. Harris reassured David, who was afraid of looking egotistical, that he “could hide in his own biography”, due to it including interviews with people other than himself. When he heard Harris was talking to friends and collaborators, David urged him not to “bother them”. Sarah Silverman allayed the biographer’s fears: “That’s so Larry. What he doesn’t realise is what a joy it is for us to speak to you about him.”

Harris describes his subject as the “idealised version of the artist we all wish we were”, a man far more concerned with artistic integrity than financial gain. In the 1980s, long before the fame and fortune, Larry wrote a screenplay entitled Prognosis: Negative. His manager sold the script and was thrilled when she secured a hefty payday for a rewrite. In an unprecedented move, the struggling comic asked for the fee to be negotiated down from $35,000 to $5,000 because he thought the material was good and had no wish to make wholesale changes.

Through Harris’s biography, we learn that this strange combination of unerring belief in his own ability on the one hand and low self-esteem on the other has defined the career of the comic genius. During his standup days, he would routinely open with the following esoteric bit: “You seem like a very good audience tonight. I’m wondering, may I use the tu form with you people? Because I feel very close to you. Do you mind if I jump into the tu form?”

By David’s own admission, it got nothing “60 to 70% of the time”. When Seinfeld asked his future collaborator why he persisted in opening with a routine that rarely worked, the answer was unequivocal: “I think that’s funny! And if that’s not funny, why am I even doing standup? What’s the point?” Typically defiant, he extended it: “You know, Caesar used the tu form even after Brutus stabbed him.” Thus, Seinfeld got an early glimpse of a man who would not be cowed by outside interference.

Harris was grateful that David largely chose not to interfere with his manuscript. His only real notes were asking for sections to be toned down where he appeared “too nice”, especially in relation to his daughters (“What father doesn’t love his daughters?”). He did, however, witness one trademark David rant when he was invited to appear as a background actor in the Curb finale, a story he is delighted to relay over the phone.

Harris and Ken David, Larry’s older brother, were sitting at a table in the background while Larry and Richard Lewis improvised an argument. The pair of extras were instructed to mouth their words, but not speak audibly. Larry’s sibling, however, appeared not to have got the memo and audibly started trying to talk sports with Harris. Harris tells me: “In the middle of the take, Larry seamlessly turned from yelling at Richard Lewis to yelling at his brother and telling him he was supposed to be quiet and that he was ruining the take.”

As an early Curb tagline made clear: “Just because he’s made it, doesn’t mean he’s got it made.” David, it seems, will never stop shouting. Emperor of Nothing perfectly captures the evolution of an artist – even as the man steadfastly refuses to change.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Natasha Bedingfield looks back: ‘I had hits in the US that weren’t released in England. It was like being banished’
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Harriet Gibsone
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
The singer-songwriter on her unconventional education, her brother Daniel, and her quest to write a classic like Purple Rain

Born in London in 1981, Natasha Bedingfield is a singer and songwriter. Her 2004 debut album, Unwritten, sold more than 2.3m copies and featured the No 1 single These Words. She has released three further albums, scoring UK Top 10 hits and success in the US with Pocketful of Sunshine. Nearly two decades after it was released, her single Unwritten became a viral TikTok hit in 2021. Her new single, Dot Dot Dot, is out now.

This was taken at Hilly Fields park in south-east London. I’m dressed in a sweet little tracksuit. I was a cute kid: I sucked my thumb until I was 11 and I had a sheepskin that I sniffed. But if anyone actually said I was cute, I’d reply: “No, I’m not!” I wanted to be taken seriously. That word made me think that nobody was listening to what I had to say.

My parents come from New Zealand, and when they had my brother Daniel they emigrated to England where they then had me and my two younger siblings. We lived in the inner city, so our backyard was a saviour. Together we were a pack and would spend all day making forts and watching frogs in the pond. We didn’t have much money, but I was rich in love.

I come from a family of big thinkers. My parents are social workers and raised us to believe that everyone is equal. We were taught that you should talk to everyone, as you never know when you could be standing in front of an angel. Mum and Dad wanted each of us to learn in our own way, outside of a system, so I was home-schooled from 11 until 16. Back then it was a rebellious thing to do, but I loved self-study. I am overwhelmed by loudness, so the fact I didn’t have to learn in a full class of students worked for me. It’s ironic, really, considering my profession, but too much noise makes me shut down. Is that a neurodiversity thing? Probably.

As well as my parents’ outside-the-box approach, another big influence on my childhood was church. Every week we would go to a Jamaican church, one that really encouraged kids to get into music. I loved the culture there – as well as singing, we had a strong community of people of all ages.

When I was 18, I started travelling on the tube and doing late-night writing sessions with producers. My brother was the more obvious musician in the family. Daniel would be at home, saying things like, “Everyone be quiet – I’m recording!” Whereas I was more private – writing but keeping it to myself. Why? Some friendly acquaintances – family, friends – warned me that it might be hard to have two Bedingfields in the industry. “It’s very rare that it would happen for both of you,” they’d say. So I decided to get on with it quietly. In the end I said to my brother: “I know this is your thing, but it’s actually my thing, too. And I’m not trying to take over from you.” He, of course, supported me entirely.

Around the same time, I started studying psychology at university. I found the whole process stressful – I often felt dizzy, and struggled to learn all of the names and dates. My dad ended up saying: “We all know that you’re a singer-songwriter – that is what you should be doing.” He was the one who encouraged me to leave university and I will be for ever grateful.

When I started out, my label told me that I was a pop artist. But I wasn’t Britney. I didn’t even know what pop meant at the time, because I wasn’t keeping an eye on the charts, I didn’t listen to the radio. Even as a teenager I never had boybands on my wall. I was a fan of Coldplay, Björk, India Arie and Stevie Wonder. I didn’t want to mime, or pole dance. I was just trying to be authentic. The only time I did learn a dance routine was for the video for Single. I did a few moves, then felt weird. They wanted to make me sexy, but the whole thing looked forced. It was frustrating. Female artists often get boiled down to how we look and it takes away from the substance of what we’re actually saying.

I wrote Unwritten for my younger brother. It started as a poem, and then I tried to make it into a song with other writers, but they wanted to take a different approach, to do the whole blond bombshell pop type of thing. Then I met Danielle Brisebois [from New Radicals] and together we clicked and made Unwritten. The whole process felt simple. I wasn’t showing off vocally. I was just singing to my brother. I didn’t think about whether it would be a hit.

After the success of my first album, I started taking myself less seriously in my lyrics. I’d grown into my humour, which is where a song like I Wanna Have Your Babies comes from. The track was restricted by BBC Radio 2 as they thought it was encouraging young people to have kids. But, really, it was meant to make people laugh as it was about the thoughts you never say out loud when you are dating someone new. In the end, my label sent me to the US – a way to test out my career without other parts of the world watching. They essentially geo-blocked me. I had hits in the US, but they were not released in England. I even sang at the White House for Obama, and my mum couldn’t watch it. It was a bit like being banished. The only bonus was that being a Briton in the US meant I could get away with certain things. Because I taught myself to read, there were some words I knew how to write but not say out loud. In my song These Words, I use the word hyperbole. A word I had never said out loud before. I sang it wrong for a long time, but told the Americans that was how you pronounced it in England.

After that I left my label and had a 10-year period where I was doing a lot of corporate shows and touring. I got married, had a baby and kept on songwriting. I wrote with some Swedish songwriters, but the songs didn’t show much growth. Then around the pandemic, people started making up dances to Unwritten. It went viral and I started having a resurgence. Some friends called and said: “Natasha, you have to become part of the conversation.” I didn’t get it at first. I thought TikTok was just a dance app and I didn’t want to dance. But once I saw the videos I realised it was a creative place to be. I’ve embraced the song’s new life ever since.

My goal now is to write my Purple Rain. I haven’t written my best songs yet and I want a timeless classic. Getting older doesn’t threaten me – artists like Tina Turner had careers that took off when they were my age. I find that so inspiring, as so often it’s, like, women are written off when they reach a certain age.

I still feel so alive when I am making songs. It’s that buzz of expressing an emotion that everyone feels, but is hard to articulate without music. I don’t get excited about the things other people do – I don’t like going to Disneyland or holiday resorts. Even on my birthday I would rather be in a recording studio, making songs and geeking out about a triple entendre, than at a party. I don’t think that will ever change.

1 min Peep peep! Leeds, in their yellow change strip, kick off from left to right as we watch.

Prokofiev is on the tannoy at the Stadium of Light, which means the teams are about to take the field.

Subs: Ellborg, Methalie, Talbi, Alderete, Diarra, Ahoka, Fofana, Juan Angulo, Tutierov.

After Bruno Fernandes was dropped for “pure football” reasons - according to Michael Carrick - could Manchester United actually win a game of football?

The answer, again, was a resounding, humiliating no, and if the manager’s job remains in real peril, you have to wonder, too, if this beleaguered team should steel itself for a relegation dogfight. They lack imagination, cohesion, fight, confidence, and anything resembling joy and so now hovering a point above the drop zone, survival cannot be taken for granted.

Brighton’s emphatic run was blown off course at Anfield as Liverpool moved up to fourth with an appetite and urgency at both ends of the pitch that showed Andoni Iraola’s methods taking root. It is Liverpool, convincing winners on home soil for the first time this season in the Premier League, who looked upwardly mobile.

Florian Wirtz was instrumental in an opening goal officially credited to Brighton’s Pascal Gross and Alexander Isak converted his sixth league goal of the campaign to shatter the visitors’ sequence of four successive Premier League wins. Brighton’s winning streak had included 15 goals and none against but there was neither attacking verve nor defensive resilience on show from Fabian Hürzeler’s side. Liverpool had a monopoly on both, and the sight of Bradley Barcola racing back to defend and Ronald Araújo thundering into challenges will have satisified Iraola just as much as the incisiveness up front.

Sunderland v Leeds evokes one game more than any other. You know the one. It’s 1973. Never mind the Sunday roast, who’s ’avin ’oops?

Daniel Harris has reaction to another dreadful day for Manchester United (and much else besides).

The talismanic Brian Brobbey returns to the Sunderland attack after injury. Leeds are without Nico Elvedi, Anton Stach and Noah Okafor; in come Jaka Bijol, Harry Wilson and Brenden Aaronson.

You can follow all the action at Old Trafford and elsewhere with Daniel Harris.

Hello and welcome to live, minute-by-minute coverage of Sunderland v Leeds at the Stadium of Light. Last season, these teams breathed new life into the English football pyramid by comfortably avoiding relegation on their return to the Premier League. Leeds have started 2026-27 in a similar vein – but Sunderland, almost unnoticed, have slipped to the bottom of the table after taking four points from the first seven games.

The distraction of the Europa League, in which Sunderland have started superbly, is probably the main reason for that. And three of their seven league games were against the top three, so there’s nothing to worry about yet.

Nor will Sunderland – or Leeds, for that matter – take anything for granted. This is only the third Premier League meeting between the sides since 2002, a reflection of how much these two huge clubs have struggled. English football is a better place when they are in the top flight.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.title: Serbia votes as strongman Vučić faces grassroots challenge to 12-year rule – Europe live
https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.author: Jakub Krupa
https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.text:
The Student List movement is taking on authoritarian leader following nearly two years of protests against government and institutional corruption

Aleksandar Vučić’s SNS anchors the “United Serbia” list. The party relies on control of the public purse, favourable media coverage and strong nationalist backing, but its campaign has been overshadowed by accusations of systemic voter manipulation.

The Student List eschews party hierarchies or a single figurehead, preferring locally respected academics and professionals, and operates through university networks. Its quickfire, humorous campaign has mobilised large numbers of disengaged voters.

That means Serbia’s traditional opposition parties have been largely marginalised, with their collective support falling from 30% to 10-15%. Some parties have switched allegiance to the Student List. Others, such as European Serbia, may not clear the 3% electoral threshold.

Meanwhile, Serbia’s rightwing, nationalist bloc is riven with disagreements and has been further weakened by the unexpected withdrawal of the We the Power of the People party over allegations of Russian influence. Some of the nationalist vote may switch to the SNS.

Serbia’s former president and now prime ministerial candidate (again) Aleksandar Vučić rose to prominence in the 1990s as a radical nationalist, who supported the policies of Serbian expansion and ethnic cleansing led by Slobodan Milošević, who died of a heart attack in detention in The Hague during his trial on charges of genocide and crimes against humanity committed in Croatia, Bosnia and Kosovo.

He served as Milošević’s information minister throughout the Kosovo conflict. His Serbian Progressive Party, or SNS, has been in government since 2012.

He first spent three years as the prime minister from 2014, before switching to the role of the president in 2017. Unable to run for the third term, he resigned from the post in September, and now wants to lead the government again.

As president, Vučić has not emulated his predecessor’s militarism, but he has maintained his nationalist playbook in domestic politics, dismissing the opposition as stooges of unspecified foreign powers.

He maintains close ties with Putin’s Russia and Xi’s China, which regularly gets him criticism from the EU and complicates Serbia’s path to the bloc.

Serbia has regressed in international rankings for press freedom and corruption in recent years, and its process of joining the EU is effectively stalled. More on that shortly.

Vučić is also fairly close with Donald Trump and his associates. He hosted Donald Trump Jr and Jared Kushner in Belgrade, and, as we revealed, personally intervened to advance an allegedly illegal – and definitely very controversial – scheme to hand over a protected site in Belgrade for a Trump tower.

Dobro veče, or good evening, and welcome to our live coverage of Serbian election night.

The grassroots protest movement, the Student List, is taking on the country’s increasingly authoritarian leader, Aleksandar Vučić, in what is shaping up to be the sternest test of his 12-year grip on power.

The vote is a culmination of two years of student-led protests triggered by the collapse of the Novi Sad railway station canopy in November 2024, which killed 16 people and uncovered massive government and institutional corruption.

The bottom-up leaderless movement, with 250 candidates democratically elected from people with limited political experience but distinguished professional careers, seeks to end Vučić’s rule and rewire the state, with focus on fighting alleged corruption, clientelism and power abuses of the past.

Polls opened at 7am (6am UK time) and close at 8pm (7pm UK time). Until then, we’ll bring you all the key background, explain why it matters for Europe, Ukraine, and you, and give you a flavour of the chatter in the queues outside polling stations from Belgrade to London.

I will also keep one eye on the first round of the presidential election in Bulgaria, so expect an odd update on this or two on this.

It’s Sunday, 25 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/202.title: Is having urine the color of Mountain Dew normal?
https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/202.author: Keren Landman
https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/202.text:
A Trump administration doctor says neon yellow urine is normal because of diets consisting entirely of meat and fermented foods. Here’s what experts say

A doctor who advises several Trump cabinet members on their diets rhapsodized this summer about having urine the color of Mountain Dew, thanks to a diet consisting entirely of meat and fermented foods.

What you consume does determine what you see in the toilet. But should urine be neon yellow – or some other hue? Here’s what you need to know.

Urine is normally a shade of yellow owing to a pigment called urobilin, which your gut bacteria produce. The more diluted it is by extra fluid intake, the lighter its shade – so urine is typically darker in the morning or when you’re dehydrated.

You may have seen charts that indicate what color and shade urine “should” be, but “they are considered imprecise” and experts don’t rely on them for serious purposes such as managing kidney disease, says Suzanne Watnick, a nephrologist at the University of Washington. Urine’s darkness or lightness loosely corresponds with hydration status, but for most people, it’s best to rely on your sense of thirst rather than what’s in the toilet to determine when to drink water.

That said, in people who need to stay highly hydrated, urine shade can be a helpful hydration indicator. For example, people prone to kidney stones should aim for very pale urine, Watnick says.

Your kidneys constantly filter blood to remove excess water and waste products, which trickle down to the bladder to get peed out as urine. These organs’ goal is to ensure your blood consistently has exactly the right balance of fluid, minerals, salts and acid.

“Your kidneys are really smart,” says Sharon Moe, a nephrologist at Indiana University School of Medicine. As long as they’re healthy, you can’t really override their settings. For instance, if you consume more water-soluble nutrients than you need, anything “extra” ends up in the toilet. This includes the by-products your body makes when it breaks down food and medicines, as well as the majority of any vitamins and supplements you might be taking.

Some of these compounds won’t visibly change urine – for instance, digesting a lot of beef is likely to turn urine more acidic but not change its color, says Watnick. But some can change the color of urine or make it exceptionally bright. B vitamins (like riboflavin) can turn it fluorescent yellow, rhubarb a reddish-brown, and beets a festive pink.

Anything but the usual yellow – including Mountain-Dew-adjacent hues – may signal your body is consuming something it can’t use. “If you get super fluorescent or super red, you’re eating too much of something or taking too many supplements,” says Moe.

For most healthy people, urine color changes are rarely an emergency. Notable exceptions include people with kidney disease, or if the color change is accompanied by other concerning symptoms like new pain, a new rash or severe leg swelling. These types of changes might signify a medical problem – get it checked out.

Otherwise, to troubleshoot a strange new urine hue, first stop any supplements you’re taking, says Moe. If it doesn’t go back to normal, cut out brightly colored foods next.

Additionally, look over your medication list. If you recently started a new drug, ask your clinician whether it could cause urine color changes. But don’t stop taking any prescribed medicines before that conversation, as urinary changes are an expected and harmless side-effect of some drugs.

If your urine is red or brown, you haven’t had any red flag symptoms, and the color persists after you’ve ruled out any recent dietary or medication changes, get checked out.

Bleeding in the kidneys, the bladder or the urinary tract can also turn it red or brown, and your clinician can assess that with a simple urine test. (In people who menstruate, it can occasionally be challenging to determine where blood in the toilet is coming from. Talk to your clinician if you’re not sure.)

Foamy urine can mean protein is leaking from your kidneys – a few bubbles aren’t worrying, but you should be concerned if you see anything that looks “like a beer head in the toilet”, says Moe.

Odor, frequency and transparency are also important. A sweet or foul smell, peeing much more or less than usual, and cloudy urine are all reasons to get checked.

Although urine changes can occasionally herald kidney problems, most kidney disease is invisible; 37 million US adults have chronic kidney disease, but only one in 10 of them is aware. Moe says the best prevention is keeping your blood pressure in a healthy range and eating lots of fruits and vegetables, with meat in moderation. “The carnivore diet is not a healthy diet,” she says.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Matthew McConaughey has read all his bad reviews – and I applaud him | Polly Hudson
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Polly Hudson
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The Hollywood actor revealed he once read two-decades’ worth of pans in one fell swoop, during two days in the desert. It’s the kind of preposterous self-flagellation we can all learn from and enjoy

To assume makes an ass out of you and me, but as sweeping generalisations go, this seems fairly uncontroversial: nobody likes hearing themselves being criticised. Obviously there are exceptions to the rule – no kink shaming here – but most people aren’t fans.

Which is why a recent admission from Matthew McConaughey is unusual. The Hollywood actor revealed that he once spent two days in the desert reading 20 years’ worth of negative reviews about himself.

I love everything about this. Each detail is perfect: the setting, the duration of the pursuit and the period spanned by the reviews, the narcissistic/anti-narcissistic intent, the ridiculousness, the pretension, the commitment.

“I read every one,” McConaughey said on the podcast Build or Break, while wearing tinted sunglasses inside and the sort of hat last seen on The Only Way Is Essex. “I sat with them – I spent two days looking. It was hard.”

The mental image this conjures up is a gift – nay, payback. This is why McConaughey is paid the big bucks; why, as the world burns, we need celebrities more than ever. Thinking about a 56-year-old tortured artist-millionaire, hunkered down in a barren landscape, nobly forcing himself to pore over his harshest critiques, is a wonderful distraction from proper news. It’s like a ludicrous minibreak from reality.

There are a few gaps we’ll have to fill in ourselves. When McConaughey says he “collected 20 years” of slatings and “went away to the desert for a weekend and took them all in this thick book”, do we imagine him sitting by the printer with his Pritt Stick, constructing his burn book with his own fair hands? Or is it more likely that this endeavour fell to an assistant in his employ? (In which case, talk about a fool’s errand.) Did McConaughey’s wife and kids join him on the multi-day desert jaunt and, if so, how was his 48-hour absence explained? “Sorry darling, Daddy can’t play Uno, he’s wallowing in painful self-reflection.”

In summary: this column will definitely not feature in any of his handmade tomes of the future. Ten out of 10, Mr McConaughey, no notes. And thank you.
