39 governorships. Voters will choose governors in 36 states and three US territories.

Thousands of state legislative seats, as well as local offices, judicial contests and ballot measures on issues including taxes, abortion rights and voting rules.

The elections for Congress will determine which party controls Congress for the final two years of Trump’s second term. The governorships and state legislative contests will shape policymaking closer to home, from education and reproductive rights to taxation and the administration of elections.

They have a long history of punishing the occupant of the White House. The president’s party has lost House seats in 18 of the past 20 midterm elections, a 90% rate of loss that stretches back to 1946.

The pattern is not inevitable. George W Bush’s Republicans gained seats in the 2002 midterms, following the September 11 attacks. But Barack Obama’s Democrats suffered a “shellacking” in 2010 and Trump’s Republicans lost the House in 2018.

Republicans enter this election with a narrow margin for error in the House and a more substantial advantage in the Senate. The RealClearPolitics average of national generic polls showed Democrats leading Republicans by 8.2 points in early October. Trump has been forced to hold campaign rallies in what should be safe Republican states.

But political polarisation and years of redistricting have reduced the number of genuinely competitive House districts, making it harder for either party to translate a national swing into a big change in seats. The Reuters news agency has estimated that only about 40 to 50 House races are truly competitive.

Several Senate contests have emerged as key battlegrounds. In Michigan, progressive Abdul El-Sayed is seeking to hold an open seat for Democrats after Gary Peters, the incumbent senator, decided not to seek re-election. In Georgia, Jon Ossoff, a Democratic senator, enjoys a healthy poll lead over Republican challenger Mike Collins.

In Maine, a state won by Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024, Susan Collins, the Republican senator, is defending her seat against Democrat Troy Jackson. Ohio offers another major test, with Democrat Sherrod Brown seeking to return to the Senate against Republican Jon Husted.

Texas has become especially closely watched. Democrat James Talarico is taking on Republican Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general. Republicans have spent about $210m to help the scandal-plagued Paxton. No Democrat has won a statewide election in Texas since 1994. Trump won Texas by nearly 14 points in 2024.

Other contests in Alaska, Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina and New Hampshire could help determine which party controls the chamber (if there is a 50-50 split, JD Vance, the vice-president, a Republican, wields the tiebreaker vote). Latest polls show Democrats ahead in Maine, North Carolina and Kansas, and competitive in Alaska and Ohio.

In the House, the contest is spread across dozens of districts. Republicans are defending vulnerable seats in places including New York, Texas and Iowa, while Democrats are also fighting to protect members in districts made more difficult by redrawn congressional boundaries. Notable gubernatorial elections include Alaska, Iowa, Florida, Georgia, Ohio and Texas.

The cost of living regularly tops opinion polls. Democrats are campaigning hard on affordability related to food prices, housing, fuel and healthcare. The war in Iran has added a further complication for Republicans.

Immigration remains another defining issue, with polls suggesting that many voters feel Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) hardline approach has gone too far. This could wipe out many of the gains that Trump made with Latino voters in 2024.

Datacentres, AI, tariffs, trade, abortion rights, voting rules and the future of democracy also remain important themes. Democratic socialists scored some notable victories in Democratic primaries, creating momentum on the left of the party.

But in closely fought races, personal credibility, local connections, the ability to appeal to independent voters and a blitz of TV advertising can outweigh the national party message.

The integrity of the midterms is under scrutiny, with concerns ranging from voter registration to the certification of results. Trump has sought to amplify these fears, putting forward a litany of misleading and false claims about threats to US elections.

The justice department has sued states for access to their unredacted voter rolls, seeking to cross-check them against a federal immigration database in an effort to identify ineligible voters. A federal judge ruled that the department’s policy was unlawful, citing limits on its authority and the risks of inaccurate data.

There are also concerns about the use of immigration-enforcement data in voter-fraud investigations, the administration’s efforts to change mail-voting rules and the prospect of federal election monitors at polling places. The NAACP has sued over the planned deployment of monitors, arguing that their presence could intimidate voters.

The risks do not end when polling stations close. Voting-rights advocates are also watching for pressure on local officials to certify results, mass challenges to ballots and legal disputes that could delay or undermine the transition of power.

A Democratic victory in either chamber would significantly constrain Trump’s ability to advance his domestic agenda and hasten the president’s decline into “lame duck” status.

If Democrats take the House, Republicans would lose their ability to pass legislation through that chamber without Democratic support. A Democratic majority could launch investigations into the administration, demand documents and testimony, and subject senior officials to sustained congressional scrutiny. They might come under pressure from their support base to impeach Trump.

The Senate confirms cabinet officials, ambassadors and federal judges, including supreme court nominees. A Democratic majority could block or delay many of Trump’s appointments, and force the White House to negotiate over legislation.

Even if Republicans retain one or both chambers, a reduced majority could make governing more difficult, particularly when legislation requires near-unanimous support from the party’s own members.

Governors and state legislatures have influence over abortion access, education, taxation and voting procedures. State legislatures also play a central role in drawing congressional district boundaries, although the precise arrangements vary by state and some maps are subject to court challenges or independent commissions.

Voting rules are another source of contention. New restrictions on identification, registration and mail-in voting have taken effect in several Republican-controlled states. Supporters describe such measures as safeguards for election integrity; critics argue that they risk making it harder for eligible citizens to vote.

These disputes are especially significant in a political climate in which Trump has repeatedly questioned election procedures and the legitimacy of results he dislikes.

Voting takes place on Tuesday 3 November, but the results may not be known that night. Close contests, different state rules for counting early and postal ballots, and possible recounts or legal challenges could delay the final outcome.

Once the dust has settled, there will be no respite in this – the land of the endless campaign. Attention will soon turn to the 2028 presidential election campaign, when both parties will seek to turn the results of this November into a foundation for the next fight for the White House.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: ‘He was like 10 men after taking cocaine‘: how Britain’s drug habit is fuelling domestic abuse
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Robyn Vinter North of England correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
Home Office figures show nearly two-thirds of drug tests carried out on arrested abuse suspects detected use of a drug that ‘boosts confidence but increases paranoia’

During lockdown, Charlotte and her ex-partner would spend evenings cooped up in their flat, listening to music, watching YouTube videos and chatting until the small hours. Those nights would be fuelled by alcohol and lines of cocaine.

“I wanted to be loved, and when he told me he loved me like nobody ever would and nobody ever will, I drank the Kool-Aid,” Charlotte says. “I wanted to believe that. And there’s a point when you’re with somebody and you’re drinking, you’re doing coke, where you think you have this bond, you think it’s just you two in the world.”

But that emotional high would be fleeting. “Without a doubt, without any exception, it would never end peacefully. My ex-partner would get so ridiculously paranoid once he was using cocaine. It was just crazy,” she says. Charlotte’s partner would accuse her of taking more than him, messaging men and hiding things from him. When she denied it, he would subject her to brutal physical assaults.

“And then the next day it was all apologies and it’ll all be fine, it’ll all be different.”

Data suggests it is a common scenario. Home Office figures sent to the Guardian show nearly six in 10 police drug tests carried out on people arrested on suspicion of domestic abuse were positive for cocaine between July 2025 and June this year.

It is not possible to see the whole picture, as some of the tests were carried out after the police suspected drug-taking, but it tallies with a 2023 pilot study that found 59% of domestic abuse suspects tested positive for cocaine or opiates.

A wider Guardian investigation has found that Britain’s record-breaking cocaine habit is also driving crimes from assault to dangerous driving. The stimulant is increasingly ubiquitous, fuelling situations ranging from fights on nights out to violence at football matches.

Cocaine has featured in a number of domestic murder cases in recent years. Victoria Thomas, a 45-year-old mother-of-two from Cardiff, was strangled to death by her husband, Alcwyn Thomas, who was “argumentative and moody”, having been filmed on CCTV taking cocaine shortly before he killed her on 19 August 2024.

On 13 June last year, 32-year-old Izzy Knight was murdered by her husband, Paul Knight, in the house they shared in Northamptonshire while their two daughters slept upstairs. In a note, he blamed “having an addiction to cocaine and spending money I don’t have”.

Cat Chappell, a BACP-registered therapist specialising in domestic abuse who previously volunteered on the National Domestic Violence Helpline, says cocaine boosts confidence but increases paranoia, “and so much of abuse is around paranoia”. “It’s taking what’s already there, making it like 10 times worse,” she says.

It can also make it more difficult to leave, she says, because perpetrators will often offer to get help with their cocaine problem. “And [for victims], that’s what you want to hear in those moments.”

Charlotte and her ex-partner got together just before the pandemic and, though it was not the first time she had taken cocaine, it was not something she had done regularly. Her ex, on the other hand, was a habitual user.

“My ex was a really small man, and after cocaine use he’d be like 10 men. He was like the Incredible Hulk, it was like there was this beast in him and he would get this strength. And I can’t tell you where it was from. Then he would come at me and he would absolutely beat me to a pulp. It was absolutely terrifying,” she says.

He would routinely trap her in the bedroom. “I remember one night he got really paranoid that somebody was in the house and he brought knives upstairs. He would pace about all night. It was really, really horrific.

“For somebody who’s already [controlling and abusive] it’s like adding fuel to the fire, it really is, with coke.”

He often stole from her to fund his habit, using her phone to take money from her bank account, including times when he had knocked her unconscious.

Charlotte remembers police visited their flat about 19 times, as a result of her own calls and those made by neighbours, but she would always cover up her ex’s cocaine use.

“I would deny a lot of it because I didn’t want to say, ‘Yes, I’ve been doing it as well’, so you’re in this absolute no-win situation because you’re then sticking up for them all the time.”

She began to abuse alcohol to cope with the situation she was in. “I didn’t want to be there,” Charlotte says. “I was just drinking because I didn’t want to feel anything. I’d wake up, drink all day. I just wanted to feel numb, numb, numb, numb, numb.”

She was finally able to leave on Boxing Day in 2021 when her ex went out to score drugs and she wrote an email to her father asking him to pick her up. She has been free of alcohol and cocaine since.

After initially attempting to pursue her ex for knocking her teeth out, police later decided to take no action against Charlotte’s abuser. She fears he will go on to abuse someone else.

It was Women’s Aid that helped her get her life back on track and she is now an advocate for the charity in her home city of Leeds. She also works for another charity, Smart Works, which helps women get into employment.

Nik Peasgood, the chief executive of Leeds Women’s Aid, says Charlotte’s story is increasingly common. She thinks cocaine is having an effect on the levels of violence perpetrated by abusers and she is calling for more research to help understand the relationship between cocaine, domestic abuse and mental health.

“If they’re already abusive and the relationship’s abusive, [cocaine] might lower their inhibitions, it might make the frequency worse, it might make the severity worse, it might mean that they can’t control how they normally control the relationship and the situation. But it doesn’t make somebody abusive or violent if they’re not already. It’s not an excuse for that violence.”

Peasgood says that cocaine, unlike a lot of other drugs, is used by a broad range of people, including middle- and upper-class people and those who are well-respected within society and do not fit the stereotype of what people think domestic abusers looks like.

The drug can be a barrier to people seeking help, particularly for victims in professional jobs who feel they have a lot to lose if they are caught using illegal substances.

“[Contacting the police] has ramifications away from just the perpetrator when there are drugs involved, and [there is] fear around that,” says Peasgood. “Especially if people have got children, it’s something they wouldn’t necessarily want others to know about.”

Through her work, Charlotte has now met many others who faced similar situations. “I’m in recovery now and it’s alarming how many people tell the same tale of drinking, doing coke, and it just becoming an absolute explosion of rows and just horrific violence,” she says.

“I think it’s not a problem that’s actually going away. If anything, it’s getting worse. You only have to speak to people in the rehab or recovery world and they’ll tell you this is going nowhere. It’s really scary.”

She believes the figures don’t show the true scale of the issue. “I think this is much wider reaching than we realise, due to the stigma of reporting it and the shame of the victim using the drug.”

For many people, she says, cocaine use is “very much seen as our weekend thing”. “It’s very much behind closed doors and not spoken about. People would be gobsmacked at how many people actually do it. It’s so widespread, it’s unbelievable.”

In the UK, call the national domestic abuse helpline on 0808 2000 247, or visit Women’s Aid. In the US, the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the national family violence counselling service is on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found via www.befrienders.org.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Creaking, smug … and a contender? Aaron Rodgers may yet get his Super Bowl farewell
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Melissa Jacobs
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.text:
The 42-year-old remains a polarizing figure. But the Steelers have a formidable defense and a quarterback who has seen it all before

Aaron Rodgers is nowhere near this season’s MVP conversation. At times in his second season with the Steelers, the almost 43-year-old has shown glimpses of the player he was in his prime, slinging the ball with zest and precision, able to suss out any coverage. Other times he has looked like, well, a guy in his 40s playing a young man’s game.

Rodgers looked more like prime Rodgers in the Steelers’ gritty 16-10 win over the Saints in Paris. He wasn’t satisfied with his side of the ball, telling reporter Molly McGrath, “I don’t think we played very good on offense today.” But Rodgers did enough to secure the win, including a 51-yard strike to DK Metcalf in the second quarter. He later scrambled for a first down on third-and-six to secure the win.

Sure, there were points left on the table – the Steelers had several stalled drives and only scored one touchdown in four red-zone trips – and 16 points against a two-win team isn’t impressive. But the Steelers left France with a win, a 5-2 record and a ton of upside.

So here’s a crazy thought: Could Rodgers win a Super Bowl in his final NFL season?

But when you consider the parts around Rodgers, perhaps it’s not so crazy. As competent as Rodgers was against the Saints, the defense stole the show. They smothered Saints quarterback Tyler Shough, and shut down the Saints run game as Steelers linebacker Patrick Queen had predicted. This Steelers run defense is punishing and only improving. In Weeks 1-4, they allowed 4.5 yards per carry. Over the last three weeks, it has dropped to 2.8 yards per carry. All told, Pittsburgh’s defense has allowed just three touchdowns in the last 15 quarters. That is some 2025 Seahawks-level domination.

Offensively, Rodgers is no worse than Sam Darnold was last year when the Seahawks won the Super Bowl. He’s thrown 13 touchdowns and five interceptions for 1,699 yards through his first seven games this season – Darnold had 12 TDs, four picks and 1,754 yards over the same span in 2025. Saints linebacker Kaden Elliss likened Rodgers to a point guard, noting the advantage he has over other NFL quarterbacks. “Even though he’s up there in age, I think that’s an advantage to him, his mind,” Elliss said after Sunday’s game. “And I think he used that today.”

Maybe Rodgers’s football IQ could catapult Pittsburgh to a deep playoff run in the AFC. Yes, there are the perennial Super Bowl contenders like Kansas City and Buffalo, but no AFC team this season is a winning machine like the Patriots in the Brady-Belichick era.

And, after a ho-hum Super Bowl from a star power perspective, a Rodgers return to the big stage would set off fireworks.

Of course, Rodgers comes with plenty of baggage due to his commitment to his “own research” during Covid, his ridiculous antipathy towards Anthony Fauci and his habit of calling out coaches and teammates. Recently, though, he appears to have realized keeping his opinions to himself is probably the best course of action. His worst take over the weekend was appearing to think Peaky Blinders was set in France rather than England. He’s not exactly likable, but considering what he’s said in the past, his recent behavior seems like progress.

Not that he’s completely quiet. In Paris, when asked about the International Series, he let it be known that team owners had considered a 16-game schedule with an entire international week, where teams play all over the world and two byes. Instead, according to Rodgers, they opted for the 17-game schedule to rake in extra cash. Rodgers added that the league “may be a little tight on money,” a refreshing level of shade that will win him some fans.

Realistically, Rodgers and the Steelers will need a good deal of luck to make it to the Super Bowl this year. But that’s the case for plenty of teams. A run to the title game would send Rodgers’s smugness of the charts, but you have to admit that his final game coming on Super Bowl Sunday would be interesting.

Joe Burrow, QB, Cincinnati Bengals. Down 13-0 at the half, the Bengals looked destined for an infuriating loss, an art they specialize in. They had mustered just 49 passing yards, and were struggling to sustain drives. Meanwhile, the supposedly retooled Bengals defense couldn’t get the Ravens off the field. At the half, Baltimore, led by a backup quarterback, had dominated the time of possession 22:20 to 7:40. Yet again, Cincinnati looked like a fringe playoff team not meeting their full potential. And after locking up star receivers Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins for Joe Burrow in his prime, being a fringe playoff team isn’t acceptable.

Chase’s halftime team talk seems to have worked. “I told our offense [that] we can’t look at our defense the whole time. We’ve got to step this shit up and make something work,” he said after the game. Burrow, who is chasing his first league MVP, duly played out of his mind. He was essentially perfect after the break, dicing up the Ravens secondary for four touchdowns on four drives with 243 yards and an 89% completion percentage. Burrow made it look effortless as he tends to do at his best.

64. How do the Bucs win a game 43-13 when Baker Mayfield only throws 64 passing yards? They faced a Panthers team who were a walking comedy of errors. Mayfield only threw 11 passes in his first game back from dislocating his thumb, and did connect with Tez Johnson for a score. The damage unsurprisingly came on the ground – Tampa rushed for 258 yards and three touchdowns, including two from Bucky Irving, who eclipsed 100 yards. The Bucs also strip-sacked Bryce Young and returned it for a touchdown. Imagine the score if Mayfield was slinging the rock.

This article includes content hosted on embed.bsky.app. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

Bo Nix came into Sunday’s game with just 37 rushing yards all season. So when the Broncos quarterback nearly doubled that total in one play – a 62-yard touchdown run that gave Denver a late second-quarter lead over Arizona – hell yeah, he was going to add a flourish.

The spin move at the goalline may not have been necessary, but it must have been cathartic. Nix has been criticized for not providing an offensive spark, even though Denver came into the game at 4-2 after negotiating one of the league’s toughest schedules. But Nix looked far more comfortable – and at times electric – in Sunday’s 30-16 win. He finished with the one long rushing touchdown, and 222 passing yards.

-- The Chiefs were undefeated going into their game with the Super Bowl champion Seahawks but we knew Kansas City had flaws. Patrick Mahomes has been good rather than great, the receiving corps is ravaged and their schedule had been soft to start the season. On Sunday Night Football, they were overwhelmed by Seattle, whose defense became the first unit this season to make former Seahawk Kenneth Walker III look human. And Seattle’s Jaxon Smith-Njigba was terrifying once again, hauling in 150 receiving yards in his team’s 20-3 win. “One hell of a game from Sam Darnold,” said Smith-Njigba, slightly underplaying his own contribution.

–- The Dolphins are no longer winless after humiliating the Jets 28-25 at MetLife. Geno Smith was outplayed by Malik Willis, who played clean football and was able to scramble at will, especially in the first half. Jeff Hafley outcoached Aaron Glenn, not a hard feat. Given New York’s talent advantage, they have no business losing at home to a 0-5 team with severe salary cap issues. But when the Dolphins have the ball for the final nine minutes of the first half and Glenn enters the break with all three timeouts remaining, winning is difficult. The Jets’ star receiver, Garrett Wilson, has cut a frustrated figure recently and was only targeted three times on Sunday. CBS cameras caught him yelling on the sidelines, although he later denied his anger was directed at his quarterback, Geno Smith. “We were collaborating,” said Wilson. “I don’t even think I was talking to Geno.” This fan on Reddit summed it up best.

–- The Minnesota Vikings moved to 6-0 after an ugly 16-10 win over the Indianapolis Colts. This was not the game that will leave the rest of the NFL believing the Vikings are a juggernaut. Colts kicker Spencer Shrader missed two field goals, and Minnesota sealed the win after Daniel Jones delivered a ball right to Harrison Smith. But the Vikings are the only undefeated team left in the league, something few would have predicted at the start of the season.

–- The Houston Texans fell to 2-5 after a 27-21 overtime loss to the New York Giants, who move to 4-2-1 and are very much in contention in a weak NFC East. It was a masterclass by the Giants’ offensive line and running backs against a Houston team who were favored by 10.5 points. Cam Skattebo tore through the Texans line with 18 carries, 124 yards and a touchdown, a week after being benched. In his first start for New York, JJ McCarthy was sensational. While he had no passing touchdowns, McCarthy (20-of-28, 252 yards and no turnovers) was comfortable in the pocket and able to anticipate coverage under pressure. One bright spot amid the disappointment for Houston: Tank Dell caught his first pass in 673 days. Dell suffered a torn ACL, MCL, LCL and a dislocated kneecap in late 2024, and his return is miraculous after a plethora of surgeries.

–- The Atlanta Falcons handed the San Francisco 49ers their first loss of the season. The Falcons were opportunistic in the 29-20 win after a series of miscues by the 49ers. Brock Purdy threw two interceptions, including one on a pass he meant to be thrown away. The injured Mike Evans’s absence was felt keenly, and Christian McCaffrey missed a chunk of the game with a thigh injury, though he did return. Given the thin wide receiver corps in San Francisco, perhaps there’s an unhappy camper they can pursue.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.title: Kimi Antonelli looks forward to drivers’ title after victory in US Grand Prix
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/o.author: Giles Richards at the Circuit of the Americas

Kimi Antonelli has acknowledged the Formula One world championship is within his grasp after the Italian took a dominant victory at the US Grand Prix which has put him just two points away from clinching his first title at the Mexican Grand Prix next weekend.

Antonelli beat the Ferrari of Charles Leclerc into second place and the Red Bull of Max Verstappen into third. With his title rivals George Russell and Lewis Hamilton finishing eighth and fourth respectively, Antonelli will take the title if he finishes ninth or better in Mexico City.

The 20-year-old, who stands to become Formula 1’s youngest champion, was jubilant as he crossed the line at the Circuit of the Americas. “Yeah! That’s how we do it,” he exclaimed to his engineer Peter Bonnington.

“Another small step,” the Mercedes team principal, Toto Wolff, told Antonelli over the radio after the victory. “Another small step.”

With Mercedes having worked hard to iron out issues with their recent upgrades to the car, the victory was important to the team, who pulled off a coup in opting for a one-stop strategy which paid off handsomely for their world champion-elect driver. Antonelli paid tribute to his team.

“We’re very close [to the title], hopefully we can clinch it soon,” he said. “It was a result we needed, to be fair, the whole team deserved it all this time – working to bring this new package and finally seeing the result is very pleasant. It was a perfect execution of strategy to call the one stop. Today was a great team effort.”

This view was echoed by the Mercedes deputy team principal, Bradley Lord. “It felt like everyone was getting a bit excited but all Kimi could do today is go out and win,” he said. “Amazing job by everyone on the pit wall and the strategists back at base. What a drive, what a win.”

However Verstappen, whose Red Bull team opted for a two-stop strategy, was far from enamoured with his afternoon and a car that was suffering from problems. “Yeah, that was terrible,” he said. “The pace, the wrong tyre, shit pit stop, shit engine braking. Nothing worked.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: If Democrats win big, will they learn the right lessons from their victory? | Jan-Werner Mueller
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Jan-Werner Müller
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
No election outcome ever interprets itself. So how will Democrats interpret these results once they are known?

Whichever metaphor one prefers – landslide, earthquake, wave – it seems increasingly like the Democrats can expect a significant victory in the midterms.

As the joke goes, every gas station display of prices has become an ad for Democrats; what’s more, some of them have managed to connect the relatively abstract issue of corruption to the daily misery of many Americans.

But, in the end, no election outcome ever interprets itself; Democrats should not rest content with the conclusion that only what moderate leaders (and consultants) like to call kitchen table issues really mattered.

They have a historic opportunity to dislodge the image of the Republicans as the party of national security and the party best trusted with the economy.

After 2024, Republicans massively benefited from elite actors – Silicon Valley oligarchs, no less than many journalists – reading a globally important “vibe shift” into the presidential election outcome; we now know that what political scientists politely call “low-information voters” were simply fed up with inflation, as opposed to a large majority thirsting for a far-right agenda.

But Trumpists turned the perception to their advantage; and to be sure, successful politicians are entitled to interpret a vote as they see fit.

Democrats could stay relatively timid and read the outcome as simply a rejection of Donald Trump and the most egregious elements of his misrule since January 2025; they certainly should make the point that the spectacular cruelty of ICE and the incitement to hatred in which Stephen Miller and JD Vance regularly engage is deeply unpopular with the public. But it would be a mistake to see the outcome as only a referendum on Trumpism.

True, the US president’s catastrophic record in foreign policy is partly explained by conduct the old Republican establishment could never have imagined: recklessly alienating allies, with the result that the US may never be trusted by Nato countries again; massively destroying soft power by mistreating foreign students and undermining the capacity of American universities to attract talent internationally; blatant interference in elections to favor the global far right.

But the Iran war shows continuities with the George W Bush era that neoconservatives probably find uncomfortable to contemplate: an inability to think strategically and an apparent indifference to loss of human life. In fact, a line can be drawn from the torture memos to the murders at sea and the plans for a public execution under the US secretary of defense, Pete Hegseth.

Yet the Republican party still lives off an image that the party of Ronald Reagan is supremely competent in matters of national security. The right response is not that Democrats should not enter a competition of how often they can use the word “lethality” in one sentence; they should simply point out how shameful it is that Republicans, some murmuring on the part of has-beens like Thom Tillis aside, have betrayed Ukraine; how damaging the loss of bases in the Middle East will turn out to be; and that, from the very beginning of Trump 2.0, it was a sign of deep unseriousness to put a second-rate TV host in charge of the world’s most powerful military force. There might be monuments to both Trump and Hegseth in Moscow and Beijing one day; after all, they effectively capitulated to the former and sped up the rise of the latter.

The Republican party has also long benefited from the notion that, as the party of business, they are best qualified to boost the economy (no doubt, some low-information voters still buy into the myth of Trump as the great entrepreneur).

The actual record has long shown something different: not just when it comes to Trump and his string of bankruptcies, but for the party as a whole. Since Trump engaged in policies so irrational and damaging that the old Republican establishment would never have contemplated them – tariffs being the obvious example – it is again easy to overlook continuities.

The party that claims to be deeply concerned about debt and deficits (one of Elon Musk’s disingenuous justifications for Doge’s chainsaw massacres) has given us Reagan, Bush and Trump – all of whom managed massively to increase the national debt. The reason is, of course, that they pushed through enormous tax cuts that overwhelmingly benefited the wealthy.

In the postwar period, economic growth, job creation and even stock market returns have on the whole been higher under Democratic administrations; it just seems that average gains are not enough for the uber-wealthy, who can buy themselves tax cuts by donating massively to Republicans.

Needless to say, as soon as Democrats are in charge, Republicans discover that the very debt they were instrumental in causing constitutes a national crisis and requires deep cuts to social security.

Conventional wisdom has it that the Biden administration overreached: too woke, too ambitious a Green New Deal, too harsh in its criticisms of Maga Republicans (with the next claim usually being that such overreach made a “backlash” inevitable and, so the implication goes, at least somewhat legitimate).

But what if the opposite is true? What if Joe Biden’s mistake was to assume that there were still many Republicans who cared about policy – as opposed to endless culture war performance a la Hegseth – and long-term success for the country?

What if Democrats seized the opportunity to discredit their opponents in the way Franklin D Roosevelt made the most of the Great Depression (as opposed to pining for bipartisanship); what if they showed people that all the Republicans who will soon be running away from Trump were not just complicit in the misrule, but that the misrule has been part of a larger story predating Trump?

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: ‘Zero-energy companionship’: bizarre hobby takes seed among China’s stressed young adults
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Amy Hawkins in Beijing
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Faced with a stagnant jobs market, many are spurning children or pets in favour of ‘raising bricks’

Chinese young adults looking for a cheaper, low-maintenance alternative to having pets or children have found an answer: raising bricks.

Bricks may not be as cuddly as cats or as life-affirming as human offspring, but they also cost next to nothing. “No cats, no dating, I started raising a brick,” wrote one brick parent on social media.

Raising “brick babies” is easier than house plants, involving spraying them with water a few times a day and waiting for moss spores already present in the atmosphere to attach themselves and grow. One Chinese media article praised the bricks as being “practically immortal”: “If you forget to water them, the moss goes dormant. If you remember to water them again, the greenery returns.”

A hashtag related to the trend has attracted more than 5m views on Weibo, a Chinese social media platform.

Chinese commentators have linked the trend to young people looking for low-effort routes to finding meaning in life. One brick parent told Chinese media that the hobby created “a sense of accomplishment no less than completing a long-term project”.

One user on Xiaohongshu, an Instagram-like platform, also known as Rednote, posted a picture of their rusty-coloured brick baby, saying “no output required, no KPIs to hit, no need to beg it to bloom [and] no comparing its growth with others”.

Another user wrote: “My friends asked if I’d lost my mind. I said no, I’m just starting to raise a brick.”

“A brick gives me a sense of certainty that feels way more grounded than a lot of relationships. Psychologists call this ‘zero-energy emotional companionship.’ It fulfils your need for company without demanding any obligation to give love in return.”

Chinese young people are increasingly shunning the traditional expectations of society such as having children and grinding out long hours in strenuous jobs, assuming they can find one in the first place. Nearly one in five 16- 24-year-olds, excluding students, are unemployed, according to official statistics. Some estimates put the employment rate much higher.

China’s birthrate is in stubborn decline and fell to a record low last year. Faced with a sluggish job market after years of studying in an intensely competitive educational environment, many young people are choosing to drop out of the rat race, and opting instead for “lying flat” – pursuing a low effort, low stress lifestyle, well-suited to raising bricks.

The trend of raising bricks has become so popular that Chinese media has started to warn about the health risks.

Cultivating moss could lead to the spread of mould, with some “brick parents” reportedly complaining of suffering from itchy eyes and a runny nose. Xuedong Li, a retired moss professor from Beijing’s Capital Normal University, urged brick parents to raise their mossy babies in an enclosed environment. “It is best to wear disposable gloves and a mask during handling to reduce spore inhalation and skin contact,” Li told Chinese media.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/liv.title: AI cloud computing firms face ‘guppy-level death’, Elon Musk warns; French bonds rally after avoiding downgrade – business live
https://www.theguardian.com/business/liv.author: Graeme Wearden
https://www.theguardian.com/business/liv.text:
Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy.

The flow of funding which has helped the AI industry to grow rapidly could be running dry, at least for some firms in the cloud computing world, Elon Musk has warned.

The world’s richest person declared last night that at least 200 ‘neoclouds’ – companies which provide specialised cloud infrastructure to run AI workloads – could die or consolidate because they will struggle to access capital.

Musk made the claim while also declaring that his SpaceX business has closed a $40bn debt deal to pay for the chips it needs for its artificial intelligence work.

He posted on X that firms who rely on revenue streams from AI datacentres are being cold-shouldered by lenders, saying:

double quotation markAs of the past few weeks, debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn’t have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers.

SpaceX closed $40B of debt for GPUs, but we’re investment grade and have Starlink & launch revenue.

That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation. Some will make it through, but not many.

[Musk is referring to the guppy fish, the colourful freshwater aquarium fish notorious for suddenly dying in the aquarium, especially if there is a change in its environment.]

Neoclouds are specialist cloud providers that rent out clusters of high-speed Nvidia chips to firms looking to conduct AI training and inference.

They include CoreWeave, the US firm whose share price has fallen 60% in the last year as investors have questioned whether the huge investment in AI datacentres will be rewarded with lucrative cash flows.

The cost of insuring CoreWeave’s debt against default has climbed in recent weeks to levels that typically suggest credit distress – Musk’s comments are unlikely ease investors concerns!

UK government borrowing costs are dropping this morning, a welcome sign ahead of Wednesday’s budget.

The yield (or interest rate) on 10 and 30-year UK gilts have both dropped by around three basis points (0.03 of a percentage point) this morning.

City investors are hoping that chancellor John Healey avoids rocking the boat when he delivers his first budget, prioritising rebuilding fiscal headroom – although the jump in bond yields in recent months will have eaten into that borrowing cushion.

There were reports last weekend that Healey will put billions of pounds into public financial institutions including the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank.

Fresh funding into these so-called “PuFins” could boost the UK’s AI, defence and green energy sectors.

Crucially for the chancellor, if a PuFin makes a loan or investment, the value of this financial asset is netted off against public liabilities, and the PSNFL measure of UK debt does not go up.

However, the City may be wary of any trickery to keep government debt off the books.

double quotation markIssuing loans to public financial institutions creates a financial asset that offsets the increase in outstanding government debt. If the investments that the PuFins make generate sufficient returns for the PuFins to repay their government loans, then long term debt sustainability is little affected.

Limited transparency and the risk that the PuFins may suffer impairments on their investments will probably make bond market investors skeptical of the extra gilt issuance. Chancellor Healey should avoid a big increase in gilt issuance to fund such intra-public sector lending.

Shares in AI cloud computing companies are dropping in pre-market trading after Elon Musk warned they face “guppy-level death and consolidation”.

Coreweave are down 2.4% in pre-market. Nebius, another neocloud operator, are on track for a 2.1% drop when Wall Street opens, while Iren are down 1.9%.

double quotation markNebius, CoreWeave and Iren were slammed in premarket trading on Monday after SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk said more than 200 neoclouds are “going to see guppy-level death and consolidation.”

That’s the guppy fish – prone to suddenly dying in household fisk tanks – not the GBPJPY FX cross...In a post on X Musk said “debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn’t have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers”.

Business sentiment in Germany has improved, as hopes build that its economic stagnation may be ending.

Economic research institute Ifo’s Business Climate Index has risen to 90.2 points in October, up from 89.9 points in September.

double quotation markThis was due to more optimistic expectations. Companies, however, assessed their current situation as slightly worse. The economic recovery is continuing.

Elsewhere in the bond markets, Brazil’s debt is dropping in value after president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won a dramatic victory over his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, to claim a historic fourth term in power.

Bolsonaro, son of the former president, had been expected to oust Lula, but instead the left-wing incumbent triumphed, with 51.79% of the vote to his 45-year-old rival’s 48.21%.

Investors had anticipated that a Bolsonaro win would have led to a new push to rein in Brazil’s public debt, and may now be keen to sell Brazilian debt and the real.

Reuters reports that Brazil’s international bonds have dropped more than 1 cent after Lula’s election win.

Viktor Szabó, investment director for emerging market debt at Aberdeen Investments, explains why bond investors are nervous:

double quotation markLula’s campaign did pledge fiscal consolidation, but at a slower pace than his rival and with the explicit condition that spending cuts should not fall on lower-income Brazilians. The government’s own projections show the primary balance improving only gradually, to a surplus of 1.3% of GDP by 2030. His running mate, Geraldo Alckmin, pointed to campaign funding and excessive public-sector salaries as areas for savings. Neither comes close to the scale of the problem.

Brazil has little room left for this kind of politics. Gross public debt has climbed to around 83% of GDP, up more than 10 percentage points during this administration, and a deficit close to 10% of GDP is now almost entirely interest. Brazil pays one of the highest real interest rates in the world on a debt that keeps growing, which is the definition of an unsustainable path, and the bill falls on companies and households as much as on the Treasury.

Elon Musk’s warning that AI cloud funding could dry up is a reminder that companies may not provide the revenues that hyperscalers and neoclouds are relying on.

Steve Daheb, Head of AI GTM Strategy at enterprise software firm Flexera, explains:

double quotation mark“We have spent the past few years debating whether AI will replace people. But the more immediate question for many businesses is whether AI could end up costing more than the people and processes it replaces.

“Businesses need to remember every decision an AI makes and every action an agent takes has a price tag. The AI people see and the prompt they enter is only part of the story. AI doesn’t just answer questions: it reasons, retries, checks and refines its response, drawing on models, enterprises data and computing power just to complete a single task. That iterative process and response refinement are what drive AI costs. Once agents are embedded across applications and running tasks throughout a business, the metre is always running – yet many companies still have no idea how many tokens they are using or what a particular task will cost because of this AI cost domino effect.

“That is why we are seeing such whiplash. Businesses went from board-level mandates to use AI as quickly as possible to cancelling licences, imposing token limits and slamming the brakes on projects when the bills arrived.”

French government bonds are rallying this morning after Paris avoided being downgrade by rating agency Moody’s last Friday night.

The yield, or interest rate, on French 10-year bonds has dropped by 3.5 basis points to 4.98%, away from the 24-year high set last week.

Moody’s surprised investors late on Friday night by announcing it had maintained its rating of Aa3 with a negative outlook; the City had expected a cut.

Moody’s warned, though, that France’s debt position has worsened, explaining:

double quotation markSince our previous periodic review of the sovereign rating, slower growth and a higher deficit have pushed France’s debt burden somewhat higher than previously expected. In addition, government bond yields have risen more rapidly than we expected, while widespread social protests have erupted which could constrain fiscal consolidation efforts.

The Aa3 rating assumes that a deficit-reducing budget for 2027 will be adopted, while financing costs and social tensions will abate somewhat in the next few months.

France’s public debt soared to 119% of GDP this summer, the highest level since 1946. The proposed budget for 2027, which has yet to be approved, aims to cut France’s budget deficit from 5.4% to 5% through wage freezes and tax rises.

This morning, Computacenter raised its financial outlook for this financial year, after “a very strong first half performance”.

Computercenter is winning business from the neoclouds – the AI cloud computing companies which Elon Musk reckons face ‘guppy-level death’.

double quotation markSourcing revenue continued to grow strongly, primarily driven by hyperscale and neocloud customers in North America and the UK.

Group Services revenue was also ahead of last year, as strong organic growth in Professional Services, also driven by North America, more than offset a decline in Managed Services revenue.

There’s such demand that Computercenter now has a ‘committed product order backlog’ of £12.6bn, up from £9.3bn at the end of June, and “a strong pipeline of opportunities in North America and the UK”.

It now expects adjusted profit before tax for FY 2026 to be at least £425m, ahead of forecasts of £387.1m.

Musk also claimed on X overnight that some partly-built datacentres simply won’t be completed.

double quotation markI think we’re going to see a lot of stranded compute in partially complete datacenters

Bloomberg, intriguingly, are questioning Elon Musk’s claim that SpaceX has closed a $40bn debt deal to fund more chip purchases.

They’ve heard that talks over the pricing of this deal are still ongoing, and report:

double quotation markAs of late Sunday in New York, those conversations remained ongoing and the deal hadn’t priced, people with knowledge of the discussions said. The parties are still working on finalizing the debt package in the coming days, the people said.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/liv.title: I would like to rejoin EU, says Burnham, but ‘British public are the bosses’ – UK politics live
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/liv.author: Andrew Sparrow
https://www.theguardian.com/politics/liv.text:
PM says talking about changing the relationship with the bloc would not be divisive but ‘can start to bring people together’

Andy Burnham has claimed that the welfare changes he is planning to get more young people into work could over time save a “significant amount of money”.

Ahead of the budget, the Conservatives and Reform UK are both calling for massive cuts in welfare spending, which they say could be used in part to fund more defence investment. At their conference the Tories identified welfare cuts worth £36bn a year, and today Reform UK is saying it would cut welfare spending by £40bn a year.

Burnham has repeatedly rejected what he calls “crude cuts”. But the government will soon publish recommendations from the Alan Milburn review into Neets (young people not in education, employment or training), and it is expected to recommend more spending on support getting young people into work, offset by some cuts to benefits. Milburn has said this would cost more in the short term, but would save money over time.

double quotation markI think a big change is needed here where we move to a situation where the spending is not to sustain people on benefits, but we give people the right support when they need it as they are growing up, coming through their teenage years.

Asked how much this could save, he replied: “A significant amount of money, and that’s what the Milburn review is all about.”

Burnham also said the cuts proposed by the Tories and Reform UK would just lead to “more failure and crisis and spending”. He said:

double quotation markThe opposition parties are out there today saying just make crude cuts to the welfare budget.

I personally think that won’t work, and it isn’t right to do that anyway, because it just leads to more and more failure and crisis and spending that isn’t helpful for anybody.

Andy Burnham has said that Shabana Mahmood is right to want to make migrant workers wait longer until they can claim indefinite leave to remain (ILR) in the UK.

Under plans announced last year, migrant workers would normally have to wait 10 years for ILR, instead of five years as they do now, and care workers would normally have to wait 15 years. Some cabinet ministers have made it clear they believe 15 years is too long.

Asked about the split, Burnham broadly defended the home secretary in his Good Morning Britain interview. He said:

double quotation markWhy has this problem arisen? It’s arisen because if you look back to the early 2020s, people call it the Boriswave, a huge number of people came in seeking permanent settlement on longer-term visas …

And the home secretary is right, in my view, to bring forward changes that are based on the principle that settlement is a right to be earned, not just something that is granted automatically.

But, when asked if he was sticking to the 15-year element of the plan, Burnham just said that he stood by “the principle” of what Mahmood was proposing. He also said the government would take into account the results of its consultation on the plans.

In fact, Burnham himself is one of the ministers who have signalled they are unhappy about care workers being singled out for particularly harsh treatment. And Mahmood has already indicated that some aspects of the plan announced last year will be revised in response to objections.

In his Good Morning Britain interview, Andy Burnham was twice asked about an early election.

At the start, Susanna Reid asked him if he was softening people up for an early election. Burnham replied:

Asked if that was absolutely the case, he said it was. He said he had made that clear before the Labour conference. He went on:

double quotation markI just don’t think people want another backward-looking squabble. I think they want me to get on with the job.

And, when Reid raised the subject again at the end of the interview, Burnham said:

double quotation markMy mind is not on that [an early election]. I don’t know if that is coming over here, but it genuinely is not on that. There is no election coming anytime soon. People may as well just put that out of their mind.

Reid did not ask specifically about polling, but two polls came out over the weekend both giving Labour an eight-point lead.

📊Labour on 32% with a lead of +8 – the largest Labour lead Ipsos have recorded this parliament

🚨 Labour continues to lead in the polls, 8 points ahead of Reform in second place.

These polls have attracted a lot of attention in part because they both give Labour a bigger lead than other recent polls. The Politico poll of polls, which averages the results of all polls, has Labour just four points ahead of Reform UK in second place. But that has not been updated to take into account the most recent Ipsos and Opinium numbers.

In one pre-conference interview, Burnham said that he would not hold the next election until 2029. But mostly he just rules out an “early” general election, while leaving it unclear what “early” means.

At Westminster no one is expecting an election before the end of the year. But the weekend polls have revived speculation about Burnham being tempted to call one in May next year, not least because having the rightwing vote split almost 50/50 between the Conservatives and Reform UK is an ideal backdrop for Labour.

Good morning. Andy Burnham started budget week with an interview on ITV’s Good Morning Britain with Susanna Reid and Richard Madeley. There were plenty of decent lines in it, but some of his most intriguing comments were about Brexit. Yesterday opposition parties (and even in private some Labour MPs) were criticising the PM for saying in a Sunday Times interview that he would be willing to consider going into the next election proposing accepting EU free movement rules. This was treated as if it was a novel outrage – even though at Labour conference Burnham announced that rejoining the EU could end up as the best option to emerge from his proposed renegotiation of the Brexit settlement, which of course would automatically involve accepting free movement.

Neil Kinnock said recently he thought Burnham was determined to take Britain back in the EU, but in his interview this morning Burnham insisted that he was not dogmatic in that way. When Madeley asked him if he saw himself as someone “destined” to be the PM that would take Britain back in, Burnham replied:

I see it as my job to be pragmatic about the whole situation. Can I make it work better? Can I add growth to the British economy?

And when Reid asked him bluntly to be honest and say if he wanted the UK to rejoin, Burnham replied:

double quotation markI’ve said – I’m going to be honest – in my lifetime I would like to see that happen, but I am not going to move ahead of the public. I am not going to dictate in terms of my own opinions here. You have to make sure that the British public are the bosses here.

When it was put to him that he had broken a promise he made during the Makerfield byelection campaign not to reopen the Brexit referendum campaign, Burnham said that was not what he was doing.

He repeated the argument he made in his Labour conference speech – that it was worth revising the relationship with the EU because the current, post-Brexit settlement was not working.

But he also claimed that, rather than being divisive, this new debate could bring people together. Later in the interview, he returned to Brexit unprompted.

double quotation markAnd [to] go back to Brexit, by just talking about it in a more practical way, by being honest about it … that can start to bring people together who voted in different ways.

The divides that we’ve lived through in the last decade really do need to end, and we need to pull people together …

I’m trying to give the country a direction and there is no way I can do that without coming back to the relationship with Europe and saying, ‘Look, here are some options as to how we got this right.’

Not for the first time, Burnham categorically ruled out trying to rejoin the EU before the election.

And, on the timing of the election, Burnham also insisted that it would be “no time soon”. He went on:

Morning: Andy Burnham is on a visit in London ahead of attending a summit on rough sleeping in Downing Street.

2pm: Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, and Robert Jenrick, his Treasury spokesperson, hold a press conference to present what they call their “economic rescue plan”.

2.30pm: Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, takes questions in the Commons.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘We don’t have inflation’? Five charts show the US economic reality of Trump’s second term so far
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Lauren Aratani in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
As the US midterm elections approach, we take a look at data to see a true picture of the US economy under Trump

With the midterm elections fast approaching, many Americans have the economy on their minds.

US voters are exhausted by years of higher prices. Donald Trump won the presidency in 2024 on promises to lower inflation and undo the damage he said the Biden administration had inflicted on the economy.

In Trump’s view, his plan is working. At a recent rally in Montana, Trump boasted about the current economy, framing it as a booming time for Americans. “We’re richer now,” he said. “We don’t have inflation.”

Economic data paints a different picture. Inflation, especially gas prices, have soared over the last year. The job market has been in stasis, and higher interest rates have meant it’s more expensive for Americans to borrow money for loans and mortgages.

These fluctuations have a concrete impact on the lives of Americans. A recent Harris poll for the Guardian found that a majority of Americans, including some Republicans, disagree. Nearly two-thirds said they believe the country is experiencing a recession, and many said higher prices have been a pain point. Americans are reporting having trouble saving, and a third polled said one surprise bill could sink them financially.

The rate of price increases has dramatically cooled since its peak in 2022, when the pandemic’s economic stimulus packages found their way into consumer prices. Inflation peaked at 9.1%, a 40-year high, in June 2022.

In January 2025, the month when Trump started his second term, inflation was down to 3%. By April 2025, it would be 2.3% – the lowest rate since 2021.

That’s when things start to get bumpy. After Trump placed tariffs on nearly everything that the US imports, inflation started to heat up again, climbing back up to 3% in September 2025. After many of his tariffs were paused and eventually found to be illegal, prices started going down again. In January and February 2026, inflation was back down to 2.4%.

The Iran war, specifically its impact on oil prices, has brought inflation back up to levels not seen since 2023. In May, inflation reached 4.2% and has hovered above 3.4% since.

It’s been nearly six years since Americans has seen inflation at a manageable 2% level. Price increases build up over time and can put a squeeze on budgets, which is why it’s such a sensitive point for voters during a crucial election.

In the Guardian’s recent poll with the Harris Poll, gas prices were the most common pain point for Americans, with 83% saying they’re making a dent in their current finances.

Soon after the war in Iran began, the strait of Hormuz, a key route that a fifth of the world’s oil typically passes through, was blocked off. Its closure has pushed up prices all around the world. Though the US itself is a major oil producer, prices have still surged since the war. The average price of gas was $4.32 per gallon in mid-October, according to AAA, nearly $1.30 a gallon higher than a year ago.

Even for an oil-producing state like Texas, a gallon of gas is $3.81 compared with $2.64 a year ago. Meanwhile, drivers in California, a state that imports much of its gas from overseas, are paying $6.21 per gallon.

The labor market is another metric used to measure the health of the economy, and while the US job market has seen some growth since Trump took office again, figures have fluctuated over the last year. In 2025, altogether 181,000 new jobs were added to the economy, compared with 2.2m jobs in 2024.

Employers have been dealing with a mixed landscape for hiring: harsher immigration policies, uncertainty from tariffs and higher prices for supplies have all meant slow job growth. The unemployment rate has remained low, though, at just over 4%. Economists call this a “low-hire, low-fire” economy, in which employers are neither hiring or laying off workers.

Though many Americans report struggling in today’s economy, a small handful have never been wealthier. The stock market has continued to soar since Trump took office, recovering from dips seen during his initial tariff announcement and the early days of the Iran war.

Economists largely see AI investment as the leading factor in the stock market’s acceleration. Tech companies are spending billions of dollars investing in datacenters and for chips that are needed to power AI.

While many Americans are invested in the stock market through their retirement and pension funds, this growth has really been a boon for the top 1% wealthiest Americans, who own nearly half of the stock market investments.

Economists say higher prices paired with an exuberant stock market has led to a K-shaped economy, where the wealthier have never felt richer while everyday Americans continue to deal with tightened budgets from high prices.

Interest rates are often not as noticeable to consumers as gas or grocery prices, which they come across every day. The impact that higher interest rates have on the economy takes longer to appear and runs deep. Interest rates shape how much Americans pay to borrow money – to run their businesses, pay off car loans and buy their homes.

For the Federal Reserve, shifting interest rates is the tool it uses to balance the economy. Raising rates can cool the economy, bringing prices down, though at the risk of hurting the job market. Lowering rates can stimulate the economy at the risk of leading to more inflation.

When Trump entered office in January 2025, the Fed was in the middle of a series of interest rate reductions. Officials said they were seeing inflation cooling and slower growth in the labor market. Interest rates were at a range of 4.25% to 4.5% – 1% lower than they were a year ago.

Uncertainty around Trump’s new tariffs would ultimately lead officials to pause the reduction, though the president was still demanding lower rates. As tariffs proved to have less of a long-term effect on prices, the Fed started lowering rates again in fall 2025.

For months, the Fed held off on changing rates as the economic impacts of the war of Iran bore out. But in September, the Fed hiked rates for the first time since 2023, by a quarter point. The Trump-appointed Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, said that “inflation is too high and has been for too long”.

Higher interest rates have already had an impact on mortgage rates, which had dipped down to below 6% (for a 30-year mortgage) for the first time since 2022, in February, but are now up past 7%.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: What you need to know about the most consequential election in Israel’s history
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Emma Graham-Harrison in Jerusalem
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Benjamin Netanyahu is seeking a new mandate in Israel’s first election since the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks

On Tuesday Israel holds its first election since the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks, the deadliest day in the country’s history, which resulted in the deaths of about 1,200 people, the majority of them civilians.

Since then Israel has pursued a war of annihilation in Gaza, launched two inconclusive wars with Iran, and intensified a campaign of state-backed ethnic cleansing in the occupied West Bank.

Domestically the coalition formed by Benjamin Netanyahu has taken aim at democratic institutions, including the supreme court. Many Israelis have described this election as the most consequential in their country’s history.

The prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has led Israel for 19 out of the last 30 years, most recently at the head of a far-right coalition. He is seeking a new mandate with the endorsement of the US president, Donald Trump, and the fight is personal as well as political. He is on trial for corruption; losing power may mean a greater risk of jail time.

His main rival is Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the Israeli military and relative political newcomer, the son of Moroccan immigrants who rose to the heart of Israel’s establishment from humble beginnings. His son and two nephews were killed fighting in Gaza in 2024.

He lacks Netanyahu’s charisma, but has embraced that as part of a campaign positioning him as the opposite of Israel’s current leader, down to the name of his new party – Yashar, or “Honesty”.

Israel’s security is at the heart of the election, overshadowing even the soaring cost of living. Opponents of the current government point to the catastrophe of the 7 October attacks, the erosion of democratic institutions, rise of religious extremism and the cost of open-ended, multi-front wars.

They have promised a state commission of inquiry into 7 October, and most have pledged to end draft exemption for ultra-Orthodox men, a source of deep resentment among families whose loved ones are serving or have been killed.

They are also concerned about international isolation, amid broadening sanctions over settlement expansion, and an accelerating brain drain among the elite.

Netanyahu has tried to shift blame for 7 October on to Israel’s security establishment, and despite presiding over the deadliest day in Israel’s history, he claims to be the only leader with the experience and international contacts to keep the country safe.

He recently posted an AI image of a nuclear bomb hitting Tel Aviv on social media, with the claim “anyone who cares about their physical existence” should pause before voting for the opposition.

His far-right allies have called for the ethnic cleansing of Gaza and the occupied West Bank, and expansion of settlements.

His ultra-Orthodox partners want to preserve a decades-old exemption from conscription and subsidies for religious study.

Most polls show Netanyahu’s Likud and his current coalition parters losing their majority. That fall in voter support has been fairly consistent for more than two years.

They also show a clear anti-Netanyahu majority. However, those opposition seats are divided between the bloc of Jewish Israeli parties, led by Eisenkot’s Yashar, and parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel.

The Jewish Israeli parties are unlikely to have a majority on their own, but have mostly ruled out going into coalition with Palestinians.

Palestinian politicians have indicated they might support a minority government of the Jewish Israeli parties in order to unseat Netanyahu’s far-right coalition.

The Knesset has 120 seats, with lawmakers voted in through a system of proportional representation. No single party has ever claimed a majority of 61 seats, so Israel has always been governed by coalitions.

When the results are in, the president invites the party with the largest number of seats to try to agree a governing coalition.

Exit polls are released at 10pm Israeli time (8pm GMT), and the first indication of actual voting counts usually emerges in the early hours of the morning.

Getting full results could take much longer, with the outcome potentially hanging on the electoral fortunes of two small parties, which need to win 3.25% of the overall vote to take up seats in the Knesset. Polling puts both around this threshold. If they cross it, they each get four seats, which would have a significant impact on coalition building options.

The far-right Amcha Yisrael is led by the former general Ofer Winter, who has pledged to back Netanyahu for prime minister if he gets into the Knesset. The Reservists is a rightwing Zionist party focused on ensuring universal conscription whose leaders sit between the two blocs. They have ruled out joining any government supported by either the ultra-Orthodox – key Netanyahu allies – or Palestinian parties whose backing Eisenkot is likely to need.

About 15 million people live in areas under Israeli control. Just over 7 million Jewish Israelis and 1.7 million Palestinian citizens of Israel live within the country’s pre-1967 borders, known as the “green line”, and have full voting rights.

In the occupied West Bank, more than 500,000 Israeli settlers can vote. They live among 3.1 million Palestinians who are subject to military rule and do not have the right to vote.

In occupied East Jerusalem more than 230,000 Israelis with voting rights live among 350,000 Palestinians who cannot vote.

Two million Palestinians in Gaza, who live under Israeli military occupation, according to the international court of justice, also have no vote.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Anthropic’s Claude AI model accessed Georgia voter data in US
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Dan Milmo Global technology editor
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Latest example of unauthorised behaviour shows AI model bypassed paywall to access data as part of statistics project

Anthropic’s Claude model accessed voter data in the US state of Georgia, the AI company has confirmed, in the latest example of unauthorised behaviour by the technology.

The AI model managed to bypass a paywall to reach data that is publicly available but is typically accessible only after paying a fee. Claude accessed aggregate vote counts as part of a statistics project at Anthropic, which is preparing for a $1.5tn (£1.1tn) flotation.

“Claude did not access the state’s voter registration system, change any voting records, or pull any individual voter records,” Anthropic said.

Anthropic said the AI found a loophole in an old version of the state agency’s website, discovering that it issued a digital entry pass – an “access token” – to visitors. It then requested a token and gained access to the information.

The AI developer said it had since put in place guardrails to prevent similar actions happening again. The incident was first reported by the news website Axios.

Anthropic had pointed out the unauthorised behaviour earlier in the month when it said in a blogpost that it had found examples of ​Claude “working around a restriction to reach data that ‌was ⁠gated by a token or a fee” and that some of these cases involved websites run by US ​government agencies. At the time, it said the incidents had “minimal real-world impact”.

The unintended actions flagged by Anthropic included a model submitting a fake tip about an unsolved murder to the Philadelphia police department. The US state department also revealed this month that an Anthropic model had filed 19 visa applications in August.

Examples of unauthorised behaviour by AI agents – programs powered by AI models that carry out tasks autonomously – have been mounting since OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, revealed in July that its bots had hacked an AI startup.

Since then, it has emerged that an OpenAI agent hacked the Australian healthcare system, and the UK’s AI security institute revealed that Anthropic agents had carried out a hacking campaign against real people during a cybersecurity test.

This month, the UK’s AI minister said he expected an AI-driven cyber-attack similar to the Australia hack, describing such an incident as likely, “if not inevitable”. Kanishka Narayan said the government would consider using the cyber security and resilience bill as a vehicle for introducing AI safety regulations, including making it mandatory to report AI safety incidents.

In the US, the White House’s newly formed Super Intelligence Force – a federal body overseeing AI development – is mandating that all AI companies report security incidents involving their technology.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: ‘It’s a mess right now’: RFK’s sweeping changes place new vaccines in limbo
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Melody Schreiber
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Health secretary’s effort to alter makeup of ACIP panel means no new recommendations coming – even as new vaccines are approved

US vaccine recommendations are in limbo, access to vaccines is suffering, and some of the uncertainty may continue for years following major blows to vaccination by the Trump administration, experts say.

Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), has made sweeping changes to vaccination policy, cutting childhood immunization recommendations by a third and replacing experts on the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) with his own handpicked allies.

A judge’s order halted these changes because they were not done correctly, but Kennedy has not nominated any new ACIP members – which means there are no new vaccination recommendations coming from the committee, even as new vaccines are approved.

Ron Kroening, 63, has asthma and bad allergies this time of year, so his doctor recommended the new Moderna mRNA flu vaccine, approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in August for ages 50 and up. Trials suggest it provides even stronger protection than traditional flu shots.

It took time to locate the one pharmacy in his area that stocked the shot – and then Kroening was shocked to be charged a $40 co-pay.

“I figured that was an error because I’ve never had to pay for a flu shot in my life,” he said. But his insurance company told him it’s because there’s no recommendation from the ACIP, Kroening said: “The reason the mRNA isn’t covered is because it’s not listed as an ACIP vaccine.”

If the ACIP doesn’t recommend the new shot by the end of the year – a scenario experts say is likely – insurers won’t be required to cover it until January 2029 at the earliest.

“This is really a barrier. And any barrier to immunizations is going to keep people from getting them,” said Kroening, a retired public health employee who worked on immunizations at the state level in Oklahoma. “A $40 co-pay is going to turn people off,” he added, noting that his pharmacist also didn’t inform him that there were other flu shot options.

Insurers usually have at least a year after FDA approval to add coverage of a new vaccine to their plans, so a co-pay like Kroening’s isn’t unusual in the first year or so. But the difference now is it’s not clear when the vaccine will be fully covered.

Typically, when a vaccine is approved for a new group of people – either because it’s new to the market or because the approval expanded to include more people – insurers have a year from the recommendation to implement it by the next plan year, which usually starts in January. That means if a vaccine is recommended by ACIP in December 2026, insurers are required to cover it by January 2028. If it’s recommended a month later, in January 2027, then the coverage requirement is pushed to January 2029.

“The legal requirement doesn’t go into effect very quickly. The process takes time,” said Lindsay Wiley, professor of law and faculty director of the Health Law and Policy Program at UCLA Law.

For the new flu shot, “it seems likely that at best we would get a recommendation next year,” Wiley said, “but there’s no reason to think” they will do so. “It’s just delaying more and more and more,” she said.

The only exception to the law on coverage is for Covid vaccines, because Congress amended the Affordable Care Act to specifically include coverage of Covid immunizations within 15 days of ACIP recommendation.

The uncertainty around ACIP has other ripple effects. Some states won’t allow pharmacists to give vaccines without an ACIP recommendation. Some of the decisions the committee made before it was disbanded were also halted, including the September 2025 recommendation on new shots to prevent RSV – though insurers appear to be covering them anyway. A now-voided vote to end the universal birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccine is influencing potential state-level laws.

There have also been delays reported for insurers covering the new flu shots for seniors under Medicare, which is mandated by law even without an ACIP recommendation.

The US government has appealed the part of the judge’s order that disbanded the vaccines committee, but there’s nothing to stop Kennedy from undergoing the correct process for appointing new members, experts say. He hasn’t.

“This White House and DoJ are making no serious attempt to actually revive the vaccine committee,” Aaron Siri, who has served as Kennedy’s lawyer and has litigated cases against vaccine makers, wrote on Monday. Siri added: “It appears the DOJ and the White House are doing everything they can to make sure that there is no functioning vaccine committee.”

“The federal government is choosing not to put in place a new ACIP,” she said. She also noted that Kennedy’s slate of advisers were clearly “uninformed” about vaccine policy and it was “embarrassing”, even for anti-vaccine activists, to watch the public meetings.

There are some advantages for Kennedy not to have a functioning ACIP, Reiss said. “Kennedy, in appointing his ACIP, wanted to change the schedule, and they haven’t been anywhere near as quick as he’d like them to be. So, going around ACIP is a plus,” she said. Delaying the reconstitution of the committee may allow him to make his own recommendations, she added.

Even after the lengthy court case concludes, the way forward for ACIP is shaky, because Kennedy has “aggressively undermined” trust in the independence of the committee, Reiss said.

“Without dramatic changes, it’s probably not coming back the way it was,” she said. “This has shown that ACIP is politically vulnerable, and I think if we want ACIP to go back to the way it was, we’re going to need a statute that gives it some protection.”
