Ron Kroening’s insurer is a member of the insurance industry group AHIP, which vowed to continue covering all shots recommended as of September 2025. And insurers can decide to cover vaccines before they’re required to do so.

“Vaccines are more cost-effective than getting the flu,” Kroening said. He said he still would choose the new vaccine despite the co-pay. “I’m able to pay the $40, and I’m happy I did, but still not happy that insurance didn’t cover it,” he said.

He’s worried about what all of this means for the future of immunizations in America. “They’re harder to get now,” Kroening said. “It’s a mess right now, what they’re doing with our vaccines.”

https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.title: US forces accused of ‘weaponising’ Somalia’s floods by trapping women and children in the path of El Niño
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.author: Mark Townsend in Kismayo
https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.text:
Exclusive: Coordinated airstrikes on territory held by al-Shabaab are driving the civilian population to find refuge alongside a river where rising water levels are a threat to safety. Is it a deliberate military strategy?

The water was rising rapidly. It had already reached Cayni Ali’s waist. Her home, five metres from the flooded River Juba in southern Somalia, never stood a chance. There was nowhere to go. Ali’s city of Jilib was under attack. Repeated airstrikes, said the mother of six, were pinning its population beside the rising river.

“The drones come all the time,” said the 27-year-old. “We hear them constantly. They kill animals, civilians. The town is big but destruction is everywhere.”

Asho Omar from Malenda, a village near Jilib, described “constant” airstrikes that had forced people towards the banks of the Juba.

“The airstrikes are everywhere; it is difficult to move. So many people have been killed.”

Their testimony offers a rare glimpse of life inside the stronghold of al-Shabaab, the Islamist militants who control 30% of Somalia. Closed off from the outside world, residents describe a city dealing with significant civilian casualties. Bodies, some said, lay in the streets.

The ongoing conflict is a legally ambiguous, shadowy war coordinated by the United States in east Africa, in which there is little accountability for harm to Somali civilians.

The United States Africa Command (Africom) would not share “operational security” details of a seemingly accelerating campaign that has also raised questions over potential covert US strikes. But there is, perhaps, an even darker dimension to the offensive on al-Shabaab’s de facto capital.

Sources say the military strategy appears to be seeking to drown those living in al-Shabaab territory by “weaponising” a rapidly strengthening El Niño, forecast to intensify Somalia’s rainy season from this month.

“The airstrikes are forcing people to go close to the river. It’s an extremely aggressive offensive, exploiting El Niño as a weapon of war to push the population into flood-prone areas,” said a source monitoring the Juba floodplain in southern Somalia.

Pinning the population – which includes large numbers of women and children – on the river’s floodplain has raised concerns of large-scale deaths in the months ahead.

“The official line is that they are targeting military positions and al-Shabaab, but because al-Shabaab is embedded within the community, it’s difficult to avoid collateral damage,” added the source.

When El Niño last struck Somalia in 2023, it caused the worst floods seen in the country for a century, displacing more than 1.2 million people. Analysts have questioned the ethics of the US military allegedly using mapping data from flood-prone areas – conceived to mitigate civilian casualties – to inflict harm.

Jethro Norman, a senior researcher with the Danish Institute for International Studies, said: “A weaponisation of El Niño is a reversal of process – using humanitarian remote sensing to inflict casualties rather than to mitigate harm. You capture the cumulative impact of a sustained airstrikes campaign in an El Niño flooding context.”

US officials deny exploiting climatic factors. A spokesperson said: “Africom does not target civilians, conduct operations for the purpose of displacing civilian populations or use weather or flooding as a method of warfare. Africom targets lawful military objectives and takes feasible measures to mitigate civilian harm.”

Nevertheless, many wonder if the opportunity to weaken al-Shabaab using the weather was too tempting to ignore, offering a catastrophic drowning event blamed on a supercharged El Niño.

Like many cities, Jilib’s location has been found wanting in an era of extreme weather. On a low-lying plain, the city is chronically vulnerable to flooding. In 2023, vast swathes of farmland were submerged. Halimo Abdikadir from Kamsuuma, south of Jillib, described the destruction of her home, 6 miles (10km) from the river. “The waters came quickly at night – when they left, everything was mud. A lot of animals drowned.”

Arbey Famu from Ahmed Yare, another village outside Jilib, expects this El Niño to be far worse than 2023: her crops of maize and sorghum are underwater.

US defence officials will know the early indicators of El Niño’s impact in al-Shabaab’s heartland. UN agencies say the Juba River basin is of “particular concern”. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), meanwhile, foresees “severe flooding”.

Attacking Jilib using ground forces carries much risk. Airstrikes can yield triumphs such as the death of a senior al-Shabaab commander on 1 October, but are unable to overrun a city of 100,000.

Ali Adan Ali, the commissioner for displaced people in Jubaland, is worried. In his Kismayo office, Ali identified 327 regions prone to flooding. By October, El Niño warnings had only been issued to half.

His chief concern is the lack of boats. Without them, he says, thousands in al-Shabaab territory risk being trapped on the east side of the river, unable to reach help in Kismayo, at the mouth of the Juba.

Three years ago, during the last El Niño, Ali says, 19,000 people were stranded for a week without food. “We are running out of time,” he says.

The absence of boats sums up Somalia’s funding woes. In 2023, the country’s aid budget was $2.2bn. Now it stands at about $300,000. Flood protection investment has dwindled.

Compounding concerns is al-Shabaab’s lack of preparedness in the area it controls. Ali has not received a response from the militants regarding El Niño readiness. Cayni Ali said there are no sandbags or flood defences deployed yet in Jilib. Earth walls were erected along the river but have proved insufficient.

“They are not big enough,” she said. The latest flood advisory for the River Juba urges communities to “reinforce” weak riverbanks.

Corroborating testimonies describe a prolonged – and seemingly indiscriminate – campaign of airstrikes against al-Shabaab that appears to have killed many civilians. The US would not share details of potential civilian fatalities “to protect US and partner forces and preserve operational security”.

Farhan Ahmed, who lived in Jilib until fleeing last month, described constant terror. “There were airstrikes every day, all the time.” One strike flattened five homes in his neighbourhood. Ahmed, 35, described bodies littering the city streets.

Fadumo Abdi claimed the airstrikes were largely failing to target militants. “The attacks are mostly killing civilians. Some were buried, but some were not,” she said.

Abdikadir, from Kamsuuma, added: “The drone attacks on Jilib are too much. So many people die.”

Yusuf Siidi, 27, from Araare near Jamame in al-Shabaab territory, witnessed three teenagers killed in one strike. Maryan Salah was at home near Jamame when a drone sent a shard of burning metal 20cm long into her back yard, landing next to her two-year-old daughter.

Salah’s near miss predates the current offensive. She can recall only that it happened in “mid-March”. The US admits a drone strike near Jamame on 19 March, but no other data is provided.

Although eyewitness accounts detail an extraordinary number of strikes in Jilib, official US records confirm only one airstrike in Jilib during August. Six took place last month. Between the start of August and now, the US says it conducted a total of just 11 strikes.

Allegations of ambiguity increasingly characterise US operations in Somalia. It is an opaque approach that raises questions over whether Africom has authorised covert airstrikes in the region.

Records from the nearest hospital indicate intensive airstrikes or fighting. The ICRC has treated 205 patients with “weapon-related” injuries in Kismayo this year, a 43% increase on last year.

David Sterman, analyst at the New America thinktank, said: “The possibility that we are seeing covert US strikes always looms large when there are strikes without clear attribution.”

The US, however, said it publicised “all airstrikes conducted under its authority in Somalia. We do not maintain an undisclosed or unannounced strike count.”

Turkey has also used drones to target al-Shabaab in Somalia. Operating alongside Africom, Turkey rarely divulges any details of its strikes or military operations in Somalia.

Beyond airstrikes and floods, the primary concern for Somalis is hunger. Those fleeing the Juba valley – local authorities are offering humanitarian help to those who escape – say there is insufficient food to sustain them.

Omar’s family of 13 survives on one fish a day. How big is the fish? Omar held her hands less than 30cm apart.

Habiba Ali, 55, from Jamame, said her family – like many – shares one daily meal of maize. Time in between is spent hiding from conflict. “When the fighting stops, we wait for it start again.”

Shukri Ahmed, 32, the president of Galbeed refugee camp, estimates that 6,000 might have died in Kismayo’s network of displacement sites since the Trump administration abruptly shut USAID last year. Overnight, two children had died in makeshift shelters from diarrhoea.

El Niño will “deepen [Somalia’s] hunger levels”, warns the UN-backed body responsible for identifying famine.

Zakaria Mohammed, head nurse at Kismayo’s ICRC-supported hospital for five years, says children from al-Shabaab territory arrive every day so severely malnourished or weak they cannot be saved. Cases of child malnutrition rates have risen 40% this year.

Xaawo Nacdoor made it just in time. Al-Shabaab had blocked her leaving Jamame to receive treatment for her baby. But her 14-month-old daughter Faadumo was dying, so Nacdoor fled at night.

For three days, with just a bottle of water, Nacdoor walked with her daughter strapped to her back. On the second day, the toddler lost consciousness.

“She was severely dehydrated, but I kept going.” Arriving at the hospital, Faadumo weighed 4.1kg. Three days later: 4.4kg. She survived.

Most patients here vow never to return home, saying life under al-Shabaab meant no school, education, healthcare or food. For the thousands of families straddling the Juba River – often the poorest – things are about to get much worse.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.title: Japanese prosecutors charge US marine suspected of robbing and killing woman
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.author: Ramon Antonio Vargas and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text:
Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, denies charges that he fatally strangled Anna Yagi, 39, in a hotel on the island of Okinawa

Prosecutors in Japan have filed formal charges against a US marine suspected of murdering and robbing a woman while stationed on the country’s island of Okinawa, according to Japanese media.

Devin Jacob Ballard, a 20-year-old lance corporal assigned to Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Okinawa, is charged with fatally strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in the city and stealing from her a backpack containing a wallet, the public broadcaster NHK reported.

Ballard had initially been arrested in Yagi’s killing on 4 October, about a day after she was found dead in Naha, Okinawa’s capital. Prosecutors indicted him in the case on Sunday, and he has reportedly denied the charges.

NHK and other Japanese media outlets had previously reported that Ballard was arrested after surveillance camera footage from near the scene of Yagi’s killing showed a man entering a room with a woman and later leaving the scene with her belongings.

Ballard evidently matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage, was confronted and agreed to accompany investigators voluntarily to a local police station when he was arrested, Japanese media reported.

Yagi’s killing prompted protests in Okinawa and the Japanese capital of Tokyo, with political leaders publicly condemning her killing. It also triggered a curfew and alcohol ban for US military members stationed in Okinawa, where most of the 54,000 US troops in Japan are based.

Crimes committed by US troops in Japan – including rape, assault, hit-and-run and drunk-driving – have long strained relations between the countries, which are close military allies.

A Japanese court in June 2025 sentenced US marine Jamel Clayton, then 22, to seven years in prison after he was convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a woman in her 20s.

In 2017, a former US marine and civilian military base worker named Kenneth Shinzato was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local Okinawa woman.

US military forces in Japan that same year banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated US marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing a local driver, age 61.

The Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper reported that about 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested since the US returned Okinawa to Japan after the second world war in 1972.

After Ballard’s arrest, Shinjiro Koizumi, Japan’s defense minister, said: “Incidents and accidents involving US military personnel cause great anxiety among the local community and must not be allowed to happen.”

https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.title: Chris Brown given suspended sentence over bottle attack at London club
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.author: Press Association
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/o.text:
R&B singer sentenced to eight months’ imprisonment suspended for 12 months over incident in Mayfair in 2023

The R&B singer Chris Brown has been given a suspended sentence after striking a man twice in the head with a tequila bottle in a central London club.

Brown, 37, admitted affray earlier this year after attacking a former friend with a “heavy” tequila bottle on the dancefloor at the Tape private members’ club in Mayfair in February 2023.

Brown was sentenced to eight months’ imprisonment, suspended for 12 months, at Southwark crown court on Monday. His vocal coach Omololu Akinlolu, 40, who joined the attack, was sentenced to four months’ imprisonment, suspended for 12 months, and both men were ordered to pay £1,500 costs.

In front of a packed public gallery, the singer sat looking at the floor in the dock for much of the hearing.

Judge Baumgartner called the attack “plainly dangerous” and warned that “commercial success does not attract preferential treatment” in court.

In sentencing, he said: “The repeated use of a glass bottle in that way, especially aimed at the head, was plainly dangerous. It carried the risk of delivering a more serious injury than was ultimately sustained.”

CCTV footage was shown in which Brown was seen striking Abraham Diaw four times with the bottle, connecting twice with his head and then hitting his shoulder.

Heidi Stonecliffe KC, prosecuting, told the court Brown used a “heavy square-shaped tequila bottle” to “hit Mr Diaw twice over the left-hand side of his head”. He rained down “further blows” as Diaw turned away, the court heard.

Stonecliffe said Akinlolu then grabbed Diaw in a “bear hug”. She said: “Mr Diaw falls to the ground and Mr Brown is also seen throwing punches.”

In another clip, Brown, from California, could be seen being pulled away from the victim. The incident took place at about 3am and lasted about 20 seconds, the court heard.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Peta releases video showing experiments on infant monkeys at University of Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Claire Colley and Tracy Keeling
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Animal-rights group released video footage that shows distressed baby macaques undergoing lab experiments

Footage released by the animal-rights group Peta reveals, for the first time, filmed experiments at the University of Washington’s National Primate Research Center (WaNPRC), in which newborn monkeys were separated from their mothers and subjected to neurological tests after prenatal exposure to a neurotoxin.

Records show that the infant monkeys, some just two days old, were used in research on domoic acid, a toxin produced by marine algae that accumulates in shellfish and can cause illness in humans. The experiments were part of a project that ran for six years until 2020.

The footage shows monkeys with electrodes attached to their heads, undergoing tests to investigate whether exposure to domoic acid in the womb had damaged their brains. The baby monkeys appear distressed as they clutch blankets, suck their fingers, screech, and jerk as experimenters shave their heads and test their reflexes and memory.

The infant macaques were bred at the University of Washington’s Infant Primate Research Laboratory for the project researching the developmental neurotoxicity of domoic acid in nonhuman primates. Researchers administered doses of domoic acid daily to 32 pregnant macaques. After birth, 28 infants were removed from their mothers, bottle-fed and kept in incubators before being housed individually at three weeks old.

“These monkeys are so young they still have the distinctive black fur of newborn macaques, yet instead of clinging to their mothers, they grasp blankets on metal tables,” says Peta’s chief science adviser on primate issues, Dr Lisa Jones-Engel.

In the wild, macaques live in close social groups. Infants have long-term maternal care needs for their social and behavioral development, says Dr Malene Hansen, a long-tailed macaque expert, and cannot thrive without their mothers. “It is unethical to conduct research that separates infant macaques from their mothers. Period,” she says.

The WaNBRC told the Guardian: “We recognize that research involving infant animals raises important questions about their wellbeing. Maternal relationships and early social development are important considerations in nonhuman primate welfare. Our experienced veterinary and animal care personnel have specialized expertise in primate care, including nursery rearing.”

The project ran from 2014 to 2020 and received more than $4.2m in National Institutes of Health (NIH) funding. Some experiments lasted years. According to Peta, the monkeys were killed after the experiments were concluded.

The NIH says it takes the care and use of laboratory animals very seriously: “All animals used in NIH-supported research are protected by laws, regulations and policies designed to ensure the smallest possible number of animals are used and their welfare is prioritized.”

According to the WaNBRC, there are no current infant studies at its center; however, protocols for such studies are active.

Jones-Engel says: “There is no moral escape hatch. You can’t claim primates are used because they’re so like us, then take an infant away from its mother and experiment on it. You would never do that to a human primate. The cruelty also has biological consequences: maternal separation alters an infant’s physiology, immunity, behavior and development, distorting its response to the very substance or disease being studied.”

Jones-Engel worked as a primate scientist at the University of Washington for 17 years and has spent 35 years working as a primatologist. Her transition from animal researcher to campaigner is documented in a new film, Sentient.

Now one of the University of Washington’s most outspoken critics, Jones-Engel says the footage offers a rare glimpse into experiments involving monkeys: “For decades, the term ‘primate research’ has obscured the reality inside laboratories. These videos expose the suffering and raise a fundamental question: why are these facilities still operating at all?”

Peta is calling for the closure of all seven US National Primate Research Centers.

The footage relates to a research program that has operated at the University of Washington’s Infant Primate Research Laboratory since 1971 and emerges amid a long-running dispute between Peta and the university. In a 2020 lawsuit, Peta challenged the school’s handling of public-records requests. The court ruled that the university violated laws by failing to adequately search for records, in a case that revealed systematic destruction of photos and videos at the school.

The footage was released to Peta in September 2026 in response to a records request. The videos were filmed between 2017 and 2019.

The WaNPRC says the monkey studies have contributed to an understanding how prenatal domoic acid exposure may affect learning and memory: “These findings remain relevant to public health.”

However, there is no clear evidence that the experiments led to changes in public health recommendations.

Although the domoic acid research ended in 2020, records show that the WaNPRC continued to breed, purchase and use monkeys, including infants, to study viruses such as Epstein-Barr and HIV.

In a 2021 study, 25 infant rhesus macaques were infected with SIV, which is closely related to HIV. The study was looking at why some infants develop Aids more rapidly than others. The infected baby monkeys experienced significant distress, chronic diarrhea and body wasting, before they were killed for autopsy. In another study, 10 infant monkeys were separated from their mothers within two days of birth to test an experimental Epstein-Barr vaccine.

While supporters argue that biological similarities between humans and nonhuman primates make monkeys useful for studying human disease, decades of animal research has yet to produce an approved HIV vaccine.

Research scientist Dr Jarrod Bailey argues that biological differences mean monkey experiments often fail to deliver treatments for human diseases, including HIV/Aids, Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s. “We pay the price in failed treatments; monkeys pay with their lives. A shift away from monkey experiments would benefit all primates – including humans.”

The University of Washington says it is committed to replacing, reducing and refining animal experiments through emerging technologies and improved animal care, but says that “animal studies remain necessary for some complex scientific questions”.

In the US, federal agencies are shifting towards reducing animal testing in favor of new approach methodologies, including organ-on-a-chip technology and computer modeling. The NIH is also investing in human-based alternatives. Yet primate research remains widespread: more than 106,000 monkeys were held in US facilities in 2025, up 1.5% from 2024, and more than 32,000 primates were imported from Asia and Africa for laboratory use from 2025 to 2026.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: On the campaign trail in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed rides a wave of support for Medicare for All
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Jessica Glenza in Escanaba, Michigan
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Days before the midterms, as Americans prepare for historic cuts led by Republicans, the US Senate candidate catches a rising tide of interest in single-payer healthcare

Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic US Senate candidate, starts this day on the campaign trail in Escanaba, Michigan, where nearby Wisconsin dairy country spills into dense forests and the sandy shores of Green Bay.

This is the upper peninsula – the “UP” – a rural slash of land north of Michigan’s mitt. Electorally, it’s crimson. Donald Trump won some districts near Escanaba by more than 41%. But at the county fairgrounds, past sheds labeled “Beef” and “Swine”, hundreds of locals on the political left have gathered in the hangar-size 4H Club meeting hall to hear El-Sayed speak.

“We built this campaign on three simple things. Y’all remember what they are?” El-Sayed stokes the audience, leading them to a call-and-response.

As Americans prepare for historic cuts enacted in the Republican-led “One Big Beautiful Bill Act”, which is expected to push 17 million people from their health insurance plans, El-Sayed appears to have caught a rising tide of interest in Medicare for All.

This election season, Troy Jackson, the Democratic US Senate candidate from Maine, who’s in a dead heat with Republican Susan Collins, said Medicare for All would be “great coverage”. Angie Nixon, Florida’s Democratic US Senate candidate, has made it a part of her “working families guarantee”. Chris Van Hollen, current US senator for Maryland, added Medicare for All to his platform last December after “listening to his constituents”.

El-Sayed’s supporting act in this series of stops is influential Democratic congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a longtime Medicare for All proponent and the subject of whispers about a 2028 presidential run. And, according to an October poll by the health policy thinktank the Kaiser Family Foundation, two-thirds of Americans support the idea.

Technically, Medicare for All is an insurance reform. Proposals currently before Congress would make the federal government into the nation’s health insurer, a “single-payer” system more closely aligned with health systems in peer-developed democracies, such as Canada.

Sounds simple. However, in the US, one in every five dollars goes to healthcare. The existing health insurance patchwork fuels profits of world-leading, resource-unlimited corporations and powerful local monopolies. Democrats also worry that replacing private insurance, as Medicare for All advocates call for, would provide fodder for Republicans, who have made stoking popular resentment against government into an electoral strategy.

Those enormous barriers have repeatedly relegated Medicare for All to the political hinterlands. Centrist Democrats worry that, in a nation where me-but-not-thee politics has reigned for many years, Medicare for All is nothing more than a decades-old tried-and-failed idea.

Then again, in a nation where healthcare prices are the highest in the world and climbing, when even the insured find themselves in medical debt, and where the broad-daylight assassination of an insurance executive elicits catharsis and not mourning – the yearning for change is personal and visceral.

“Not enough doctors, not enough healthcare,” says El-Sayed, who ran both the Detroit and Wayne county health departments, and received a medical degree from Columbia University.

“Not enough mental healthcare,” El-Sayed answers, tossing out a campaign slogan: “It shouldn’t be this hard.”

El-Sayed’s campaign comes as the Trump administration enacts the largest federal healthcare cut in the nation’s history – extracting $1tn from the system primarily by through severe cuts to Medicaid, the federal-state health insurance program for low-income and disabled people. Medicaid cuts are expected to close hospitals, particularly those in rural outposts like Escanaba, and the urban core.

At the same time, some of the most popular health policies of recent years – such as reigning in medical debt collections – spring directly from the policy work of Medicare for All advocates. Add to this a counterintuitive reality: almost half of all healthcare today is already paid for by federal, state or local government, according to the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.

“I’ve been at this for a while, and we have dips and peaks in the single-payer movement,” said Dr Stephanie Woolhandler, a professor of public health at the City University of New York, and a decades-long advocate for Medicare for All. Support “always comes back”, she said.

“And the reason it always comes back is because the healthcare system has not been fixed – and it may not be fixable at all without single-payer,” said Woolhandler.

To understand this system, and Republican enmity toward it, it pays to go back a century when the idea of tying health insurance to employment was born of entrepreneurial innovation and historical accident. In 1929, Baylor University hospital offered insurance to cover hospital bills for $6 per year to a group of 1,500 schoolteachers in Dallas. The idea caught on across the country and Blue Cross came to life.

This arrangement was institutionalized during the second world war. Amid government price controls, health insurance was one of the few ways businesses could compete for workers. The federal government made the benefit tax-exempt, as it still is today, according to the foremost history on the subject by author Paul Starr.

Since then, Democrats have pushed for reform and expansion – with their failures to reach universal coverage shaping the contours of the patchwork system that exists today.

In 1965, Democrat Lyndon Johnson passed Medicare, for people older than 65, and its sister program Medicaid, together providing insurance for more than one-third of Americans today. While the reform was a momentous triumph over segregationist opposition – Medicare desegregated hospitals – it came up short against its architects’ vision.

“We expected Medicare to be a first step toward universal national health insurance,” said Robert Ball, a top official in the Kennedy and Johnson administrations, according to an article in Health Affairs.

It also created important knock-on effects: it pushed the hospital industry to commercialize in the 1980s, according to Dr Luke Messac, an emergency room doctor at Mass General Brigham, and author of Your Money or Your Life, a history of medical debt. Hospitals, the majority of which are non-profit in the US, argued they could drop the explicit charitable missions many were founded with because Medicare paid patients’ bills. As a result, the hospital industry pushed the IRS to loosen its definition of community benefit, at the same time keeping their nonprofit status and scaling up billing.

This yielded “a lot of middlemen in our system that do not provide a benefit to the public”, said Messac. “One of the things Medicare for All is intended to do is take some of the power back from those actors.”

“That poses a huge threat, so the fact that there would be opposition is like the most predictable thing in the world,” he adds. “It doesn’t mean it’s a bad idea – it may mean it’s a good idea.”

Since Johnson’s Medicare bill, the only law to rival it in scope is the Affordable Care Act (ACA), passed in 2010. Better known as Obamacare, a version of the market-based reform was first proposed by scholars at the conservative Heritage Foundation. Democrats sought to reach across the aisle; to do so, they developed a bill to subsidize insurance for individuals. But that plan for bipartisan support didn’t work out.

Obamacare was passed on a party-line vote – one of the first signposts of the new era of polarization. Republicans incessantly targeted it for more than a decade. Today, it is etched it into the minds of conservative voters as the source of all that ills healthcare.

“We should almost go back to square one and start analyzing what caused this,” says Bonnie, a 70-year-old Republican in Delta county, who declines to give her last name. “When the socialistic ideas started coming in, like Obamacare, that’s what threw everything in a tailspin.”

“I want everything privatized,” says Lisa Pieczyski, a woman in her 60s from near Escanaba, who carries a homemade anti-green-energy sign. “We’ve mandated too many things under insurance that have made the premiums outrageous.” She adds that she can’t trust the government because “Obamacare did all this”.

“I’m middle class, I’ve always been middle class, and what I have done to ensure I have medical insurance is give up something else like a fucking Cadillac and pay for it, all right? OK?” said Delta county’s Republican spokesperson, Michael Glass, 77, who gets insurance through a privatized version of Medicare called Medicare Advantage.

“It is the individual who should take responsibility for their own healthcare, period.”

As El-Sayed stumps through the UP, his supporters repeat a set of ideas they believe run parallel to Medicare for All: kindness, respect and shared responsibility. In Iron Mountain, he greets an overflow crowd at the local ski lodge – one of the few public meeting places in this rural town. One “lifelong Democrat” says there hasn’t been this much excitement since Bernie Sanders came to town a few years back.

After El-Sayed’s speech – his condemnations of US support for Israel’s war in Gaza, his calls for cheaper gas, groceries and healthcare, criticisms of Islamophobia – a woman asks about how to bring people around to Medicare for All.

“I was a registered nurse for 40 years,” she says. “Can you make a video or some kind of something explaining – some easy way for people to understand how great and easy it’s going to be?” El-Sayed answers – but it’s Ocasio-Cortez that captures the room.

“Raise your hand if you have waited or delayed getting a treatment or seeing a doctor because you felt you couldn’t afford it,” says Ocasio-Cortez.

“Right now, we are waiting weeks, months, years – to wait until we can afford to see a doctor one day. Healthcare has become a luxury,” says Ocasio-Cortez. “Medicare exists – we provide a healthcare system for every American above the age of 65.”

Finally, she adds: “There is this idea that I don’t want to pay for someone else’s thing. First of all, does that mean you don’t want someone else to pay for your care? Does that mean we shouldn’t have Medicare today? Because I’m a young person and I gladly pay, because I want to live in a society where seniors” – then, she is drowned out by the cheers of people excited to share the cost.

At the end of the one-day, 131-mile trail, El-Sayed is in the gymnasium of Northern Michigan University with enormous pictures of athletes looking out at the audience. A physician assistant who is running for state representative opens the rally and – all of a sudden – public health is on the offense.

“All it took was the closure of my little Planned Parenthood clinic about 18 months ago,” says Anna Aho Rink, a Democratic candidate for Michigan’s 109th US House district, “and me being completely fed up with the system that is not working well for any of us to get me up here today and running for office.”

The rally is at a college, but students are a minority in the audience; there are elderly residents and middle-aged parents with children in tow on a school night.

“You don’t need a medical degree to recognize the symptoms of a broken economy,” says Ocasio-Cortez as she warms up the crowd. “Michigan, corruption is making this country sick.”

El-Sayed ticks off his public health victories: he got 16,000 kids free reading glasses; used vending machines to distribute Narcan, the overdose reversal medication; tested daycares and preschools for lead in the water, and then remediated dozens.

“You deserve to have a long, healthy life in the United States of America,” El-Sayed calls.

For many, this politics is in perfect relief to the worldview of the Trump administration – one where there is not enough to go around, where someone needs to lose, the government must be gutted, loyalty ranks much higher than fact.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Sunlight at night: US startup’s demonstration of lighting Earth from space draws critcism
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Oliver Milman
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Company imitates reflection of sun from mirrors, prompting pushback from some scientists, environmentalists and California locals

Locals in a rural area of California were recently startled to see dazzlingly bright light shining down from nearby mountains at night, illuminating a swathe of the desert below.

Unbeknown to them, the strange nocturnal illumination was the latest step in a company’s plan to erect thousands of giant mirrors in space to reflect sunlight on to the Earth during night-time.

The night-time light demonstration, near the town of Lone Pine in the Sierra Nevada region, was conducted by a US startup called Reflect Orbital, which has an almost sci-fi aim to launch 50,000 satellites into space in the next decade to illuminate parts of the world at night.

In July, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) approved Reflect Orbital’s proposal to launch an initial demonstration satellite next year, which will orbit the Earth and, via a 59ft-diameter mirror, reflect sunlight in 3-mile-wide beams in strengths from moonlight up to the brightness of the sun at noon.

The demonstration in California, undertaken earlier this month, showcased what this would look like on the ground, to the bewilderment of locals, one of whom called the lights “blinding”. Large mobile lights were erected near Mount Whitney, with Reflect Orbital comparing the radiance to that of a full moon.

This provided, the company said, a realistic simulation of one of the benefits of this technology: to help search-and-rescue teams and other emergency responders at night. Other planned uses include bathing crops in sunlight, replacing broken streetlights and even providing solar power for military operations, all summoned by the tap of a button on an app.

“Search-and-rescue teams are expected to be our first customers, so this was a real-world test conducted alongside teams who would use our technology,” said a spokesperson for Reflect Orbital, which partnered with a local search-and-rescue team for the demonstration.

“We’ll keep working closely with local communities and authorities wherever we operate, and are excited to show how this technology can help save lives.”

A coalition of environmentalists and astronomers are far less excited about Reflect Orbital’s ambitions, however. These groups have criticized the company and the FCC for threatening a harmful change to the separation of night and day that will affect everything from people’s sleep to wildlife and the ability to see the stars from Earth.

“This is an idiotic project,” said Jan Hasselman, a senior attorney with Earthjustice, an environmental group. “There are a huge number of unresolved questions and significant potential impacts. Literally all of life on Earth evolved based on the rhythm of day and night and there is a ton of data showing that messing with this is not a good idea.”

“There needs to be some sort of discussion and analysis before we grant these people the right to fundamentally alter the night sky,” he added. “The proposal for 50,000 of these satellite mirrors is crazy and would really end the night sky as we know it.”

In August, four groups represented by Earthjustice asked the FCC to reconsider its approval, citing concerns that opening up the skies to mirrored satellites, which would ascend to about 400 miles (645km) above the Earth’s surface before reflecting light back, would cause a litany of problems.

Animals such as birds, insects and mammals rely on the reliable change between day and night to feed, shelter and mate, with any change to this being potentially disastrous for some species.

Astronomers, meanwhile, have complained that this night-time glare would worsen existing light pollution and spur an overall rush to add more satellites to orbit – Elon Musk’s SpaceX plans to place 1 million celestial datacenters around Earth – that will obscure the stars and cause more space debris that could descend as pollution back to our world.

There are also concerns that the scrambling of night and day will harm people’s health by disrupting their circadian rhythms as they sleep. Looking directly at the unusual glaring sunlight at night would also, much like doing so during a solar eclipse, harm people’s eyes.

Reflect Orbital has said its technology will actually aid the environment by boosting the energy output of solar panels when sunlight is pointed at them during night-time, thereby reducing reliance on fossil fuels.

But some climate scientists have warned against meddling with the amount of sun’s energy reaching Earth. Proposals for solar geoengineering, in which particles are sprayed into the atmosphere to deflect sunlight away from Earth instead of toward it, have also prompted fierce opposition.

“Global warming is happening because the Earth has a radiative imbalance due to the massive amounts of greenhouse gases we’ve dumped into the atmosphere,” said David Ho, a climate scientist at the University of Hawaii.

“Some people are promoting the already unhinged idea of installing space mirrors facing away from the Earth to reflect the sun’s energy in order to decrease global warming. Imagine wanting to turn those mirrors around so that the Earth gets hotter.”

Reflect Orbital said it has had “substantive discussions” with scientists and astronomers on the use of its technology so that areas such as astronomical sites, national parks and other wildlife-rich areas are avoided.

“We welcome oversight and want to play a role in shaping it,” a spokesperson said. “We believe it is our responsibility to work alongside governments, scientists and regulators rather than ahead of them.”

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Should we tip on takeout? We weighed all angles and the answer is …
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Ward Farnsworth and Saul Levmore
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
Adding gratuity doesn’t always make sense, but the obligation to has been entrenched as a societal norm

You arrive at a pizza place to pick up your order. The credit-card screen asks if you would like to tip and gives some choices. It seems strange to tip the cashier, who did nothing but hand over the pizza. But it also seems a little harsh to select “no tip” instead of one of those more generous options.

Start with the situations where our instincts are clearest. Tipping is normal at restaurants, in taxis or after haircuts. We don’t usually tip when we buy fast food, ride on a bus or have the plumbing fixed.

What explains the difference? One way to think about it is through economics. A server’s pay, in effect, is split in two: a salary paid by the restaurant, and a tip paid directly by you, the customer. But why do you get a say in the server’s pay when you don’t have that role in other cases?

The logic is simple: you’re in a better position than the restaurant owner to judge the quality of the service.

You know whether the server was fast or slow – so your tip rates it as baseline, above baseline or below baseline. A low tip, though, can feel confrontational: you’re delivering your verdict in front of the person you’re judging.

And it’s not just restaurants. A cab company knows how far the driver went, but not how well the car was driven. You know that, so you leave a tip. The owner of a hair salon knows how many customers were served, but not whether they were served well. Or take housekeepers at a hotel: you don’t watch them work, but you still know something the hotel doesn’t know: how big a mess you left behind.

The common thread is that you know something the employer doesn’t. And that gives you a role in deciding how much the worker gets paid.

You don’t tip the cashiers at a fast-food restaurant. Why? The company trains the staff to say the same things every time, then watches them. You don’t see much that the company doesn’t. And the cashier works behind a counter where the pressure to keep moving is already strong.

When you ride the crosstown bus, you don’t usually see anything important the bus company doesn’t, and the prospect of being tipped probably wouldn’t change what the driver does. So you don’t tip.

Or a company sends you a plumber. You might know whether the problem got fixed, but not whether the plumber worked efficiently or cut corners. Since you don’t know anything the boss doesn’t, there’s no reason to give you a direct role in setting the agent’s pay.

Compare this with a case where the plumber has to climb long stairs to reach you or face off against a scary dog. Here, you do know about hidden hardships – hidden from the plumber’s boss, that is – so tipping is a sensible economic gesture as well as a kind one.

Still, the theory only gets us so far. Why don’t people usually tip employees of airlines, front-desk workers at hotels or baggers at the grocery store?

Maybe it was a mistake to imagine that there’s one explanation for tipping rather than many of them – and that they change across time and place. In some cultures, there’s little or no tipping, and a tip might even be considered an insult.

In fact, our theory above was a better fit in the United States 20 years ago than it is today, because invitations to tip have become more common in places where customers know little that management doesn’t already know.

Some people imagine that the business is trying to get out of paying its clerks what it should; it’s foisting that job on to its customers. But that’s probably the wrong way to look at it. Clerks decide whether to take jobs and keep them based on the total pay they take home, wherever it comes from. Adding tips to their pay, in the long run, will probably hold down the base salaries that they’re paid.

Look at it this way: if all tipping were banned tomorrow, you’d expect the base pay of servers to go up soon afterwards, along with prices on the menu. Otherwise the loss of tips would just be a pay cut; and if restaurants could pay less to their servers without losing them, they’d presumably (alas?) be doing it already.

More likely, the takeout place just needs to somehow raise its prices. They think you’ll react better to an invitation to tip than you would to a more expensive menu, though it comes to the same thing. You’ll use the menu to decide what to buy and won’t think about the tip. Then when tipping is invited at the end, you won’t tell yourself the cafe raised its prices. You’ll just think the culture is changing: everyone wants a tip nowadays! But in effect, the invitation to tip is just a price hike that the owner is hoping you won’t view that way.

There’s another oddity: the timing of the request. An unfamiliar invitation to tip sometimes comes early, when some of the work you’re buying hasn’t been done yet. This might give the server a chance to see your tip before performing and then retaliate on the spot with sluggish service if you seem ungenerous, or do a good job if you’ve been nice.

This order of operations isn’t very consistent with the idea that you’re tipping in order to rate the quality of the work done.

In those new settings – bakeries, coffee shop, fast food places – your choice can function as a kind of vote – not on the quality of service, but on tipping itself. Leaving a tip accepts the invitation to help set the pay and encourages the arrangement to continue. If you don’t tip, you’re saying that you’re against using tips as a way to divide decisions about pay in this situation.

But once tipping is customary – not auditioning for acceptance, but entrenched – then you should tip, at least usually. The obligation isn’t set by law, but you consent to it when you eat at the restaurant. The owner is saying, in effect: your obligation to pay for this meal will be a combination of laws (that make you pay the check) and norms (that make you pay the tip).

You should play by the rules that the business has set or not play at all, even if the rules might seem to defy your theory, or any theory, of when tipping serves a good purpose. But when deciding what to order or where to eat, just remember: 20% of the cost (or whatever the customary tip might be) isn’t shown on the menu.

To put this more generally: if you run into a norm that you aren’t sure you like, ask whether you’re in a position to help shape it or whether you can only decide whether to go along with it.

The bottom line: tipping for takeout doesn’t make sense as a custom. It should be resisted unless it’s entrenched, at which point it’s best viewed as part of the bargain.

Put differently, we would vote against the idea; but having lost the vote, we go along with it.

Ward Farnsworth is a professor at the University of Texas school of law, and Saul Levmore at the University of Chicago law school. This is an edited excerpt from their new book, Should You Tip for Takeout? Solving the Puzzles of Everyday Life, out now

https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.title: ‘Maxxing’ is Dictionary.com’s word of the year: ‘It’s cooler than saying you’re doing more’
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.author: Matthew Cantor
https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text:
As all facets of our lives are optimized, the suffix has become inescapable - and experts predict it’s around to stay

Maxxing is not a new concept. Dungeons and Dragons players have been “min-maxing” character stats for years; Will Smith was maxin’ and relaxin’ in the 90s; as far back as the 40s, the term was used in game theory.

But in the past few years, as all facets of our lives are optimized, the suffix has become inescapable. We’re personalitymaxxing to charm our peers and sleepmaxxing to get the best possible rest; the Pentagon brags about “lethalitymaxxing”.

The explosion in the word’s use has made it Dictionary.com’s word of the year for 2026.

To choose each year’s word, Dictionary.com staffers investigate search trends, social media and the news, “and then we ask ourselves what’s telling the most compelling story of the year”, says Steve Johnson, director of lexicography for the Dictionary Media Group. “This year, maxxing stood out because it really connects to so many different parts of life. People are proteinmaxxing their breakfast, tokenmaxxing their use of AI during the workday, cozymaxxing on a Friday night.”

While “maxxing” has been around in various forms for decades, it’s the phenomenon of “looksmaxxing” – putting your physical appearance above all other concerns, and going to extreme lengths to improve it – that has fueled the recent rise in the word’s use. The message board 4chan is responsible for a vast amount of current slang, according to the linguist Adam Aleksic, and looksmaxxing has roots in online “incel” communities that use it.

But the suffix has emerged from the shadow of 4chan. As associate editor of Among the New Words, which tracks emerging terms in a quarterly journal, the linguist Kelly Wright and her colleagues have documented examples of the term’s use since 1990, when it appeared in a D&D context, through looksmaxxing-related 4chan posts in the 2010s to YouTube discussions of “vibemaxxing” (“adding to my energy”) and Substack posts on “vocabularymaxxing” (“because there are some thoughts you’ll only have if you have the words for them”) in 2025.

Wright sees the word as particularly creative – it can “apply to anything”. Dictionary.com data bears this out: by August 2026, it was being used 19 times as often in digital media as its monthly average in 2025.

And these days, it says far more about our social media-driven compulsion to optimize than it does about inceldom. “If there is an aspect of life that could be improved, it can probably be maxxed,” writes Jennifer Donnelly, a researcher at RCSI University of Medicine and Health Sciences, at the Conversation.

That comes with risks, she writes, as it suggests there is some kind of endpoint to the improvement process. “But health, wellbeing, social relationships and lifestyle habits aren’t really something we complete,” and maxxing can fuel “constant self-surveillance, self-criticism and the pursuit of an idealised ‘optimal’ self”.

In fact, that obsession is emerging on both ends of the words we use: terms recently added to the dictionary include “prefixes that mean ‘much more’ – things like ‘hyper’, things like ‘ultra’, ‘super’”, Johnson says.

The suffix benefits from being “infinitely customizable but instantly recognizable”, Daria Bahtina, a continuing lecturer in the UCLA department of linguistics, writes in an email. “You can attach the pattern to practically anything while still sounding like you are participating in a particular linguistic and cultural moment.” Saying you’re “proteinmaxxing” feels much cooler than just saying you’re eating more protein.

Its popularity could also be, in part, simply related to its sound. “The sound structure of a word tells us a lot,” Wright says, “and maximalism is trending.” A similar string of sounds – “maxx” – “was maybe a little primed to get picked up”.

Bahtina and Johnson agree that it’s unlikely most people using “maxxing” are thinking about any incel connections. Still, Bahtina wonders if its constant usage could help elevate its origins into the mainstream. “Someone encounters pheromone-maxxing or some other allegedly annoying but innocent version,” she writes, “and suddenly there is a linguistic breadcrumb trail into a much broader ideological ecosystem.”

So can we expect “maxxing” to stick around as a suffix – will it have the staying power of “-gate”, which has denoted scandal ever since Watergate, or will it go the way of “-licious”, which stretched from Bubblicious bubble gum to Destiny’s Child’s Bootylicious, but, as Johnson notes, has largely disappeared?

It’s difficult to predict, the linguists say. Once a slang term gets a mainstream platform, it often loses its cachet. But “I don’t think it’s going to fizzle out,” says Wright. It’s not just young optimizers who’ve embraced it: “Middle-aged people really love this word. Corporate brands love this word. So it’s going to have some staying power.”

https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/o.title: ‘I laughed so hard my Tampax fell out’: Michael Gambon’s pranks revealed by the stars he cracked up
https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/o.author: Chris Wiegand
https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2026/o.text:
He made Daniel Radcliffe’s Harry Potter fart, left Judi Dench unable to control herself and told a fry-up fantasy about Helen Mirren. A new biography details the star’s mischief

Jasper Rees’s authorised biography of Michael Gambon, published three years after the great actor’s death, has nuanced accounts of his performances in Shakespeare, Beckett and Pinter as well as The Singing Detective and the Harry Potter films. There are even chapters devoted to his hands (“the biggest you’ve ever seen on anybody” – Brian Cox) and similarly enormous feet. But, Gambon being Gambon, there are also dozens of accounts of tomfoolery on and off stage …

David Hare’s 1995 play Skylight is set in a draughty flat where a dish of spaghetti is cooked up on stage. Those kitchen cupboards proved useful for Lia Williams to hide when Gambon’s goofing got to her at the National Theatre. Gambon would adopt a different accent or speak in tongues during a scene and “when he made me laugh it was hell on Earth because there was nothing I could do about it” said Williams, who called him “one of the funniest people I’ve ever met”. She continued: “One time I laughed so hard that my Tampax fell out and I had to deal with that for an entire act.”

Ibsen’s Ghosts was a hot potato when it was first staged in 1882 thanks to its scandalous plot involving syphilis and incest. Gambon had some fun with the spuds when playing the self-righteous Pastor Manders in an 80s BBC TV version. Director Elijah Moshinsky envisioned a tense, sombre dinner scene and Gambon sat alongside Judi Dench and Kenneth Branagh. The potatoes were duly passed around by Natasha Richardson. “I’ll just have the usual eight,” requested Gambon. His co-stars’ corpsing led them to leave the set. “We couldn’t control ourselves at all,” confessed Dench.

Not every actor’s biography includes “fart machines” in the index but toots fake and real are let off in several chapters. When Gambon took over the role of Dumbledore in Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban, he and Alan Rickman pranked Daniel Radcliffe by triggering a fart machine during a closeup of the young star when he was in a sleeping bag alongside fellow Hogwarts students. “I was initially really annoyed,” said Radcliffe, before concluding that if Rickman and Gambon had engineered it then “that is pretty funny”.

When Gambon played King Lear for the RSC in 1982, Antony Sher sported a red nose as the clownish Fool. The poster presented them as a sort of double act and Sher was widely seen as stealing the limelight. Rees likens it to Gambon taking on what is often referred to as an “actor’s Everest” only to find another climber “clambering frantically up the same rope”. Adrian Noble, who directed the tragedy, said Gambon “joshed [Sher] mercilessly”. During the storm scene he reportedly bellowed: “Come on out, you little red-nosed fucker!”

When he was appearing on stage in Arthur Miller’s A View from the Bridge, Gambon kept a signed photo of Robert De Niro – with words of admiration for Gambon’s work – on his dressing room table. The pair would appear together in the film The Good Shepherd in 2006 but had never even met by the time he was doing A View from the Bridge. The fake autograph and note – “I loved working with you Mike, you’re great – love Bobby” – were apparently written by Gambon himself.

One festive season in the late 60s, Gambon found himself starring in the Christmas show Hans, the Witch and the Gobbin at Birmingham Rep – much to his annoyance, remembered co-star Anthony Higgins. A prodigious swearer, Gambon decided to add to his stage makeup for a performance. “One night he’d written on one eyelid ‘fuck’ and on the other ‘off’,” said Higgins. Gambon blinked each eye to deliver the message to Higgins. Artistic director Peter Dews had to give him a word of warning.

When Gambon played the tramp Davies in a 2000 revival of Harold Pinter’s play The Caretaker, he revelled in repelling theatregoers – as well as the brothers played by Douglas Hodge and Rupert Graves. One night, according to Rees’s book, Gambon had his back to the audience and buried his hand in his trousers, where he had stowed away a serving of chocolate cake. He withdrew his smeared fingers and sniffed them, causing his co-stars to crack up. “Rupert was in terrible trouble,” remembered Hodge. “Rupert wet himself regularly.”

Gambon loved to supply journalists with tall tales and see who believed him. He treated one interviewer to an “insight” into how he and Helen Mirren prepared while in the wings for their roles as Antony and Cleopatra for the RSC. Mirren, he assured the journalist, got into character by performing a mime in which she prepared a dish of ham and eggs for Antony. “Absolute rubbish,” Mirren told Rees, though added: “It’s a lovely story.”

Michael Gambon: The Authorised Biography by Jasper Rees is published by Century (£30). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: The pet I’ll never forget: Clement was hit by a car and left to die in a ditch – then found his beautiful purpose
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Stephanie Israel, as told to Farryn Stock
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
Before being rescued, he had an extremely traumatic experience. You’d never know it though, from the joy his patience and sunny nature bring to those who most need him

In December 2024, my kerry blue terrier, Magnus, died suddenly from a stroke at the age of nine. Devastated, I started looking at rescue dogs on Facebook and came across Clement, who was being looked after by a shelter in Romania. It wasn’t his appearance that caught my attention, but his heartbreaking story.

An eight-year-old mixed-breed rescue, Clement had spent most of his life with a woman living with Alzheimer’s. One day, she accidentally let him out. He was hit by a car, attacked by two large dogs and left in a ditch for three days in the snow before being rescued by chance. When I read this, I knew I had to take him in.

On 11 June 2025, exactly six months after Magnus died, Clement arrived on what I called the “happy bus” from Romania. He was small, with long black fur, a greying beard, and pointy ears that stood to attention. With a gentle and calm demeanour, Clement was the perfect fit alongside our three other dogs. He settled into our family straight away.

Despite the difficult time he’d had, Clement loved being around people and other dogs. His gentle nature made me think he would make a fantastic therapy dog, particularly with elderly people. After six months with us, I decided to register him. Passing his therapy dog assessments, Clement soon began working with Ashfields care home in Norwich.

They had been looking for a therapy dog for years and Clement instantly enriched the lives of those within the home, just as he had ours. Walking around the communal spaces, you can see that spending time with him brings the elderly residents comfort and gets them talking about their own former pets.

Due to his experience in Romania, Clement came to us with limited motion. Although it doesn’t stop him getting around, I bring a stool with me to help him climb up and sit beside people. Often, he will sit for a minute or two before moving on – but on our last visit he sat with a woman, who had been quite upset all day, for five minutes without moving. It was as though he knew she needed him.

Not only has Clement brought joy to those in Ashfields care home, but he has taught me a lot in life. He has shown me that no matter your circumstances, we each have something to give to this world. No, he might not win dog shows, but that’s not his purpose. His gift is giving affection and companionship to people who need it most, and he does it beautifully.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Donald Trump has been a disaster for rural America | Steven Greenhouse
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Steven Greenhouse
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The president’s policies have taken such a toll on farmers that Republicans face trouble in deep-red states

Donald Trump’s policies have been a disaster for the nation’s farmers, so much so that a near electoral miracle may soon happen: Kansas, one of the deepest red, most rural states, may elect its first Democratic senator in nearly a century.

After Trump won farm country handily in 2024, many rural voters in Kansas, Iowa and elsewhere have soured on him because the price of diesel fuel, a key input for farming, has soared by nearly 70%, farm bankruptcies have surged and because Trump’s trade wars have significantly reduced agricultural exports.

Rural voters are so upset with Trump that polls show that Republican Senate candidates stand a good chance of losing in Kansas, Iowa, Nebraska and Texas, even though Trump won those rural states by 13 percentage points or more in 2024. No wonder Trump is hopscotching madly across Kansas, Iowa, and other states in the midterm campaign’s final weeks.

No one is saying that Trump deliberately hurt farmers, but when he plunged the US into the Iran war and his many trade wars, he showed little concern about what those decisions might mean for rural America. It was nearly inevitable that Trump’s moves would batter farmers – by pushing down soybean and other farm exports and by pushing up the price of fuel, fertilizer and farm equipment. Not only that, Trump’s proudest legislative achievement, his “big, beautiful bill”, further hammered farm country with its major cuts to food assistance and its $1tn in Medicaid cuts, which will cause an estimated 1.8 million rural Americans to lose health insurance.

“He has sold out rural America with his policies,” said Jon Tester, a third-generation Montana farmer and former US senator.

Even the Cato Institute, a Republican-friendly, conservative thinktank, slammed Trump over what he has done to farmers. A Cato commentary stated that while Trump calls this a “golden age” for farmers, the fact is that Trump’s “tariffs are inflicting serious damage” on farmers, increasing their input prices and causing their exports to decline by billions of dollars.

This helps explain why farm bankruptcies have jumped by 85% over two years ago.

Little wonder that a recent KFF/AP poll found that roughly six in 10 rural voters disapprove of how Trump is handling the economy, while around half believe the economy is in worse shape than when Trump returned to office.

Indeed, many rural voters have turned against Trump – while nearly two-thirds backed him in 2024, now less than half, 49%, of rural voters say they support GOP candidates this fall, according to a Fox News poll.

At a recent news conference in Washington, John Hansen, president of the Nebraska Farmers Union, sought to convey the pain and anger many farmers feel. “Because of the misuse of tariffs, record high agricultural input costs, soaring fertilizer costs”, and “high interest rates”, Hansen said, farmers “are facing the worst economic and financial crisis since the farm crisis of the 1980s”, when many farms went under because of sky-high interest rates.

In a direct slap at Trump, Hansen added: “Just when farmers need to expand markets for their products, the president seems to be at war with our nation’s top three trading partners: Mexico, Canada and China. When trade wars break out, farmer noses always bleed first and worst and longest.”

Many rural voters backed Trump in 2024 because he promised to cut prices, including energy prices, and vowed not to plunge the US into unnecessary, expensive wars overseas. But now many feel betrayed because Trump began an unnecessary, expensive war against Iran that caused diesel fuel – which farmers rely on for their tractors and combines – to soar to a record $6.52 a gallon in late September, before declining somewhat (to $6.32). This price spike – diesel averaged $3.75 a gallon before the war – cost most farmers thousands of extra dollars when many were barely breaking even.

“Compared to last year, our fuel bill is $50,000 higher,” Vance Ehmke, a Kansas farmer, told the Hastings (Nebraska) Tribune, while “fertilizer, that’s going to be at least another $20,000 or $40,000 increase. That’s all due to Trump and his war in Iran. We are madder than hell about it.

Last month, the American Farm Bureau Federation ran a bad news article saying “the record-high input cost environment”, meaning high diesel and fertilizer prices, means that “no major row crop”, such as soybeans or corn, “is projected to clear break-even” this year”.

In Texas, Kansas, Nebraska and other farm states, ranchers are fuming that Trump announced plans to import roughly 660m lb of tariff-free beef with the aim of cutting beef prices by 25% – one of the many ways Trump’s tariffs angered consumers was by pushing up beef prices. The National Cattlemen’s Beef Association voiced dismay about Trump’s beef imports, saying the move would undercut the struggling industry’s stability.

The North Carolina farmer Matt Bell had a warning for Republicans. Bell, who voted for Trump in 2024, told CBS News: “Everything we touch has gone up. We’re in a position now where we’re mad and ready to be heard.”

With rural America in deep pain, Bell and many other farmers who traditionally backed Republicans want to send a message to the party that controls the White House, Senate and House. Many are angry that GOP lawmakers haven’t sought to protect farmers by fighting against Trump’s tariffs and war against Iran.

“We need to get some other voices in there to push back a little bit on this stuff,” Nancy Danner, a soybean and corn farmer in Iowa, told the Wall Street Journal. “We need as many changes as we can get.” Danner said she plans to vote only for Democrats in November.

A Wall Street Journal headline had bleak news for the GOP, saying: “Republicans are facing the worst political environment in farm country in decades.”

All this dismay could go far to elect Democratic Senate candidates in rural states: Josh Turek in Iowa, Adam Hamilton in Kansas, Roy Cooper in North Carolina and James Talarico in Texas, not to mention the independent progressive Dan Osborn in Nebraska.

John Tsitrian, a South Dakota business executive who writes about rural America, didn’t mince words about who’s to blame.

“Farmers are hurting thanks to Trump’s apocalyptic screw-up,” he wrote. Perhaps the biggest screw-up, in Tsitrian’s view, has been the loss of global markets caused by Trump’s never-ending trade wars, which he said have caused long-lasting “structural damage” to US farmers.

Before Trump’s first term, the US and Brazil each provided about 40% of China’s soybean imports. But as a result of Trump’s repeated trade wars with China and China’s search for more reliable, less antagonistic trading partners, the US now provides just 23% of China’s soybeans, with Brazil providing over 60% and Argentina 10%. With China importing around $60bn worth of soybeans annually, that means a painful loss of $10bn a year in US soybean exports.

Trump has long been known to seek to shovel money, often lots of money, to people who are angry at him. Just look at his shameless plan to hand out $5,000 to every American adult.

Seeing how upset farmers are about sky-high diesel prices, Trump announced a new handout on Monday at a rally in Kansas – he promised $8bn in emergency aid to US farmers in what he called the Harvest Fuel Relief Program. It seemed like a desperate, last-ditch effort to rescue Kansas’s incumbent Republican senator, Roger Marshall. That came after Trump announced a previous $12bn bailout of farmers last December.

While acknowledging that farmers need emergency aid, South Dakota’s Tsitrian wrote, “Today’s tough farm economy, in regular need of federal cash infusions, is the result of a disaster that has a specific name attached to it: Donald Trump. Unlike most disasters, this one was utterly foreseeable.”

Across rural America, there is fast-increasing frustration, dismay and anger about economic conditions, Trump’s policies and GOP lawmakers whom farmers have long supported.

“This Republican-led Congress has not done their job,” said Hansen, the Farm Union president. “They have not helped our nation’s farmers in our time of need, and it is time for a change.”

Steven Greenhouse is a journalist and author, focusing on labor and the workplace, as well as economic and legal issues

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Harry Styles says his laptop has been dead for six years. Is he just showing off? | Emma Beddington
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Emma Beddington
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
He is either being insincere – knowing he could buy an entire Apple store if he wanted – or he is genuinely overwhelmed by tech. If it’s the latter, he has my sympathy

Clips of the “epic conversation” (rambling, blokey chat) Rolling Stone orchestrated between Harry Styles and Thom Yorke keep appearing online, and none more often than the one in which Styles declared his laptop has been dead for about six years. “I don’t know where the charger is,” Styles laughed, prompting a predictable rash of “his computer is NOT OK” jokes from 6 Music dads everywhere.

Is this charmingly relatable, or … not? One personal finance influencer declared it “a deeply unlikeable clip”, seeing it as the kind of tech-free flex you can get away with only if you are rich and famous. It’s true that the ability to protect your peace by withdrawing from the brain-liquefying churn of online life is a privilege inaccessible to most people, who need tech to function and earn a living. Opting out means delegating digital drudgery to other people: Christopher Nolan’s determination not to have email must be a massive pain for his entourage. I bet Ed Sheeran not having a smartphone is extremely inconvenient, too – someone else must always have to put the hotel into Google Maps, arrange the Deliveroo dinner and order the Uber.

This dead laptop business does feel slightly disingenuous – Styles could have an entire Apple store delivered if he fancies a tech upgrade. But I’m inclined to feel more tolerant. He says he uses his phone to write songs, and maybe there is an element of overwhelm at play? I’m always losing cables and procrastinating over tech issues. “I don’t understand why you’re waiting for it to die when you’ll really be in trouble,” my husband said crossly to me this morning as I fought to turn off my ancient phone, which had decided once again that typing was forbidden. But I’m filled with dread and confusion at the thought of replacing it (what model, how many GBs, must I engage with the Cloud?) and my life isn’t too busy or demanding; I can’t imagine what it’s like when you are a global icon on a world tour.

So, in case he is floundering not flexing – Harry, check your sock drawer. That’s where I found my charger last time I lost it.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Could Europe’s autumn of discontent threaten the survival of the EU? | Catherine De Vries
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Catherine De Vries
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Anger on the streets could increasingly turn against the EU itself if it can’t show why cooperation makes people’s lives better

Europe is living through an autumn of unusual discontent. What protesters from Paris to Milan to Madrid share is a deepening anxiety about the future and a growing anger at the gap between what they expect from their governments and what they feel governments are delivering, whether the issue is unaffordable housing, stagnant wages, the spiralling cost of living or failing schools.

The electoral consequences of the failure to get a grip on this public anger are already with us. Spain goes to the polls next month in a snap election called after parliament voted down key housing reforms. France begins the process of electing a new president in April, while Poland, Italy and a string of smaller states will vote before the end of 2027. The stakes could not be higher.

At the same time, national leaders face mounting pressures from abroad. Issues such as Ukraine, uncertainty over US security guarantees and economic competition with China demand more European cooperation, even as national politics makes this increasingly difficult. Governments face popular demands to deliver security and prosperity, just as their capacity to do so independently is shrinking. This leaves Europe with a difficult question: how can countries whose leaders are increasingly struggling at home find the common ground needed to act together abroad?

If the EU did not exist, Europeans would have every reason to invent it. Together, its members form a market of 450 million people and an economy of almost €19tn, the third largest after the US and China. No individual EU country comes close to that weight on its own. Germany, the largest, has 84 million people and an economy about a sixth the size of the US’s. Twenty of the 27 member states have fewer than 12 million inhabitants, less than half of Shanghai’s. In a world of tariffs and export controls, it is scale that secures a seat at the table.

But this rationale for cooperation does not make the EU’s survival inevitable. This political project has often been declared on the brink of collapse; the most recent crises include Brexit, the pandemic and energy shocks. Yet it has proved remarkably durable, responding with improvised solutions that previously seemed impossible.

The very traits that infuriate Eurosceptics – slow decision-making, endless negotiations and messy compromises – are, counterintuitively, sources of strength for Europe. The dispersion of power between governments, parliaments, courts and EU institutions makes the system hard to capture and compromises tend to stick.

The EU’s staying power lies in its capacity to adapt despite disagreements, while helping countries achieve what is termed “effective sovereignty”. Nominal sovereignty is the right to decide alone, even when deciding alone – as the UK has discovered to its cost since it left the club supposedly to regain its sovereignty – changes little. Effective sovereignty is the capacity to shape outcomes on energy, trade, migration or defence that no European state can control by itself. And the EU has itself adapted: its fully paid-up members remain the core but non-members such as Norway and Switzerland participate on defence, security, energy and economic policy. The EU has an interest in bringing Britain back into closer cooperation too, even if not exactly as it looked pre-Brexit.

But the EU’s resilience should not be taken for granted. Negotiations over the next seven-year budget, worth almost €2tn, show just how hard it is to achieve consensus. While everyone agrees on the need for greater European security and economic competitiveness, countries can’t agree on who should foot the bill. France, for example, is pushing for new EU-wide taxes, which others resist.

Even so, growing domestic political instability does not necessarily mean there will be paralysis in Brussels. Quite the opposite – it creates an impetus to act. With France’s presidential election approaching, Emmanuel Macron has urged fellow leaders to strike a budget deal by Christmas, warning that political room for manoeuvre would shrink in the new year if Marine Le Pen succeeds him.

Le Pen no longer talks about taking France out of the euro or a Brexit-style referendum. But her platform would undermine the union from within, turning the EU into a “Europe of Nations” and threatening cuts to France’s contribution to the EU budget.

Whether political change comes through elections, protests or new compromises in Brussels, public discontent cannot simply be negotiated away. This brings us back to the streets. French, Italian and Spanish citizens want functioning public services, affordable housing, economic and national security, and a sense that they have some control over their futures.

Younger Europeans, in particular, face growing uncertainty about their economic prospects, from finding affordable housing to securing stable employment. So far, this pessimism has not translated into widespread rejection of the EU. Recent polling suggests that young Europeans remain among the EU’s strongest supporters, with 90% favouring greater unity among member states and 78% wanting the EU to have more resources to act.

This gives Europe an opportunity, but also a responsibility, to turn that support into tangible improvements in their lives. That is the real test in the years ahead. Decisions about defence, industrial policy and social protection will involve difficult trade-offs, and not everyone will benefit equally. But if European cooperation becomes better at preserving institutions than at responding to citizens’ concerns, the discontent now spilling on to the streets could increasingly turn against the EU itself. The EU has repeatedly shown that it can survive political crises. Now it must ensure that the people living through them can do more than merely get by.

Catherine De Vries is professor of political science at IE University in Madrid. She is the co-author with Alexandros Kentikelenis of How Europe Survives

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s action
